name: AP Chemistry
blurb: Nine units, from the mole to the cell, and the two tables

units.title: Atomic Structure and Properties
units.blurb: Moles and molar mass, mass spectra and average atomic mass, empirical and molecular formulas, electron configurations, PES spectra, periodic trends explained with Coulomb's law, and the polyatomic ions to memorize.
keys: A mole is a count of 6.022 x 10^23 particles, and n = m/M links a measured mass in grams to moles through the molar mass in g/mol.
A mass spectrum shows one peak per isotope, and average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of those isotope masses.
An empirical formula is the smallest whole-number atom ratio from percent composition, and the molar mass scales it up to the molecular formula.
Mixtures separate by physical properties, so filtration uses particle size, distillation boiling point, and chromatography phase attraction.
Coulomb's law says attraction grows with charge and shrinks with distance, and shielding by core electrons sets the effective nuclear charge.
Electron configurations fill by Aufbau, Pauli and Hund, and a PES spectrum shows one peak per subshell whose height counts its electrons.
Rising effective nuclear charge across a period shrinks atoms and raises ionization energy, while added shells down a group reverse both.
Main-group atoms form ions that reach a noble-gas configuration, and polyatomic ions like nitrate, sulfate and ammonium must be memorized.

excl.s: Interpreting mass spectra of samples containing multiple elements or peaks arising from species other than singly charged monatomic ions will not be assessed on the AP Exam.
The assignment of quantum numbers to electrons in subshells of an atom will not be assessed on the AP Exam.
Writing the electron configuration of elements that are exceptions to the aufbau principle will not be assessed on the AP Exam.

frq.title: Gallium: mass spectrum to oxide formula
frq.stem: The mass spectrum of a sample of pure gallium shows two peaks: one at m/z = 69 with relative height 60.1 and one at m/z = 71 with relative height 39.9 (the two heights total 100). The isotope masses are 68.93 amu (⁶⁹Ga) and 70.92 amu (⁷¹Ga). In a separate experiment a 2.00 g sample of gallium metal is heated in excess oxygen until its mass no longer changes; the gallium oxide formed has a mass of 2.688 g. Use Ga = 69.72 g/mol and O = 16.00 g/mol.

parts.q: Identify the two isotopes of gallium present in the sample and give the percent abundance of each.
parts.a: ⁶⁹Ga at 60.1% and ⁷¹Ga at 39.9%. Each peak is one isotope: its m/z gives the mass number (for a singly charged monatomic ion) and its relative height, since the heights total 100, is the percent abundance directly.
parts.n: Reading the heights as masses, or the positions as abundances, earns nothing.

parts.q: Calculate the average atomic mass of gallium from the spectrum and the isotope masses given.
parts.a: 69.72 amu. Average = Σ(mass × fractional abundance) = 0.601 × 68.93 amu + 0.399 × 70.92 amu = 41.43 + 28.30 = 69.73 amu, which agrees with the periodic-table value of 69.72 amu to within rounding. One point for the correct setup with decimal fractions, one for the answer with units.
parts.n: A plain average of 68.93 and 70.92 (69.93 amu) earns the setup point at most; the weighting by abundance is what scores.

parts.q: Explain why the average atomic mass of gallium is closer to 69 than to 71.
parts.a: The average is weighted by abundance, and about 60% of gallium atoms are ⁶⁹Ga while only 40% are ⁷¹Ga; the more abundant isotope contributes more to the sum, so the average is pulled toward 69.
parts.n: 'Because 69 is the first peak' or 'because the lighter isotope is more stable' earns nothing.

parts.q: Calculate the number of moles of gallium and the number of moles of oxygen in the 2.688 g of gallium oxide.
parts.a: n(Ga) = 2.00 g ÷ 69.72 g/mol = 0.0287 mol. The mass of oxygen combined is 2.688 − 2.00 = 0.688 g, so n(O) = 0.688 g ÷ 16.00 g/mol = 0.0430 mol. One point for each amount, provided the oxygen mass is found by difference.
parts.n: Using 2.688 g as the mass of oxygen earns nothing for the oxygen point; the metal is still in the product.

parts.q: Determine the empirical formula of the gallium oxide.
parts.a: Ga₂O₃. Dividing by the smaller amount: Ga 0.0287/0.0287 = 1.00, O 0.0430/0.0287 = 1.50; a 1:1.5 ratio is multiplied by 2 to give whole numbers, 2:3.
parts.n: Rounding 1.5 to 1 or 2 (GaO or GaO₂) earns nothing; ratios ending in .5 are doubled.

parts.q: Write the complete ground-state electron configuration of a gallium atom (Z = 31) and predict the charge of the gallium ion in the oxide. Explain whether the prediction is consistent with your answer to part (e).
parts.a: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s²3d¹⁰4p¹ (or [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰4p¹). Gallium is in group 13 with three valence electrons (4s²4p¹), so it loses all three to form Ga³⁺. With O²⁻, two Ga³⁺ (+6) balance three O²⁻ (−6), giving Ga₂O₃, exactly the empirical formula from part (e), so the two results are consistent.
parts.n: Counting the filled 3d¹⁰ as valence electrons (13 valence electrons) earns nothing for the charge; only the n = 4 electrons are valence.

parts.q: A student claims that a Ga³⁺ ion is smaller than a Ga atom. Justify the claim using Coulomb's law.
parts.a: The claim is correct. Forming Ga³⁺ removes the three n = 4 electrons, so the entire outer shell is lost and the outermost electrons are now the n = 3 shell, much closer to the nucleus. The 31 protons now attract only 28 electrons, so each remaining electron feels a stronger net Coulombic attraction and the electron cloud contracts further.
parts.n: 'It lost electrons so it is smaller' without naming the lost shell or the increased attraction per electron earns nothing.

frq.title: Photoelectron spectrum of element X
frq.stem:
The photoelectron spectrum of element X shows five peaks. Binding energy (MJ/mol) · relative height:
151 · 2
12.1 · 2
7.79 · 6
1.09 · 2
0.58 · 1
For comparison, the spectrum of magnesium shows four peaks:
126 · 2
9.07 · 2
5.31 · 6
0.74 · 2
The first four successive ionization energies of element X are 578, 1817, 2745 and 11,577 kJ/mol.

parts.q: Write the ground-state electron configuration of element X and identify the element.
parts.a: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹; the element is aluminum (Z = 13). Reading peaks from highest to lowest binding energy, the heights give the subshell populations 2, 2, 6, 2, 1 for 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p; the superscripts sum to 13 electrons. One point for the configuration, one for the identity.
parts.n: Identifying X from the number of peaks (5) rather than from the electron total earns nothing for the second point.

parts.q: Explain why the peak at 151 MJ/mol is at a much higher binding energy than any other peak in the spectrum of X.
parts.a: That peak is the 1s subshell. Its electrons are in the shell closest to the nucleus and have no inner electrons shielding them, so they feel nearly the full +13 nuclear charge at a very short distance; by Coulomb's law the attraction is far stronger than for any electron in the n = 2 or n = 3 shells, which are farther out and shielded by the core.
parts.n: 'Because it is the first peak' or 'core electrons are always hardest to remove' without distance and shielding earns nothing.

parts.q: Describe two ways in which a sketch of magnesium's spectrum differs from the spectrum of X.
parts.a: (1) Magnesium has four peaks, not five: it lacks the 3p peak at 0.58 MJ/mol (height 1) because Mg is [Ne]3s² with no 3p electron. (2) Each of the four shared peaks is at LOWER binding energy in Mg (126 vs 151, 9.07 vs 12.1, 5.31 vs 7.79, 0.74 vs 1.09 MJ/mol) because Mg has one fewer proton acting on the same shells; the heights of those shared peaks (2, 2, 6, 2) are identical.
parts.n: Saying Mg's peaks are 'shorter' earns nothing: the shared subshells hold the same numbers of electrons in both atoms.

parts.q: The 3p electron of X (0.58 MJ/mol) requires less energy to remove than the 3s electron of magnesium (0.74 MJ/mol), even though X has one more proton. Explain.
parts.a: The electron removed from X comes from the 3p subshell, while magnesium's comes from the 3s. A 3p electron penetrates the core less than a 3s electron, so it is shielded more effectively and feels a smaller effective nuclear charge than a 3s electron in the same atom. That weaker attraction outweighs the one extra proton of X, so less energy is needed. (Within X itself, the 3s peak at 1.09 MJ/mol is above Mg's 3s at 0.74, as the extra proton predicts.)
parts.n: Z_eff reasoning alone predicts the opposite and earns nothing; the point requires the change of subshell and its shielding.

parts.q: Use the successive ionization energies of X to explain why the fourth ionization energy is so much larger than the third.
parts.a: The first three electrons removed are the valence electrons (3s²3p¹), each from the n = 3 shell, shielded by the 10 core electrons. The fourth electron must come from the 2p subshell of the core: it is in a shell closer to the nucleus and shielded only by the 2 electrons of the 1s shell, so it feels a much larger effective nuclear charge at a shorter distance and is held far more tightly, giving the jump from 2745 to 11,577 kJ/mol.
parts.n: 'The ion is more positive' explains the gradual rise from IE₁ to IE₃, not the four-fold jump; the change of shell must be named.

parts.q: Predict the formula of the compound formed between X and oxygen, and justify the charge of the X ion using your electron configuration from part (a).
parts.a: Al₂O₃. X has three valence electrons (3s²3p¹) that are removed at modest cost (578, 1817, 2745 kJ/mol) while the fourth is prohibitive, so it forms X³⁺; two X³⁺ (+6) balance three O²⁻ (−6).
parts.n: XO or X₃O₂ earns nothing; the charge must follow from three valence electrons and the formula from charge balance.

parts.q: Compare the radius of the X³⁺ ion with that of the Mg²⁺ ion and justify your comparison.
parts.a: X³⁺ (Al³⁺) is smaller. Both ions have 10 electrons in the configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶, so the shielding is identical, but Al has 13 protons to Mg's 12. The same electron cloud is attracted by a larger nuclear charge, so by Coulomb's law it is pulled in more tightly and Al³⁺ is the smaller ion.
parts.n: 'Al³⁺ has a higher charge' without the isoelectronic proton-count argument earns nothing.

frq.title: Combustion analysis of compound Q
frq.stem: Compound Q contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. When a 1.000 g sample of pure Q is burned completely in excess oxygen, 1.466 g of CO₂ and 0.600 g of H₂O are produced. A separate experiment gives the molar mass of Q as 60.05 g/mol. A second sample of Q, bought from a different supplier, is found by elemental analysis to be 39.0% carbon by mass. Use C = 12.01, H = 1.008, O = 16.00 g/mol; M(CO₂) = 44.01 g/mol, M(H₂O) = 18.02 g/mol.

parts.q: Calculate the number of moles of carbon atoms and the number of moles of hydrogen atoms in the 1.000 g sample of Q.
parts.a: n(C) = n(CO₂) = 1.466 g ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 0.03331 mol C. n(H) = 2 × n(H₂O) = 2 × (0.600 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol) = 2 × 0.03330 = 0.0666 mol H. One point each; the factor of 2 for hydrogen is required.
parts.n: Forgetting that each H₂O carries two H atoms halves the hydrogen and earns nothing for that point.

parts.q: Calculate the mass of oxygen in the 1.000 g sample and convert it to moles of oxygen atoms.
parts.n: Taking the oxygen from the CO₂ and H₂O masses (which include oxygen from the air) earns nothing; oxygen in Q is found by difference from the sample mass.

parts.q: Determine the empirical formula of Q.
parts.a: CH₂O. Dividing by the smallest amount (0.03330 mol): C 1.00, H 2.00, O 1.00, so the lowest whole-number ratio is 1:2:1.
parts.n: Any formula whose ratio is not 1:2:1 with the data above earns nothing; an incorrect part (b) carried through consistently still earns this point.

parts.q: Determine the molecular formula of Q.
parts.a: C₂H₄O₂. Empirical formula mass = 12.01 + 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 30.03 g/mol; n = 60.05 ÷ 30.03 = 2.00, so every subscript is doubled.
parts.n: Reporting CH₂O as the molecular formula ignores the given molar mass and earns nothing.

parts.q: Calculate the number of molecules of Q in a 12.0 g sample.
parts.a: 1.20 × 10²³ molecules. n = 12.0 g ÷ 60.05 g/mol = 0.200 mol; N = 0.200 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.20 × 10²³ molecules.
parts.n: Using the empirical formula mass (30.03) doubles the count and earns nothing; the molecule is C₂H₄O₂.

parts.q: Determine whether the second sample is pure Q. If it is not, estimate its percent purity, assuming the impurity contains no carbon.
parts.a: It is not pure. Pure Q is (2 × 12.01 ÷ 60.05) × 100 = 40.0% C, and the sample is only 39.0% C, so some of its mass is a substance that contains less carbon (one point for the comparison with the theoretical value). If the impurity has no carbon, all the carbon is in Q, so purity = 39.0 ÷ 40.0 × 100 = 97.5% Q by mass (one point).
parts.n: '39.0% is close to 40.0% so it is pure' earns nothing; a pure compound has a fixed composition and any shortfall means impurity.

parts.q: Explain, in terms of the law of definite proportions, why the mass ratio of C:H:O is the same for every pure sample of Q regardless of the sample's size or source.
parts.a: Q is a pure compound, so every one of its molecules has the same formula, C₂H₄O₂, with the same two carbon, four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms of fixed masses. Any sample is just a larger or smaller number of identical molecules, so the total mass of each element scales by the same factor and the ratio 24.02:4.03:32.00 never changes.
parts.n: 'Mass is conserved' is the wrong law and earns nothing; the fixed molecular formula is the reason.

frq.title: Isotopes of chlorine
frq.stem: Naturally occurring chlorine consists of two isotopes, ³⁵Cl (mass 34.97 amu) and ³⁷Cl (mass 36.97 amu). The average atomic mass of chlorine is 35.45 amu. Chlorine has atomic number 17.

parts.q: Calculate the fractional abundance of each isotope.
parts.a: ³⁵Cl ≈ 0.76 and ³⁷Cl ≈ 0.24. Let x be the fraction of ³⁵Cl, so ³⁷Cl is 1 − x: 34.97x + 36.97(1 − x) = 35.45 → 36.97 − 2.00x = 35.45 → x = 1.52 ÷ 2.00 = 0.76. One point for the setup with the two fractions summing to 1, one for the values.
parts.n: Two unknowns with no x + y = 1 constraint cannot be solved and earn only the setup point if the equation is otherwise right.

parts.q: Sketch the mass spectrum of chlorine, labeling the axes and indicating the position and relative height of each peak.
parts.a: Horizontal axis: mass-to-charge ratio m/z (amu); vertical axis: relative abundance. Two vertical lines: at m/z = 35 with height 76 (or 100 if normalized) and at m/z = 37 with height 24 (32 normalized), so the 35 peak is about three times taller. No peak at 35.45.
parts.n: A single peak at 35.45, or two peaks of equal height, earns nothing.

parts.q: State the number of neutrons in a ³⁷Cl atom, and explain why ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl react identically with sodium.
parts.a: 20 neutrons (37 − 17). Both isotopes have 17 protons and therefore 17 electrons in the same configuration, [Ne]3s²3p⁵; chemical behavior is set by the electrons, and the extra neutrons change only the nuclear mass, not the nuclear charge that governs the electrons, so both form NaCl the same way.
parts.n: 'They are the same element' restates the observation; the point needs the identical electron configuration from the identical proton count.

frq.title: Potassium and calcium ions
frq.stem:
Potassium (Z = 19) and calcium (Z = 20) are neighbors in period 4. Their first two ionization energies (kJ/mol) are:
K · IE₁ = 419 · IE₂ = 3052
Ca · IE₁ = 590 · IE₂ = 1145

parts.q: Write the ground-state electron configuration of the K⁺ ion and of the Ca²⁺ ion.
parts.a: K⁺: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶ ([Ar], 18 electrons). Ca²⁺: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶ ([Ar], 18 electrons). Both lose their 4s electron(s) and are isoelectronic with argon.
parts.n: Writing the ions with 4s electrons still present earns nothing; the superscripts must total 18.

parts.q: Identify which ion, K⁺ or Ca²⁺, has the smaller radius, and justify your answer using Coulomb's law.
parts.a: Ca²⁺ is smaller (one point). Both ions have the same 18 electrons in the same configuration, so the shielding of the outer 3p electrons is identical; Ca²⁺ has 20 protons to K⁺'s 19, so the same electron cloud is attracted by a larger nuclear charge and, by Coulomb's law, is pulled closer to the nucleus (one point).
parts.n: 'Ca²⁺ has a bigger charge' without the equal-electron, unequal-proton argument earns only the claim point.

parts.q: Explain why the second ionization energy of potassium (3052 kJ/mol) is so much larger than the second ionization energy of calcium (1145 kJ/mol).
parts.a: Calcium's second electron is its other 4s valence electron, still in the outer n = 4 shell and shielded by 18 core electrons. Potassium's second electron must come from the 3p subshell of the argon core, which is closer to the nucleus and shielded by only 10 inner electrons, so it feels a much larger effective nuclear charge at a shorter distance and is far harder to remove.
parts.n: 'K⁺ has a noble-gas configuration so it is stable' earns nothing on its own; the distance and shielding of the core electron must be stated.

units.ced: AP Chemistry Course and Exam Description, Effective Fall 2024

units.title: Compound Structure and Properties
units.blurb: Bond types from electronegativity, lattice energy, metals and alloys, Lewis structures with formal charge and resonance, then VSEPR geometries, hybridization and molecular polarity, mostly as predict-and-justify cards.
keys: Electronegativity difference classifies a bond as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent or ionic, and metal plus nonmetal is the quick sign of ionic.
A potential energy curve bottoms out at the bond length, and higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond that costs more energy to break.
Lattice energy grows with larger ion charges and smaller radii by Coulomb's law, so ionic solids melt high and conduct only when molten or dissolved.
In the electron-sea model delocalized electrons let metals conduct and bend, and alloy atoms of a different size make the layers harder to slide.
Lewis structures place every valence electron, and the best one keeps formal charges near zero with negative charge on the most electronegative atom.
Resonance structures average into a single hybrid, so the bonds in nitrate or carbonate are all equal with a fractional bond order like 4/3.
VSEPR spreads electron domains as far apart as possible, and lone pairs repel more strongly, so they squeeze bond angles below the ideal value.
Hybridization follows domain count as sp, sp2 or sp3, and a molecule is polar only when its bond dipoles fail to cancel by symmetry.

units.title: Properties of Substances and Mixtures
units.blurb: Intermolecular forces, solid types and phase diagrams, the ideal gas law and kinetic molecular theory, molarity, solubility and chromatography, then photons, the photoelectric effect and Beer-Lambert absorbance.
keys: Every substance has London dispersion forces that grow with polarizability, and hydrogen bonding needs an H bonded directly to N, O or F.
Stronger intermolecular forces raise boiling point, viscosity and surface tension while lowering vapor pressure.
Ionic, molecular, covalent network and metallic solids are told apart by melting point and by whether they conduct as solids or only when molten.
PV = nRT with T in kelvin contains every gas law, and each gas in a mixture exerts a partial pressure equal to its mole fraction times the total.
Kinetic molecular theory sets average kinetic energy by temperature alone, so at equal T lighter gas particles move faster than heavier ones.
Real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature, where particle volume and intermolecular attractions stop being negligible.
Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution, and like dissolves like because solute-solvent attractions must match the forces being broken.
Photon energy E = hc/lambda sets whether one photon can eject an electron, and absorbance A = ebc grows in direct proportion to concentration.

excl.s: Understanding/ interpreting phase diagrams will not be assessed on the AP Exam.
Colligative properties will not be assessed on the AP Exam.
Calculations of molality, percent by mass, and percent by volume for solutions will not be assessed on the AP Exam.

frq.title: A gas mixture in a rigid vessel
frq.stem: A rigid 5.00 L steel vessel contains 0.200 mol of N₂(g) and 4.00 g of Ar(g) at 25 °C. Assume ideal behavior unless a part says otherwise. Use R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K), Ar = 39.95 g/mol and N₂ = 28.02 g/mol.

parts.q: Calculate the total pressure in the vessel at 25 °C.
parts.a: 1.47 atm. n(Ar) = 4.00 g ÷ 39.95 g/mol = 0.100 mol, so n(total) = 0.200 + 0.100 = 0.300 mol, and T = 25 + 273 = 298 K. P = nRT/V = (0.300 mol)(0.08206 L·atm/mol·K)(298 K) ÷ 5.00 L = 1.47 atm. One point for the total moles of gas, one for the pressure with units.
parts.n: Using only the N₂ moles, or T = 25 K, earns at most the first point.

parts.q: Calculate the partial pressure of Ar in the vessel.
parts.a: 0.490 atm. X(Ar) = 0.100 mol ÷ 0.300 mol = 0.333, and P(Ar) = X(Ar) × P(total) = 0.333 × 1.47 atm = 0.490 atm (equivalently, P(Ar) = n(Ar)RT/V).
parts.n: Using the mass fraction of argon (4.00 g of 9.60 g) gives 0.61 atm and earns nothing; partial pressure follows moles.

parts.q: The vessel is heated to 125 °C. Calculate the new total pressure.
parts.a: 1.96 atm. With n and V fixed, P is proportional to kelvin temperature: P₂ = 1.47 atm × (398 K ÷ 298 K) = 1.96 atm.
parts.n: Using the Celsius ratio 125/25 (7.35 atm) earns nothing.

parts.q: On one set of axes, sketch the Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions of molecular speeds for the N₂ in the vessel at 25 °C and at 125 °C. Label the axes and each curve.
parts.a: Horizontal axis: molecular speed (m/s); vertical axis: number (or fraction) of N₂ molecules. Both curves start at the origin, rise to a single peak and trail off in a long tail to the right. The 125 °C curve peaks at a higher speed (by about √(398/298) ≈ 1.16 times), is lower at its peak and broader, with more molecules at high speeds; the two curves enclose equal areas because the number of N₂ molecules is unchanged. One point for the shift of the peak to higher speed, one for the lower, broader curve of equal area.
parts.n: Drawing the 125 °C curve taller, or with visibly more area, loses the second point.

parts.q: Explain, in terms of kinetic molecular theory, why the pressure increased when the vessel was heated.
parts.a: Heating raises the average kinetic energy, and so the average speed, of the gas particles. With the same number of particles in the same volume, they strike the walls more often and each collision delivers more momentum, so the force per unit area on the walls, the pressure, increases.
parts.n: 'There are more collisions' without the higher particle speed caused by the higher temperature earns nothing; 'the gas expands' is impossible in a rigid vessel.

parts.q: At 125 °C, compare the average kinetic energy of the Ar atoms with that of the N₂ molecules, and identify which has the greater average speed. Justify your answer.
parts.a: Their average kinetic energies are equal, because average kinetic energy depends only on the kelvin temperature, which both gases share. Since KE = ½mv², the lighter N₂ (28.02 g/mol) must have the greater average speed than Ar (39.95 g/mol), by a factor of about √(39.95/28.02) ≈ 1.19.
parts.n: 'Ar has more kinetic energy because it is heavier' earns nothing; the point requires equal average kinetic energy and the lighter gas moving faster.

parts.q: In a separate experiment, 80.0 mol of N₂ is forced into the same 5.00 L vessel at 25 °C, where the ideal gas law predicts a pressure of 391 atm. Predict whether the measured pressure is greater than or less than 391 atm, and justify your prediction in terms of the particles.
parts.a: Greater than 391 atm. At 16 mol/L the N₂ molecules are so crowded that their own volume is a significant fraction of the 5.00 L, so the free space in which they move is less than 5.00 L; they reach the walls more often than ideal particles would, and the pressure exceeds the PV = nRT value. Attractions between small, weakly polarizable N₂ molecules would lower the pressure only slightly, so at this extreme pressure the particle-volume effect dominates. One point for the claim, one for the particle-volume reasoning.
parts.n: Reasoning from attractions alone, and so predicting a lower pressure, earns nothing at this extreme pressure, where particle volume dominates.

frq.title: Three compounds of similar molar mass
frq.stem:
The table gives data for three substances of similar molar mass.
Substance · Structural formula · Molar mass (g/mol) · Boiling point (°C)
propane · CH₃CH₂CH₃ · 44.10 · −42
dimethyl ether · CH₃OCH₃ · 46.07 · −24
ethanol · CH₃CH₂OH · 46.07 · 78
In addition, potassium chloride, KCl, melts at 770 °C, and solid ethanol melts at −114 °C.

parts.q: Identify the strongest type of intermolecular force in liquid dimethyl ether and in liquid ethanol.
parts.a: Dimethyl ether: dipole-dipole forces (the molecule is polar, bent at the O, but has no H bonded to O). Ethanol: hydrogen bonding (the H of its O–H is attracted to a lone pair on the O of a neighboring molecule).
parts.n: Naming hydrogen bonding for dimethyl ether because it contains O and H earns nothing; all of its H atoms are bonded to C.

parts.q: Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol boils about 100 °C higher than dimethyl ether even though the two have the same molar mass.
parts.a: Ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to one another: the strongly δ+ H of each O–H is attracted to a lone pair on the O of a neighbor. Dimethyl ether has no O–H, so its molecules attract only through dipole-dipole and dispersion forces. With the same formula and electron count their dispersion forces are similar, so the much stronger hydrogen bonds in ethanol need much more energy to overcome when the liquid boils. One point for hydrogen bonding in ethanol only, one for linking its greater strength to the energy needed to separate the molecules.
parts.n: 'Ethanol has stronger bonds' earns nothing; boiling overcomes attractions between molecules, and no covalent bonds break.

parts.q: Propane and dimethyl ether have the same number of electrons. Explain why dimethyl ether has the higher boiling point.
parts.a: Both have 26 electrons, so their London dispersion forces are comparable. Dimethyl ether is polar (the bent C–O–C unit with polar C–O bonds gives a net dipole), so its molecules also attract through dipole-dipole forces, while essentially nonpolar propane has only dispersion forces. The additional attraction requires more energy to separate the molecules, so dimethyl ether boils higher.
parts.n: 'Dimethyl ether is heavier' earns nothing (46 vs 44 g/mol is a trivial difference); the point is the additional dipole-dipole attraction.

parts.q: Describe a particulate drawing that shows a hydrogen bond between one ethanol molecule and one water molecule, identifying the atoms joined by the hydrogen bond.
parts.a: Two intact molecules, CH₃CH₂–O–H and H–O–H. A dashed line runs from the H of ethanol's O–H to a lone pair on the O of the water molecule (or from an H of water to a lone pair on ethanol's O), roughly in line with the O–H bond. The dashed line joins an H bonded to O on one molecule with an O atom of the other molecule.
parts.n: A dashed line to a C–H hydrogen, or one drawn along a covalent bond inside one molecule, earns nothing.

parts.q: Predict which is more soluble in water, propane or ethanol. Justify your answer in terms of the interactions between each solute and water.
parts.a: Ethanol, which is miscible with water in all proportions. Ethanol's –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water, attractions comparable to the water-water hydrogen bonds broken to make room for it. Propane can form only weak dispersion and dipole-induced dipole attractions with water, far weaker than the water-water hydrogen bonds it would disrupt, so it is only very slightly soluble. One point for the claim, one for comparing the solute-water interactions.
parts.n: 'Like dissolves like' with no interactions named earns only the claim point.

parts.q: Explain why KCl melts at 770 °C while solid ethanol melts at −114 °C, in terms of the particles present and the forces between them.
parts.a: KCl is an ionic solid: K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held in a lattice by strong Coulombic attractions between full opposite charges, so melting, which loosens those ion-ion attractions, takes a great deal of energy. Solid ethanol is a molecular solid: neutral molecules held by hydrogen bonds and dispersion forces, which are much weaker than ion-ion attractions, so far less energy, and a much lower temperature, is needed. One point for the particles and forces in each solid, one for linking their relative strength to the melting points.
parts.n: Saying that ethanol's covalent bonds break on melting earns nothing; only intermolecular attractions are overcome and the molecules stay intact.

parts.q: A student claims that both KCl and ethanol conduct electricity in the liquid state. Explain whether the claim is correct for each substance.
parts.a: Correct for KCl, incorrect for ethanol. Molten KCl contains K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that are free to move and carry charge. Liquid ethanol consists of neutral molecules whose electrons are held in covalent bonds and lone pairs; with no ions or delocalized electrons there are no mobile charge carriers, so it does not conduct.
parts.n: 'Ethanol conducts because it hydrogen bonds' earns nothing; conduction requires mobile charged particles.

frq.title: Permanganate by spectrophotometry
frq.stem:
A student prepares a stock solution by dissolving 0.158 g of KMnO₄ (molar mass 158.03 g/mol) in distilled water in a 100.0 mL volumetric flask and diluting to the mark. Standards are made by transferring 1.00, 2.00, 3.00 and 4.00 mL of the stock into separate 100.0 mL volumetric flasks and diluting each to the mark. The absorbance of each standard is measured in a 1.00 cm cuvette at 525 nm, the wavelength of maximum absorbance of MnO₄⁻(aq).
Standard · [MnO₄⁻] (M) · Absorbance
1 · 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ · 0.241
2 · 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ · 0.478
3 · (see part b) · 0.722
4 · 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ · 0.959
An unknown KMnO₄ solution measured the same way has an absorbance of 0.600. Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.q: Calculate the molarity of MnO₄⁻ in the stock solution.
parts.a: 1.00 × 10⁻² M. n(KMnO₄) = 0.158 g ÷ 158.03 g/mol = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol; KMnO₄ dissociates completely into K⁺ and MnO₄⁻, one MnO₄⁻ per formula unit, so [MnO₄⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.1000 L = 1.00 × 10⁻² M.
parts.n: Dividing by 100.0 instead of 0.1000 L, or reporting 1.58 g/L, earns nothing.

parts.q: Calculate the concentration of MnO₄⁻ in standard 3.
parts.a: 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ M. M₂ = M₁V₁/V₂ = (1.00 × 10⁻² M)(3.00 mL) ÷ 100.0 mL = 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ M; the moles of MnO₄⁻ transferred in 3.00 mL are unchanged by dilution to 100.0 mL.
parts.n: Using 97.0 mL (the water added) as V₂ earns nothing; V₂ is the final volume of the diluted solution.

parts.q: Explain why the student measured the absorbances at 525 nm rather than at another visible wavelength.
parts.a: At 525 nm, the wavelength of maximum absorbance, MnO₄⁻ has its largest molar absorptivity, so the absorbance changes most for a given change in concentration: the calibration line is steepest and the measurement most sensitive, and the reading is least affected by a small error in the wavelength setting.
parts.n: 'Because the solution is purple' earns nothing; the reason is maximum molar absorptivity and sensitivity.

parts.q: Use the data to determine the molar absorptivity, ε, of MnO₄⁻ at 525 nm. Include units with your answer.
parts.a: ε ≈ 2.40 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹. A plot of absorbance against [MnO₄⁻] is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals εb: from standards 1 and 4, slope = (0.959 − 0.241) ÷ (4.00 × 10⁻⁴ M − 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ M) = 2.39 × 10³ M⁻¹ (a best-fit line gives 2.40 × 10³ M⁻¹). With b = 1.00 cm, ε = slope ÷ b = 2.40 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹. One point for the slope (or for ε from one standard, such as 0.478 ÷ [(1.00 cm)(2.00 × 10⁻⁴ M)] = 2.39 × 10³), one for the value with correct units.
parts.n: Omitting the units M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, or inverting the ratio (c ÷ A), loses the second point.

parts.q: Determine the concentration of MnO₄⁻ in the unknown solution.
parts.a: 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ M. c = A ÷ (εb) = 0.600 ÷ [(2.40 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹)(1.00 cm)] = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ M, which lies between standards 2 and 3, so no extrapolation beyond the calibration range is needed.
parts.n: Using a remembered or textbook ε instead of the value from this calibration earns nothing when calibration data are given.

parts.q: Calculate the energy of one photon of the 525 nm light.
parts.n: Leaving λ in nm gives 3.79 × 10⁻²⁸ J and earns nothing.

parts.q: Identify the type of transition that occurs when an MnO₄⁻ ion absorbs a 525 nm photon, and state how the energy of the ion changes.
parts.a: An electronic transition: visible photons promote an electron to a higher electronic energy level. The ion's energy increases by exactly the energy of the absorbed photon, 3.79 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
parts.n: Naming a vibrational or rotational transition earns nothing; those are caused by infrared and microwave photons.

parts.q: Before measuring the unknown, the student rinses the cuvette with distilled water and does not dry it, so a few drops of water remain inside. Predict whether the calculated concentration of the unknown will be greater than, less than, or equal to its true value, and justify your answer.
parts.a: Less than the true value. The leftover water dilutes the unknown in the cuvette, so fewer MnO₄⁻ ions are in the light path and the measured absorbance is lower than it should be; because the calculated concentration is proportional to the absorbance (c = A/εb), it comes out too low. One point for the direction, one for linking the dilution to a lower absorbance and so a lower calculated concentration.
parts.n: 'The result is inaccurate' with no direction earns nothing, and so does 'too high because water absorbs light'.

frq.title: Separating two dyes by TLC
frq.stem: A student separates a mixture of two dyes by thin-layer chromatography. The stationary phase is silica gel, whose surface is covered with polar Si–OH groups; the mobile phase is a nonpolar solvent mixture. After development the solvent front is 7.5 cm above the origin line. The mixture gives a yellow spot centered 5.4 cm above the origin and a blue spot centered 1.8 cm above the origin.

parts.q: Calculate the $R_f$ value of the yellow spot.
parts.a: 0.72. $R_f$ = distance traveled by the spot ÷ distance traveled by the solvent front = 5.4 cm ÷ 7.5 cm = 0.72.
parts.n: Dividing 7.5 by 5.4 (1.4) earns nothing; an $R_f$ cannot exceed 1.

parts.q: Identify which dye is more polar, and justify your answer in terms of intermolecular interactions.
parts.a: The blue dye. It traveled a shorter distance ($R_f$ = 1.8 ÷ 7.5 = 0.24), so it is held more strongly by the polar stationary phase: stronger dipole-dipole or hydrogen-bond attractions to the Si–OH groups keep it adsorbed longer, while the less polar yellow dye dissolves better in the nonpolar solvent and moves farther.
parts.n: 'The blue dye is heavier' earns nothing; the justification must compare attractions to the stationary and mobile phases.

parts.q: The experiment is repeated with a more polar mobile phase. Predict how the $R_f$ value of the blue dye changes, and justify your prediction.
parts.a: It increases. A more polar solvent attracts the polar blue dye more strongly and competes with it for the polar sites on the silica, so the dye spends more time dissolved in the moving phase and travels a larger fraction of the solvent-front distance.
parts.n: 'It stays the same because R_f is a constant' earns nothing; R_f is constant only for a fixed stationary phase and solvent.

parts.q: A pure sample of dye Y, run beside the mixture on the same plate, also travels 5.4 cm. Explain whether this result supports the claim that the yellow dye is dye Y.
parts.a: Yes. On the same plate with the same solvent, Y and the yellow dye have the same $R_f$ (0.72), and a compound's $R_f$ is characteristic of it under fixed conditions, so the match supports the identification. It is evidence rather than proof: a different compound with similar interactions could share the value, and a second solvent system could confirm it.
parts.n: Comparing with an $R_f$ measured on a different plate or with a different solvent would earn nothing; the match counts only under identical conditions.

frq.title: A sodium sulfate solution
frq.stem: A student dissolves 2.84 g of Na₂SO₄ (molar mass 142.04 g/mol) in distilled water and dilutes the solution to exactly 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask.

parts.q: Calculate the molarity of Na₂SO₄ in the solution.
parts.n: Dividing by 250.0 instead of 0.2500 L earns nothing.

parts.q: Calculate the concentration of Na⁺ ions in the solution.
parts.a: 0.160 M. Na₂SO₄ dissociates completely, Na₂SO₄ → 2 Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻, so [Na⁺] = 2 × 0.0800 M = 0.160 M.
parts.n: Reporting 0.0800 M for Na⁺ ignores the subscript 2 and earns nothing.

parts.q: A box drawn to represent a small volume of the solution contains eight Na⁺ ions. Describe what else a correct particulate drawing must show in the box, including how the water molecules are oriented around the ions.
parts.a: Four intact SO₄²⁻ ions (one for every two Na⁺), with no Na₂SO₄ units and no separate S or O atoms, all separated from one another; water molecules surround the ions and far outnumber them, with the O ends of water toward each Na⁺ and the H ends toward each SO₄²⁻.
parts.n: Drawing eight SO₄²⁻, splitting sulfate into atoms, or pointing water's H atoms at Na⁺ earns nothing.

parts.q: The student dilutes 25.00 mL of the solution to a final volume of 100.0 mL. Calculate the new concentration of Na₂SO₄, and state how many Na⁺ ions a box of the same size as in part (c) would contain.
parts.a: 0.0200 M. M₂ = M₁V₁/V₂ = (0.0800 M)(25.00 mL) ÷ 100.0 mL = 0.0200 M, one-fourth of the original concentration, so a box of the same volume contains one-fourth as many solute particles: 2 Na⁺ ions (and 1 SO₄²⁻ ion).
parts.n: Keeping eight Na⁺ ions but spreading them farther apart earns nothing; a same-size box of a solution one-fourth as concentrated holds one-fourth as many ions.

units.ced: AP Chemistry Course and Exam Description, Effective Fall 2024

units.title: Chemical Reactions
units.blurb: Net ionic equations and particulate reaction diagrams, stoichiometry with limiting reactants and percent yield, titration and gravimetric error analysis, then oxidation numbers and balancing redox half-reactions.
keys: A chemical change breaks and forms bonds to make new substances, while a physical change like dissolving only disrupts attractions between particles.
A net ionic equation splits only strong electrolytes into ions, drops the spectator ions, and must balance both mass and charge.
Balanced coefficients give mole ratios, so masses are converted to moles before the ratio is applied to find any other species.
The limiting reactant is found by dividing each reactant's moles by its coefficient, and percent yield is actual over theoretical times 100.
A titration finds an unknown concentration from moles of titrant at the equivalence point, which the indicator endpoint only approximates.
Gravimetric analysis precipitates a target ion with excess reagent, and the washed, dried precipitate mass gives the moles of that ion.
Oxidation is loss of electrons and a rise in oxidation number, and the oxidizing agent is the species that is itself reduced.
Redox equations balance by half-reactions, adding H2O for O, H+ for H and electrons for charge, then adding OH- in basic solution.

units.title: Kinetics
units.blurb: Reaction rates and rate laws from initial-rate tables, integrated rate laws and half-life, collision theory and the Arrhenius equation, mechanisms with a rate-determining step, catalysts, and reading energy profiles.
keys: Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time, divided by each species' coefficient so the whole reaction has one rate.
Rate laws take the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, and the orders come from initial-rate experiments, never from the balanced equation's coefficients.
A straight-line plot reveals the order, [A] for zero, ln[A] for first and 1/[A] for second, and only first order has a constant half-life.
Collision theory needs enough energy to top the activation energy plus the right orientation, so raising temperature raises k exponentially.
The Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT) gives a straight ln k versus 1/T plot whose slope equals -Ea/R.
A mechanism's elementary steps must add to the overall equation, and the slow rate-determining step dictates the observed rate law.
An intermediate is made then consumed and never appears in a rate law, while a catalyst is consumed then regenerated and lowers Ea without moving K.
On an energy profile Ea is the climb to the peak, delta H is products minus reactants, and the step with the biggest climb is rate-determining.

excl.s: Calculations involving the Arrhenius equation will not be assessed on the AP Exam.
Collection of data pertaining to detection of a reaction intermediate will not be assessed on the AP Exam.
Collection of data pertaining to detection of a reaction intermediate will not be assessed on the AP Exam.

frq.title: Nitrogen monoxide and hydrogen: initial rates to mechanism
frq.stem:
Nitrogen monoxide reacts with hydrogen according to the equation 2 NO(g) + 2 H₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2 H₂O(g). A student measures the initial rate of formation of N₂ at a constant temperature for several starting mixtures:
Trial · [NO]₀ (M) · [H₂]₀ (M) · initial rate of N₂ formation (M/s)
1 · 0.0100 · 0.0100 · 1.20 × 10⁻⁵
2 · 0.0200 · 0.0100 · 4.80 × 10⁻⁵
3 · 0.0100 · 0.0200 · 2.40 × 10⁻⁵
4 · 0.0300 · 0.0150 · ?
Two mechanisms are proposed.
Mechanism I: Step 1 (fast, reversible): 2 NO ⇌ N₂O₂; Step 2 (slow): N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂O + H₂O; Step 3 (fast): N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O.
Mechanism II: Step 1 (slow): NO + H₂ → N + H₂O; Step 2 (fast): N + NO → N₂O; Step 3 (fast): N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O.

parts.q: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to NO and with respect to H₂. Justify each answer using the data.
parts.a: Second order in NO: in trials 1 and 2 [H₂] is constant at 0.0100 M while [NO] doubles, and the rate rises from 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ to 4.80 × 10⁻⁵ M/s, a factor of 4 = 2², so the order in NO is 2 (1 point). First order in H₂: in trials 1 and 3 [NO] is constant while [H₂] doubles, and the rate doubles (2.40 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ = 2 = 2¹), so the order in H₂ is 1 (1 point).
parts.n: Comparing trials 2 and 3, in which both concentrations change, earns nothing; so does reading the orders from the coefficients (2 and 2).

parts.q: Write the rate law for the reaction.
parts.a: rate = k[NO]²[H₂], third order overall. The exponents are the orders found in part (a).
parts.n: A rate law with exponents taken from the balanced equation, k[NO]²[H₂]², earns nothing; an answer consistent with an incorrect part (a) can still earn this point.

parts.q: Calculate the value of the rate constant, k, and include its units.
parts.a: k = 12.0 M⁻²·s⁻¹. From trial 1: k = rate ÷ ([NO]²[H₂]) = 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ M/s ÷ [(0.0100 M)²(0.0100 M)] = 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ M/s ÷ 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ M³ = 12.0 M⁻²·s⁻¹ (equivalently L²·mol⁻²·s⁻¹). Any trial gives the same value.
parts.n: A value with no units, or with s⁻¹ or M⁻¹·s⁻¹, does not earn the point; a third-order k carries M⁻²·s⁻¹.

parts.q: Calculate the initial rate of formation of N₂ in trial 4.
parts.n: Multiplying the trial 1 rate by 3 × 1.5 (ignoring the square on [NO]) gives 5.40 × 10⁻⁵ M/s and earns nothing.

parts.q: In trial 1, calculate the initial rate at which H₂ is consumed.
parts.a: 2.40 × 10⁻⁵ M/s. From the balanced equation, (1/2)(−Δ[H₂]/Δt) = Δ[N₂]/Δt, so H₂ is consumed twice as fast as N₂ forms: 2 × 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ M/s = 2.40 × 10⁻⁵ M/s.
parts.n: Halving instead of doubling (6.00 × 10⁻⁶ M/s) inverts the ratio; the species with the larger coefficient changes faster.

parts.q: Show that the steps of Mechanism I add up to the overall equation, and identify every intermediate in Mechanism I.
parts.a: Adding the steps: 2 NO + N₂O₂ + H₂ + N₂O + H₂ → N₂O₂ + N₂O + H₂O + N₂ + H₂O. N₂O₂ and N₂O appear on both sides and cancel, leaving 2 NO + 2 H₂ → N₂ + 2 H₂O, the overall equation. The intermediates are N₂O₂ (formed in step 1, consumed in step 2) and N₂O (formed in step 2, consumed in step 3).
parts.n: Naming H₂O as an intermediate earns nothing: it is formed twice and never consumed, so it is a product.

parts.q: Show that Mechanism I is consistent with the rate law you wrote in part (b).
parts.a: The rate-determining step is step 2, so rate = k₂[N₂O₂][H₂] (1 point). N₂O₂ is an intermediate, so its concentration must be eliminated: because step 1 is a fast equilibrium, its forward and reverse rates are equal, k₁[NO]² = k₋₁[N₂O₂], giving [N₂O₂] = (k₁/k₋₁)[NO]². Substituting: rate = (k₂k₁/k₋₁)[NO]²[H₂] = k[NO]²[H₂], which matches the observed rate law, with k = k₂k₁/k₋₁ (1 point).
parts.n: Stopping at rate = k₂[N₂O₂][H₂] earns only the first point; a rate law containing an intermediate cannot be compared with experiment.

parts.q: Explain why Mechanism II is not consistent with the experimental rate law.
parts.a: Mechanism II sums correctly to the overall equation (N and N₂O cancel), but its slow step is the bimolecular collision NO + H₂ → N + H₂O, which predicts rate = k[NO][H₂], first order in NO. The data show the reaction is second order in NO, so Mechanism II is ruled out.
parts.n: 'Mechanism II has the wrong intermediates' earns nothing; the point requires the predicted first order in NO set against the observed second order.

frq.title: Fading of crystal violet: integrated rate law
frq.stem:
The violet dye crystal violet, CV⁺(aq), reacts with hydroxide ion to form a colorless product: CV⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CVOH(aq). A student mixes a solution of CV⁺ with NaOH so that [OH⁻] = 0.100 M, far larger than the initial [CV⁺] of 2.00 × 10⁻⁵ M, and follows [CV⁺] with a spectrophotometer at constant temperature. The results are:
Time (s) · [CV⁺] (M) · ln[CV⁺] · 1/[CV⁺] (M⁻¹)
0 · 2.00 × 10⁻⁵ · −10.820 · 5.00 × 10⁴
150. · 1.41 × 10⁻⁵ · −11.167 · 7.07 × 10⁴
300. · 1.00 × 10⁻⁵ · −11.513 · 1.00 × 10⁵
450. · 7.07 × 10⁻⁶ · −11.860 · 1.41 × 10⁵
600. · 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ · −12.206 · 2.00 × 10⁵
900. · 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ · −12.899 · 4.00 × 10⁵
In separate experiments the reaction is found to be first order with respect to OH⁻.

parts.q: Explain how the spectrophotometer readings can be used to monitor the concentration of CV⁺ over time.
parts.a: The absorbance is measured at a wavelength that the violet CV⁺ absorbs strongly (the product is colorless). By Beer's law, A = εbc, so at a fixed wavelength and path length the absorbance is directly proportional to [CV⁺]; recording absorbance at regular times therefore tracks [CV⁺] as a function of time.
parts.n: 'The color fades' earns nothing without the proportionality between absorbance and concentration. This part borrows Beer's law from Unit 3.

parts.q: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to CV⁺ under these conditions. Justify your answer using the data.
parts.a: First order in CV⁺ (1 point). The values of ln[CV⁺] fall by a constant 0.346 to 0.347 in every 150 s interval, so ln[CV⁺] versus time is linear. By contrast, [CV⁺] falls by unequal amounts (0.59 × 10⁻⁵ M, then 0.41 × 10⁻⁵ M), ruling out zero order, and 1/[CV⁺] rises by unequal amounts (2.07 × 10⁴, then 2.93 × 10⁴ M⁻¹), ruling out second order. The half-life is also constant, 300 s, as [CV⁺] halves from 2.00 to 1.00 to 0.500 × 10⁻⁵ M (1 point).
parts.n: Choosing the order from the plot that 'looks straightest' without citing constant differences, or a constant half-life, earns only the claim point.

parts.q: Calculate the value of the rate constant, k′, for the reaction under these conditions, including units.
parts.a: k′ = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. For first order, the slope of ln[CV⁺] versus t is −k′: slope = (−12.899 − (−10.820)) ÷ (900. s − 0 s) = −2.079 ÷ 900. s = −2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, so k′ = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
parts.n: Reporting k′ as a negative number, or with units of M/s or M⁻¹·s⁻¹, earns nothing; a first-order constant is positive, in s⁻¹.

parts.q: Calculate the half-life of CV⁺ under these conditions and show that it agrees with the data.
parts.a: t½ = 0.693 ÷ k′ = 0.693 ÷ 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ = 300. s. The table agrees: [CV⁺] is 2.00 × 10⁻⁵ M at 0 s, 1.00 × 10⁻⁵ M at 300. s and 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ M at 600. s, halving every 300 s.
parts.n: Using the second-order or zero-order half-life relations earns nothing; t½ = 0.693/k applies because part (b) established first order.

parts.q: Calculate the time at which [CV⁺] would reach 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ M.
parts.n: Using the zero-order form ([A]₀ − [A] = kt) or dropping the logarithm earns nothing; the first-order law uses the ratio of concentrations.

parts.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, the graph of ln[CV⁺] versus time for these data, including the axes, the intercept and the slope.
parts.a: Horizontal axis: time from 0 to 900 s; vertical axis: ln[CV⁺] from about −10.8 down to −12.9. The six points lie on a single straight line falling from the intercept (0 s, −10.820) through (300 s, −11.513) and (600 s, −12.206) to (900 s, −12.899); the slope is −2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (= −k′).
parts.n: A curved line, a line with positive slope, or an intercept at 2.00 × 10⁻⁵ (the concentration rather than its logarithm) earns nothing.

parts.q: The full rate law is rate = k[CV⁺][OH⁻]. Explain why the data behave as first order overall, and calculate the value of k, including units.
parts.a: [OH⁻] = 0.100 M is about 5000 times the initial [CV⁺], so even when all the CV⁺ has reacted [OH⁻] falls by only 2 × 10⁻⁵ M and is effectively constant. Then rate = (k[OH⁻])[CV⁺] = k′[CV⁺], which is first order in CV⁺ with k′ = k[OH⁻] (1 point). k = k′ ÷ [OH⁻] = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ ÷ 0.100 M = 2.31 × 10⁻² M⁻¹·s⁻¹ (1 point).
parts.n: Saying OH⁻ 'does not take part' earns nothing; it is in the rate law, but its large, nearly constant concentration folds into k′.

parts.q: The experiment is repeated at the same temperature with [OH⁻] = 0.0500 M. Predict the value of k′ and the half-life of CV⁺ in the new experiment.
parts.a: k′ = k[OH⁻] = (2.31 × 10⁻² M⁻¹·s⁻¹)(0.0500 M) = 1.16 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, half its earlier value, so the half-life doubles: t½ = 0.693 ÷ 1.16 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ ≈ 600 s. The true rate constant k is unchanged because the temperature is unchanged.
parts.n: Keeping k′ = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ ('same temperature, same constant') earns nothing: k is constant, but k′ contains [OH⁻].

frq.title: Hydrogen peroxide with and without iodide
frq.stem:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly at room temperature: 2 H₂O₂(aq) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Adding iodide ion speeds up the decomposition greatly. A proposed mechanism for the catalyzed reaction is:
Step 1 (slow): H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻
Step 2 (fast): H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + I⁻
Use these values for this problem, in kJ per mole of reaction as written, with the reactants at 0 kJ/mol: ΔH = −196 kJ/mol. Uncatalyzed reaction, treated as passing through a single transition state: Ea = 76 kJ/mol. Catalyzed pathway: step 1 has Ea = 56 kJ/mol and leads to the state H₂O + IO⁻ + H₂O₂ at −70 kJ/mol; step 2 has Ea = 30 kJ/mol measured from that state. In one trial at 25 °C with [H₂O₂]₀ = 0.200 M and [I⁻] = 0.0500 M, the initial rate of formation of O₂ is 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ M/s.

parts.q: Identify the catalyst and the intermediate in the mechanism. Justify each identification.
parts.a: I⁻ is the catalyst: it is consumed as a reactant in step 1 and regenerated as a product in step 2, so its net amount is unchanged. IO⁻ is the intermediate: it is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, so it exists only while the reaction is running.
parts.n: Swapping the two, or justifying only with 'it cancels out' (both cancel), earns nothing; the order of consumption and formation is the evidence.

parts.q: Show that the two steps add up to the overall equation.
parts.a: Adding: 2 H₂O₂ + I⁻ + IO⁻ → 2 H₂O + IO⁻ + O₂ + I⁻. I⁻ and IO⁻ appear on both sides and cancel, leaving 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂, the overall equation.
parts.n: Cancelling H₂O₂ or H₂O between the two steps earns nothing; only species that appear on both sides of the summed equation cancel.

parts.q: Write the rate law predicted by the mechanism.
parts.a: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]. The rate law is that of the slow step, a bimolecular collision of one H₂O₂ with one I⁻; the catalyst appears because it takes part in the rate-determining step.
parts.n: rate = k[H₂O₂]² from the overall coefficients, or leaving out [I⁻] because it is not in the overall equation, earns nothing.

parts.q: Using the data from the trial, calculate the value of k in your rate law, including units.
parts.a: k = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M⁻¹·s⁻¹. Each slow step 1 event is followed by one fast step 2 event that releases one O₂, so the rate of O₂ formation equals the rate of step 1: k = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ M/s ÷ [(0.200 M)(0.0500 M)] = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 1.00 × 10⁻² = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M⁻¹·s⁻¹.
parts.n: Units of s⁻¹ (treating the reaction as first order) do not earn the point; the rate law is second order overall.

parts.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, the reaction energy profiles of the uncatalyzed and the catalyzed reactions on the same set of axes. Label the energies of the reactants, products, transition states and the intermediate state.
parts.a: Axes: reaction coordinate (horizontal), potential energy in kJ/mol (vertical). Uncatalyzed curve (1 point): reactants flat at 0, one smooth hump to a peak at +76, then down to products flat at −196. Catalyzed curve, drawn dashed (1 point): from 0 up to a first peak at +56, down to a valley at −70 (the state with IO⁻), up to a second, smaller peak at −40 (climb of 30), then down to −196; the first climb (56) is larger than the second (30), consistent with step 1 being slow. Both curves begin at 0 and end at −196, with the same ΔH = −196 kJ/mol marked for each, and every catalyzed peak lies below +76 (1 point).
parts.n: A catalyzed curve that ends at a different level (a changed ΔH), or one whose second hump is the larger climb, contradicts the data and loses that point.

parts.q: Explain, in terms of collisions between particles, why the catalyzed reaction is faster than the uncatalyzed reaction at the same temperature.
parts.a: At a given temperature the distribution of collision energies is the same for both pathways. The catalyzed pathway's rate-determining step has Ea = 56 kJ/mol instead of 76 kJ/mol, so a much larger fraction of collisions (the area beyond Ea under the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve) has enough energy to react; more effective collisions per second means a faster reaction.
parts.n: 'The catalyst lowers the activation energy' alone earns nothing unless it is tied to a larger fraction of collisions with sufficient energy.

parts.q: A student claims that because the catalyzed reaction is faster, it releases more energy per mole of H₂O₂ decomposed. Evaluate the claim.
parts.a: The claim is incorrect. The catalyst changes the pathway between reactants and products, not their energies: both profiles start at 0 and end at −196 kJ/mol, so ΔH = −196 kJ/mol for either pathway, or −98 kJ per mole of H₂O₂. The heat released is the same; it is only released faster.
parts.n: 'The catalyst makes ΔH more negative' earns nothing; a catalyst never changes ΔH.

parts.q: The enzyme catalase also catalyzes the decomposition of H₂O₂ by binding H₂O₂ in its active site. Describe how binding the reactant can increase the reaction rate.
parts.a: Binding forms a new intermediate, the enzyme–H₂O₂ complex, and so a new pathway. In the active site the H₂O₂ is held in the orientation that lets bonds rearrange and the transition state is stabilized, so the bound pathway has a lower activation energy and a larger fraction of collisions, or of bound molecules, reacts; the enzyme is released unchanged afterward.
parts.n: 'The enzyme gives the H₂O₂ extra energy' earns nothing; binding improves orientation and lowers the barrier.

frq.title: Reading a two-step energy profile
frq.stem:
The reaction A + 2 B → AB₂ is proposed to occur by the mechanism
Step 1: A + B → AB
Step 2: AB + B → AB₂
Its reaction energy profile, read from left to right along the reaction coordinate, shows: the reactants (A + 2 B) on a plateau at 50 kJ/mol; a peak at 130 kJ/mol; a valley at 60 kJ/mol; a second peak at 85 kJ/mol; and the product AB₂ on a plateau at 10 kJ/mol.

parts.q: Identify the species present at the valley at 60 kJ/mol, and explain why it is not a transition state.
parts.a: AB, the intermediate (with the remaining B). It sits at a local energy minimum: a real species with complete bonds that must climb a barrier to react further or to go back. Transition states are the peaks at 130 and 85 kJ/mol, energy maxima with bonds partly broken and partly formed.
parts.n: Calling the valley an activated complex or transition state earns nothing; minima are intermediates and maxima are transition states.

parts.q: Determine which step is the rate-determining step. Justify your answer using the energy profile.
parts.a: Step 1. Its activation energy is 130 − 50 = 80 kJ/mol, while step 2's is 85 − 60 = 25 kJ/mol. The larger barrier means a much smaller fraction of collisions has enough energy to cross it, so step 1 is the slowest step.
parts.n: Measuring step 2's barrier from the reactants (85 − 50 = 35 kJ/mol) or from zero earns nothing; each step's Ea starts at the level before its hump.

parts.q: Write a rate law for the reaction that is consistent with the mechanism and the energy profile.
parts.a: rate = k[A][B]. The rate law is that of the rate-determining step 1, a bimolecular collision of one A with one B, so it is first order in each; the second B reacts only in the fast step after the bottleneck.
parts.n: rate = k[A][B]² from the overall coefficients earns nothing; the second B does not take part in the slow step.

parts.q: Calculate ΔE for step 1 and ΔE for the overall reaction, and classify each as exothermic or endothermic.
parts.a: Step 1: ΔE = 60 − 50 = +10 kJ/mol, endothermic (the intermediate lies above the reactants). Overall: ΔE = 10 − 50 = −40 kJ/mol, exothermic (the product lies below the reactants). Check: step 2 has ΔE = 10 − 60 = −50 kJ/mol, and +10 + (−50) = −40 kJ/mol.
parts.n: Using peak heights (such as 130 − 50) as ΔE earns nothing; ΔE compares the level after a step with the level before it.

frq.title: Ammonia on a hot tungsten surface
frq.stem:
At high pressure, ammonia gas decomposes on the surface of hot tungsten metal: 2 NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g). In one experiment at constant temperature the concentration of NH₃ was measured over time. Take the rate as −Δ[NH₃]/Δt.
Time (s) · [NH₃] (M)
0 · 2.00 × 10⁻³
100. · 1.75 × 10⁻³
200. · 1.50 × 10⁻³
300. · 1.25 × 10⁻³
400. · 1.00 × 10⁻³

parts.q: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to NH₃ under these conditions. Justify your answer using the data.
parts.a: Zero order. [NH₃] falls by the same 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M in every 100 s interval, so [NH₃] versus time is a straight line and the rate is constant even as [NH₃] halves. A first-order reaction would lose a constant fraction instead; here the fraction lost per interval grows (12.5% in the first interval, 20% in the last).
parts.n: 'First order, because the concentration decreases' earns nothing; equal drops in equal times mean zero order.

parts.q: Calculate the value of the rate constant, k, including units.
parts.a: k = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ M/s. For zero order, [NH₃]t − [NH₃]₀ = −kt, so k is the magnitude of the slope of [NH₃] versus t: k = (2.00 × 10⁻³ M − 1.00 × 10⁻³ M) ÷ 400. s = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ M/s (mol·L⁻¹·s⁻¹).
parts.n: A value in s⁻¹ from a first-order treatment, or a negative k, earns nothing; a zero-order constant has the units of a rate, M/s.

parts.q: Explain, at the particulate level, why the reaction is zero order in NH₃ under these conditions.
parts.a: The reaction occurs only among NH₃ molecules bound to active sites on the tungsten surface, and the number of sites is fixed. At high pressure essentially every site is occupied, so the rate depends only on how fast the bound molecules react, not on how many NH₃ molecules remain in the gas; changing [NH₃] cannot change the number of reacting molecules.
parts.n: 'NH₃ is not involved in the rate-determining step' or 'the catalyst is used up' earns nothing; the saturated surface is the scored idea.

parts.q: The experiment is repeated at the same temperature and NH₃ pressure with a tungsten sample of twice the surface area. Predict the effect on the rate of decomposition, and justify your prediction.
parts.a: The rate doubles, to 5.00 × 10⁻⁶ M/s (the observed zero-order k doubles). Twice the surface area provides twice as many active sites, and at high pressure all of them are occupied, so twice as many NH₃ molecules react per second.
parts.n: 'No change, because the reaction is zero order' earns nothing; zero order describes the dependence on [NH₃], not on the number of surface sites.

units.title: Thermochemistry
units.blurb: Heat, work and the first law, specific heat and calorimetry, heating curves and enthalpies of phase change, then enthalpy of reaction three ways, from bond enthalpies, Hess's law and standard enthalpies of formation.
keys: The first law says delta E = q + w, with q positive when heat enters the system and w positive when work is done on it.
Heat is energy transferred by a temperature difference, while temperature measures average kinetic energy and ignores sample size.
Heat for a temperature change is q = mc delta T, so a substance with a high specific heat like water warms and cools slowly.
Coffee-cup calorimetry sets q of the reaction equal to minus mc delta T of the solution, and dividing by moles gives delta H at constant pressure.
During a phase change temperature holds constant and q = n delta H, so a heating curve alternates sloped mc delta T segments with flat plateaus.
Enthalpy is a state function, so reversing a reaction flips the sign of delta H and scaling its coefficients scales delta H by the same factor.
Delta H from bond enthalpies equals bonds broken minus bonds formed, an estimate because the tabulated values are gas-phase averages.
Hess's law adds step enthalpies that sum to the target reaction, and standard delta H also equals formation enthalpies of products minus reactants.

units.title: Equilibrium
units.blurb: Kc and Kp expressions, ICE tables and the small-x approximation, Q against K, Le Chatelier shifts justified through Q, then Ksp, molar solubility, the common-ion effect and how pH changes solubility.
keys: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant even though both reactions continue.
K is products over reactants with equilibrium concentrations or pressures raised to their coefficients, leaving out pure solids and liquids.
A large K means the equilibrium mixture is mostly product, but K says nothing about how fast that state is reached.
Reversing a reaction inverts K, multiplying its coefficients by n raises K to the nth power, and adding reactions multiplies their K values.
An ICE table tracks initial, change as coefficient times x, and equilibrium values, and x is dropped from I minus x when it stays under 5 percent.
Q below K drives a reaction forward and Q above K drives it in reverse, which is the justification behind every Le Chatelier shift.
Only a temperature change alters K itself, since heat acts like a product of an exothermic reaction and a reactant of an endothermic one.
Ksp is the ion product at saturation, so molar solubility follows the salt's ion ratio, drops with a common ion and rises in acid for basic anions.

units.title: Acids and Bases
units.blurb: Conjugate pairs, pH and pOH, Ka and Kb calculations, percent ionization, structure and acid strength, salt solutions, titration curves and indicators, then buffers through Henderson-Hasselbalch and buffer capacity.
keys: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and its conjugate base differs by exactly one H+, so a strong acid has a negligibly weak conjugate base.
Kw = [H3O+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14 at 25 °C, so pH + pOH = 14.00 and a strong acid's pH comes straight from its molarity.
A weak acid's Ka comes from an ICE table with x = [H3O+], and Ka times Kb equals Kw for any conjugate pair.
Percent ionization rises on dilution because Ka stays fixed while the acid concentration falls.
Acid strength rises with a weaker H-X bond, more terminal oxygens on an oxyacid, or electronegative groups that stabilize the conjugate base.
A salt's pH is set by whichever ion hydrolyzes, so sodium acetate is basic, ammonium chloride is acidic and NaCl is neutral.
In a weak acid-strong base titration pH equals pKa at half-equivalence and the equivalence point sits above 7, which fixes the indicator choice.
A buffer of a weak acid and its conjugate base follows pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), and its capacity depends on the absolute amounts of both.

units.title: Thermodynamics and Electrochemistry
units.blurb: Entropy and ΔS° from S° values, Gibbs free energy and its temperature cases, ΔG° against K, coupled reactions, then galvanic and electrolytic cells, E°cell from reduction potentials and electrolysis stoichiometry.
keys: Entropy counts the ways energy and matter can be dispersed, so it rises from solid to liquid to gas and whenever moles of gas increase.
Standard delta S is the sum of absolute S° of products minus reactants, and elements have nonzero S° unlike their delta H of formation.
Delta G = delta H minus T delta S is negative for a favorable process, and the signs of delta H and delta S set the temperatures where that holds.
Delta G° = -RT ln K, so K above 1 means a negative delta G°, yet a favorable reaction can still be too slow if its activation energy is large.
Coupling an unfavorable reaction to a strongly favorable one through a shared intermediate makes the summed delta G negative overall.
Oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode in every cell, and a galvanic cell runs a favorable reaction while electrolysis is forced.
E°cell equals E°cathode minus E°anode from unscaled reduction potentials, and a positive E°cell means a negative delta G° = -nFE°.
E falls toward zero as Q rises toward K by the Nernst equation, and electrolysis deposits mass in proportion to the moles of electrons, It over F.

units.title: Exam Craft
units.blurb: Exam format and calculator rules, the six science practices, what readers score in justifications, CER answers, particulate drawings and sig figs, pacing for both sections, plus mixed practice items from every unit.
keys: The AP Chemistry exam splits 50/50 between 60 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes and 7 free-response questions in 105 minutes.
No calculator is allowed on Section I, so every multiple-choice item is built to be reasoned or estimated, while Section II permits one.
Section II has 3 long questions worth 10 points and 4 short ones worth 4, so pacing follows the points at about 23 and 9 minutes each.
Readers score shown setup, units and sig figs matched to the least precise datum, and a later part earns credit for using an earlier wrong answer.
A justification names the chemistry principle and ties it to the given data, and a full CER answer needs claim, evidence and reasoning all linked.
A particulate drawing needs correct particle counts, phase spacing and a key, and a graph needs both axes labeled with quantity and unit.
An error-analysis answer names one specific, plausible error and argues which direction it pushes the result, never generic human error.
There is no guessing penalty, so every bubble gets filled, and a question set's shared stimulus is read once in full before its first question.

units.title: Polyatomic ions
units.blurb: The ion table: formula to name.

units.title: VSEPR shapes
units.blurb: The VSEPR chart: electron domains and lone pairs to shape and bond angle.

cards.q: Define the mole and state Avogadro's number.
cards.a: A mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units); that number is Avogadro's number, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. It is a counting unit that links the particulate scale to laboratory masses: one mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its molar mass.
cards.h: → a count, then the number with its unit
cards.n: 'A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ grams' earns nothing: the mole counts particles; its mass depends on which substance it is.

cards.q: State the equation relating moles, mass, and molar mass.
cards.a: n = m/M, where n is the amount in moles (mol), m the mass in grams (g) and M the molar mass in g/mol. Rearranged: m = nM and M = m/n. Units check the direction: g ÷ (g/mol) = mol.
cards.n: Multiplying by M instead of dividing gives an absurd number of moles; the unit cancellation g ÷ g/mol = mol is the check that earns the point.

cards.q: Define molar mass and give its units.
cards.a: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol. It is the sum of the atomic masses of every atom in the formula (H₂O: 2 × 1.008 + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol) and is numerically equal to the average mass of one particle in amu (one H₂O molecule: 18.02 amu).
cards.h: → definition + unit + how it is found
cards.n: g/mol and amu are numerically equal but never interchangeable inside a calculation: 18.02 amu is one molecule, 18.02 g is 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.

cards.q: State the equation relating the number of particles, moles, and Avogadro's number.
cards.a: N = n × N_A, where N is the number of particles, n the amount in moles and N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Rearranged, n = N/N_A converts a particle count back to moles.
cards.n: Particles can be atoms, molecules, ions or formula units; say which, because 1 mol of CO₂ is 6.022 × 10²³ molecules but three times as many atoms.

cards.q: Compute the number of molecules in 36.0 g of H₂O.
cards.a: 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules. n = m/M = 36.0 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 2.00 mol; N = n × N_A = 2.00 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.20 × 10²⁴ molecules (3 sig figs, set by 36.0 g).
cards.n: If the question asked for ATOMS you would multiply by 3 (3.61 × 10²⁴); answering molecules when atoms were asked earns nothing.

cards.q: Compute the mass of 3.01×10²³ formula units of $CaCl_2$ (M = 111.0 g/mol).
cards.n: Formula units of an ionic solid are counted with Avogadro's number exactly like molecules; multiplying by N_A instead of dividing is the classic slip.

cards.q: Compute the number of moles of oxygen atoms in 2.50 mol of $Al_2(SO_4)_3$.
cards.a: 30.0 mol O. Each formula unit contains 3 sulfate groups × 4 O = 12 O atoms, so 2.50 mol × 12 = 30.0 mol of oxygen atoms.
cards.h: → O atoms per formula unit × moles
cards.n: The subscript 3 outside the parentheses multiplies everything inside; answering 10.0 mol (4 O) or 7.50 mol (3 O) means the parentheses were ignored.

cards.q: Compute the number of moles of glucose, $C_6H_{12}O_6$ (M = 180. g/mol), in a 45.0 g sample.
cards.n: Keep molar mass in the denominator; 45.0 × 180 = 8100 mol is impossible for a 45 g sample and a quick size check catches it.

cards.q: Compute the mass of 0.750 mol of NaOH (M = 40.0 g/mol).
cards.n: Less than one mole must weigh less than the molar mass in grams; a result above 40.0 g means the equation was inverted.

cards.q: Compute the number of moles of oxygen atoms in 3.00 mol of $Ca(NO_3)_2.$
cards.a: 18.0 mol O. Each formula unit of Ca(NO₃)₂ has 2 nitrate groups × 3 O = 6 oxygen atoms; 3.00 mol × 6 = 18.0 mol of O atoms.
cards.h: → atoms per formula unit × moles given
cards.n: Count atoms per formula unit first (the subscript 2 doubles the 3 oxygens of each nitrate); 9.00 mol means the parenthesis subscript was dropped.

cards.q: Calculate the molar mass of $Ca(NO_3)_2$ from the atomic masses Ca = 40.08, N = 14.01 and O = 16.00 g/mol.
cards.a: 164.10 g/mol. One formula unit holds 1 Ca, 2 N and 6 O: 40.08 + 2(14.01) + 6(16.00) = 40.08 + 28.02 + 96.00 = 164.10 g/mol. One formula unit therefore has an average mass of 164.10 amu.
cards.h: → count each atom, sum the products
cards.n: Forgetting to multiply the nitrate group by 2 gives 102.09 g/mol; write the atom count of each element before adding.

cards.q: Calculate the mass in grams of a single molecule of water (M = 18.02 g/mol).
cards.a: 2.992 × 10⁻²³ g. One mole (18.02 g) contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules, so one molecule has mass 18.02 g ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.992 × 10⁻²³ g. Equivalently 18.02 amu × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁴ g/amu.
cards.n: An answer of 18.02 g is the mass of a MOLE of molecules, not one molecule; the per-particle mass must be a number around 10⁻²³ g.

cards.q: Determine which sample contains more atoms: 10.0 g of helium (M = 4.00 g/mol) or 10.0 g of neon (M = 20.18 g/mol).
cards.a: The helium sample, by about five times. n(He) = 10.0 g ÷ 4.00 g/mol = 2.50 mol; n(Ne) = 10.0 g ÷ 20.18 g/mol = 0.496 mol. Both are monatomic, so the atom count is proportional to moles: He holds 1.51 × 10²⁴ atoms, Ne 2.99 × 10²³ atoms.
cards.n: Equal masses never mean equal numbers of particles; 'same mass so same atoms' earns nothing. The lighter atom gives more moles per gram.

cards.q: Calculate the number of chloride ions in 0.250 mol of $CaCl_2$.
cards.a: 3.01 × 10²³ Cl⁻ ions. Each formula unit releases 2 Cl⁻, so 0.250 mol CaCl₂ × 2 = 0.500 mol Cl⁻; N = 0.500 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³ ions.
cards.h: → ions per formula unit, then × N_A
cards.n: 1.51 × 10²³ is the number of formula units (or of Ca²⁺ ions); the factor of 2 chloride ions per CaCl₂ is the point of the question.

cards.q: Identify the quantities and relationships needed to find the number of atoms in a given mass of a monatomic element such as argon.
cards.a: Needed: the sample mass m (given), the molar mass M from the periodic table (39.95 g/mol for Ar) and Avogadro's number. Pathway: n = m/M gives moles; N = n × N_A gives atoms. For a molecular substance a third factor, atoms per molecule, would be needed.
cards.h: → list the quantities, then the two-step path
cards.n: Jumping from grams straight to Avogadro's number (m × N_A) skips the mole and gives a meaningless number; every path from mass to particles passes through n = m/M.

cards.q: Explain why chemists count particles by weighing a sample rather than by counting the particles directly.
cards.a: Atoms and molecules are far too small and numerous to count, so mass is measured instead and converted to a count. Because one mole of any substance has a mass equal to its molar mass, n = m/M gives moles and N = n × N_A gives the number of particles reacting.
cards.h: → particles uncountable → mass measurable → molar mass and N_A convert mass to a count
cards.n: 'Because it is easier' earns nothing; the point is that molar mass and Avogadro's number make mass a proxy for number.
o: Mass is the measurable macroscopic quantity, and molar mass converts it to the particle count that governs a reaction.
Reactions happen particle by particle, so the balance reading must be turned into moles before ratios of reacting particles can be used.

w.a: Chemists weigh samples because counting particles would take too long.
w.why: states a convenience, not the mass-to-number link through molar mass

w.a: Chemists weigh samples because mass is conserved in a reaction.
w.why: true but irrelevant; conservation of mass does not give a particle count

w.a: Chemists weigh samples because one gram of any substance contains one mole.
w.why: false: one MOLE has a mass of one molar mass, which differs for every substance

cards.q: Explain why the molar mass of a substance in g/mol is numerically equal to the mass of one of its particles in amu.
cards.a: The two units are defined together: the amu is set so that Avogadro's number of amu equals exactly one gram (1 g = 6.022 × 10²³ amu). So a particle of mass 18.02 amu, multiplied by N_A particles per mole, has a molar mass of 18.02 g/mol: the same number, scaled by N_A.
cards.h: → 1 g = N_A amu by definition → particle mass × N_A = molar mass with the same digits
cards.n: 'Because the periodic table lists both' describes the coincidence without the definition that causes it and earns nothing.
o: Multiplying a particle's mass in amu by N_A particles and by the conversion 1 g per N_A amu leaves the number unchanged, in g/mol.
The mole is defined as the number of amu in one gram, so per-particle and per-mole masses share the same digits.

w.a: They are equal because the amu and the gram are the same unit written two ways.
w.why: an amu is 1.661 × 10⁻²⁴ g; the units differ by a factor of N_A

w.a: They are equal because every atom has a mass of exactly one amu.
w.why: false; atomic masses range from 1 to over 200 amu

w.a: They are equal because molar mass is measured in amu per mole.
w.why: molar mass is in g/mol; the sentence just renames the units

cards.q: Explain why 1.0 mol of CO₂ contains more atoms than 1.0 mol of CO even though both samples contain the same number of molecules.
cards.a: Both samples hold 6.022 × 10²³ molecules, but each CO₂ molecule contains 3 atoms while each CO molecule contains 2. The atom count is molecules × atoms per molecule: 1.8 × 10²⁴ atoms in CO₂ versus 1.2 × 10²⁴ in CO.
cards.h: → same molecule count → multiply by atoms per molecule → 3 vs 2
cards.n: 'CO₂ has a bigger molar mass' earns nothing; mass does not decide atom count, the formula's atom total does.
o: A mole counts molecules; the formula subscripts then multiply that count by the atoms in each molecule, 3 for CO₂ and 2 for CO.
N_atoms = n × N_A × (atoms per molecule), and only the last factor differs: 3 versus 2.

w.a: CO₂ contains more atoms because it is heavier than CO.
w.why: mass is irrelevant to the count; the subscripts are

w.a: Both contain the same number of atoms because both are one mole.
w.why: a mole counts molecules, not atoms; the samples have equal molecules and unequal atoms

w.a: CO₂ contains more atoms because oxygen atoms are larger than carbon atoms.
w.why: atomic size has nothing to do with how many atoms are present

cards.q: Explain how to read a mass spectrum of a pure element.
cards.a: Each peak is one isotope. The x-axis is mass-to-charge ratio (m/z); for the singly charged monatomic ions the exam uses, m/z equals the isotope's mass in amu (close to its mass number). The y-axis is relative abundance: the height of each peak is proportional to the fraction of atoms that are that isotope, and the heights, normalized to a total of 1, weight the isotope masses to give the average atomic mass.
cards.h: → what each axis means, what a peak is
cards.n: Reading a peak's HEIGHT as its mass, or its POSITION as abundance, earns nothing; position is mass, height is abundance.

cards.q: Compute average atomic mass from isotopic masses and abundances.
cards.a: Average atomic mass = Σ (isotope mass × fractional abundance). Convert each percent to a decimal, multiply by that isotope's mass, add. Example: chlorine, 75.8% ³⁵Cl (34.97 amu) and 24.2% ³⁷Cl (36.97 amu): 0.758(34.97) + 0.242(36.97) = 26.51 + 8.95 = 35.45 amu.
cards.n: A plain average of the isotope masses (35.97 for Cl) earns nothing; the fractions must weight the sum and must total 1.

cards.q: Compute the average atomic mass of copper from 69.17% $^{63}Cu$ (62.93 amu) and 30.83% $^{65}Cu$ (64.93 amu).
cards.a: 63.55 amu. 0.6917 × 62.93 amu + 0.3083 × 64.93 amu = 43.53 + 20.02 = 63.55 amu, which matches the periodic-table value for copper.
