cards.n: The answer must fall between 62.93 and 64.93 and closer to 62.93 (the more abundant isotope); anything outside that window is an arithmetic slip.

cards.q: Identify the element whose mass spectrum shows only two peaks, at m/z 63 and 65, with relative heights near 7:3.
cards.a: Copper. The peaks are ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu; heights 7:3 mean fractional abundances of about 0.7 and 0.3, so the average mass is about 0.7(63) + 0.3(65) ≈ 63.6 amu, matching copper (63.55 amu) on the periodic table.
cards.h: → estimate the average, match the table
cards.n: Naming the element from the FIRST peak alone (63 → Cu is lucky here) is not reasoning; the weighted average matched to the periodic table is what scores.

cards.q: Predict what happens to a mass spectrum peak's relative height if that isotope's natural abundance increases while the others stay fixed.
cards.a: The peak grows taller in direct proportion to the abundance, and its position on the m/z axis does not move. Peak height encodes the fraction of atoms with that mass; the mass of the isotope, and so its m/z, is a fixed property of that nucleus.
cards.n: Saying the peak 'moves right' or 'gets heavier' earns nothing; abundance changes height only.

cards.q: Compute the average atomic mass of boron from 19.9% $^{10}B$ (10.01 amu) and 80.1% $^{11}B$ (11.01 amu).
cards.a: 10.8 amu. 0.199 × 10.01 amu + 0.801 × 11.01 amu = 1.99 + 8.82 = 10.81 ≈ 10.8 amu (3 sig figs from the abundances).
cards.n: The result must sit between 10.01 and 11.01 and lean toward ¹¹B (80% abundant); 10.5 (the plain average) earns nothing.

cards.q: Compute the average atomic mass of lithium from 7.59% $^6Li$ (6.02 amu) and 92.41% $^7Li$ (7.02 amu).
cards.a: 6.94 amu. 0.0759 × 6.02 amu + 0.9241 × 7.02 amu = 0.457 + 6.487 = 6.94 amu, the value tabulated for lithium.
cards.n: 7.59% is 0.0759, not 0.759; a misplaced decimal drags the average far outside the 6.02–7.02 window.

cards.q: Determine the percent abundance of each bromine isotope, given that bromine's average atomic mass is 79.90 amu and its isotopes have masses 78.92 amu (⁷⁹Br) and 80.92 amu (⁸¹Br).
cards.a: About 51% ⁷⁹Br and 49% ⁸¹Br. Let x be the fraction of ⁷⁹Br, so ⁸¹Br is 1 − x: 78.92x + 80.92(1 − x) = 79.90 → 80.92 − 2.00x = 79.90 → x = 1.02/2.00 = 0.51. So ⁷⁹Br ≈ 51% and ⁸¹Br ≈ 49%; the near-equal split is why 79.90 lies almost midway between the isotope masses.
cards.h: → one unknown x, fractions sum to 1
cards.n: Using two independent unknowns without the constraint x + y = 1 leaves the system unsolvable; that constraint is the point that earns credit.

cards.q: Sketch the mass spectrum of naturally occurring chlorine (75.8% ³⁵Cl, 24.2% ³⁷Cl), describing the axes and every peak.
cards.a: Horizontal axis: mass-to-charge ratio m/z (amu), scaled to show 34 to 38. Vertical axis: relative abundance (or relative intensity). Two vertical lines only: one at m/z = 35 with height 75.8 (or 100 if normalized to the tallest peak) and one at m/z = 37 with height 24.2 (32 normalized), so the 35 peak is about three times taller. No peak at 35.45 and nothing between the two lines.
cards.h: → axes with labels, two lines, 3:1 heights
cards.n: A peak drawn at 35.45 earns nothing: no atom has the average mass. Labeling the y-axis 'mass' or the x-axis 'abundance' also loses the axis point.

cards.q: Estimate the average atomic mass of gallium from a mass spectrum with peaks at m/z 69 (relative height 60) and m/z 71 (relative height 40).
cards.a: About 69.8 amu. The heights total 100, so the fractional abundances are 0.60 (⁶⁹Ga) and 0.40 (⁷¹Ga). Using the mass numbers as the isotope masses: 0.60 × 69 + 0.40 × 71 = 41.4 + 28.4 = 69.8 amu, close to the tabulated 69.72 amu (the exact isotope masses are slightly below the mass numbers).
cards.n: Answering 70 (the midpoint) ignores the unequal heights; the weighted average must lean toward the taller peak at 69.

cards.q: Determine the fractional abundances of silver's isotopes from a mass spectrum with peaks at m/z 107 (relative height 100) and m/z 109 (relative height 93), then estimate the average atomic mass.
cards.a: (¹⁰⁷Ag) 0.518 and (¹⁰⁹Ag) 0.482; average ≈ 107.9 amu. The heights sum to 193, so the fractions are 100/193 = 0.518 and 93/193 = 0.482. Average ≈ 0.518 × 107 + 0.482 × 109 = 55.4 + 52.5 = 107.9 amu, matching silver's tabulated 107.87 amu.
cards.h: → normalize heights to a total of 1, then weight
cards.n: Relative heights are not percentages unless they sum to 100; using 1.00 and 0.93 as fractions gives an average near 208 and earns nothing.

cards.q: Estimate the average atomic mass of magnesium from a mass spectrum with three peaks: m/z 24 (79.0%), m/z 25 (10.0%) and m/z 26 (11.0%).
cards.a: About 24.3 amu. Weighted sum using the mass numbers: 0.790 × 24 + 0.100 × 25 + 0.110 × 26 = 18.96 + 2.50 + 2.86 = 24.32 amu, matching the periodic-table value 24.31 amu. Three peaks means three naturally occurring isotopes.
cards.n: Dividing by 3 after adding the products earns nothing; the fractions already sum to 1, so the weighted sum IS the average.

cards.q: Contrast the mass number of an isotope with the average atomic mass of the element.
cards.a: Mass number is the integer count of protons plus neutrons in ONE nucleus (³⁷Cl: 17 + 20 = 37) and labels a single isotope. Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of the isotope masses of the natural mixture, a non-integer in amu (Cl: 35.45), and is the number on the periodic table. Neutrons are counted from a mass number, never from the average.
cards.h: → one nucleus vs the natural mixture
cards.n: Subtracting Z from the periodic-table mass (35.45 − 17 = 18.45 neutrons) is the classic confusion; neutron counts come from the mass number of a specific isotope.

cards.q: Determine which isotope is most abundant, and identify the element, from a mass spectrum with peaks at m/z 20 (relative height 100), m/z 21 (relative height 0.3) and m/z 22 (relative height 10).
cards.a: The m/z 20 isotope is most abundant (about 90% of atoms), and the element is neon. Fractions: 100/110.3 = 0.907, 0.003, 0.091; average ≈ 0.907(20) + 0.003(21) + 0.091(22) = 18.14 + 0.06 + 2.00 = 20.2 amu, matching neon (20.18 amu), whose isotopes are ²⁰Ne, ²¹Ne and ²²Ne.
cards.h: → tallest peak, then match the average to the table
cards.n: Identifying the element from 'the peak at 20' alone is not evidence; the weighted average compared with the periodic table is.

cards.q: Explain why an element's average atomic mass lies closer to the mass of one particular isotope.
cards.a: The average is weighted by abundance, so it is pulled toward the most abundant isotope. Chlorine's average of 35.45 amu sits near ³⁵Cl (34.97) because about 76% of chlorine atoms are ³⁵Cl and only 24% are the heavier ³⁷Cl.
cards.h: → abundance-weighted sum → the most common isotope dominates → average lands near its mass
cards.n: Saying the average 'rounds to the nearest isotope' earns nothing; the weighting by abundance is the reason.
o: Each isotope contributes mass × fraction, and the isotope with the largest fraction contributes most of the total.
If one isotope were 100% abundant the average would equal its mass; each minority isotope only shifts it a little.

w.a: The average lies near the heaviest isotope because heavier atoms count for more.
w.why: weighting is by abundance, not by mass

w.a: The average lies near one isotope because most elements have only one isotope.
w.why: most elements have several; abundance, not isotope count, sets the average

w.a: The average lies near one isotope because the periodic table rounds atomic masses.
w.why: rounding is not the cause; the weighted sum is

cards.q: Explain why the mass spectrum of a pure element can show several peaks.
cards.a: A pure element is a mixture of isotopes: atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Each isotope has a different mass, so its singly charged ion appears at a different m/z, one peak per isotope; the peak heights give the relative abundance of each isotope.
cards.h: → same protons, different neutrons → different masses → one peak per isotope
cards.n: 'The sample is impure' earns nothing; the exam's spectra are of single elements and the peaks are isotopes.
o: Neutron number varies among atoms of one element, so their ions are separated by mass in the spectrometer.
Elements with one stable isotope (fluorine, sodium) show a single peak; several peaks means several isotopes.

w.a: A pure element shows several peaks because some atoms lose more than one electron.
w.why: the exam limits spectra to singly charged monatomic ions; multiple charges are excluded

w.a: A pure element shows several peaks because it contains molecules of different sizes.
w.why: monatomic ions of an element are all the same size; only the nucleus differs

w.a: A pure element shows several peaks because atoms have different numbers of protons.
w.why: different proton numbers would be different elements, not isotopes

cards.q: Explain why no single chlorine atom has a mass of 35.45 amu even though 35.45 is the atomic mass listed for chlorine.
cards.a: 35.45 amu is an average, not a mass any atom has. Natural chlorine is about 76% ³⁵Cl (34.97 amu) and 24% ³⁷Cl (36.97 amu); the abundance-weighted sum 0.76(34.97) + 0.24(36.97) = 35.45 amu describes the mixture, and every individual atom is one isotope or the other.
cards.h: → two isotopes → weighted average of the mixture → the average is not either atom's mass
cards.n: Claiming that chlorine atoms have 18.45 neutrons treats the average as a real nucleus and earns nothing.
o: The periodic table reports the mean mass per atom of the natural isotope mixture, which need not coincide with any isotope.
In a mass spectrum of chlorine there are peaks at 35 and 37 and none at 35.45.

w.a: No chlorine atom has that mass because atomic masses are rounded on the periodic table.
w.why: rounding is not the reason; 35.45 is a weighted average of two different isotopes

w.a: No chlorine atom has that mass because electrons add a fraction of an amu.
w.why: electron mass is tiny and would not produce a value between two isotopes

w.a: Every chlorine atom does have a mass of 35.45 amu, since that is chlorine's atomic mass.
w.why: false: atoms are ³⁵Cl or ³⁷Cl; 35.45 is the mixture's average

cards.q: Explain why the isotopes of an element show the same chemical behavior even though their masses differ.
cards.a: Chemical behavior is set by the electrons, and isotopes have the same number of protons and therefore the same number and configuration of electrons. They differ only in neutron count, which changes nuclear mass but not the nuclear charge that holds the electrons, so bonding is essentially unchanged.
cards.h: → same protons → same electrons and configuration → same bonding; neutrons change mass only
cards.n: 'Isotopes are the same element' restates the claim; the point comes from saying the electron configuration is identical because the proton count is.
o: Valence electrons decide reactivity, and the valence configuration depends on nuclear charge, which all isotopes share.
Neutrons are uncharged, so adding them does not change the Coulombic attraction between nucleus and electrons.

w.a: Isotopes behave the same because they have the same mass number.
w.why: isotopes have DIFFERENT mass numbers; that is what makes them isotopes

w.a: Isotopes behave the same because neutrons and protons are both in the nucleus.
w.why: location is irrelevant; the proton count fixing the electron count is the reason

w.a: Isotopes behave differently because heavier atoms react more slowly.
w.why: mass effects on rate are negligible for most elements and the question concerns chemical identity

cards.q: Define percent composition by mass and give the equation.
cards.a: Percent composition is the mass fraction of each element in a compound expressed as a percent: % element = (mass of that element in one mole of compound ÷ molar mass of the compound) × 100%. For H₂O: %H = (2 × 1.008 ÷ 18.02) × 100 = 11.19%, %O = 88.81%; the percentages of all elements total 100%.
cards.n: Dividing the atomic mass by the molar mass without multiplying by the subscript (1.008/18.02 for H) is the usual slip; the numerator is the mass of ALL atoms of that element.

cards.q: Contrast an empirical formula with a molecular formula.
cards.a: The empirical formula gives the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms (CH₂O); the molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in one molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) and is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Mass-percent data yield only the empirical formula; the molar mass is needed to find the multiple.
cards.n: Percent composition alone can never give a molecular formula: CH₂O, C₂H₄O₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆ all have identical mass percents.

cards.q: Apply the standard procedure for finding an empirical formula from percent composition.
cards.a: 1) Assume a 100 g sample so each percent becomes grams. 2) Divide each mass by that element's molar mass to get moles. 3) Divide every mole value by the smallest. 4) If a ratio is not near a whole number, multiply all by the smallest integer that clears it (1.5 → ×2, 1.33 → ×3, 1.25 → ×4). Write the subscripts.
cards.n: Rounding 1:1.5 to 1:2 earns nothing; ratios ending in .5, .33 or .25 must be multiplied up, not rounded.

cards.q: Compute a molecular formula given an empirical formula and molar mass.
cards.a: Find the whole number n = (molar mass of compound) ÷ (empirical formula mass), then multiply every subscript by n. Example: empirical formula NO₂ (46.01 g/mol) and molar mass 92.0 g/mol give n = 92.0/46.01 = 2.00, so the molecular formula is N₂O₄.
cards.h: → divide the masses, scale every subscript
cards.n: n must come out close to a whole number; 2.4 means the empirical formula mass or the molar mass was miscomputed, not that you should round.

cards.q: Compute the empirical formula of a compound that is 40.0% C, 6.7% H, and 53.3% O by mass.
cards.a: CH₂O. In 100 g: C = 40.0 g ÷ 12.01 g/mol = 3.33 mol; H = 6.7 g ÷ 1.008 g/mol = 6.6 mol; O = 53.3 g ÷ 16.00 g/mol = 3.33 mol. Dividing by 3.33 gives C:H:O = 1:2:1.
cards.n: This ratio fits glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), formaldehyde (CH₂O) and acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂) alike; without a molar mass, CH₂O is all the data support.

cards.q: Combustion of 2.20 g of a hydrocarbon produces 6.60 g $CO_2$ and 3.60 g $H_2O$. Compute its empirical formula.
cards.a: C₃H₈. Moles C = 6.60 g ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 0.150 mol (1.80 g C); moles H = 2 × (3.60 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol) = 0.400 mol (0.403 g H). The C and H masses total 2.20 g, the whole sample, so no oxygen is present. Ratio C:H = 0.150:0.400 = 3:8.
cards.h: → CO₂ gives C, H₂O gives H, check the mass balance
cards.n: Forgetting the factor of 2 hydrogens per H₂O gives C₃H₄; and if recovered C + H mass fell short of the sample mass, the difference would be oxygen.

cards.q: Compute the empirical formula of a compound that is 43.4% Na, 11.3% C, and 45.3% O by mass.
cards.h: → three mole values, divide by the smallest
cards.n: Dividing by the LARGEST mole value gives fractions below 1 and no formula; always divide by the smallest.

cards.q: Compute the percent composition by mass of Fe and O in $Fe_2O_3$ (M = 159.7 g/mol; Fe = 55.85, O = 16.00 g/mol).
cards.h: → (mass of element in formula ÷ M) × 100, twice
cards.n: Using 55.85 instead of 2 × 55.85 gives 35.0% Fe; a pair of percentages that do not add to 100 signals a dropped subscript.

cards.q: Compute the molecular formula of a compound with empirical formula $CH_2O$ and molar mass 180. g/mol.
cards.a: C₆H₁₂O₆. Empirical formula mass = 12.01 + 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 30.03 g/mol; n = 180. ÷ 30.03 = 5.99 ≈ 6, so every subscript is multiplied by 6.
cards.h: → M ÷ empirical mass, then ×6 on all subscripts
cards.n: Multiplying only the hydrogen subscript (CH₁₂O) is the usual slip; every subscript, including the implied 1 on C and O, scales by n.

cards.q: Compute the percent by mass of water in $MgSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O$ (M = 246.5 g/mol).
cards.n: Dividing by the anhydrous MgSO₄ mass (120.4) instead of the full hydrate mass earns nothing; the waters are part of the formula and of the denominator.

cards.q: Determine the empirical formula of the oxide formed when 1.20 g of magnesium burns completely in oxygen to give 2.00 g of magnesium oxide (Mg = 24.31, O = 16.00 g/mol).
cards.h: → mass of O by difference, then mole ratio
cards.n: Using 2.00 g as the mass of oxygen (instead of the product) gives Mg:O = 1:2.5 and earns nothing; the oxygen is the mass GAINED.

cards.q: Determine the value of x in $CuSO_4 \cdot xH_2O$ if a 5.00 g sample of the hydrate leaves 3.20 g of anhydrous $CuSO_4$ (M = 159.6 g/mol) after heating to constant mass.
cards.a: x = 5. Water driven off = 5.00 − 3.20 = 1.80 g = 1.80 ÷ 18.02 = 0.0999 mol H₂O; CuSO₄ = 3.20 ÷ 159.6 = 0.0201 mol. Ratio H₂O:CuSO₄ = 0.0999 ÷ 0.0201 = 4.97 ≈ 5, so the hydrate is CuSO₄·5H₂O.
cards.h: → two mole values, ratio water to salt
cards.n: Ratio of MASSES (1.80/3.20 = 0.56) earns nothing; x is a mole ratio. 'Constant mass' is the evidence that all water has left.

cards.q: Determine whether two samples of a copper chloride are the same compound: sample 1 (3.00 g) contains 1.42 g of Cu, and sample 2 (5.00 g) contains 2.36 g of Cu.
cards.a: They are the same compound. Mass percent Cu: sample 1 = 1.42 ÷ 3.00 × 100 = 47.3%; sample 2 = 2.36 ÷ 5.00 × 100 = 47.2%. Equal mass ratios in different-sized samples is exactly the law of definite proportions; both match CuCl₂ (63.55 ÷ 134.45 = 47.3% Cu), not CuCl (64.2% Cu).
cards.h: → compare mass fractions, cite definite proportions
cards.n: Comparing the raw copper masses (1.42 vs 2.36 g) and concluding 'different' earns nothing; only the RATIO of element masses is fixed for a compound.

cards.q: Classify each substance as made of molecules, of formula units, or of individual atoms: H₂O · NaCl · CO₂ · MgO · NH₃ · KNO₃ · He · Cu · C₆H₁₂O₆ · CaCl₂ · SO₂ · Fe₂O₃ · Ar · Ne · NH₄Cl · Br₂
cards.a:
H₂O → molecules
NaCl → formula units (ionic)
CO₂ → molecules
MgO → formula units
NH₃ → molecules
KNO₃ → formula units (K⁺ and polyatomic NO₃⁻)
He → individual atoms
Cu → individual atoms (metallic lattice)
C₆H₁₂O₆ → molecules
CaCl₂ → formula units
SO₂ → molecules
Fe₂O₃ → formula units
Ar → individual atoms
Ne → individual atoms
NH₄Cl → formula units (two polyatomic/simple ions)
Br₂ → molecules
cards.h: → ions → formula unit; nonmetals only → molecule
cards.n: Calling NaCl 'a molecule' earns nothing on the exam: an ionic solid has no discrete molecules, only a lattice described by its lowest ratio.

cards.q: Determine the molecular formula of a hydrocarbon that is 85.6% C and 14.4% H by mass and has a molar mass of 56.1 g/mol.
cards.a: C₄H₈. In 100 g: C = 85.6 ÷ 12.01 = 7.13 mol; H = 14.4 ÷ 1.008 = 14.3 mol; ratio 1:2.00 gives empirical formula CH₂ (14.03 g/mol). n = 56.1 ÷ 14.03 = 4.00, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.
cards.h: → empirical formula, then M ÷ empirical mass
cards.n: Stopping at CH₂ loses the final point; the molar mass was given precisely so the multiple n = 4 could be found.

cards.q: Identify one testable question that percent-composition data for a newly isolated white solid can answer, and one it cannot answer.
cards.a: Can answer: 'What is the lowest whole-number ratio of the elements (the empirical formula)?' or 'Is the mass ratio consistent with a proposed compound such as Na₂CO₃?' Cannot answer: 'What is the molecular formula?' (needs the molar mass, since CH₂O and C₆H₁₂O₆ have the same percents) or 'How are the atoms connected?' (needs structural data).
cards.h: → one question the ratio answers, one it cannot
cards.n: 'What is the compound?' is not testable from mass percents alone; two compounds with the same empirical formula give identical data.

cards.q: Explain why percent-composition data alone cannot distinguish acetylene (C₂H₂) from benzene (C₆H₆).
cards.a: Both have the empirical formula CH, so both are 92.3% C and 7.7% H by mass. Mass percent depends only on the RATIO of atoms, and a ratio of 1:1 is the same whether a molecule holds 2 atoms or 12. Distinguishing them needs the molar mass (26.0 vs 78.1 g/mol).
cards.h: → same empirical formula → same atom ratio → identical mass percents → molar mass needed
cards.n: 'They are different compounds so the percents differ' is false and earns nothing; identical ratios give identical percents.
o: Percent composition reduces to the empirical formula, and C₆H₆ is (CH)₆ while C₂H₂ is (CH)₂, the same ratio.
Only a measurement of molar mass fixes the multiple n that turns CH into C₂H₂ or C₆H₆.

w.a: Percent composition cannot tell them apart because both are hydrocarbons.
w.why: being hydrocarbons is not the reason; C₃H₈ is also a hydrocarbon and has different percents

w.a: Percent composition can tell them apart because benzene has more carbon atoms.
w.why: more atoms in the same ratio give the same mass percent

w.a: Percent composition cannot tell them apart because the samples were the same mass.
w.why: sample size never affects percent composition; the identical ratio does

cards.q: Explain why the mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in pure water is always about 1:8, whatever the source or size of the sample.
cards.a: Water is a pure compound with a fixed formula, H₂O: every molecule has 2 H atoms (2 × 1.008 = 2.016 amu) bonded to 1 O atom (16.00 amu). Because every molecule has the same composition, any sample, however large, has the same element mass ratio, 2.016:16.00 ≈ 1:7.9. This is the law of definite proportions.
cards.h: → fixed formula → every molecule identical → same mass ratio in any sample
cards.n: Citing 'conservation of mass' earns nothing here; the relevant law is definite proportions, and it follows from the fixed formula.
o: A sample is just many identical H₂O molecules, so scaling the sample scales both element masses by the same factor.
If the ratio varied, the substance would be a mixture, not a compound; a compound's formula fixes its composition.

w.a: The ratio is fixed because water is always made in the same laboratory way.
w.why: origin is irrelevant; the molecular formula fixes the ratio

w.a: The ratio is fixed because hydrogen and oxygen atoms have the same mass.
w.why: false, and it would not produce a 1:8 ratio

w.a: The ratio is fixed because mass is conserved when water forms.
w.why: conservation of mass says nothing about the ratio of elements in the product

cards.q: Explain why an empirical formula obtained from mass-percent data must be combined with the molar mass to give the molecular formula.
cards.a: Mass percents fix only the ratio of atoms, which is the same for a molecule and for any whole-number multiple of it (CH₂O, C₂H₄O₂, C₆H₁₂O₆ all give 40.0% C). The molar mass tells how many empirical units one molecule contains: n = M ÷ (empirical formula mass), and the subscripts are scaled by n.
cards.h: → percents give a ratio only → multiples share the ratio → M picks the multiple
cards.n: 'The molar mass makes the answer more accurate' earns nothing; it supplies a different quantity, the multiple n, not extra precision.
o: The empirical formula is a ratio; the molecular formula is a count, and a count needs the mass of one molecule to fix it.
Dividing the molar mass by the empirical formula mass gives the integer that turns the ratio into actual atom numbers.

w.a: The molar mass is needed because percent data are usually measured imprecisely.
w.why: precision is not the issue; even perfect percents give only a ratio

w.a: The molar mass is needed to convert the percents into grams.
w.why: the 100 g assumption already does that; the molar mass sets the multiple

w.a: The molar mass is not needed, because the empirical formula is the molecular formula.
w.why: true only when n = 1, which cannot be known without the molar mass

cards.q: Explain why sodium chloride is described by a formula unit, NaCl, rather than by a molecular formula.
cards.a: Solid NaCl is a lattice in which every Na⁺ is surrounded by Cl⁻ ions and every Cl⁻ by Na⁺ ions, with no separate two-atom molecules. The formula NaCl states only the lowest whole-number ratio of ions (1:1) needed for the solid to be neutral, which is what a formula unit means.
cards.h: → ionic lattice → no discrete molecules → formula gives the neutral ratio only
cards.n: 'NaCl is a molecule with one bond' earns nothing; ionic solids have extended lattices, not molecules.
o: Ionic compounds are held together by attractions between many ions in fixed proportion, so the smallest neutral ratio is the only meaningful formula.
Contrast H₂O, where two H and one O are bonded into a discrete unit that exists on its own; no such NaCl unit exists in the crystal.

w.a: NaCl is a formula unit because it is a solid at room temperature.
w.why: being solid is not the reason; ice is a solid made of molecules

w.a: NaCl is a formula unit because it contains only two atoms.
w.why: atom count is irrelevant; CO also has two atoms and is a molecule

w.a: NaCl is called a formula unit because it has no fixed composition.
w.why: false: the 1:1 ratio is fixed, which is exactly what the formula unit states

cards.q: Contrast a pure substance with a mixture.
cards.a: A pure substance (an element or a compound) contains atoms, molecules or formula units of a single type, so its composition is fixed and its properties are characteristic. A mixture contains two or more substances whose relative proportions can vary, so its composition and properties (density, boiling range) vary from sample to sample, and it can be separated by physical means.
cards.h: → one kind of particle vs several, fixed vs variable
cards.n: A compound is a pure substance although it holds two elements; 'pure means one element' earns nothing. Pure means one kind of particle.

cards.q: Contrast the particle-level appearance of a homogeneous mixture with that of a heterogeneous mixture.
cards.a: In a homogeneous mixture (solution, alloy, air) the different particles are evenly intermixed, so any region drawn at the particle level has the same composition. In a heterogeneous mixture the components sit in distinct regions or phases, so a particle diagram shows clumps or layers of one kind of particle beside another.
cards.n: Uniform to the eye is not the criterion; the exam draws particle boxes, and a box with one region rich in particle A and another in particle B is heterogeneous.

cards.q: Compute the mass percent of NaCl in a mixture formed by dissolving 15.0 g of NaCl in 235 g of water.
cards.n: Dividing by the water mass alone (15.0/235 = 6.38%) earns nothing; the denominator is the whole mixture.

cards.q: Define parts per million (ppm) and state when it is preferred over percent composition.
cards.a: ppm = (mass of component ÷ total mass of mixture) × 10⁶. It is used for very dilute mixtures where a percent would be an awkward decimal: 0.0002% is 2 ppm. For dilute aqueous solutions 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg of solute per liter, since a liter of water has a mass of about 1 kg.
cards.n: ppm is mass ÷ mass × 10⁶, so 1 ppm = 0.0001%; multiplying a percent by 10⁴ to get ppm is the conversion, not by 10⁶.

cards.q: Explain the physical property that filtration exploits.
cards.a: Filtration separates by particle size: an undissolved solid is held back by the pores of the filter while the liquid, and anything dissolved in it at the ion or molecule level, passes through. It works only for a heterogeneous mixture in which one component is not dissolved.
cards.n: Filtration cannot separate a dissolved solute from its solvent; the ions pass through the paper. Borrowed from Unit 3 (separations).

cards.q: Explain the physical property that distillation exploits.
cards.a: Distillation separates by boiling point. The component with the lower boiling point, the one with weaker intermolecular forces, vaporizes first when the mixture is heated; its vapor is condensed and collected, leaving the higher-boiling component behind.
cards.n: 'It evaporates faster' earns nothing; tie the boiling-point difference to intermolecular force strength (Unit 3 content, borrowed).

cards.q: Explain the principle behind chromatographic separation.
cards.a: The components distribute between a mobile phase (solvent) and a stationary phase (paper, silica). A component attracted more strongly to the mobile phase and less strongly to the stationary phase travels farther; one attracted more strongly to the stationary phase lags behind. The differing strengths of these intermolecular attractions separate the components.
cards.h: → two competing attractions, who moves farther
cards.n: Naming only 'polarity' without saying which phase each component is attracted to earns nothing. Borrowed from Unit 3 (3.9).

cards.q: Explain why a solution cannot be separated into its components by simple filtration.
cards.a: In a true solution the solute is dispersed as individual ions or molecules, far smaller than the pores of any filter, so solute and solvent both pass through and nothing is retained. Separating them requires a property difference, such as boiling point (distillation) or evaporation of the solvent.
cards.n: 'The solute is invisible' is not chemistry; the point is that dissolved particles are at the molecular scale. Borrowed from Unit 3.

cards.q: Classify each as an element, a compound, a homogeneous mixture, or a heterogeneous mixture: air · brass · salt water · granite · distilled water · oxygen gas · carbon dioxide · Italian salad dressing · 14-karat gold · table sugar · muddy water · ozone · stainless steel · diamond · vinegar · concrete
cards.a:
air → homogeneous mixture (N₂, O₂, Ar...)
brass → homogeneous mixture (Cu–Zn alloy)
salt water → homogeneous mixture (solution)
granite → heterogeneous mixture (visible mineral grains)
distilled water → compound (H₂O)
oxygen gas → element (O₂)
carbon dioxide → compound
Italian salad dressing → heterogeneous mixture (oil and water layers)
14-karat gold → homogeneous mixture (Au alloy)
table sugar → compound (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁)
muddy water → heterogeneous mixture
ozone → element (O₃)
stainless steel → homogeneous mixture (Fe–Cr–Ni alloy)
diamond → element (C)
vinegar → homogeneous mixture (acetic acid in water)
concrete → heterogeneous mixture
cards.h: → one kind of particle? fixed ratio? uniform?
cards.n: Alloys and air are mixtures although they look uniform; 'looks the same everywhere' identifies homogeneous, not pure. Ozone and O₂ are both the element oxygen.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, three particle diagrams: a sample of pure O₂ gas, a sample of pure NO gas, and a mixture of the two gases.
cards.a: Box 1 (pure O₂): only identical two-atom particles, each made of two same-colored circles (say two red), spread randomly. Box 2 (pure NO): only two-atom particles, each one red circle joined to one blue circle. Box 3 (mixture): both kinds of particle in the same box, randomly intermixed, in any ratio (say 5 O₂ and 3 NO); no free single atoms and no red-red-blue units.
cards.h: → three boxes: one particle type, one type, both types
cards.n: Drawing separate O and N atoms in the mixture earns nothing: the gases keep their molecular identity in a mixture; only the proportion is free.

cards.q: Determine the mass percent of NaCl in a 5.00 g sample of impure NaCl that contains 2.73 g of chlorine, given that the impurity contains no chlorine (Na = 22.99, Cl = 35.45 g/mol).
cards.a: 90.0% NaCl. All the chlorine is in NaCl, and the mass fraction of Cl in NaCl is 35.45 ÷ 58.44 = 0.6066, so mass of NaCl = 2.73 g ÷ 0.6066 = 4.50 g. Purity = (4.50 ÷ 5.00) × 100 = 90.0%.
cards.h: → element mass ÷ its mass fraction in the compound
cards.n: Reporting 2.73/5.00 = 54.6% gives the percent CHLORINE, not the percent NaCl; the chloride mass must be scaled up to the whole compound first.

cards.q: Determine the mass percent of NH₄NO₃ in a fertilizer sample that is 15.0% nitrogen by mass, given that pure NH₄NO₃ is 35.0% N and the other components contain no nitrogen.
cards.a: 42.9% NH₄NO₃. In 100 g of fertilizer there are 15.0 g N; since every 100 g of NH₄NO₃ carries 35.0 g N, the mass of NH₄NO₃ = 15.0 ÷ 0.350 = 42.9 g, i.e. 42.9% of the sample. (35.0% N checks: 2 × 14.01 ÷ 80.05 = 0.350.)
cards.h: → element percent ÷ element fraction in the compound
cards.n: 15.0/35.0 only works because both are per 100 g of their sample; forgetting that and answering 15.0% earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the quantities needed to find the mass of each component of a two-component mixture of NaCl and KCl from the total mass of the sample and the total mass of chloride it contains.
cards.a: Needed: the total sample mass (x + y, with x = mass NaCl and y = mass KCl); the chloride mass; and the mass fraction of Cl in each salt from the molar masses (35.45/58.44 = 0.6066 for NaCl, 35.45/74.55 = 0.4755 for KCl). Two equations, x + y = total and 0.6066x + 0.4755y = mass of Cl, fix x and y.
cards.h: → two unknowns, two equations, the fractions from M
cards.n: A single measurement (total mass alone, or chloride alone) cannot fix two unknowns; the point is that two independent data are required.

cards.q: Calculate the mass percent of each component in a 10.00 g mixture of NaCl and KCl that contains 5.50 g of chloride, given NaCl is 60.66% Cl and KCl is 47.55% Cl by mass.
cards.n: Writing 0.6066x + 0.4755y = 5.50 and stopping earns partial credit only; the mass constraint y = 10.00 − x is what makes it solvable.

cards.q: Determine whether a white solid that is 39.3% Na and 60.7% Cl by mass could be pure NaCl (Na = 22.99, Cl = 35.45 g/mol), and state what the data do not prove.
cards.a: It could be pure NaCl: the theoretical composition is %Na = 22.99 ÷ 58.44 × 100 = 39.3% and %Cl = 60.7%, matching the data. The match is consistent with purity but does not prove it, because an impurity that contributes Na and Cl in the same 1:1 ratio, or is present below the precision of the analysis, would not change the percents.
cards.h: → compute the theoretical percents, compare, state the limit
cards.n: 'The percents match, so it is pure' overstates the evidence; the earned phrasing is 'consistent with' plus the reason the data cannot rule out impurity.

cards.q: Explain why the mass percent of sodium in NaCl is fixed at 39.3%, while the mass percent of NaCl in salt water can take any value.
cards.a: NaCl is a pure compound: every formula unit has one Na⁺ and one Cl⁻, so the element ratio and the mass percent are fixed by the formula (definite proportions). Salt water is a mixture: NaCl and H₂O keep their identities and combine in any proportion, so its composition depends on how much salt was dissolved.
cards.h: → compound: fixed formula → fixed ratio; mixture: independent substances → any proportion
cards.n: 'Salt water is not pure' restates the claim; the point comes from saying a mixture's components are not bonded in a fixed ratio.
o: Formula units all have the same composition, whereas the number of water molecules per formula unit in a solution is not fixed by any formula.
A compound's percent is a property of the substance; a mixture's percent is a property of the particular sample.

w.a: The percent of NaCl in salt water varies because salt dissolves at different rates.
w.why: rate is irrelevant; the amount dissolved, not the speed, sets the composition

w.a: The percent of Na in NaCl is fixed because sodium is a metal.
w.why: metallic character has nothing to do with definite proportions

w.a: Both percents are fixed because both substances contain NaCl.
w.why: false; a mixture's composition varies with the sample

cards.q: Explain how elemental analysis can reveal that a sample of a compound is impure.
cards.a: A pure compound has a fixed mass percent of each element set by its formula. Measure the percent of one element (say % N in a fertilizer) and compare it with the theoretical value; a lower percent means part of the mass is something else, and the ratio measured ÷ theoretical estimates the purity.
cards.h: → formula fixes the percent → measured percent below it → mass of other substances present
cards.n: 'Test whether it melts sharply' is a valid purity check but is not elemental analysis; the point requires comparing element percents.
o: Because definite proportions holds for the pure compound, any deviation of the measured composition from the formula's composition implies added material.
If an impurity contains none of the analyzed element, purity = measured percent ÷ theoretical percent.

w.a: Elemental analysis shows impurity because impure samples weigh more.
w.why: mass alone says nothing about composition

w.a: Elemental analysis shows impurity because a pure compound contains only one element.
w.why: a compound contains at least two elements; purity concerns fixed ratio, not element count

w.a: Elemental analysis cannot detect impurity because mixtures also have fixed percents.
w.why: false; a mixture's composition is variable, a compound's is fixed

cards.q: Explain why the elemental composition of a mixture of NaCl and KCl cannot be used to write a single chemical formula for the mixture.
cards.a: A formula expresses a fixed ratio of atoms held together in one substance. The mixture contains two separate substances, NaCl and KCl, each with its own formula, in a proportion that can be anything; its overall Na:K:Cl ratio depends on how the sample was made, so no single formula describes it.
cards.h: → two independent substances → variable proportion → no fixed ratio → no formula
cards.n: Writing 'NaKCl₂' earns nothing; a formula implies definite proportions, which a mixture lacks.
o: Definite proportions applies to each compound in the mixture, not to the mixture as a whole.
Another sample with more KCl would give a different Na:K ratio, which a fixed formula cannot represent.

w.a: A formula cannot be written because the mixture contains too many elements.
w.why: element count is not the issue; Na₂CO₃ has three elements and a formula

w.a: A formula can be written by averaging the two formulas.
w.why: an average ratio changes from sample to sample and is not a formula

w.a: A formula cannot be written because NaCl and KCl are both ionic.
w.why: bonding type is irrelevant; variable proportion is the reason

cards.q: Explain why a sample whose measured percent composition matches a compound's theoretical values is consistent with purity but not proof of it.
cards.a: The analysis shows only that the element mass ratio equals the compound's. An impurity with the same elements in the same ratio (an isomer, or one with the same empirical formula) leaves the percents unchanged, and a small impurity hides within the precision of the analysis. The data rule out some impurities, not all.
cards.h: → analysis tests the ratio only → same-ratio impurity invisible → consistent, not proven
cards.n: 'It matches, therefore it is pure' overclaims and earns nothing; the point is naming a kind of impurity the analysis cannot see.
o: Percent composition is a necessary but not sufficient test: a pure sample must match, but a matching sample need not be pure.
Adding a second test, such as a sharp melting point, is needed because composition alone cannot detect same-ratio contaminants.

w.a: A match proves purity because definite proportions applies only to pure compounds.
w.why: an impurity of the same composition also obeys definite proportions

w.a: A match is not proof because percent composition is never measured accurately.
w.why: the limitation is conceptual, not instrumental

w.a: A match is not proof because the sample might be a different element.
w.why: a different element would change the percents

cards.q: State Coulomb's law as it is used to explain atomic and ionic attractions.
cards.a: The force between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F ∝ q₁q₂/r² (the CED form); the potential energy of the pair goes as q₁q₂/r. For an electron and a nucleus, more nuclear charge or a shorter distance means a stronger attraction and more energy needed to remove the electron.
cards.n: Every 'why' about radius, ionization energy and lattice energy is scored on two words, CHARGE and DISTANCE; a trend described without them earns nothing.

cards.q: Define effective nuclear charge and shielding.
cards.a: Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) is the net positive charge an electron actually experiences: the full nuclear charge reduced by the repulsion of the other electrons. Shielding is that reduction, done mainly by core electrons that lie between the nucleus and the outer electrons. Simple model: Z_eff ≈ Z − (number of core electrons), e.g. about +1 for the 3s electron of Na (11 − 10).
cards.h: → net pull, what reduces it, a number
cards.n: Same-shell electrons shield each other only weakly, so Z_eff on valence electrons rises across a period; 'more shielding' without naming the core shells earns nothing.

cards.q: State the maximum number of electrons in the s, p, d, and f subshells.
cards.a: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14. Each orbital holds 2 electrons and the subshells have 1, 3, 5 and 7 orbitals; shell n holds 2n² electrons in all (2, 8, 18, 32).
cards.n: These capacities are the peak heights in a PES spectrum and the lengths of the periodic table's blocks; a 2s peak taller than height 2 is impossible.

cards.q: State the three rules that govern the order of filling atomic orbitals.
cards.a: Aufbau principle: electrons occupy the lowest-energy subshells first (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p ...). Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins. Hund's rule: within a subshell, electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before any orbital gets a second electron.
cards.h: → three named rules with one clause each
cards.n: Hund's rule is what gives P three unpaired 3p electrons; writing 3p as ↑↓ ↑ _ earns nothing. Aufbau exceptions (Cr, Cu) are not assessed.

cards.q: State the rule for writing the electron configuration of a transition metal cation.
cards.a: Write the neutral atom's configuration, then remove electrons from the shell with the highest n first: the 4s electrons leave before any 3d electrons. Fe is [Ar]4s²3d⁶, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. The 4s electrons are outermost and least tightly held once the 3d subshell is occupied.
cards.h: → which subshell empties first, one example
cards.n: Fe²⁺ written as [Ar]4s²3d⁴ earns nothing; electrons are removed from the highest n, not from the last subshell filled.

cards.q: Identify the number of unpaired electrons in a ground-state phosphorus atom.
cards.a: Three. P is [Ne]3s²3p³; by Hund's rule the three 3p electrons occupy the three 3p orbitals singly with parallel spins, so all three are unpaired.
cards.n: Answering 1 (pairing two of the 3p electrons) violates Hund's rule; a half-filled p subshell is the maximum, 3 unpaired.

cards.q: Predict whether ground-state $Fe^{2+}$ or $Fe^{3+}$ has more unpaired electrons, and explain.
cards.a: Fe³⁺ has more: 5 unpaired versus 4. Fe is [Ar]4s²3d⁶; the 4s electrons leave first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ (five orbitals: one pair plus four singles → 4 unpaired) and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵ (one electron in each of the five 3d orbitals → 5 unpaired).
cards.n: 'More electrons, more unpaired' earns nothing; the sixth d electron must pair, so removing it INCREASES the unpaired count.

cards.q: Identify the complete ground-state electron configuration of a neutral iron atom (Z = 26).
cards.a: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s²3d⁶ (or [Ar]4s²3d⁶). Subshells fill in order of increasing energy, 4s before 3d, until all 26 electrons are placed; the superscripts sum to 26.
cards.n: The superscripts must total Z; a configuration ending 3d⁸ (skipping 4s) sums to 26 but is not the ground state.

cards.q: Identify the number of unpaired electrons in a ground-state $Cu^{2+}$ ion.
cards.a: One. Cu has 29 electrons, so Cu²⁺ has 27: the argon core (18) plus 9 electrons in 3d, [Ar]3d⁹, because the 4s electrons (highest n) leave first. Nine electrons in five 3d orbitals means four pairs and one single, so 1 unpaired electron.
cards.n: Neutral copper is an aufbau exception and is not assessed; whichever way you write neutral Cu, the ion is [Ar]3d⁹ and the answer is 1.

cards.q: Compute the number of neutrons in the more abundant chlorine isotope, mass number 35 (Z = 17).
cards.a: 18 neutrons. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 35 − 17 = 18. The isotope has 17 protons and, as a neutral atom, 17 electrons.
cards.n: Subtracting Z from the periodic-table mass 35.45 gives 18.45, a meaningless non-integer; neutron counts come from a specific isotope's mass number.

cards.q: Represent the ground-state electron configuration in noble-gas shorthand for each: Na · Cl · Ca · Ti · Zn · Br · K⁺ · S²⁻ · Fe³⁺ · Zn²⁺ · Ni²⁺ · Al³⁺ · Se · Sr²⁺
cards.a:
Na → [Ne]3s¹
Cl → [Ne]3s²3p⁵
Ca → [Ar]4s²
Ti → [Ar]4s²3d²
Zn → [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰
Br → [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰4p⁵
K⁺ → [Ar] (18 electrons)
S²⁻ → [Ne]3s²3p⁶, i.e. [Ar]
Fe³⁺ → [Ar]3d⁵ (4s electrons removed first)
Zn²⁺ → [Ar]3d¹⁰
Ni²⁺ → [Ar]3d⁸ (from [Ar]4s²3d⁸)
Al³⁺ → [Ne] (10 electrons)
Se → [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰4p⁴
Sr²⁺ → [Kr] (36 electrons)
cards.h: → count electrons, fill in order, cations lose highest n
cards.n: For cations, superscripts must sum to Z minus the charge and the 4s electrons go first: Ni²⁺ as [Ar]4s²3d⁶ earns nothing. Aufbau exceptions are not assessed.

cards.q: Determine the number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in each species: ³⁷Cl⁻ · ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ · ²³Na⁺ · ¹⁸O²⁻ · ⁴⁰Ca²⁺ · ²⁷Al³⁺ · ¹⁴C · ²³⁸U
cards.a:
³⁷Cl⁻ → 17 p, 20 n, 18 e⁻
⁵⁶Fe³⁺ → 26 p, 30 n, 23 e⁻
²³Na⁺ → 11 p, 12 n, 10 e⁻
¹⁸O²⁻ → 8 p, 10 n, 10 e⁻
⁴⁰Ca²⁺ → 20 p, 20 n, 18 e⁻
²⁷Al³⁺ → 13 p, 14 n, 10 e⁻
¹⁴C → 6 p, 8 n, 6 e⁻
²³⁸U → 92 p, 146 n, 92 e⁻
cards.h: → p = Z, n = A − Z, e = Z − charge
cards.n: A positive ion has FEWER electrons than protons; giving Fe³⁺ 29 electrons (adding instead of removing) is the standard slip.

cards.q: Identify the element whose ground-state configuration is [Ar]4s²3d¹⁰4p³, and state how many of its electrons are valence electrons and how many are core electrons.
cards.a: Arsenic (Z = 33): 18 + 2 + 10 + 3 = 33 electrons. Valence electrons are those in the outermost shell, n = 4: 4s²4p³ = 5, which matches group 15. The other 28 (the argon core plus the filled 3d¹⁰) are core electrons.
cards.h: → sum the superscripts, count the highest-n shell
cards.n: Counting the 3d¹⁰ as valence gives 15 and earns nothing; for a main-group element only the highest n shell is valence.

cards.q: Compare the Coulombic attraction between a +2 charge and a −1 charge with that between a +1 charge and a −1 charge at the same separation, and state how the +1/−1 attraction changes when the separation doubles.
cards.a: The +2/−1 pair attracts twice as strongly, because F ∝ q₁q₂/r² and the product of charges doubles at fixed r. Doubling r for the +1/−1 pair cuts the force to one quarter (1/2²); the potential energy, which goes as 1/r, is halved. More charge or less distance always means a stronger attraction.
cards.n: Saying the force halves when distance doubles confuses force (1/r²) with energy (1/r); either quantity is accepted if its dependence is stated correctly.

cards.q: Determine the approximate effective nuclear charge felt by a valence electron of chlorine, using the simple model in which core electrons shield fully and valence electrons do not shield each other.
cards.a: About +7. Cl has Z = 17 and configuration [Ne]3s²3p⁵; the 10 core electrons in n = 1 and n = 2 each cancel one unit of nuclear charge, so Z_eff ≈ 17 − 10 = +7 on the 3s and 3p electrons. Compare Na, +1, and Ar, +8, in the same period: Z_eff climbs across the period.
cards.h: → Z minus the core electron count
cards.n: This is the simplest model (real Z_eff on Cl 3p is about +6); the exam only needs the qualitative point that Z_eff increases across a period and is roughly constant down a group.

cards.q: Describe the structure of an atom: the location, charge, and relative mass of protons, neutrons, and electrons, and where nearly all of the mass is found.
cards.a: Protons (+1, about 1 amu) and neutrons (0, about 1 amu) are packed in a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus, which holds essentially all the mass. Electrons (−1, about 1/1800 amu) occupy the space around the nucleus, arranged in shells and subshells, and set the atom's size and chemistry. Z = number of protons fixes the element; electrons = Z in a neutral atom.
cards.h: → three particles: place, charge, mass; then the nucleus
cards.n: Saying neutrons are 'neutral and massless' earns nothing; neutrons carry about half the mass of most nuclei.

cards.q: Explain why the 4s electrons of iron are removed before the 3d electrons when the Fe²⁺ ion forms.
cards.a: The 4s electrons are in the outermost shell (n = 4): on average they are farther from the nucleus and are shielded by the 3d electrons, so by Coulomb's law they are held least tightly. Once the 3d subshell is occupied, 4s is the higher-energy, easiest-to-remove subshell, and Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶.
cards.h: → 4s is highest n → farther, more shielded → weakest attraction → removed first
cards.n: 'Because 4s was filled last' is false (it fills first) and earns nothing; the point rests on distance and shielding, not filling order.
o: Ionization removes the electron with the weakest Coulombic attraction, and that is the one at the largest average distance, the 4s.
In the ion the remaining 3d electrons feel a larger effective nuclear charge than the 4s electrons would, so losing 4s costs the least energy.

w.a: The 4s electrons are removed first because 4s is lower in energy than 3d.
w.why: in the atom with 3d occupied, 4s is the higher-energy, more loosely held subshell

w.a: The 3d electrons stay because a half-filled or filled d subshell is stable.
w.why: stability of d⁶ is not the reason; Fe²⁺ is d⁶, neither half nor fully filled

w.a: The 4s electrons are removed first because they were added last.
w.why: 4s fills before 3d; filling order is not removal order

cards.q: Explain why removing a 1s electron from a sodium atom requires far more energy than removing its 3s electron.
cards.a: The 1s electron is in the shell closest to the nucleus, with no inner electrons shielding it, so it feels nearly the full +11 charge at a short distance; by Coulomb's law that attraction is enormous. The 3s electron is three shells out and shielded by 10 core electrons to a Z_eff near +1, so it is held far more weakly.
cards.h: → 1s: closest, unshielded, full charge → huge attraction; 3s: far, shielded → weak
cards.n: 'Core electrons are harder to remove' restates the claim; the point needs distance AND shielding (charge) from Coulomb's law.
o: PES shows the difference directly: Na's 1s peak is at 104 MJ/mol and its 3s peak at 0.50 MJ/mol, a factor of about 200.
Both the distance term and the effective charge term of Coulomb's law favor the 1s electron: smaller r and larger Z_eff.

w.a: The 1s electron is harder to remove because it was the first electron added.
w.why: filling order is not a cause; attraction is

w.a: The 3s electron is easier to remove because there is more shielding.
w.why: 'more shielding' without naming the 10 core electrons and the larger distance is not scored

w.a: The 1s electron is harder to remove because it has the lowest quantum number.
w.why: quantum numbers are not assessed and n alone is not the reasoning; distance and charge are

cards.q: Explain why the outermost electron of a magnesium atom is harder to remove than the outermost electron of a sodium atom.
cards.a: Both outer electrons are 3s electrons shielded by the same 10 core electrons, but Mg has 12 protons to Na's 11. The Mg valence electron feels a larger effective nuclear charge (about +2 vs +1) at a similar distance, so by Coulomb's law it is held more strongly and costs more energy to remove (738 vs 496 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → same shell and shielding → one more proton → larger Z_eff → stronger attraction
cards.n: 'Mg has more electrons so more attraction' earns nothing; more PROTONS with the same core shielding is the argument.
o: Effective nuclear charge rises across a period because added electrons enter the same shell and shield poorly, while nuclear charge rises by one.
Mg's PES 3s peak sits at 0.74 MJ/mol versus Na's 0.50 MJ/mol, consistent with the stronger attraction.

w.a: Magnesium's electron is harder to remove because magnesium has two valence electrons that pair up.
w.why: pairing in 3s is not the cause; the larger nuclear charge is

w.a: Magnesium's electron is harder to remove because magnesium is a smaller atom.
w.why: smaller size is a consequence of the same Coulombic pull, not the reasoning

w.a: Sodium's electron is easier to remove because sodium is more reactive.
w.why: reactivity is the observation being explained, not the explanation

cards.q: Explain why the 2p electrons in Na⁺ are held more tightly than the 2p electrons in Ne, even though both species have the electron configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶.
cards.a: The two species are isoelectronic, so the shielding of the 2p electrons is the same, but Na⁺ has 11 protons and Ne only 10. The 2p electrons in Na⁺ feel a larger effective nuclear charge and are pulled closer to the nucleus, so by Coulomb's law the attraction is stronger and more energy is needed to remove them.
cards.h: → same electrons and shielding → more protons in Na⁺ → larger Z_eff → tighter hold
cards.n: Saying 'Na⁺ is positive so it holds electrons' is not Coulomb reasoning; the proton count with equal shielding is what scores.
o: In an isoelectronic series the only variable is nuclear charge, and attraction increases with it.
Na⁺ is smaller than Ne for the same reason: the extra proton draws the identical electron cloud inward.

w.a: Na⁺ holds its 2p electrons more tightly because it has fewer electrons than Na.
w.why: the comparison is with Ne, which has the same number of electrons

w.a: Ne holds its 2p electrons more tightly because it is a noble gas with a full octet.
w.why: both species have the full octet; the proton count decides

w.a: Na⁺ holds its electrons more tightly because it is more electronegative.
w.why: electronegativity concerns bonded atoms and is not the mechanism here

cards.q: Explain why the effective nuclear charge felt by valence electrons increases from left to right across a period.
cards.a: Across a period each successive element adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same outer shell. The core electron count, which does the shielding, stays constant, and electrons in the same shell shield one another only weakly, so Z_eff ≈ Z − core rises by about one unit per element (Na +1 ... Ar +8).
cards.h: → +1 proton each step → same core → same-shell electrons shield poorly → Z_eff rises
cards.n: 'More protons' alone is half the point; the earned answer also says the shielding does not increase because the core is unchanged.
o: Nuclear charge increases while the number of inner electrons between nucleus and valence shell is fixed, so the net pull grows.

w.a: Effective nuclear charge increases because atoms get smaller across a period.
w.why: the smaller radius is the consequence, not the cause

w.a: Effective nuclear charge increases because more electrons are added.
w.why: added electrons, if anything, add shielding; the extra protons are the cause

w.a: Effective nuclear charge stays the same across a period because shielding increases with each electron.
w.why: same-shell electrons shield poorly, so Z_eff does rise

cards.q: Explain why the second ionization energy of sodium (4562 kJ/mol) is about nine times its first ionization energy (496 kJ/mol).
cards.a: The first electron removed is the lone 3s valence electron, far out and shielded by 10 core electrons. The second comes from the 2p core, a shell closer to the nucleus shielded only by the two 1s electrons, so it feels a much larger effective nuclear charge at a shorter distance and is held far more tightly.
cards.h: → 1st: shielded 3s far out; 2nd: core 2p, closer, larger Z_eff → far stronger attraction
cards.n: 'The second electron is removed from a positive ion' is a minor contribution; the point requires the change of SHELL (n = 3 to n = 2) with its distance and shielding.
o: Na⁺ has the neon configuration; breaking into a filled, inner shell needs core-level energy, which PES also shows (Na 2p at 3.67 MJ/mol versus 3s at 0.50).
The jump marks the boundary between valence and core electrons and is why sodium forms only Na⁺, never Na²⁺.

w.a: The second ionization energy is larger because the ion has fewer electrons to lose.
w.why: the number remaining does not set the energy; which shell the electron leaves does

w.a: The second ionization energy is larger because it is always harder to remove a second electron.
w.why: true in general but gives no reason for the nine-fold jump

w.a: The second ionization energy is larger because sodium wants a full octet.
w.why: 'wants' is not a mechanism; the core electron's distance and Z_eff are

cards.q: Explain why core electrons shield valence electrons from the nucleus much more effectively than other valence electrons do.
cards.a: Core electrons occupy inner shells, between the nucleus and the valence electrons, so their negative charge cancels part of the nuclear charge seen from outside. Electrons in the same valence shell sit at about the same distance from the nucleus, beside rather than inside, so they cancel little of the nuclear pull.
cards.h: → core electrons lie inside → cancel nuclear charge → same-shell electrons beside, not inside → weak shielding
cards.n: Counting all electrons as equal shielders gives Z_eff ≈ 0 for every atom and earns nothing; only inner-shell electrons shield strongly.
o: Shielding is effective only from charge located closer to the nucleus than the electron in question; core shells satisfy this, valence neighbors do not.
This is why Z_eff ≈ Z − core is a usable model: core electrons count fully and valence electrons are ignored.

w.a: Core electrons shield better because there are more of them.
w.why: number is not the reason; position between nucleus and valence shell is

w.a: Core electrons shield better because they carry more negative charge each.
w.why: every electron has the same charge

w.a: Valence electrons shield each other just as well because all electrons repel equally.
w.why: repulsion is equal, but only charge located inside the electron's orbit cancels nuclear attraction

cards.q: Explain, using Coulomb's law, why the ground-state configuration of an atom places electrons in the 1s subshell before the 2s subshell.
cards.a: The ground state is the lowest-energy arrangement. A 1s electron is on average much closer to the nucleus than a 2s electron, and Coulombic potential energy falls as the distance between opposite charges shrinks, so a 1s electron is more tightly bound and lower in energy. Aufbau fills the lowest-energy subshell first.
cards.h: → ground state = lowest energy → 1s closer to nucleus → stronger attraction, lower energy → filled first
cards.n: 'Because 1 comes before 2' earns nothing; the ordering is by energy, which Coulomb's law ties to distance from the nucleus.
o: Removing a 1s electron always costs more than removing a 2s electron in the same atom (PES), which shows 1s is the more stable, lower-energy subshell.
Electrons fill closest to the nucleus first because that arrangement minimizes the atom's potential energy.

w.a: 1s fills first because it is the smallest orbital and small orbitals fill fastest.
w.why: 'fills fastest' is not an energy argument

w.a: 1s fills first because the Aufbau principle says so.
w.why: names the rule without the Coulombic reason behind it

w.a: 1s fills first because electrons repel each other into the lowest shell.
w.why: repulsion pushes electrons apart; attraction to the nucleus draws them to 1s

cards.q: Explain what a photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) spectrum measures and how its axes are arranged.
cards.a: PES measures the energy needed to remove an electron from each subshell (binding energy, in MJ/mol or eV). The x-axis is binding energy, conventionally increasing to the LEFT, so core peaks (1s) sit at the far left and valence peaks at the right; the y-axis is relative number of electrons. Each peak is one subshell; its position gives the subshell's binding energy and its height the number of electrons in it.
cards.h: → what is measured, axis direction, what a peak is
cards.n: Reading a peak's height as an energy, or its position as an electron count, earns nothing; position = energy, height = count.

cards.q: Identify what the height (relative intensity) of a PES peak tells you.
cards.a: The number of electrons in that subshell: peak height is (ideally) proportional to the electron count. Heights in the ratio 2:2:6:2 mean 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²; a 2p peak is three times the height of a full 2s peak because 6 electrons versus 2. The heights, scaled so they total the atomic number, identify the element.
cards.h: → proportional to a count, with the ratio check
cards.n: A relative height of 6 does not mean 6 MJ/mol; and a height above 2 for an s peak or above 6 for a p peak is impossible and signals a misread.

cards.q: Apply PES data to identify an element: peaks at 126, 9.07, 5.31, and 0.74 MJ/mol with relative heights 2, 2, 6, 2.
cards.a: Magnesium. Reading from highest to lowest binding energy, the heights give 1s² (126) 2s² (9.07) 2p⁶ (5.31) 3s² (0.74), a total of 12 electrons, so Z = 12, Mg. The large gap between 126 and 9.07 marks the n = 1 to n = 2 shell boundary; the smaller 9.07/5.31 gap is the 2s/2p subshell split within one shell.
cards.n: Assigning the 0.74 peak to 1s because it comes 'first' when read left to right on a reversed axis is the classic misread; the highest energy is the innermost subshell.

cards.q: Apply PES reasoning: a spectrum shows peak heights 2, 2, 6, 2, 1 in order of decreasing binding energy. Identify the element.
cards.a: Aluminum. In decreasing binding energy the subshells are 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, so the heights read 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹; the superscripts sum to 13, so Z = 13, Al. The final peak of height 1 is the single 3p valence electron.
cards.h: → subshell order, heights to superscripts, sum
cards.n: Summing to 13 but naming the element from the number of peaks (5) earns nothing; the electron total, not the peak count, gives Z.

cards.q: Predict how the 2p peak positions of chlorine and argon compare on a PES spectrum.
cards.a: Argon's 2p peak sits at higher binding energy (24.1 MJ/mol) than chlorine's (20.2 MJ/mol). The 2p electrons of both are shielded by the same inner electrons, but argon has one more proton, so its 2p electrons feel a larger effective nuclear charge and need more energy to remove.
cards.h: → which is higher, then charge with equal shielding
cards.n: Stating the direction without the proton count and equal shielding earns nothing; both charge and distance/shielding must appear.

cards.q: Identify the number of peaks expected in the photoelectron spectrum of a ground-state nitrogen atom (Z = 7).
cards.a: Three peaks. N is 1s²2s²2p³, three occupied subshells, each giving one peak: 1s (height 2, at about 39.6 MJ/mol), 2s (height 2, 2.45 MJ/mol) and 2p (height 3, 1.40 MJ/mol). The three 2p orbitals are degenerate and share one peak.
cards.n: Counting shells (2) or orbitals (5) instead of subshells earns nothing; one peak per occupied subshell.

cards.q: Identify the number of PES peaks expected for a ground-state oxygen atom (Z = 8), and give the relative height of each.
cards.a: Three peaks with relative heights 2:2:4, for 1s² (highest binding energy, about 52.6 MJ/mol), 2s² (3.12 MJ/mol) and 2p⁴ (1.31 MJ/mol, lowest). The heights total 8, the atomic number.
cards.h: → one peak per subshell, height = electron count
cards.n: Giving the 2p peak height 6 (a full subshell) for oxygen earns nothing; heights must sum to Z = 8.

cards.q: Predict how the 1s peak binding energy of neon compares to that of fluorine on a PES spectrum.
cards.a: Neon's 1s peak sits at higher binding energy (84.0 MJ/mol versus 67.2 for fluorine). The 1s electrons of both are unshielded and at similar distance, but neon has 10 protons to fluorine's 9, so its 1s electrons feel a larger nuclear charge and are held more tightly.
cards.h: → which is higher, then proton count
cards.n: 'Neon is a noble gas so it holds electrons better' earns nothing; the extra proton acting on an unshielded shell is the reasoning.

cards.q: Sketch the photoelectron spectrum of sodium, whose subshell binding energies are 104, 6.84, 3.67, and 0.50 MJ/mol, describing the axes, each peak's position, and its relative height.
cards.a: x-axis: binding energy in MJ/mol, increasing to the left (usually a broken or log scale); y-axis: relative number of electrons. Four vertical peaks: 1s at 104 MJ/mol, height 2; 2s at 6.84, height 2; 2p at 3.67, height 6 (the tallest, three times the 2s); 3s at 0.50, height 1 (the shortest, at the far right). Label each peak with its subshell.
cards.n: A 3s peak drawn as tall as the 2s earns nothing (Na has one 3s electron); and the 2p must be the tallest peak, not the highest-energy one.

cards.q: Determine the electron configuration and the identity of the element whose PES spectrum has peaks at 19.3 MJ/mol (relative height 2), 1.36 MJ/mol (height 2), and 0.80 MJ/mol (height 1).
cards.a: 1s²2s²2p¹, boron (Z = 5). The 19.3 peak is the 1s core (height 2); the two close-lying peaks at 1.36 and 0.80 are the n = 2 subshells, 2s (height 2) and 2p (height 1). The heights sum to 5 electrons.
cards.h: → assign subshells by energy, heights to superscripts
cards.n: Assigning 0.80 to 3s because it is the third peak earns nothing; the second shell has two subshells, and B has only 5 electrons.

cards.q: Estimate the first ionization energy of sodium from its PES spectrum, whose lowest-energy peak is at 0.50 MJ/mol, and compare it with the tabulated value of 496 kJ/mol.
cards.a: About 0.50 MJ/mol = 500 kJ/mol. The first ionization energy removes the most loosely bound electron, the 3s, and that is exactly the binding energy of the lowest-energy PES peak. 500 kJ/mol agrees with the tabulated 496 kJ/mol within the precision of the spectrum.
cards.h: → lowest-energy peak = IE₁, convert MJ to kJ
cards.n: Using the 1s peak (104 MJ/mol) as IE₁ earns nothing; ionization energy is for the OUTERMOST electron, the rightmost peak.

cards.q: Compare the PES spectra of magnesium and aluminum: the number of peaks, and the direction in which each peak they share is shifted.
cards.a: Al has five peaks (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p) to Mg's four (1s 2s 2p 3s): the extra peak is Al's single 3p electron at 0.58 MJ/mol, height 1. Every shared peak is at higher binding energy in Al (1s 151 vs 126, 2s 12.1 vs 9.07, 2p 7.79 vs 5.31, 3s 1.09 vs 0.74 MJ/mol) because Al has one more proton acting on the same shells. Peak heights of the shared subshells are identical (2, 2, 6, 2).
cards.h: → peak count, then shift direction with reason
cards.n: Predicting that Al's 3s peak is LOWER than Mg's because Al's first ionization energy is lower confuses IE₁ (the 3p electron) with the 3s peak.

cards.q: Evaluate a student's sketch of the PES spectrum of carbon: peaks at 28.6 MJ/mol (height 2), 1.72 MJ/mol (height 4), and 1.09 MJ/mol (height 2). Is the sketch consistent with carbon's electron configuration?
cards.a: No. Carbon is 1s²2s²2p², so the 2s peak (1.72 MJ/mol) must have height 2, not 4: an s subshell holds at most two electrons. The 2p peak (1.09 MJ/mol) should also be height 2. Peak positions are right (1s highest, 2s above 2p within n = 2) and the total of 6 electrons is right, but the heights are distributed wrongly.
cards.h: → check positions, then heights vs subshell capacity
cards.n: Accepting the sketch because the heights sum to 6 earns nothing; each height must also respect the capacity of its subshell.

cards.q: Identify the subshell responsible for a single PES peak at 1.31 MJ/mol with relative height 1, in a spectrum that shows no other peaks, and name the element.
cards.a: The 1s subshell of hydrogen. One peak means one occupied subshell; a height of 1 means one electron, so the atom is 1s¹, H (Z = 1). The binding energy 1.31 MJ/mol is hydrogen's ionization energy, 1312 kJ/mol.
cards.n: Helium also has a single peak, but with height 2 and at 2.37 MJ/mol; the height, not just the peak count, identifies the element.

cards.q: Explain why the 2s peak appears at higher binding energy than the 2p peak in the same atom.
cards.a: A 2s electron spends part of its time close to the nucleus, inside the 1s core, so it is shielded less and feels a larger effective nuclear charge than a 2p electron of the same shell. By Coulomb's law the stronger attraction makes the 2s electron harder to remove, so its peak is at higher energy.
cards.h: → 2s penetrates closer → less shielded, larger Z_eff → stronger attraction → higher energy
cards.n: '2s is lower in energy because s comes before p' earns nothing; penetration and shielding are the reason.
o: Within one shell the subshells differ by how much the inner electrons shield them, and s electrons are the least shielded.
The same ordering appears in every shell: 3s above 3p above 3d in binding energy.

w.a: The 2s peak is higher because 2s electrons are closer to the nucleus than 2p electrons.
w.why: the average distances are similar; the difference is penetration inside the core, which changes shielding

w.a: The 2s peak is higher because the 2s subshell holds fewer electrons.
w.why: capacity sets peak height, not position

w.a: The 2s peak is higher because 2s electrons are paired.
w.why: pairing is irrelevant; 2p electrons in Ne are also paired and still lower

cards.q: Explain why the 1s peak in a PES spectrum sits at higher binding energy for magnesium than for sodium.
cards.a: The 1s electrons are the innermost electrons in both atoms, with no inner electrons to shield them, so they feel almost the full nuclear charge. Magnesium has 12 protons to sodium's 11, so its 1s electrons experience a stronger Coulombic attraction and require more energy to remove (126 versus 104 MJ/mol).
cards.h: → 1s unshielded in both → Mg has one more proton → stronger attraction → higher energy
cards.n: 'Mg has more electrons' earns nothing; the extra PROTON, with unchanged shielding, is the point.
o: Every subshell of Mg is more tightly bound than the same subshell of Na, because nuclear charge increased by one while shielding of that subshell did not.
Core binding energies climb steadily across a period for the same reason: each step adds a proton.

w.a: Magnesium's 1s peak is higher because magnesium has two valence electrons.
w.why: valence electron count does not affect the 1s binding energy

w.a: Magnesium's 1s peak is higher because magnesium is a smaller atom.
w.why: size is a consequence of the same nuclear charge, not the reasoning

w.a: Sodium's 1s peak is higher because sodium is more reactive.
w.why: reactivity concerns the valence electron and the direction is wrong

cards.q: Explain why lithium's 2s electron (binding energy 0.52 MJ/mol) is easier to remove than hydrogen's 1s electron (1.31 MJ/mol), even though lithium has three protons and hydrogen only one.
cards.a: Lithium's 2s electron is in the second shell, farther from the nucleus, and is shielded by the two 1s electrons, so it feels an effective nuclear charge of only about +1. Hydrogen's electron is in the first shell, close to its +1 nucleus, unshielded. Similar net charge at a larger distance means weaker attraction.
cards.h: → Li 2s: farther, shielded by 1s² → Z_eff ≈ +1 at larger r → weaker attraction
cards.n: 'Lithium has more protons so it should be harder' is the trap; shielding by the core cancels the extra protons and distance decides.
o: Both atoms present a net +1 charge to their outer electron, so the distance term of Coulomb's law decides, and Li's n = 2 electron is farther out.
Lithium's own 1s peak at 6.26 MJ/mol shows how tightly the unshielded inner electrons are held; the 2s electron is outside that core.

w.a: Lithium's electron is easier to remove because lithium is a metal.
w.why: classification is not a reason; distance and shielding are

w.a: Lithium's electron is easier to remove because it has more shielding.
w.why: 'more shielding' without naming the 1s core electrons and the larger distance is not scored

w.a: Hydrogen's electron is harder to remove because hydrogen has no core electrons to help it leave.
w.why: core electrons do not 'help' removal; they shield, and H's electron is simply closer to an unshielded nucleus

cards.q: Explain why the 2p peak in the PES spectrum of neon is three times as tall as its 2s peak.
cards.a: Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in the subshell. Neon is 1s²2s²2p⁶: the 2p subshell holds six electrons (three orbitals, two each) and the 2s holds two, so the 2p peak is 6/2 = 3 times taller. All six 2p electrons have the same binding energy and appear in one peak.
cards.n: '2p is higher in energy so its peak is taller' mixes up position and height and earns nothing.
o: The three degenerate 2p orbitals contribute to one peak, so a full p subshell always gives a peak three times the height of a full s subshell.
Heights read as a ratio 2:2:6 for Ne, and the total of 10 confirms the atomic number.

w.a: The 2p peak is taller because 2p electrons are easier to remove, so more of them are ejected.
w.why: ease of removal sets the position, not the height

w.a: The 2p peak is taller because p orbitals are larger than s orbitals.
w.why: orbital size does not set peak height; electron count does

w.a: The peaks should be the same height because both subshells are full.
w.why: full subshells of different capacity hold different numbers of electrons

cards.q: Explain how a photoelectron spectrum supports the shell model of the atom, using sodium's peaks at 104, 6.84, 3.67, and 0.50 MJ/mol.
cards.a: The peaks fall into three widely separated groups: 104 alone, 6.84 and 3.67 close together, then 0.50. Electrons at similar distance from the nucleus (one shell) have similar binding energies, so the groups are shells n = 1, 2, 3, each farther out and more shielded than the last; the small 2s/2p gap is subshells.
cards.h: → energies cluster in groups → each group = one shell at one distance → large gaps between shells
cards.n: Listing the peaks without noting the GAPS between groups earns nothing; the grouping is the evidence for shells.
o: If electrons were all at one distance the energies would form one cluster; the enormous jump from 104 to 6.84 MJ/mol shows a distinct inner shell.
The heights 2, 8 (2 + 6), 1 reproduce the shell populations 2-8-1 of the Bohr-style model for sodium.

w.a: PES supports the shell model because it shows four peaks, one for each shell.
w.why: the peaks are subshells; Na has three shells and four peaks

w.a: PES supports the shell model because the peaks get taller as energy decreases.
w.why: heights are electron counts and do not follow a trend; the energy grouping is the evidence

w.a: PES supports the shell model because all electrons have different energies.
w.why: electrons in one subshell share an energy, which is why they form one peak

cards.q: Explain why every peak in the PES spectrum of an element shifts to higher binding energy when you move one element to the right in the same period.
cards.a: Moving one element right adds a proton and an electron in the same outer shell. The extra proton raises the nuclear charge felt by every electron, while each subshell's shielding barely changes: the core is the same and the new electron is outermost. So every electron is held more tightly and every peak rises.
cards.h: → +1 proton → same core shielding → larger Z_eff on every subshell → every peak higher
cards.n: Claiming only the valence peak shifts earns nothing; the added proton acts on the core electrons too (Na 1s 104 → Mg 1s 126 MJ/mol).
o: Compare Na and Mg peak by peak: 104 → 126, 6.84 → 9.07, 3.67 → 5.31, 0.50 → 0.74 MJ/mol, all up, all by the same cause.
The one exception in position is a NEW subshell (Al's 3p) which appears below the 3s, but the shared peaks still all rise.

w.a: The peaks shift because the atom to the right has more electrons and more shielding.
w.why: the added electron is in the outer shell and shields the others poorly; the proton dominates

w.a: The peaks shift because the atom to the right is smaller.
w.why: size is a consequence of the same Coulombic pull, not the reasoning

w.a: Only the outermost peak shifts, because only valence electrons change across a period.
w.why: false; core peaks shift too, since the nuclear charge acts on all electrons

cards.q: Explain why the photoelectron spectrum of the Na⁺ ion has one fewer peak than the spectrum of the Na atom.
cards.a: Na is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹ and forming Na⁺ removes the single 3s electron. With the 3s subshell empty there is no electron to eject from it, so the 0.50 MJ/mol peak disappears and only the 1s, 2s and 2p peaks remain (heights 2, 2, 6), at slightly higher energy in the ion because the remaining electrons repel each other less.
cards.h: → Na⁺ lost the 3s electron → empty subshell gives no peak → three peaks remain
cards.n: 'Na⁺ has fewer electrons so all peaks get shorter' earns nothing; the 1s, 2s and 2p populations are unchanged, one whole peak is gone.
o: Na⁺ is isoelectronic with Ne, so its spectrum has the same three peaks as neon, shifted to higher energy by the extra proton.
A peak exists only for an occupied subshell; ionization empties the 3s, so the peak count drops from four to three.

w.a: Na⁺ has one fewer peak because losing an electron removes one orbital from the atom.
w.why: orbitals still exist when empty; the peak vanishes because no electron occupies the subshell

w.a: Na⁺ has one fewer peak because the 1s and 2s peaks merge in the ion.
w.why: 1s and 2s are in different shells and remain far apart

w.a: Na⁺ has the same number of peaks, only shorter, because it has fewer electrons overall.
w.why: only the 3s electron was lost; the other subshells keep their full counts

cards.q: Explain the periodic trend in atomic radius and its cause.
cards.a: Radius decreases left to right across a period and increases down a group. Across: each element adds a proton and an electron in the same shell; the core shielding is unchanged, so Z_eff rises and pulls the valence shell closer (Coulomb's law, larger charge). Down: the valence electrons occupy a shell of higher n, farther from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so the atom is larger.
cards.h: → two directions, each with charge and distance
cards.n: Naming only one of charge (Z_eff) and distance (shell number) usually costs the justification point; 'more shielding' must come with the count of inner shells.

cards.q: Contrast the size of a cation and an anion with the neutral parent atom.
cards.a: A cation is smaller than its parent atom: it has lost electrons, often its whole outer shell (Na → Na⁺ loses the n = 3 shell), and the remaining electrons feel less repulsion and a larger Z_eff per electron, so they are pulled in. An anion is larger: added electrons increase electron-electron repulsion in the valence shell while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so the cloud expands (Cl → Cl⁻).
cards.h: → two comparisons, each with the reason
cards.n: 'Cations are smaller because they are positive' earns nothing; the lost shell and the reduced repulsion at constant nuclear charge are the reasoning.

cards.q: Rank the isoelectronic ions N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, and Mg²⁺ by radius, largest first.
cards.a: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺.
