All five have 10 electrons in the same 1s²2s²2p⁶ configuration, so the shielding is identical; the ion with the most protons (Mg, 12) pulls that electron cloud in most tightly and is the smallest, and nitrogen (7 protons) holds it most loosely and is the largest.
cards.h: → same electrons, rank by proton count
cards.n: Ranking by periodic-table position or by charge sign earns nothing; an isoelectronic series is ordered by nuclear charge only.

cards.q: Explain the periodic trend in first ionization energy and its cause.
cards.a: First ionization energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. Across: Z_eff rises (one more proton, same core shielding) and the radius shrinks, so the valence electron is held more tightly. Down: the valence electron is in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so the Coulombic attraction is weaker and less energy is needed to remove it.
cards.h: → two directions, charge and distance each time
cards.n: The two dips (group 2 → 13, group 15 → 16) mean the across-period rise is not smooth; describing the trend without Z_eff and distance earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the two places where first ionization energy dips against the general trend.
cards.a: Group 2 → 13 (Be 899 > B 801 kJ/mol): boron's electron is removed from the higher-energy, more shielded 2p subshell rather than the 2s. Group 15 → 16 (N 1402 > O 1314 kJ/mol): oxygen's fourth 2p electron shares an orbital, and the extra electron-electron repulsion makes it easier to remove than one of nitrogen's three unpaired 2p electrons.
cards.h: → two group pairs, a subshell reason and a pairing reason
cards.n: These dips must be argued from subshell energy and pairing, not Z_eff, which would predict the opposite; 'it is an exception' earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain what a large jump between successive ionization energies reveals.
cards.a: A large jump means the next electron must be removed from a lower, core shell that is closer to the nucleus and far less shielded, so the attraction is much stronger. The number of electrons removed before the jump equals the number of valence electrons and identifies the element's group: Mg (738, 1451, then 7733 kJ/mol) has 2 valence electrons and is in group 2.
cards.h: → what the jump marks, what you count
cards.n: A modest rise from one IE to the next is normal (each electron leaves a more positive ion); only a jump of several times marks the core boundary.

cards.q: Define electronegativity and state its periodic trend.
cards.a: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electrons toward itself. It increases across a period (larger Z_eff, smaller radius pull bonding electrons more strongly) and decreases down a group (bonding electrons are farther from a more shielded nucleus); fluorine (3.98) is the most electronegative element and cesium among the least.
cards.n: Electronegativity applies to atoms IN a bond; ionization energy and electron affinity apply to isolated gaseous atoms. Mixing them up earns nothing.

cards.q: Define electron affinity and state how it varies across a period.
cards.a: Electron affinity is the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). Across a period it generally becomes more negative (more energy released), because the added electron enters the same shell while Z_eff rises, so it is attracted more strongly; halogens have the most negative values (Cl −349 kJ/mol), and noble gases and group 2 have positive or near-zero values because the electron would enter a new, shielded subshell.
cards.h: → definition with sign, then the trend and its reason
cards.n: A MORE negative electron affinity means the added electron is held more tightly; calling −349 'smaller' than −141 reverses the meaning.

cards.q: Rank $K^{+}$, $Ca^{2+}$, and $Sc^{3+}$ by ionic radius, and justify using effective nuclear charge.
cards.a: K⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Sc³⁺. All three are isoelectronic with argon (18 electrons, 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶), so shielding is the same; the nuclear charge rises from 19 to 20 to 21 protons, so the identical electron cloud is pulled in more tightly and the ion shrinks from K⁺ to Sc³⁺.
cards.n: Argon itself, with only 18 protons, would be the largest of the series; ranking by ionic charge without the proton count earns nothing.

cards.q: Predict which has the larger radius, a Ca atom or a $Ca^{2+}$ ion, and explain in terms of electron shells.
cards.a: The Ca atom is larger. Ca is [Ar]4s²; forming Ca²⁺ removes both 4s electrons, so the entire n = 4 shell is gone and the outermost electrons are now the n = 3 shell of the argon core, which is much closer to the nucleus. The 20 protons also hold the remaining 18 electrons more tightly than they held 20.
cards.h: → whole outer shell lost, then charge per electron
cards.n: The shell loss is the main effect; 'the ion is positive so it is smaller' without the shell argument earns nothing.

cards.q: Determine the group of an element whose successive ionization energies are IE₁ = 578, IE₂ = 1817, IE₃ = 2745, and IE₄ = 11,577 kJ/mol.
cards.a: Group 13. The first three ionization energies rise gradually (each electron leaves a more positive ion), then IE₄ jumps by a factor of about 4: the fourth electron comes from a core shell that is closer to the nucleus and much less shielded. Three electrons removed before the jump means three valence electrons, group 13 (the values are aluminum's).
cards.h: → find the jump, count electrons before it
cards.n: Counting the jump itself as a valence electron (answering group 14) is the standard slip; the group equals the number of easy removals.

cards.q: Rank each set by atomic radius, largest first: (i) Na, Mg, Al · (ii) Li, Na, K · (iii) F, Cl, Br · (iv) C, N, O · (v) Cs, Ca, Cl · (vi) S, Se, Te · (vii) Si, P, S · (viii) Be, Mg, Sr
cards.a:
(i) Na > Mg > Al (same period, Z_eff rises left to right)
(ii) K > Na > Li (more shells down the group)
(iii) Br > Cl > F (more shells)
(iv) C > N > O (Z_eff rises across)
(v) Cs > Ca > Cl (Cs has 6 shells, Ca 4, Cl 3 with high Z_eff)
(vi) Te > Se > S (more shells)
(vii) Si > P > S (Z_eff rises across)
(viii) Sr > Mg > Be (more shells)
cards.h: → more shells beats higher Z_eff; same shell → count protons
cards.n: For elements in different periods AND groups (set v), the shell count decides first; ranking Cl above Ca because 'it is farther right' earns nothing.

cards.q: Rank each set as indicated. By first ionization energy, largest first: (i) Li, Na, K · (ii) B, C, N · (iii) Cl, Br, I · (iv) Na, Si, Cl · (v) Be, B · (vi) N, O. By electronegativity, largest first: (vii) C, N, O · (viii) F, Cl, Br · (ix) Na, Al, Cl · (x) K, Ca, Br
cards.a:
(i) Li > Na > K (valence electron farther out down the group)
(ii) N > C > B (Z_eff rises across)
(iii) Cl > Br > I (more shells down the group)
(iv) Cl > Si > Na (Z_eff rises across period 3)
(v) Be > B (B's electron leaves the higher-energy 2p subshell)
(vi) N > O (O's paired 2p electron is easier to remove)
(vii) O > N > C (Z_eff rises across)
(viii) F > Cl > Br (bonding electrons closer to a less shielded nucleus)
(ix) Cl > Al > Na (Z_eff rises across)
(x) Br > Ca > K (Br: highest Z_eff, smallest radius)
cards.h: → across: Z_eff; down: shells; watch the two IE dips
cards.n: Sets (v) and (vi) are the exam's favorite dips; ranking B > Be or O > N from Z_eff alone earns nothing.

cards.q: Estimate the first ionization energy of rubidium, given that the first ionization energies of sodium and potassium are 496 and 419 kJ/mol.
cards.a: Below 419 kJ/mol, roughly 400 kJ/mol (the tabulated value is 403 kJ/mol). Rb is the next alkali metal down the group: its 5s electron is one shell farther from the nucleus and shielded by one more filled shell than K's 4s electron, so the Coulombic attraction is weaker and the value continues to fall, though by a smaller step (496 → 419 fell by 77).
cards.h: → continue the group trend, smaller step
cards.n: An estimate above 419 kJ/mol contradicts the group trend and earns nothing; the point is placing Rb below K with the shell reason.

cards.q: Estimate the covalent radius of germanium, given the covalent radii of silicon (111 pm) and tin (139 pm), and justify the estimate.
cards.a: Between the two, roughly 120 to 125 pm (the tabulated value is about 120 pm). Ge sits between Si and Sn in group 14: its valence electrons are in the n = 4 shell, one farther out than Si's n = 3 and one closer than Sn's n = 5, so its radius lies between theirs. Periodicity lets a missing value be interpolated from its neighbors.
cards.h: → interpolate down the group, give the shell reason
cards.n: An estimate outside the 111–139 pm window earns nothing; also do not claim exact linearity, the steps down a group are unequal.

cards.q: Rank Cl⁻, K⁺, and S²⁻ by radius, largest first, and justify.
cards.a: S²⁻ > Cl⁻ > K⁺. All three have 18 electrons (the argon configuration), so the shielding is identical and only the nuclear charge differs: S has 16 protons, Cl 17, K 19. The fewer the protons acting on the same electron cloud, the weaker the attraction and the larger the ion, so S²⁻ is largest and K⁺ smallest.
cards.n: Ranking K⁺ largest because potassium is the largest ATOM earns nothing; the ions share one electron configuration and differ only in Z.

cards.q: Explain why atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period.
cards.a: Each element to the right adds a proton and an electron in the same valence shell. Core shielding is unchanged and same-shell electrons shield poorly, so the effective nuclear charge on them rises. By Coulomb's law the stronger attraction pulls the valence shell closer to the nucleus, so the atom shrinks.
cards.h: → +1 proton, same shell → larger Z_eff → stronger attraction → valence shell pulled in
cards.n: 'Atoms get smaller because they get heavier' or 'because more electrons fit' earns nothing; the Z_eff argument is required.
o: Nuclear charge increases while the number of shielding core electrons stays fixed, so the net pull on the outer electrons grows and r decreases.
Compare Na and Cl: both have 10 core electrons, but Cl's 17 protons give Z_eff ≈ +7 versus Na's +1, so Cl's outer electrons sit much closer.

w.a: Atomic radius decreases across a period because the atoms have more electrons and more shielding.
w.why: the added electrons are in the same shell and shield poorly; more shielding would ENLARGE the atom

w.a: Atomic radius decreases across a period because the number of shells decreases.
w.why: the shell count is constant across a period

w.a: Atomic radius decreases across a period because nonmetals are smaller than metals.
w.why: restates the observation without the Coulombic cause

cards.q: Explain why atomic radius increases down a group.
cards.a: Each step down a group adds a whole shell: the valence electrons occupy an orbital of higher n, farther from the nucleus, and the extra filled inner shell shields them from the added protons. The effective nuclear charge on the valence electrons stays about the same while their distance grows, so the atom is larger.
cards.h: → new shell → valence electrons farther out → extra core shell shields the extra protons → larger
cards.n: 'More electrons make it bigger' earns nothing; the earned point names the additional SHELL and its shielding.
o: Down the group Z_eff on the outer electron is roughly constant (about +1 for every alkali metal), so the distance term of Coulomb's law decides, and n increases.
Li's valence electron is in n = 2, Na's in n = 3, K's in n = 4; each shell is farther out than the last.

w.a: Atomic radius increases down a group because the atoms have more protons pulling electrons in.
w.why: more protons would make the atom smaller; the added shell and its shielding dominate

w.a: Atomic radius increases down a group because there is more shielding.
w.why: 'more shielding' without naming the extra inner shell and larger n is not scored

w.a: Atomic radius increases down a group because heavier atoms take up more space.
w.why: mass is not a cause of size

cards.q: Explain why first ionization energy increases from left to right across a period.
cards.a: Across a period the nuclear charge rises by one proton each step while the core shielding is unchanged, so the effective nuclear charge on the valence electrons rises and the atom shrinks. The valence electron is held more strongly (larger charge, shorter distance in Coulomb's law), so it costs more energy to remove.
cards.h: → larger Z_eff and smaller radius → stronger Coulombic attraction → more energy to remove
cards.n: 'Because nonmetals hold electrons tightly' restates the claim and earns nothing; charge and distance must appear.
o: Same shell, more protons, same shielding: the electron being removed feels a larger net charge at a shorter distance.
PES makes the same point: Na's outer peak is at 0.50 MJ/mol, Mg's at 0.74, Cl's 3p at 1.25.

w.a: Ionization energy increases across a period because atoms want to complete their octet.
w.why: 'wants' is not a mechanism and earns nothing

w.a: Ionization energy increases across a period because more electrons repel the one being removed.
w.why: repulsion would lower IE; the increase comes from nuclear charge

w.a: Ionization energy increases across a period because the elements become more electronegative.
w.why: electronegativity is a parallel trend, not the cause

cards.q: Explain why first ionization energy decreases down a group.
cards.a: Down a group the electron removed is in a shell of higher n, farther from the nucleus, and the added inner shells shield it from the extra protons, so the effective nuclear charge it feels barely changes. A similar charge at a greater distance means a weaker Coulombic attraction, so the electron costs less to remove.
cards.h: → higher shell → farther out → extra shells shield → weaker attraction → lower IE
cards.n: 'More protons but more shielding' with no count of shells is not scored; say the outer electron is a whole shell farther out.
o: Li 520, Na 496, K 419, Rb 403 kJ/mol: each valence electron sits one shell farther from a nucleus whose extra charge is cancelled by a filled inner shell.
In Coulomb's law the charge term is roughly constant down the group while r grows, so attraction and IE fall.

w.a: Ionization energy decreases down a group because the atoms have more protons.
w.why: more protons would raise IE; the extra shell and shielding are the cause

w.a: Ionization energy decreases down a group because larger atoms are more reactive.
w.why: reactivity is the consequence of low IE, not its cause

w.a: Ionization energy decreases down a group because there are more electrons to remove.
w.why: the number of electrons does not set the energy to remove one

cards.q: Explain why boron's first ionization energy (801 kJ/mol) is lower than beryllium's (899 kJ/mol) despite boron's greater nuclear charge.
cards.a: Beryllium loses a 2s electron, but boron loses a 2p electron, which is higher in energy: a 2p electron penetrates the core less than a 2s electron, so it is better shielded and feels a smaller effective nuclear charge. That weaker attraction outweighs the one extra proton, so boron's electron is easier to remove.
cards.h: → Be loses 2s, B loses 2p → 2p less penetrating, more shielded → weaker hold despite +1 proton
cards.n: 'B is an exception' or Z_eff reasoning alone (which predicts the opposite) earns nothing; the subshell change is the point.
o: The same subshell effect shows in PES: B's 2p electron is at 0.80 MJ/mol, below its own 2s at 1.36, so the first electron out of B is a comparatively loosely held one.
Be's filled 2s subshell means the next electron must go into 2p, and removing it from that higher-energy subshell costs less.

w.a: Boron's ionization energy is lower because boron has more electrons and more shielding.
w.why: the extra electron is in the same shell; the shielding difference is between 2s and 2p, which must be named

w.a: Boron's ionization energy is lower because its 2p electron is unpaired.
w.why: being unpaired does not lower the energy; the subshell energy does (the unpaired argument is for N versus O in reverse)

w.a: Boron's ionization energy is lower because boron is larger than beryllium.
w.why: boron is smaller; the subshell change is the reason

cards.q: Explain why oxygen's first ionization energy is slightly lower than nitrogen's even though oxygen has greater nuclear charge.
cards.a: Nitrogen's three 2p electrons have their own orbitals, but oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair in one orbital. The two electrons sharing an orbital repel each other, which raises that electron's energy and offsets oxygen's extra proton, so the paired electron is easier to remove than one of nitrogen's unpaired ones.
cards.h: → N: 2p³ all unpaired; O: 2p⁴ one pair → repulsion in the shared orbital → easier removal
cards.n: 'Nitrogen's half-filled subshell is stable' without the electron-repulsion mechanism earns nothing; name the paired electrons.
o: Removing oxygen's paired electron relieves repulsion within the shared orbital, lowering the cost below what Z_eff alone predicts.
Draw the orbital diagrams: N 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ versus O 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑; the ↑↓ pair is the source of the extra repulsion.

w.a: Oxygen's ionization energy is lower because oxygen is larger than nitrogen.
w.why: oxygen is smaller; size does not explain the dip

w.a: Oxygen's ionization energy is lower because oxygen has more shielding from its extra electron.
w.why: same-shell electrons shield poorly; the specific pairing repulsion is the reason

w.a: Oxygen's ionization energy is lower because oxygen wants to gain electrons, not lose them.
w.why: 'wants' is not a mechanism

cards.q: Explain why a sodium ion is much smaller than a sodium atom.
cards.a: Na is [Ne]3s¹; forming Na⁺ removes the single 3s electron, so the whole n = 3 shell is emptied and the outermost electrons are now the n = 2 shell, much closer to the nucleus. The 11 protons now attract only 10 electrons, so each remaining electron feels a stronger net pull and the cloud contracts further.
cards.h: → outer shell lost → outermost electrons now n = 2 → plus 11 protons on 10 electrons → smaller
cards.n: 'It lost an electron so it is smaller' earns nothing without naming the lost SHELL and the increased attraction per electron.
o: The ion has the neon configuration, and Ne-like electron clouds are small; the extra proton in Na⁺ makes it even smaller than Ne.
Losing the valence shell removes the electron that was farthest from the nucleus, so the ion's radius is set by the core.

w.a: A sodium ion is smaller because it has a positive charge, and positive things are small.
w.why: charge sign is not a mechanism; the shell loss and Coulombic pull are

w.a: A sodium ion is smaller because it has fewer protons.
w.why: the proton count is unchanged at 11

w.a: A sodium ion is smaller because its electrons pair up when one is removed.
w.why: the 3s electron was alone; nothing pairs up

cards.q: Explain why a chloride ion is larger than a chlorine atom.
cards.a: Cl⁻ has one more electron than Cl in the same n = 3 valence shell but the same 17 protons. The added electron increases electron-electron repulsion in the shell, and the nuclear charge is now spread over 18 electrons instead of 17, so each valence electron feels a weaker net attraction and the electron cloud expands.
cards.h: → same protons, one more valence electron → more repulsion, less pull per electron → larger
cards.n: 'It gained an electron so it has more stuff' earns nothing; repulsion at constant nuclear charge is the reasoning.
o: Coulomb's law: the attractive charge is unchanged while the repulsion among electrons grows, so the balance point of the valence shell moves outward.
Cl⁻ is isoelectronic with Ar but has one fewer proton, so it is larger than argon for the same reason.

w.a: A chloride ion is larger because it gains a whole new shell.
w.why: the electron enters the existing n = 3 shell, not a new one

w.a: A chloride ion is larger because negative ions always have more protons.
w.why: proton count never changes when an ion forms

w.a: A chloride ion is larger because the added electron shields the nucleus completely.
w.why: a same-shell electron shields only partially; the extra repulsion is the point

cards.q: Explain why Mg²⁺ is smaller than Na⁺ even though both ions have 10 electrons.
cards.a: The two ions are isoelectronic (1s²2s²2p⁶), so their electrons are shielded identically. Magnesium has 12 protons to sodium's 11, so the same electron cloud is attracted by a larger nuclear charge; by Coulomb's law the electrons are pulled closer and Mg²⁺ is the smaller ion.
cards.h: → same electrons, same shielding → Mg has 12 protons vs 11 → stronger pull → smaller
cards.n: 'Mg²⁺ has a bigger charge' without the proton count earns nothing; the ionic charge is only a consequence of Z with equal electrons.
o: In an isoelectronic series radius falls as Z rises: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.
With shielding fixed, Z_eff on the outer electrons is 2 for Mg²⁺ and 1 for Na⁺ in the simple model, so the pull is roughly doubled.

w.a: Mg²⁺ is smaller because it lost two electrons and Na⁺ lost only one.
w.why: the number lost is irrelevant once both have 10 electrons; the proton count decides

w.a: Mg²⁺ is smaller because magnesium is to the right of sodium and atoms shrink across a period.
w.why: the atomic trend is not the reasoning for isoelectronic ions; nuclear charge on equal electrons is

w.a: Na⁺ is smaller because sodium is a smaller atom than magnesium.
w.why: false direction, and atomic size does not transfer to isoelectronic ions

cards.q: Explain why electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.
cards.a: Electronegativity is how strongly a bonded atom pulls shared electrons. Across a period Z_eff rises and the radius shrinks, so bonding electrons sit closer to a larger effective charge and are pulled harder. Down a group they are a shell farther from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so the pull is weaker.
cards.h: → across: larger Z_eff, smaller r → stronger pull; down: farther, more shielded → weaker
cards.n: Describing the trend ('F is highest, Cs lowest') without the charge-and-distance cause earns nothing.
o: The same Coulombic factors that raise ionization energy raise electronegativity, since both measure attraction of the nucleus for outer electrons.
Fluorine combines the highest Z_eff of period 2 with a tiny radius, which is why it is the most electronegative element.

w.a: Electronegativity increases across a period because nonmetals need electrons to fill their octet.
w.why: 'need' is not a mechanism

w.a: Electronegativity decreases down a group because heavier atoms hold electrons more loosely.
w.why: mass is not the cause; distance and shielding are

w.a: Electronegativity increases across a period because the atoms have more electrons to share.
w.why: electron count does not set attraction for bonding electrons

cards.q: Explain why the noble gases have the highest first ionization energies in their periods.
cards.a: A noble gas ends its period, so it has the largest nuclear charge of the period acting on a valence shell whose core shielding is the same as its neighbors': Z_eff is highest and the radius smallest. Its outermost electron is held by the strongest Coulombic attraction in the period and costs the most to remove.
cards.h: → most protons in the period, same shielding → largest Z_eff, smallest radius → highest IE
cards.n: 'Because the octet is full and stable' earns nothing on its own; the point requires Z_eff and distance.
o: The filled shell is the configuration that results from the maximum Z_eff of the period; it is the Coulombic pull, not 'fullness', that makes removal hard.
Ne (2081 kJ/mol) exceeds F (1681) for the same reason F exceeds O: one more proton on the same shell.

w.a: Noble gases have the highest ionization energy because they do not react.
w.why: unreactivity is the consequence, not the reason

w.a: Noble gases have the highest ionization energy because they have the most electrons.
w.why: electron count is not the cause; nuclear charge on the same shell is

w.a: Noble gases have the highest ionization energy because a full octet is stable.
w.why: stability without the Coulombic mechanism earns nothing

cards.q: Explain why chlorine's electron affinity (−349 kJ/mol) is more negative than sulfur's (−200 kJ/mol).
cards.a: In both atoms the added electron enters the n = 3 shell, shielded by the same 10 core electrons, but chlorine has 17 protons to sulfur's 16. The added electron therefore feels a larger effective nuclear charge in a smaller atom, so it is attracted more strongly and more energy is released when it is captured.
cards.h: → same shell and shielding → Cl has one more proton → stronger attraction for the added electron → more energy released
cards.n: 'Chlorine needs only one electron for an octet' earns nothing; the earned answer uses Z_eff and distance.
o: Electron affinity tracks Z_eff across a period just as ionization energy does; Cl has the larger Z_eff.
Coulomb's law: greater nuclear charge at a shorter distance means a more negative potential energy for the new electron.

w.a: Chlorine's electron affinity is more negative because chlorine is a halogen.
w.why: the label is not a reason; the proton count with equal shielding is

w.a: Chlorine's electron affinity is more negative because chlorine has more electrons to shield the new one.
w.why: the extra electron is in the same shell and shields poorly; more shielding would REDUCE the attraction

w.a: Sulfur's electron affinity should be more negative because sulfur needs two electrons.
w.why: 'needs' is not a mechanism and the direction is wrong

cards.q: Identify the number of valence electrons for main-group elements from the periodic table.
cards.a: Groups 1, 2, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18 have 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 valence electrons respectively (the group number's last digit). Valence electrons are those in the outermost shell (highest n), the ns and np electrons; the count matches the electron configuration, e.g. Cl [Ne]3s²3p⁵ has 7.
cards.h: → group number's last digit, from the configuration
cards.n: Helium is the exception, with 2 valence electrons in group 18, and transition metals do not follow this mapping at all.

cards.q: Predict the ion charge formed by each main group: 1, 2, 13, 15, 16, 17.
cards.a: Group 1 → 1+, group 2 → 2+, group 13 → 3+, group 15 → 3−, group 16 → 2−, group 17 → 1−. Metals lose their few valence electrons (low ionization energies) and nonmetals gain enough to fill the valence shell (high electron affinities), so each ion reaches a noble-gas configuration.
cards.h: → six charges, then the electron count reason
cards.n: Group 14 and the transition metals are left out because their charges vary; that is why their compound names carry Roman numerals.

cards.q: Name and give the formulas of the nitrogen oxyanions.
cards.a: Nitrate NO₃⁻ and nitrite NO₂⁻; both carry a 1− charge. The -ate ion has one more oxygen than the -ite ion.
cards.h: → two names, two formulas, one rule
cards.n: Giving nitrite a 2− charge because it has fewer oxygens earns nothing; oxygen count changes, the charge does not.

cards.q: Name and give the formulas of the sulfur oxyanions.
cards.a: Sulfate SO₄²⁻ and sulfite SO₃²⁻; both carry a 2− charge. Adding one H⁺ to sulfate gives hydrogen sulfate (bisulfate), HSO₄⁻.
cards.h: → two names, two formulas, one charge
cards.n: Sulfite and sulfate differ by one oxygen and share the 2− charge; -ite does not mean a smaller charge.

cards.q: Recall the formulas and charges of phosphate and ammonium.
cards.a: Phosphate PO₄³⁻ (3−) and ammonium NH₄⁺ (1+). Ammonium is the common polyatomic CATION; it pairs with anions exactly as a group 1 metal ion would, e.g. (NH₄)₂SO₄.
cards.n: Writing ammonium as NH₃⁺ or phosphate as PO₄²⁻ earns nothing; the 3− on phosphate is what forces formulas like Ca₃(PO₄)₂.

cards.q: Recall the formulas and charges of carbonate and bicarbonate.
cards.a: Carbonate CO₃²⁻ (2−) and bicarbonate, also called hydrogen carbonate, HCO₃⁻ (1−). Adding one H⁺ to a polyatomic anion raises its charge by one unit.
cards.n: Hydrogen carbonate keeps the 1− charge; writing HCO₃²⁻ ignores that the added proton is positive.

cards.q: Recall the formulas of hydroxide, cyanide, and peroxide.
cards.a: Hydroxide OH⁻, cyanide CN⁻, peroxide O₂²⁻. In peroxide each oxygen is −1 rather than the usual −2, which is why sodium peroxide is Na₂O₂, not NaO.
cards.n: Writing peroxide as O₂⁻ (that is superoxide) or hydroxide as OH²⁻ earns nothing; the charges are 1−, 1−, 2−.

cards.q: Recall the formula of the acetate ion.
cards.a: Acetate is CH₃COO⁻ (also written C₂H₃O₂⁻), charge 1−. It is the anion left when acetic acid, CH₃COOH, loses its acidic H⁺.
cards.n: Only the H on the COOH group is acidic; writing acetate as C₂H₂O₂²⁻ (removing two H) earns nothing.

cards.q: Recall the formulas and charges of chromate, dichromate, and permanganate.
cards.a: Chromate CrO₄²⁻ (2−), dichromate Cr₂O₇²⁻ (2−), permanganate MnO₄⁻ (1−). These transition-metal oxyanions carry the metal in a high oxidation state (Cr +6, Mn +7).
cards.n: Dichromate keeps the 2− charge of chromate even though it has twice the chromium; doubling to 4− earns nothing.

cards.q: State the naming pattern for the four chlorine oxyanions and give their formulas.
cards.a: Hypochlorite ClO⁻, chlorite ClO₂⁻, chlorate ClO₃⁻, perchlorate ClO₄⁻; all carry 1−. Pattern: hypo- -ite has one fewer O than -ite, -ate has one more than -ite, and per- -ate one more than -ate. The same prefixes work for bromine and iodine oxyanions.
cards.h: → four names in order + the prefix rule
cards.n: The charge stays 1− through the whole series; adding oxygens changes the name, not the charge.

cards.q: Identify the formulas and charges of the sulfite ion and the hydrogen sulfate (bisulfate) ion.
cards.a: Sulfite SO₃²⁻ (2−) and hydrogen sulfate HSO₄⁻ (1−). Hydrogen sulfate is sulfate SO₄²⁻ with one H⁺ attached, which raises the charge from 2− to 1−.
cards.n: Sulfite (SO₃²⁻) is not sulfate (SO₄²⁻): -ite means one fewer oxygen, same charge.

cards.q: Identify the formula and charge of the oxalate ion.
cards.a: Oxalate is C₂O₄²⁻, charge 2−. It is the anion of oxalic acid, H₂C₂O₄, which has lost both acidic protons.
cards.n: Confusing oxalate with acetate (C₂H₃O₂⁻) earns nothing; oxalate has no hydrogen and a 2− charge.

cards.q: Identify the formulas and charges of the hydrogen phosphate and dihydrogen phosphate ions.
cards.a: Hydrogen phosphate HPO₄²⁻ (2−) and dihydrogen phosphate H₂PO₄⁻ (1−). Each H⁺ added to phosphate, PO₄³⁻, raises the charge by one: 3− → 2− → 1−.
cards.h: → two formulas, charge steps by one per H
cards.n: The charge must fall by one per added proton; H₂PO₄²⁻ or HPO₄³⁻ earns nothing.

cards.q: Predict the formula of the ionic compound formed between aluminum ions and sulfate ions.
cards.a: Al₂(SO₄)₃. Aluminum (group 13) forms Al³⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻; the lowest ratio that makes the total charge zero is two Al³⁺ (+6) with three SO₄²⁻ (−6). Parentheses hold the polyatomic ion so the subscript applies to the whole group.
cards.h: → charges, then the lowest neutral ratio
cards.n: AlSO₄ or Al₃(SO₄)₂ earns nothing; the formula is set by charge balance, and the polyatomic ion needs parentheses when it appears more than once.

cards.q: Predict the formula of the ionic compound formed from each pair: Ca and N · Al and O · Mg and Cl · Na and S · K and P · Ba and F · Fe³⁺ and O · NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ · Ca and PO₄³⁻ · Mg and OH⁻ · Na and CO₃²⁻ · Al and NO₃⁻
cards.a:
Ca and N → Ca₃N₂ (Ca²⁺, N³⁻)
Al and O → Al₂O₃ (Al³⁺, O²⁻)
Mg and Cl → MgCl₂
Na and S → Na₂S
K and P → K₃P
Ba and F → BaF₂
Fe³⁺ and O → Fe₂O₃
NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ → (NH₄)₂SO₄
Ca and PO₄³⁻ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂
Mg and OH⁻ → Mg(OH)₂
Na and CO₃²⁻ → Na₂CO₃
Al and NO₃⁻ → Al(NO₃)₃
cards.h: → charge from the group, then the lowest neutral ratio
cards.n: Forgetting parentheses around a repeated polyatomic ion (MgOH₂, AlNO₃₃) or writing a formula that is not the lowest ratio (Ca₂O₂) earns nothing.

cards.q: Predict, from each known compound, the formula of the analogous compound formed by the element in the same column: CaBr₂ → Sr with Br · SiO₂ → Ge with O · H₂S → H with Se · NaOH → K with OH · AlCl₃ → Ga with Cl · MgSO₄ → Ba with SO₄ · PH₃ → As with H · Na₂O → Li with O · KNO₃ → Rb with NO₃ · CCl₄ → Si with Cl
cards.a:
CaBr₂ → SrBr₂
SiO₂ → GeO₂
H₂S → H₂Se
NaOH → KOH
AlCl₃ → GaCl₃
MgSO₄ → BaSO₄
PH₃ → AsH₃
Na₂O → Li₂O
KNO₃ → RbNO₃
CCl₄ → SiCl₄
cards.h: → same column = same valence count = same formula pattern
cards.n: Elements in one column share a valence configuration, so they form the same ion charge or the same number of bonds; switching the subscript when swapping Sr for Ca earns nothing.

cards.q: Recall the formula and charge of each polyatomic ion: ammonium · hydronium · acetate · cyanide · carbonate · hydrogen carbonate · oxalate · hypochlorite · chlorite · chlorate · perchlorate · chromate · dichromate · permanganate · nitrite · nitrate · peroxide · hydroxide · phosphate · hydrogen phosphate · dihydrogen phosphate · sulfite · sulfate · hydrogen sulfate · thiosulfate · thiocyanate
cards.a:
ammonium → NH₄⁺
hydronium → H₃O⁺
acetate → CH₃COO⁻ (C₂H₃O₂⁻)
cyanide → CN⁻
carbonate → CO₃²⁻
hydrogen carbonate → HCO₃⁻
oxalate → C₂O₄²⁻
hypochlorite → ClO⁻
chlorite → ClO₂⁻
chlorate → ClO₃⁻
perchlorate → ClO₄⁻
chromate → CrO₄²⁻
dichromate → Cr₂O₇²⁻
permanganate → MnO₄⁻
nitrite → NO₂⁻
nitrate → NO₃⁻
peroxide → O₂²⁻
hydroxide → OH⁻
phosphate → PO₄³⁻
hydrogen phosphate → HPO₄²⁻
dihydrogen phosphate → H₂PO₄⁻
sulfite → SO₃²⁻
sulfate → SO₄²⁻
hydrogen sulfate → HSO₄⁻
thiosulfate → S₂O₃²⁻
thiocyanate → SCN⁻
cards.h: → -ate/-ite oxygen count; each H⁺ raises the charge by one
cards.n: The exam never gives these; a wrong charge on one ion wrecks every formula and equation built on it, so learn charge and formula together.

cards.q: Determine the charge on iron in Fe₂O₃ and in FeO from charge balance, and explain why the names of these compounds need Roman numerals.
cards.a: Fe₂O₃: three O²⁻ total −6, so two Fe must total +6, Fe³⁺ (iron(III) oxide). FeO: one O²⁻, so Fe²⁺ (iron(II) oxide). Iron is a transition metal whose ionic charge is not fixed by its group, so the name must state the charge with a Roman numeral, unlike Na₂O or MgO where the group fixes the charge.
cards.h: → anion total, solve for the metal, then the naming reason
cards.n: Assigning iron a charge from its column earns nothing; for transition metals the charge is read from the formula by balancing the anions.

cards.q: Predict whether magnesium and chlorine will form an ionic compound, give its formula, and justify using their valence electrons and their ionization energy and electron affinity.
cards.a: Yes: MgCl₂. Mg ([Ne]3s²) has two valence electrons held by a low ionization energy (738 and 1451 kJ/mol), so its nucleus loses them easily; Cl ([Ne]3s²3p⁵) has a high Z_eff and a strongly negative electron affinity (−349 kJ/mol), so each Cl nucleus captures one electron. Two Cl⁻ per Mg²⁺ gives a neutral formula, and the resulting Mg²⁺/Cl⁻ attraction forms the ionic solid.
cards.h: → valence counts, IE vs EA, then the charge-balanced formula
cards.n: 'Mg wants to give two and Cl wants one' earns nothing; the point uses the energies (low IE, negative EA) that describe the valence electron/nucleus interactions.

cards.q: Explain why metals form cations and nonmetals form anions.
cards.a: Metals have few valence electrons, far from the nucleus and well shielded, so their ionization energies are low and they lose electrons easily, forming cations. Nonmetals have high Z_eff and small radii, so they attract extra electrons strongly (very negative electron affinities) and fill the valence shell as anions.
cards.h: → metals: low IE → lose electrons; nonmetals: high Z_eff, negative EA → gain electrons
cards.n: 'Atoms want a full octet' earns nothing; the comparison of ionization energy and electron affinity, tied to Z_eff and distance, is what scores.
o: The valence electrons of a metal feel a weak Coulombic attraction, so they transfer to the nonmetal, whose nucleus attracts them more strongly.
Ionization energy rises and electron affinity becomes more negative across a period, so left-side elements lose electrons and right-side elements gain them.

w.a: Metals form cations because they want to have a full outer shell like a noble gas.
w.why: 'want' is not a mechanism; the low ionization energy is

w.a: Nonmetals form anions because they have more electrons than metals.
w.why: electron count is irrelevant; Z_eff and electron affinity decide

w.a: Metals form cations because they are shiny and conduct electricity.
w.why: macroscopic properties are consequences, not the cause

cards.q: Explain why sodium and potassium form analogous compounds, such as NaCl and KCl.
cards.a: Both are in group 1 with the same valence configuration, ns¹: one electron in the outermost shell beyond a noble-gas core. Each loses that single electron at low ionization energy to form a 1+ ion, so each combines with Cl⁻ in a 1:1 ratio. Same valence structure gives the same charge and the same formula pattern.
cards.h: → same column → same valence configuration (ns¹) → same 1+ ion → same formula
cards.n: 'They are both metals' earns nothing; the point is the identical number of valence electrons.
o: The periodic table is arranged so that elements in a column repeat the same outer configuration, and it is the outer electrons that determine bonding.
Predicting RbCl and CsCl follows from the same reasoning: every alkali metal has one valence electron.

w.a: Sodium and potassium form analogous compounds because they have similar atomic masses.
w.why: mass is not related to bonding; the valence configuration is

w.a: Sodium and potassium form analogous compounds because they are both in period 3.
w.why: they are in different periods; the shared column is the point

w.a: Sodium and potassium form analogous compounds because both have eight electrons in the outer shell.
w.why: both have ONE valence electron; eight is the core

cards.q: Explain why calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions rather than Ca³⁺ ions in ionic compounds.
cards.a: Ca is [Ar]4s²: its two valence electrons are in the n = 4 shell, shielded by 18 core electrons, so removing them is cheap (590 and 1145 kJ/mol). A third electron would come from the filled 3p of the argon core, closer to the nucleus and far less shielded, costing about 4900 kJ/mol, more than bond formation can repay.
cards.h: → two shielded 4s electrons cheap → third from the core: closer, less shielded → prohibitive
cards.n: 'Ca has only two valence electrons' states the count without the reason; the point requires the core electron's distance and shielding.
o: The huge jump between IE₂ and IE₃ marks the core boundary; charges stop where the jump begins.
With the 4s shell emptied, Ca²⁺ has the argon configuration, and breaking into a noble-gas core is Coulombically very expensive.

w.a: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ because it wants the argon configuration.
w.why: 'wants' is not a mechanism; the ionization-energy jump is

w.a: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ because it can only ever lose two electrons.
w.why: more can be removed at enormous cost; the energy, not an impossibility, is the reason

w.a: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ because group 2 elements always have a 2+ charge.
w.why: restates the pattern without explaining it

cards.q: Explain why chlorine forms Cl⁻ ions but not Cl²⁻ ions.
cards.a: Cl is [Ne]3s²3p⁵, so the first added electron enters the 3p subshell, feels a high Z_eff and is bound, releasing energy (−349 kJ/mol). A second electron would have to enter the n = 4 shell, far out, shielded by 18 electrons and repelled by the ion's negative charge, so it is not attracted and would cost energy to add.
cards.h: → first electron: into 3p, high Z_eff, energy released; second: new shell, shielded, repelled → not bound
cards.n: 'Chlorine only needs one electron for an octet' earns nothing without the Coulombic reason the second electron is not held.
o: Electron affinity becomes positive (endothermic) once the valence shell is filled, because the next electron must occupy a distant, shielded shell.
Cl⁻ has the argon configuration; adding to a noble-gas configuration is as unfavorable for Cl⁻ as it is for Ar itself.

w.a: Chlorine forms only Cl⁻ because it has seven valence electrons and eight is the maximum.
w.why: states the count without the reason the ninth electron is not bound

w.a: Chlorine forms only Cl⁻ because a 2− charge is always unstable.
w.why: O²⁻ and S²⁻ exist in ionic solids; the argument must be about Cl's shells

w.a: Chlorine forms only Cl⁻ because it is more electronegative than any 2− ion.
w.why: electronegativity concerns bonded atoms and does not address the second electron

cards.q: Explain why neon does not form ionic compounds while sodium, its neighbor, readily does.
cards.a: Neon's filled valence shell feels the highest Z_eff in period 2, so its ionization energy is huge (2081 kJ/mol) and no cation forms; an added electron would enter the shielded n = 3 shell, so no anion forms. Sodium's lone 3s electron is far out, shielded to Z_eff ≈ +1, and is lost cheaply (496 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → Ne: high IE and no attraction for an extra electron; Na: one shielded electron cheaply lost
cards.n: 'Neon is a noble gas so it is stable' earns nothing; the point compares the electron/nucleus interactions (IE and EA) of the two atoms.
o: Bond formation needs a valence electron that one nucleus holds weakly and another attracts strongly; neon offers neither, sodium offers the first.
Na and Ne are adjacent in Z but differ by a whole shell for the outer electron, which changes the attraction by a factor of about four in IE.

w.a: Neon does not form compounds because it has no valence electrons.
w.why: it has eight; they are just very tightly held

w.a: Neon does not form compounds because it is a gas.
w.why: physical state is irrelevant; chlorine is a gas and forms compounds

w.a: Sodium forms compounds because it has more electrons than neon.
w.why: having one more electron is not the reason; that electron's weak attraction is

cards.q: Explain why the alkali metals react more vigorously with chlorine going down the group from lithium to cesium.
cards.a: Each alkali metal gives its one valence electron to chlorine. Down the group that electron is in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus and shielded by more core shells, so it is held more weakly and the ionization energy falls (Li 520, K 419, Cs 376 kJ/mol). The easier the loss, the faster the metal reacts.
cards.h: → valence electron farther out and more shielded down the group → lower IE → more easily lost → more reactive
cards.n: 'Bigger atoms are more reactive' earns nothing; tie reactivity to the ionization energy and the distance/shielding that lowers it.
o: Reactivity tracks how weakly the outer electron is held; for a metal that is the ionization energy, which decreases with shell number.
Cesium's 6s electron is five shells out from a nucleus screened by 54 core electrons, so almost nothing holds it.

w.a: Alkali metals get more reactive down the group because they have more electrons to lose.
w.why: each loses exactly one; the ease of losing it is the point

w.a: Alkali metals get more reactive down the group because their electronegativity increases.
w.why: electronegativity decreases down the group, and it is not the mechanism here

w.a: Alkali metals get more reactive down the group because they melt at lower temperatures.
w.why: melting point is unrelated to electron loss

cards.q: Contrast ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding in terms of what happens to valence electrons.
cards.a: Ionic: electrons are transferred from metal to nonmetal, and the resulting cations and anions attract electrostatically. Covalent: electrons are shared between two nonmetals. Metallic: valence electrons are delocalized over a lattice of metal cations.
cards.h: → three bond types, one clause each
cards.n: Classify from the periodic table first: metal plus nonmetal is ionic, nonmetal plus nonmetal covalent, metal plus metal metallic.

cards.q: Predict bond type from an electronegativity difference (ΔEN).
cards.a: ΔEN below about 0.4 gives a nonpolar covalent bond; roughly 0.4 to 1.7 gives a polar covalent bond; above about 1.7 gives an ionic bond. Metal + nonmetal is the quick check for ionic.
cards.n: AP prefers reasoning from position in the periodic table over memorized cut-offs; treat the numbers as a guide, not a law.

cards.q: Contrast a polar covalent bond with a nonpolar covalent bond.
cards.a: In a polar covalent bond the atoms have different electronegativities, so the shared electron density sits closer to the more electronegative atom, creating partial charges (δ+ / δ-). In a nonpolar bond the electronegativities are equal or nearly equal and sharing is even.
cards.n: A polar bond does not guarantee a polar molecule. CO2 holds two polar bonds whose dipoles cancel by symmetry.

cards.q: Explain what the minimum of a potential energy versus internuclear distance curve represents.
cards.a: The minimum occurs at the equilibrium bond length, where attraction between each nucleus and the shared electrons exactly balances nuclear-nuclear and electron-electron repulsion. The depth of the well below zero is the bond energy.
cards.n: Trap: at distances shorter than the minimum the energy rises steeply because of nucleus-nucleus repulsion, not because the bond weakens.

cards.q: State how bond order, bond length, and bond strength are related.
cards.a: Higher bond order means a shorter bond and a stronger bond (larger bond energy). C-C > C=C > C≡C in length; C≡C > C=C > C-C in strength.
cards.n: Stronger and shorter always travel together, so a bond that takes more energy to break is never the longer one.

cards.q: Explain why breaking a chemical bond always requires energy input.
cards.a: The bonded state is lower in potential energy than the separated atoms, so energy must be added to climb out of the potential energy well. Bond breaking is always endothermic; bond forming is always exothermic.
cards.n: This sign rule is why enthalpy from bond enthalpies is bonds broken minus bonds formed; reversing that subtraction flips the answer.

cards.q: Define lattice energy and list the two factors that control its magnitude.
cards.a: Lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions combine into one mole of an ionic solid (or the energy needed to separate it). By Coulomb's law it increases with larger ion charges and with smaller ionic radii.
cards.n: Charge outweighs radius: MgO beats NaCl chiefly because the charges are 2+/2- rather than 1+/1-, not because the ions are smaller.

cards.q: Rank the lattice energies of NaCl, MgO, and KCl and justify the order.
cards.a: MgO > NaCl > KCl. MgO has 2+/2- charges rather than 1+/1-, which dominates. NaCl beats KCl because Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺, giving a shorter interionic distance.
cards.n: Charge always outweighs size on the AP exam; compare charges first, then radii only as a tiebreaker.

cards.q: Explain why ionic solids are hard but brittle.
cards.a: The lattice of alternating charges is held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions, so it is hard. When a layer is displaced, like charges align, and the sudden repulsion splits the crystal along that plane.
cards.n: Contrast with a metal, where a displaced layer still meets the same delocalized electron sea, so metals bend instead of shattering.

cards.q: Explain why an ionic compound conducts electricity when molten or dissolved but not as a solid.
cards.a: Conduction requires mobile charge carriers. In the solid, ions are locked in fixed lattice positions; melting or dissolving frees the ions to move and carry current.
cards.n: Trap: a molten metal also conducts, but its carriers are electrons. For the ionic melt the carriers are the ions themselves.

cards.q: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.
cards.a: Melting requires overcoming strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions throughout a three-dimensional lattice. Because these Coulombic forces are far stronger than intermolecular forces, a large amount of thermal energy is needed.
cards.n: Rank within the ionic class using Coulomb's law: larger ion charges or smaller radii push the melting point higher still.

cards.q: Explain metallic bonding using the sea-of-electrons model and use it to account for two metal properties.
cards.a: Metal atoms release valence electrons into a delocalized 'sea' surrounding a lattice of cations. The mobile electrons carry charge and heat (conductivity), and because the bonding is nondirectional the cations can slide past one another without breaking bonds (malleability and ductility).
cards.n: Electrical and thermal conductivity share one cause here, so a free-response answer can cite the mobile electrons for both.

cards.q: Contrast a substitutional alloy with an interstitial alloy.
cards.a: In a substitutional alloy, atoms of similar radius replace host atoms in the lattice (brass: Zn in Cu). In an interstitial alloy, much smaller atoms fit into the holes between host atoms (steel: C in Fe).
cards.n: Radius is the test: an atom within roughly 15 percent of the host size substitutes, while much smaller C, N or H fit in the holes.

cards.q: Explain why alloys are generally harder and less malleable than the pure metal.
cards.a: Atoms of a different size disrupt the regular lattice, so layers of atoms can no longer slide smoothly past one another. Interstitial atoms also lock the lattice in place, which raises hardness and strength.
cards.n: Alloys still conduct, because the delocalized electrons survive. Only the sliding of atom layers is what gets blocked.

cards.q: State the procedure for drawing a Lewis structure.
cards.a: 1) Total the valence electrons, adjusting for overall charge. 2) Place the least electronegative atom (never H) in the center and connect with single bonds. 3) Complete octets on outer atoms. 4) Put leftovers on the central atom. 5) Form double or triple bonds if the central atom is short of an octet.
cards.n: Recount the electrons at the end. A structure using more or fewer than step 1 allows is wrong however reasonable it looks.

cards.q: Apply valence-electron counting to draw the Lewis structure of a polyatomic ion such as SO₄²⁻.
cards.a: Sum the group valence electrons (S = 6, four O = 24, total 30), then ADD one electron for each unit of negative charge (30 + 2 = 32) or subtract for positive charge. Distribute those 32 electrons, then enclose the structure in brackets with the charge outside.
cards.n: Trap: adding electrons for a cation instead of subtracting. NH₄⁺ has 5 + 4 - 1 = 8 valence electrons.

cards.q: Identify the common exceptions to the octet rule.
cards.a: H holds 2 electrons; Be is stable with 4 and B with 6 (electron deficient); central atoms in period 3 and below (P, S, Cl, Xe) can be surrounded by more than 8 (expanded octet), which smaller period-2 atoms cannot accommodate. Odd-electron species such as NO also cannot obey it.
cards.n: The old "it uses empty d orbitals" explanation is no longer used, and the CED dropped sp³d and sp³d² in 2019. Recognise instead that a period-3-or-below central atom is simply big enough to hold more than 8.

cards.q: State the formula for formal charge.
cards.a: Formal charge = (valence electrons) - (nonbonding electrons) - ½(bonding electrons). Equivalently, valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus number of bonds.
cards.n: Formal charge is bookkeeping that assumes perfectly equal sharing, so it is neither the real charge nor the oxidation number.

cards.q: Apply formal charge to decide which of several valid Lewis structures is preferred.
cards.a: The best structure has formal charges closest to zero, has no like charges on adjacent atoms, and places any negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom. The sum of formal charges must equal the overall charge.
cards.n: The CED dropped expanded octets, so do not add extra bonds to S or P just to zero out a formal charge on the AP exam.

cards.q: Define resonance and explain what the true structure is.
cards.a: Resonance occurs when more than one valid Lewis structure can be drawn by moving only electrons, not atoms. The real molecule is a single averaged hybrid of all contributors, not a mixture that flips between them.
cards.h: → definition + nature of the real species
cards.n: Trap: the molecule does not oscillate between structures. Use a double-headed arrow, never an equilibrium arrow.

cards.q: Predict the bond lengths in the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻.
cards.a: All three C-O bonds are identical and intermediate between a single and a double bond, because the three resonance structures average to a bond order of 4/3 on each bond.
cards.n: A measured length between the single and double bond values is the experimental evidence that resonance, not one fixed structure, is real.

cards.q: Explain why a molecule with resonance is more stable than any single contributing structure.
cards.a: The electrons in the pi system are delocalized over several atoms rather than confined between two. Spreading electron density over a larger volume lowers the potential energy of the molecule, an effect called resonance stabilization.
cards.n: Resonance is not rapid flipping between structures. The real ion is one averaged structure that never looks like any single drawing.

cards.q: State the central principle of VSEPR theory.
cards.a: Electron domains around a central atom (bonding groups plus lone pairs) repel each other and arrange themselves as far apart as possible, which sets the molecular geometry. A single, double, or triple bond each counts as one domain.
cards.n: Electron-domain geometry and molecular shape differ whenever a lone pair sits on the central atom, so answer the one actually asked for.

cards.q: Contrast electron-domain geometry with molecular geometry.
cards.a: Electron-domain (electron-pair) geometry counts ALL domains, including lone pairs. Molecular geometry describes the positions of the ATOMS only. NH₃ has tetrahedral electron-domain geometry but trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.
cards.n: Read the question wording carefully: 'shape of the molecule' means molecular geometry, so lone pairs are invisible in the name.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for a central atom with 2 electron domains and no lone pairs.
cards.a: Linear, with a 180° bond angle. Examples: CO₂, BeCl₂, HCN.
cards.n: Trap: a triple bond still counts as a single domain, which is why HCN is linear even though carbon carries four bonds.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 3 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Trigonal planar, with 120° bond angles. Examples: BF₃, SO₃, CO₃²⁻.
cards.n: All four atoms lie in one plane, so the bond dipoles cancel and BF3 is nonpolar even though every B-F bond is strongly polar.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 3 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Bent (angular), with a bond angle slightly less than 120° (about 118°). Examples: SO₂, O₃, NO₂⁻.
cards.h: → shape name + angle relative to ideal
cards.n: Compare with the four-domain bent case, water at about 104.5 degrees. The angle, not the shape name, reveals the domain count.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 4 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Tetrahedral, with 109.5° bond angles. Examples: CH₄, NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻.
cards.n: The 109.5 degree value holds only when all four outer atoms are identical; CH2Cl2 is still tetrahedral but measurably distorted.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 4 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Trigonal pyramidal, with bond angles of about 107°, compressed from 109.5° by the lone pair. Example: NH₃.
cards.n: The electron-domain geometry here is still tetrahedral. Only the shape name changes, because the lone pair is not counted as a position.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 4 electron domains with 2 lone pairs.
cards.a: Bent, with a bond angle of about 104.5°. Example: H₂O.
cards.n: Both SO₂ (3 domains) and H₂O (4 domains) are 'bent' but have different angles; state the domain count to justify which.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angles for 5 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Trigonal bipyramidal, with 120° angles in the equatorial plane and 90° between axial and equatorial positions. Example: PCl₅.
cards.n: Axial bonds are slightly longer than equatorial ones, since each axial bond faces three equatorial neighbors at 90 degrees.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 5 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Seesaw, because the lone pair occupies a roomier equatorial position. Example: SF₄.
cards.h: → shape name + where the lone pair sits
cards.n: An axial lone pair would face three neighbors at 90 degrees instead of two, which is why the equatorial site always wins.

cards.q: Predict the geometries for 5 electron domains with 2 and with 3 lone pairs.
cards.a: Two lone pairs gives T-shaped (ClF₃); three lone pairs gives linear (XeF₂). All lone pairs take equatorial positions.
cards.n: XeF2 is nonpolar despite three lone pairs, because the two bonds sit 180 degrees apart and their dipoles cancel exactly.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 6 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Octahedral, with 90° bond angles. Example: SF₆.
cards.n: All six positions in an octahedron are equivalent, so unlike the five-domain case there is no axial versus equatorial choice to make.

cards.q: Predict the geometries for 6 electron domains with 1 and with 2 lone pairs.
cards.a: One lone pair gives square pyramidal (BrF₅); two lone pairs gives square planar (XeF₄), with the lone pairs opposite each other at 180°.
cards.n: Square planar is nonpolar because the bond dipoles cancel, while square pyramidal keeps a net dipole pointing away from the lone pair.

cards.q: Explain why lone pairs compress bond angles below the ideal value.
cards.a: A lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so its electron cloud is broader and closer to the central atom. It repels bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, pushing the bonds together.
cards.n: The ranking is lone-lone > lone-bond > bond-bond, which is why water at 104.5 degrees is squeezed more than ammonia at 107.

cards.q: Identify the hybridization of a central atom from its number of electron domains.
cards.a: 2 domains = sp, 3 domains = sp², 4 domains = sp³. Lone pairs count as domains, so both H₂O and CH₄ are sp³.
cards.h: → three domain counts mapped to labels
cards.n: Since 2019 the AP CED only requires sp, sp², and sp³; sp³d and sp³d² are no longer assessed.

cards.q: Contrast sigma and pi bonds.
cards.a: A sigma bond forms by head-on (end-to-end) orbital overlap along the internuclear axis and allows free rotation. A pi bond forms by side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below that axis, is weaker, and blocks rotation.
cards.n: Blocked rotation about a pi bond is exactly what makes cis and trans alkenes distinct compounds rather than one substance.

cards.q: Count the sigma and pi bonds in a molecule containing double and triple bonds.
cards.a: Every bond (single, double, or triple) contains exactly one sigma bond. A double bond adds 1 pi bond and a triple bond adds 2 pi bonds. HCN has 2 sigma and 2 pi bonds.
cards.n: Count sigma bonds as connected atom pairs, not as lines drawn. Lone pairs contribute to neither the sigma nor the pi tally.

cards.q: Predict whether a molecule is polar from its geometry and bond dipoles.
cards.a: A molecule is polar if the individual bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetric arrangements with identical outer atoms and no lone pairs on the central atom cancel; asymmetry from lone pairs or different outer atoms leaves a net dipole.
cards.n: Name the geometry before the verdict. An answer that says polar without citing the shape or the cancellation rarely earns the point.

cards.q: Identify three molecules that contain polar bonds yet are nonpolar overall.
cards.a: CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), and CCl₄ (tetrahedral). In each, the symmetric arrangement of identical outer atoms makes the bond dipoles cancel to zero.
cards.n: Very common MC distractor: 'has polar bonds' is not the same as 'is a polar molecule'.

cards.q: Predict whether the bond in KF and the bond in $F_2$ is ionic or covalent, and explain using electronegativity difference.
cards.a: KF is ionic (large ΔEN, metal transfers an electron to a nonmetal). $F_2$ is nonpolar covalent (ΔEN = 0, identical atoms share the pair equally).
cards.n: Metal + nonmetal almost always signals ionic; nonmetal + nonmetal almost always signals covalent.

cards.q: Predict which has the larger lattice energy, MgO or MgS, and justify.
cards.a: MgO. Both have the same 2+/2- charges, but oxide ion is smaller than sulfide ion, giving a shorter interionic distance and a stronger electrostatic attraction.
cards.n: If the charges themselves differed (e.g. NaCl vs MgO), charge would dominate over radius instead.

cards.q: Decide which Lewis structure of $CO_2$ is preferred using formal charge: two C=O double bonds, or a C≡O triple bond paired with a C-O single bond.
cards.a: The double-bond structure (O=C=O) is preferred: every atom has a formal charge of zero, whereas the triple/single alternative carries charges of +1, 0, and -1.
cards.n: Minimizing formal charges is the tiebreaker only after every structure already satisfies the octet rule.

cards.q: Compute the average N-O bond order in the nitrate ion, $NO_3^{-}$, from its resonance structures.
cards.a: Each resonance structure has one N=O double bond and two N-O single bonds. Averaging across the three equivalent structures gives (2+1+1)/3 = 4/3 ≈ 1.33.
cards.n: Bond order need not be a whole number; resonance is exactly what produces fractional values like 4/3.

cards.q: Identify the number of lone pairs on the central atom of a T-shaped molecule such as $ClF_3$.
cards.a: Two lone pairs. $ClF_3$ has 5 electron domains (3 bonding, 2 lone pairs) arranged in a trigonal bipyramid, with both lone pairs equatorial, leaving a T-shaped molecule.
cards.n: Work back from the domain total: three bonds plus two lone pairs is five domains, so the underlying frame is trigonal bipyramidal.

cards.q: Explain why both lone pairs in $ClF_3$ occupy equatorial positions rather than one axial and one equatorial.
cards.a: Equatorial positions have fewer 90° interactions with other domains than axial positions do, so placing both lone pairs equatorially minimizes the strongest, 90°, lone-pair repulsions.
cards.n: Count the 90 degree neighbors: an axial site faces three, an equatorial site only two, and the bulkier lone pairs claim the roomier one.

cards.q: Identify the electron-domain geometry and the molecular geometry of the central atom in $XeF_4$.
cards.a: Six electron domains give an octahedral electron-domain geometry; two of them are lone pairs sitting directly across from each other, which leaves the four F atoms in one plane, so the molecular geometry is square planar.
cards.n: The CED assesses hybridization only for sp, sp² and sp³ (2, 3 or 4 domains), so a 6-domain centre gets a geometry, not a hybridization label.

cards.q: Predict whether $XeF_4$ is polar or nonpolar, and explain.
cards.a: Nonpolar. The two lone pairs sit directly across from each other, and the four Xe-F bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically in a plane, so all the dipoles cancel.
cards.n: Lone pairs do not automatically make a molecule polar. Here they sit opposite one another, so their effects cancel just as the bonds do.

cards.q: Identify a molecule with a seesaw molecular geometry, and state its electron-domain count and lone pairs.
cards.a: Sulfur tetrafluoride, $SF_4$: 5 electron domains around S, 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, in a trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry. The lone pair takes an equatorial position, giving the seesaw shape.
cards.n: Hybridization is not assigned to 5- and 6-domain centres on the current CED — answer with the geometry.

cards.q: Contrast the F-S-F bond angles at the axial and equatorial positions of $SF_4$, caused by its single lone pair.
cards.a: The two axial F-S-F bonds bend back to about 173° and the equatorial angle compresses to about 102°, both pushed away from ideal by the lone pair's stronger equatorial repulsion.
cards.n: Trap: it is not only the equatorial angle that shrinks; the axial pair also bends slightly off 180°.

cards.q: Explain the hybridization of the central carbon in $CO_2$ and how its two pi bonds form.
cards.a: Carbon is sp hybridized, since it has only 2 electron domains. Each of its two unhybridized p orbitals overlaps sideways with a p orbital on an oxygen to form the two perpendicular pi bonds.
cards.n: Each pi bond forms with a different oxygen, so the two are perpendicular to each other, not stacked.

cards.q: Predict whether $SF_4$ is polar or nonpolar, and explain.
cards.a: Polar. The seesaw shape from the single lone pair breaks the symmetry of the S-F bond dipoles, so they do not cancel and the molecule has a net dipole toward the lone pair.
cards.n: Contrast this with $XeF_4$: an even number of symmetric lone pairs cancels, an odd number usually does not.

cards.q: Compute the formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion, $NH_4^{+}$.
cards.a: Formal charge = 5 - 0 (lone-pair electrons) - 4 (bonds) = +1. Nitrogen contributes all four bonding pairs and keeps none as a lone pair, giving it the ion's full +1 charge.
cards.n: Every H atom bonded to N contributes 0 to nitrogen's own formal charge; only lone pairs and bond count matter.

cards.q: Rank NaF, NaCl, and NaBr by lattice energy from largest to smallest, and justify.
cards.a: NaF > NaCl > NaBr. All three have the same 1+/1- charges, so the smaller halide ion (F⁻) gives the shortest interionic distance and the strongest attraction.
cards.n: The same size-driven logic ranks the alkaline earth oxides (MgO, CaO, SrO) by lattice energy too.

cards.q: Predict which bond is shorter and stronger: the C-C bond in ethane or the C=C bond in ethene, using bond order.
cards.a: The C=C bond in ethene. Its bond order (2) is higher than the C-C single bond in ethane (order 1); a higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond.
cards.n: Bond order does not scale energy proportionally: a C=C bond is clearly stronger than C-C but well short of twice as strong.

cards.q: Predict which has the larger lattice energy, NaCl or $MgCl_2$, and justify using ionic charge.
cards.a: $MgCl_2$. $Mg^{2+}$ carries twice the charge of $Na^+$ while the anion is the same; lattice energy rises with the product of the ion charges, so the higher cation charge dominates.
cards.n: Charge affects lattice energy far more strongly than the modest size increase from Na⁺ to Mg²⁺.

cards.q: Predict which has the larger lattice energy, LiF or CsI, considering both ionic charge and size.
cards.a: LiF. Both compounds have 1+/1− ions, so charge is equal, but $Li^+$ and $F^-$ are much smaller than $Cs^+$ and $I^-$, giving a shorter interionic distance and stronger attraction.
cards.h: → charge is tied; compare ion size
cards.n: With the charge product tied, the comparison isolates the distance term of Coulomb's law, which is why ionic size settles it.

cards.q: Explain why CaO has a much higher melting point than NaCl, using the factors that determine lattice energy.
cards.a: CaO's ions carry 2+ and 2− charges versus NaCl's 1+ and 1−; the larger charge product gives CaO a much bigger lattice energy, so far more energy is needed to separate its ions, raising its melting point.
cards.n: Melting-point comparisons track lattice-energy trends cleanly only when the structure type is the same; this comparison isolates the charge effect.

cards.q: Compute the formal charge on each oxygen atom in one Lewis resonance structure of ozone, $O_3$.
cards.a: +1 on the central O, 0 on the double-bonded terminal O, and −1 on the single-bonded terminal O; the three charges sum to zero, matching ozone's neutral overall charge.
cards.h: → FC = valence e⁻ − lone-pair e⁻ − bonding e⁻/2
cards.n: These nonzero formal charges cannot be avoided, which is precisely why ozone is described by resonance rather than one best structure.

cards.q: Explain why the two N-O bonds in the nitrite ion, $NO_2^{-}$, are equal in length even though each Lewis structure shows one single and one double bond.
cards.a: The true structure is a resonance hybrid of both contributing structures, giving each N-O bond an intermediate bond order of 1.5; electron density is delocalized equally over both oxygens, so the bonds are identical in length.
cards.h: → resonance hybrid, not two separate molecules
cards.n: No single resonance structure is the real molecule; only the hybrid average matches experimental bond lengths.

cards.q: Predict whether the C-H bond in methane is ionic, polar covalent, or nonpolar covalent, given electronegativities C = 2.55 and H = 2.20.
cards.a: Nonpolar covalent. ΔEN = 2.55 - 2.20 = 0.35, below the ~0.4 cut-off, so the electrons are shared essentially equally. This is why hydrocarbons such as CH₄ are treated as nonpolar molecules held together only by London dispersion forces.
cards.n: The 0.4 cutoff is a teaching convention rather than physics, so a C-H bond is better called very slightly polar than truly nonpolar.

cards.q: Identify why boron in $BF_3$ is an exception to the octet rule.
cards.a: Boron ends up with only 6 valence electrons around it (three single bonds, no lone pair), an incomplete octet; boron has too few valence electrons to reach 8 while bonding to three fluorines.
cards.n: Electron-deficient central atoms like B and Be are the main incomplete-octet exceptions tested on the AP exam.

cards.q: Compute the formal charge on sulfur in $SO_4^{2-}$ using the Lewis structure with four S-O single bonds.
cards.a: +2. With four single bonds and no lone pairs, sulfur's formal charge is $6 - 0 - \frac{8}{2} = +2$.
cards.n: A structure with two S=O double bonds gives sulfur a lower formal charge, which is why it is often preferred over the all-single-bond structure used here.

cards.q: Contrast the expected melting point and electrical conductivity of an ionic compound with those of a molecular compound at room temperature.
cards.a: Ionic compounds typically have high melting points and conduct only when molten or dissolved; molecular compounds have low melting points and do not conduct in any state, since neither has mobile charges as a solid.
cards.n: Graphite and diamond are exceptions worth remembering: both are covalent network solids, not molecular, despite being pure carbon.

cards.q: Predict which bond requires more energy to break: the O-H bond in water (467 kJ/mol) or the H-H bond in $H_2$ (436 kJ/mol).
cards.a: The O-H bond. Its bond enthalpy (467 kJ/mol) is higher than the H-H bond enthalpy (436 kJ/mol), so more energy is needed to break it.
cards.n: Bond-enthalpy comparisons only make sense between specific, named bonds; there is no single universal ranking of all bond types.

cards.q: Identify the number of equivalent resonance structures needed to describe the bonding in $SO_3$.
cards.a: 3. Each resonance structure places the S=O double bond on a different one of the three equivalent oxygen atoms, and the true structure is their average.
cards.h: → one double bond, three possible positions
cards.n: Equivalent structures make the true bond order 4/3 on every S-O bond, so all three bonds measure exactly the same length.

cards.q: State the rule connecting the sum of formal charges in a Lewis structure to the overall charge of the species.
cards.a: The formal charges on all atoms in a correct Lewis structure must sum to the net charge of the molecule or ion; for a neutral molecule they sum to zero.
cards.h: → check: do the formal charges add to the ion's charge?
cards.n: A quick way to check a finished Lewis structure: the formal charges must add up to the species' actual charge.

cards.q: State the electronegativity-difference ranges used to classify a bond as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic.
cards.a: ΔEN < 0.4: nonpolar covalent. 0.4 ≤ ΔEN ≤ 1.7: polar covalent. ΔEN > 1.7: ionic.
cards.n: These cutoffs are a teaching convention, not a sharp physical boundary in nature.

cards.q: Predict the bond type between calcium and bromine, given electronegativities Ca = 1.00 and Br = 2.96.
cards.a: Ionic. ΔEN = 2.96 - 1.00 = 1.96, which is above the 1.7 cutoff for ionic bonding.
cards.n: A large ΔEN plus a metal-nonmetal pairing is the strongest signal for an ionic bond.

cards.q: Explain why bond polarity is better described as a continuum rather than three sharply divided categories.
cards.a: Electron sharing becomes gradually less equal as electronegativity difference increases; there is no physical discontinuity at ΔEN = 0.4 or 1.7. Those numbers are only a convenient teaching cutoff, not a real boundary in nature.
cards.n: Even 'ionic' compounds like LiI retain some covalent character, and some 'covalent' bonds like C-F are highly polar.

cards.q: Apply electronegativity difference to classify the N-H bond in ammonia, given N = 3.04 and H = 2.20.
cards.a: Polar covalent. ΔEN = 3.04 - 2.20 = 0.84, which falls in the 0.4-1.7 polar covalent range.
cards.n: This polarity is what lets ammonia hydrogen bond, so the same number reappears in IMF, boiling point and solubility questions.

cards.q: Contrast how electrons are shared in a nonpolar covalent bond with how they are shared in a polar covalent bond.
cards.a: In a nonpolar covalent bond the bonding electrons are shared equally between identical or near-identical atoms. In a polar covalent bond the electrons are shared unequally, spending more time near the more electronegative atom, which creates partial charges.
cards.n: Partial charges are written as delta plus and delta minus, never as full ionic charges, since no electron is handed over outright.

cards.q: Define bond dissociation energy.
cards.a: The energy required to break one mole of a specific bond in the gas phase, producing two separated atoms or fragments. It is always a positive quantity.
cards.n: Tabulated values are averages taken across many compounds, so an enthalpy built from them is an estimate rather than an exact result.

cards.q: Explain why the H-F bond is shorter and stronger than the H-I bond.
cards.a: Fluorine has a much smaller atomic radius than iodine, so the H-F internuclear distance is shorter. Shorter bonds place the shared electron density closer to both nuclei, giving a stronger, more stable bond.
cards.h: → smaller atom, shorter bond, stronger bond
cards.n: Bond strength trends with atomic radius are a fast substitute for memorizing individual bond energies.

cards.q: Compute the energy required to break all the C-H bonds in 0.500 mol of methane, given a C-H bond energy of 413 kJ/mol.
cards.a: 826 kJ. Each $CH_4$ molecule has 4 C-H bonds, so 0.500 mol x 4 = 2.00 mol of bonds; 2.00 mol x 413 kJ/mol = 826 kJ.
cards.n: Trap: multiply by the number of that bond type per molecule before multiplying by the bond energy.

cards.q: Predict which bond is longer: the C-O bond in $CO_2$ or the C-O bond in methanol, $CH_3OH$.
cards.a: The C-O bond in methanol is longer. It is a single bond (order 1), while each C-O bond in $CO_2$ has partial double-bond character (order 2), and higher bond order means a shorter bond.
cards.n: Measured bond length is the experimental evidence for bond order, which is why these comparisons show up in data-table questions.

cards.q: Contrast an intramolecular force with an intermolecular force in terms of typical magnitude.
cards.a: Intramolecular forces are the covalent, ionic, or metallic bonds holding atoms together within a particle, typically hundreds of kJ/mol. Intermolecular forces act between separate particles and are much weaker, typically only a few to a few tens of kJ/mol.
cards.h: → within a particle vs. between particles
cards.n: That order-of-magnitude gap is why a substance boils far below the temperature at which its own bonds start to break.

cards.q: Explain why lattice energy generally correlates with the boiling point of an ionic compound.
cards.a: Both properties depend on how strongly the ions attract each other in the solid. A larger lattice energy means the ions are held together more tightly, so more thermal energy (a higher temperature) is needed to separate them into a gas.
cards.n: It is a trend rather than a law, since melting and boiling also depend on the crystal structure and on the shapes of the ions.

cards.q: Use a Born-Haber cycle to compute the lattice energy of NaCl: $ΔH_f$ = -411, $ΔH_sub(Na)$ = +109, $IE_1(Na)$ = +496, $D(Cl_2)$ = +243, EA(Cl) = -349 (all kJ/mol).
cards.a: -788.5 kJ/mol. $ΔH_f$ = $ΔH_sub$ + $IE_1$ + $(1/2)D(Cl_2)$ + EA + $ΔH_lattice,$ so -411 = 109 + 496 + 121.5 - 349 + $ΔH_lattice$ = 377.5 + $ΔH_lattice,$ giving $ΔH_lattice$ = -788.5 kJ/mol.
cards.n: Trap: use half the $Cl_2$ bond energy, since only one Cl atom is needed per NaCl formula unit.

cards.q: Define an alloy.
cards.a: A mixture of two or more elements, at least one a metal, that has metallic properties overall. Alloys are classified as substitutional or interstitial based on how the atoms are arranged.
cards.n: An alloy is a mixture, so its composition varies continuously, which is why alloys soften over a range instead of melting sharply.

cards.q: Explain why metals are malleable and ductile using the electron-sea model.
cards.a: In the electron-sea model, delocalized valence electrons surround fixed cation cores rather than fixed directional bonds. When a metal is deformed, cation layers slide past one another and the mobile electron sea simply re-adjusts to hold the new shape together, so the metal bends or draws into wire instead of shattering.
cards.n: Contrast an ionic solid, where sliding one layer brings like charges together and the crystal cleaves instead of bending.

cards.q: Explain why metals are good conductors of both heat and electricity using the electron-sea model.
cards.a: The delocalized valence electrons in the electron sea are free to move throughout the metal. Under an applied voltage they carry electric current, and by colliding with neighboring particles they rapidly transmit kinetic energy, conducting heat.
cards.n: Conductivity actually falls as a metal is heated, because the vibrating cations scatter the moving electrons more often.

cards.q: Explain why metals are lustrous (shiny) using the electron-sea model.
cards.a: The mobile electrons in the electron sea can absorb photons of visible light and immediately re-emit light of nearly the same wavelength at the metal's surface, which is perceived as a reflective, shiny appearance.
cards.n: This is the same electron-sea reasoning that explains conductivity and malleability.

cards.q: Identify whether steel, in which carbon atoms occupy gaps in an iron lattice, is a substitutional or interstitial alloy.
cards.a: Interstitial. Carbon atoms are much smaller than iron atoms, so they fit into the small holes (interstices) between iron atoms rather than replacing them.
cards.n: Those trapped carbon atoms stop layers from sliding, which is why steel is much harder and far less malleable than pure iron.

cards.q: Identify whether brass, made of copper and zinc, is a substitutional or interstitial alloy.
cards.a: Substitutional. Copper and zinc atoms are similar in size, so zinc atoms directly replace copper atoms at lattice sites rather than squeezing into interstitial gaps.
