cards.n: Substitution still disturbs the lattice enough to block smooth slipping, so brass is harder than either copper or zinc alone.

cards.q: Explain the two criteria used to identify the most important resonance structure among several valid Lewis structures.
cards.a: Prefer the structure with formal charges closest to zero, and when a negative formal charge cannot be avoided, place it on the most electronegative atom rather than a less electronegative one.
cards.n: These criteria rank structures without making the others wrong. The real species is a weighted average of all of them.

cards.q: Identify the number of equivalent resonance structures needed to describe the bonding in benzene, $C_6H_6$.
cards.a: 2. Benzene's ring can be drawn with alternating single and double bonds in two equivalent ways, and the true structure is the average of both, giving every C-C bond the same intermediate length.
cards.n: Every measured C-C bond in benzene is between a single and a double bond in length, which is the evidence for this averaging.

cards.q: Rank the intermolecular forces from strongest to weakest.
cards.a: Ion-dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > dipole-induced dipole > London dispersion, for species of similar size. The order holds only at similar size: dispersion grows with the number of electrons and polarizability, so a large nonpolar molecule (I₂, a solid) has stronger net attractions than a small polar one (HCl, a gas). Every intermolecular force is far weaker than a covalent, ionic or metallic bond.
cards.n: Ranking by type alone earns nothing when sizes differ; 'heavier molecules have stronger forces' also earns nothing, the cause is more electrons and greater polarizability.

cards.q: Define London dispersion forces and state which substances have them.
cards.a: London dispersion forces are Coulombic attractions between temporary, fluctuating dipoles: at any instant the electron cloud of a particle is lopsided, giving it a momentary dipole that induces an opposite dipole in a neighbor. Every substance has them, atoms and ions included; they are the ONLY intermolecular force in nonpolar molecules and noble gases, and the strongest net force between large molecules.
cards.n: 'Only nonpolar molecules have dispersion forces' earns nothing; polar molecules have them too, and in large molecules they usually dominate.

cards.q: Explain polarizability and how it controls London dispersion strength.
cards.a: Polarizability is how easily a particle's electron cloud is distorted into a temporary dipole. A larger cloud with more electrons, held farther from the nucleus, distorts more easily, so its instantaneous dipoles are bigger and dispersion forces are stronger. Shape matters too: a long, unbranched chain presents more surface for contact with its neighbors than a compact branched isomer of the same formula.
cards.n: 'Heavier molecules have stronger forces' earns nothing; mass is a proxy, the scored cause is more electrons and greater polarizability.

cards.q: State the requirement for hydrogen bonding.
cards.a: A hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O or F in one molecule must be attracted to a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of a different molecule (or a different part of the same large molecule). Both partners are needed: the highly polarized H (large δ+) and the electronegative acceptor (δ−). It is an unusually strong intermolecular attraction, not a covalent bond.
cards.n: Naming hydrogen bonding for any molecule that contains hydrogen (HCl, CH₄, H₂S) earns nothing; CH₃OCH₃ has O but no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself.

cards.q: Explain the ion-dipole force and name a situation where it dominates.
cards.a: An ion-dipole force is the Coulombic attraction between an ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule. It dominates when an ionic solid dissolves in water: each Na⁺ is surrounded by water molecules with their δ− oxygen ends pointing inward, and each Cl⁻ by water molecules with δ+ hydrogen ends pointing inward. It is stronger than any force between neutral molecules because a full charge, not a partial one, is involved.
cards.n: Drawing the hydrogen ends of water toward Na⁺ earns nothing; the sign of the partial charge facing the ion is the scored detail.

cards.q: Define ion-induced dipole and dipole-induced dipole forces.
cards.a: An ion (or a permanent dipole) distorts the electron cloud of a nearby nonpolar particle, inducing a temporary dipole that is then attracted to it. The strength tracks the polarizability of the nonpolar partner and the charge of the inducer. Dipole-induced dipole attraction between water and O₂ is why oxygen dissolves slightly in water.
cards.n: 'O₂ dissolves in water because it is polar' earns nothing; O₂ is nonpolar and only an induced dipole attracts it to water.

cards.q: Rank $CH_4$, $SiH_4$, and $GeH_4$ by boiling point, and justify using London dispersion forces.
cards.a: CH₄ < SiH₄ < GeH₄. All three are tetrahedral and nonpolar, so London dispersion is the only intermolecular force. GeH₄ has the most electrons and the largest, most polarizable electron cloud, so its temporary dipoles are largest and its dispersion forces strongest; more energy is needed to separate its molecules, giving the highest boiling point (CH₄ −161 °C, SiH₄ −112 °C, GeH₄ −88 °C).
cards.n: Citing molar mass alone earns nothing; the point needs more electrons and greater polarizability. Polarity from Unit 2 (all tetrahedral, nonpolar).

cards.q: Rank HCl, HBr, and HI by strength of intermolecular forces, and explain why none of them hydrogen bond.
cards.a: HI > HBr > HCl. None has H bonded to N, O or F, so none hydrogen bonds; each is polar with dipole-dipole forces, but dispersion forces dominate and grow with the larger, more polarizable halogen. HCl has the largest dipole yet the weakest net force (boiling points: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C).
cards.n: 'HCl has the strongest forces because it is most polar' earns nothing; dispersion growth with polarizability outweighs the shrinking dipole here.

cards.q: Identify the strongest type of intermolecular force (hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole, or dispersion only) in a pure sample of each substance: CH₄ · NH₃ · CO₂ · H₂O · HCl · CH₃OH · CH₃OCH₃ · Ne · SO₂ · CH₃COOH · HF · C₆H₁₄ · CH₂Cl₂ · BF₃ · H₂S · CH₃NH₂ · N₂ · CCl₄
cards.a:
CH₄ → London dispersion only (nonpolar)
NH₃ → hydrogen bonding (N–H)
CO₂ → dispersion only (linear, nonpolar)
H₂O → hydrogen bonding (O–H)
HCl → dipole-dipole (Cl is not N, O or F)
CH₃OH → hydrogen bonding (O–H)
CH₃OCH₃ → dipole-dipole (has O but no O–H)
Ne → dispersion only
SO₂ → dipole-dipole (bent, polar)
CH₃COOH → hydrogen bonding (O–H)
HF → hydrogen bonding
C₆H₁₄ → dispersion only
CH₂Cl₂ → dipole-dipole (tetrahedral but unsymmetrical)
BF₃ → dispersion only (trigonal planar, nonpolar)
H₂S → dipole-dipole (S not electronegative enough)
CH₃NH₂ → hydrogen bonding (N–H)
N₂ → dispersion only
CCl₄ → dispersion only (tetrahedral, nonpolar)
cards.h: → H on N/O/F? polar? else dispersion
cards.n: Naming hydrogen bonding for any H-containing molecule (HCl, H₂S, CH₄) earns nothing. All also have dispersion forces, often the larger share. Polarity is borrowed from Unit 2.

cards.q: Identify the strongest attraction between each pair of different species: I₂ and CCl₄ · Na⁺ and H₂O · HCl and H₂O · O₂ and H₂O · NH₃ and H₂O · CH₃OH and CH₃OCH₃ · Cl⁻ and H₂O · He and Ar · K⁺ and NH₃ · CO₂ and H₂O
cards.a:
I₂ and CCl₄ → London dispersion (both nonpolar)
Na⁺ and H₂O → ion-dipole (δ− O of water toward Na⁺)
HCl and H₂O → dipole-dipole (H of HCl is not on N, O or F)
O₂ and H₂O → dipole-induced dipole
NH₃ and H₂O → hydrogen bonding (N–H···O and O–H···N)
CH₃OH and CH₃OCH₃ → hydrogen bonding (methanol's O–H to the ether's O lone pair)
Cl⁻ and H₂O → ion-dipole (δ+ H of water toward Cl⁻)
He and Ar → London dispersion
K⁺ and NH₃ → ion-dipole (N lone pair toward K⁺)
CO₂ and H₂O → dipole-induced dipole
cards.h: → ion present? both polar? H on N/O/F facing a lone pair?
cards.n: 'CH₃OCH₃ cannot hydrogen bond' is true only with itself; its O lone pairs accept a hydrogen bond from methanol's O–H. Say which molecule donates the H.

cards.q: Describe the orientation of two HCl molecules that maximizes their dipole-dipole attraction, and identify the partial charges involved.
cards.a: Cl is more electronegative than H, so each HCl has a δ+ H end and a δ− Cl end. The attraction is strongest head to tail, with the δ+ H of one molecule pointing at the δ− Cl of its neighbor (H–Cl···H–Cl), or side by side antiparallel so that each δ+ lies beside a δ−. The force is Coulombic between the partial charges of DIFFERENT molecules and depends on orientation: two δ+ ends brought together repel.
cards.h: → δ+ toward δ−, head to tail or antiparallel
cards.n: Calling the H–Cl bond the intermolecular force, or drawing the two H ends together, earns nothing; the attraction is between opposite partial charges on separate molecules.

cards.q: Describe two noncovalent interactions that hold a protein in its folded shape, and identify the parts of the molecule involved.
cards.a: Hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O groups of the backbone (and between polar side chains with –OH, –NH₂ or –COOH); London dispersion between nonpolar hydrocarbon side chains clustered in the interior; ion-ion attractions (salt bridges) between –COO⁻ and –NH₃⁺ side chains; dipole-dipole between polar groups. All act between different regions of the same large molecule, and the shape they fix determines the protein's function.
cards.n: Naming the covalent peptide bonds as what holds the fold earns nothing; folding is set by noncovalent interactions between regions of the chain.

cards.q: Explain why H₂O, HF, and NH₃ boil far higher than the trend of their families predicts.
cards.a: Each has H bonded to a small, highly electronegative N, O or F, so its molecules hydrogen bond: the strongly δ+ H is attracted to a lone pair on a neighbor's N, O or F. These attractions are much stronger than the dipole-dipole and dispersion forces in H₂S, HCl or PH₃, so more energy is needed to separate molecules.
cards.h: → H on N/O/F → hydrogen bonds → much stronger attraction → more energy to separate → higher bp
cards.n: 'They are polar' earns nothing, since H₂S and HCl are polar too; the point needs hydrogen bonding named with the H on N, O or F.
o: Down each group dispersion grows with electron count, but the first member gains hydrogen bonding, an attraction strong enough to outweigh that trend.
Vaporization must overcome all intermolecular attractions; hydrogen bonds between the H on N, O or F and a neighbor's lone pair are the strongest such attraction, so these three need the most energy.

w.a: They boil higher because their bonds are stronger and harder to break.
w.why: boiling separates molecules; covalent bonds stay intact

w.a: They boil higher because they are the lightest members of their groups.
w.why: lighter molecules have weaker dispersion forces and should boil lower

w.a: They boil higher because they are polar molecules with dipole-dipole forces.
w.why: H₂S, HCl and PH₃ are polar too; only hydrogen bonding explains the jump

cards.q: Explain why a hydrogen bond is so much stronger than an ordinary dipole-dipole attraction.
cards.a: The H bonded to N, O or F is nearly stripped of electron density, so it carries a large δ+ on a very small atom, while the neighbor's N, O or F lone pair carries a large δ−. Large opposite partial charges that approach very closely give, by Coulomb's law, a much stronger attraction than ordinary dipoles.
cards.h: → large δ+ on a tiny H + lone pair δ− → very close approach → large Coulombic attraction
cards.n: 'It is a bond between hydrogen and oxygen' earns nothing; the hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction between partial charges, not a covalent bond.
o: Coulomb's law: larger partial charges and a shorter distance between the H and the lone pair give a stronger attraction than ordinary dipoles achieve.
N, O and F are the most electronegative small atoms, so the bond to H is extremely polarized and the small H lets the two dipoles get unusually close.

w.a: Hydrogen bonds are stronger because they are covalent bonds between molecules.
w.why: a hydrogen bond is intermolecular and noncovalent; molecules stay intact

w.a: Hydrogen bonds are stronger because hydrogen is the lightest atom.
w.why: mass is irrelevant; the size of the partial charges and their separation matter

w.a: Hydrogen bonds are stronger because they occur in water, which has a high boiling point.
w.why: circular; the boiling point is the consequence, not the cause

cards.q: Explain why I₂ is a solid at room temperature although it is nonpolar, while HCl, a polar molecule, is a gas.
cards.a: I₂ has 106 electrons in a large, easily polarized cloud, so its temporary dipoles are large and its dispersion forces strong enough to hold the molecules in a solid. HCl has only 18 electrons; its weak dispersion forces plus its dipole-dipole attraction are much weaker in total, so it is a gas.
cards.h: → many electrons → high polarizability → strong dispersion in I₂ > weak dispersion + dipole-dipole in HCl
cards.n: 'I₂ is heavier' earns nothing; the point needs more electrons and greater polarizability giving stronger dispersion forces.
o: Dispersion forces are often the strongest net force between large molecules, and I₂ is large; HCl's small dipole cannot match them.
Net attraction = dispersion + dipole-dipole; for I₂ the first term is huge, for HCl both terms are small, so I₂ needs far more energy to separate its molecules.

w.a: I₂ is a solid because it has stronger covalent bonds than HCl.
w.why: the I–I bond is actually weaker than H–Cl, and bonds do not set the state of matter

w.a: I₂ is a solid because iodine molecules are heavier and sink.
w.why: mass is not a force; the scored cause is polarizability and dispersion strength

w.a: HCl is a gas because polar molecules repel each other.
w.why: polar molecules attract through dipole-dipole forces; they are just weaker here

cards.q: Explain why n-pentane boils at 36 °C while its isomer neopentane, 2,2-dimethylpropane, boils at 10 °C.
cards.a: Both are C₅H₁₂ with the same number of electrons and only dispersion forces. The long n-pentane chain lies alongside neighbors over a large contact area, so many temporary dipoles interact; compact, nearly spherical neopentane touches neighbors over a small area, so its dispersion forces are weaker and it boils lower.
cards.h: → same electrons → shape decides contact area → chain has more surface contact → stronger dispersion → higher bp
cards.n: 'n-Pentane has more dispersion forces because it is bigger' earns nothing; the two isomers have the same electrons, the difference is molecular shape and surface contact.
o: At equal electron count, dispersion strength depends on how much of two molecules' surfaces can approach; a chain offers far more than a sphere.
The spherical isomer packs with only point-like contacts, so fewer instantaneous dipoles interact and less energy is needed to separate the molecules.

w.a: n-Pentane boils higher because it has a higher molar mass.
w.why: isomers have identical molar mass

w.a: n-Pentane boils higher because it is polar and neopentane is not.
w.why: both are nonpolar hydrocarbons

w.a: Neopentane boils lower because its branches make it heavier and harder to vaporize.
w.why: contradictory and wrong; branching reduces contact area and lowers the boiling point

cards.q: Explain why nonpolar O₂ molecules are attracted to water molecules at all, even though O₂ has no permanent dipole.
cards.a: Water's permanent dipole distorts the electron cloud of a nearby O₂ molecule, inducing a temporary dipole in it; that induced dipole is then attracted to the water dipole, a dipole-induced dipole force. The attraction is weak, which is why O₂ is only slightly soluble in water.
cards.h: → water's dipole distorts O₂'s cloud → induced dipole → weak Coulombic attraction
cards.n: 'O₂ hydrogen bonds with water' earns nothing; O₂ has no H, and the only attraction is an induced dipole.
o: Any electron cloud is polarizable, so a nearby permanent dipole can induce a dipole in O₂ and attract it weakly.
The attraction exists because water's partial charges create a temporary charge separation in O₂; it is weak, consistent with oxygen's low solubility.

w.a: O₂ is attracted to water because both molecules contain oxygen atoms.
w.why: shared elements do not create forces; the induced dipole does

w.a: O₂ is attracted to water through hydrogen bonding with water's hydrogens.
w.why: hydrogen bonding needs an H on N, O or F attracted to a lone pair; O₂ only accepts an induced dipole

w.a: O₂ is not attracted to water, which is why it does not dissolve.
w.why: oxygen does dissolve slightly, and fish depend on it

cards.q: Contrast the four types of solids by particle, force, melting point, and conductivity.
cards.a: Ionic: cations and anions held by Coulombic attraction; high melting point; conducts only when molten or dissolved. Molecular: molecules held by intermolecular forces; low melting point; never conducts. Covalent network: atoms covalently bonded in a 3-D network or 2-D layers; very high melting point; nonconducting except graphite. Metallic: cations in a sea of delocalized electrons; melting point varies; conducts as solid and liquid; malleable.
cards.n: Melting point alone cannot separate ionic from covalent network; conductivity of the melt is the test that tells them apart.

cards.q: Identify three covalent network solids and explain their very high melting points.
cards.a: Diamond (C), graphite (C), silicon dioxide (SiO₂, quartz) and silicon carbide (SiC); they form only from nonmetals and metalloids. Melting requires breaking a continuous three-dimensional network of strong covalent bonds, not merely overcoming intermolecular forces, so it takes far more energy: SiO₂ melts near 1700 °C and diamond above 3500 °C.
cards.n: 'Strong intermolecular forces' earns nothing here; there are no molecules, the bonds broken on melting are covalent bonds of the network.

cards.q: Predict the type of solid from a data table of melting point and conductivity.
cards.a: High melting point + conducts only when molten or in solution → ionic. Low melting point + never conducts → molecular. Very high melting point + does not conduct as solid or liquid → covalent network. Conducts as a solid (and liquid), malleable → metallic. Water solubility adds a check: ionic solids often dissolve in water, covalent networks essentially never do.
cards.n: Deciding from melting point alone earns nothing; a table row is classified by the combination, and 'conducts when molten' is the ionic fingerprint.

cards.q: Classify each solid as ionic, molecular, covalent network or metallic: NaCl · SiO₂ · Fe · I₂ · diamond · CaF₂ · dry ice (CO₂) · graphite · brass · sucrose · SiC · MgO · Cu · S₈ · KNO₃ · ice · W · polyethylene
cards.a:
NaCl → ionic
SiO₂ → covalent network
Fe → metallic
I₂ → molecular
diamond → covalent network
CaF₂ → ionic
dry ice (CO₂) → molecular
graphite → covalent network (layered)
brass → metallic (Cu–Zn alloy)
sucrose → molecular
SiC → covalent network
MgO → ionic
Cu → metallic
S₈ → molecular
KNO₃ → ionic (K⁺ and polyatomic NO₃⁻)
ice → molecular (H₂O held by hydrogen bonds)
W → metallic
polyethylene → molecular (very large molecules held by dispersion forces)
cards.n: Calling SiO₂ molecular ('it has a formula like CO₂') earns nothing; it is a network of Si–O bonds with no discrete molecules. A polymer is still a molecular solid.

cards.q: Predict which of two substances has the higher boiling point, and justify it.
cards.a: The substance with the stronger intermolecular forces boils higher, because boiling separates the molecules completely and more energy must be supplied to overcome stronger attractions. Decide in two steps: compare the dominant force type first (hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > dispersion at similar size), then, within the same type, compare electron count and polarizability (and contact area). Cite the specific forces of both substances.
cards.n: 'It is heavier so it boils higher' earns nothing unless both substances share the same dominant force and the cause is stated as more electrons and greater polarizability.

cards.q: Contrast intermolecular forces with intramolecular forces during boiling.
cards.a: Intramolecular forces are the covalent bonds WITHIN a molecule; intermolecular forces act BETWEEN molecules. Boiling separates molecules from one another, so it overcomes only the intermolecular forces: water vapor is still H₂O molecules with every O–H bond intact. That is why boiling point and vapor pressure track intermolecular strength, not bond strength.
cards.h: → where each acts + which one is overcome
cards.n: 'Boiling water breaks the O–H bonds' earns nothing; the bonds survive, only the attractions between molecules are overcome.

cards.q: Explain how IMF strength affects vapor pressure, viscosity, and surface tension.
cards.a: Stronger intermolecular forces mean fewer molecules have enough energy to escape the liquid surface, so vapor pressure is LOWER and the boiling point higher. Stronger forces also make molecules resist flowing past one another (higher viscosity) and resist an increase in surface area (higher surface tension). Vapor pressure moves opposite to the other two.
cards.n: Reversing the vapor-pressure direction earns nothing: strong forces hold molecules in the liquid, so volatility is low. Viscosity and surface tension go beyond the EK wording.

cards.q: Predict which has a higher vapor pressure at the same temperature, pentane or octane, and explain.
cards.a: Pentane (C₅H₁₂) has the higher vapor pressure. Both are nonpolar alkanes with only London dispersion forces; octane (C₈H₁₈) has more electrons and a longer chain with more surface contact, so its dispersion forces are stronger. Pentane's weaker attractions let a larger fraction of its molecules escape into the vapor at a given temperature.
cards.n: 'Pentane is lighter' earns nothing; the point is fewer electrons and less contact area giving weaker dispersion forces.

cards.q: Define vapor pressure and state the condition for boiling.
cards.a: Vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapor in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container at a given temperature; it rises with temperature and is higher for liquids with weaker intermolecular forces. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure, so water boils below 100 °C at high altitude where the atmospheric pressure is lower.
cards.n: 'Vapor pressure is the pressure needed to make a liquid boil' earns nothing; it is the pressure of the vapor in equilibrium with the liquid, at any temperature.

cards.q: Describe the electron-sea model of a metallic solid and use it to account for electrical conductivity and malleability.
cards.a: A metal is an array of metal cations (cores) in a sea of delocalized valence electrons shared by the whole lattice. The mobile electrons carry charge (and heat) freely, so the solid conducts. Because the attraction is between the cores and the electron sea rather than between specific atoms, layers of cores can slide to new positions without breaking the bonding, so the metal deforms instead of shattering: it is malleable and ductile.
cards.n: 'Metals conduct because they have many electrons' earns nothing; the point is that the valence electrons are delocalized and free to move.

cards.q: Predict how inserting small carbon atoms between iron atoms (steel, an interstitial alloy) changes the malleability and the electrical conductivity of the metal, and explain.
cards.a: Steel is harder and less malleable than pure iron but still conducts. The interstitial carbon atoms lodge in the gaps of the iron lattice and pin the layers of metal cores so they cannot slide past one another as easily, so the lattice is more rigid and less ductile. The sea of mobile valence electrons remains, so the alloy still conducts electricity.
cards.h: → atoms in the gaps pin the layers; electron sea remains
cards.n: 'The carbon makes the bonds stronger' earns nothing; the scored mechanism is interstitial atoms blocking the sliding of the metal layers.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, particulate diagrams of solid NaCl and of molten NaCl, and use them to explain why only the molten salt conducts electricity.
cards.a: Solid: alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ spheres in a rigid, repeating 3-D lattice, each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge, no ion free to move. Molten: the same Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (no NaCl molecules, no water) in a disordered, close-packed arrangement that can flow. Conduction needs mobile charge carriers: in the solid the ions are locked in place, so no current flows; in the melt the ions migrate toward the electrodes, so it conducts.
cards.h: → two drawings: ions locked vs ions mobile
cards.n: Drawing NaCl molecules in the melt, or explaining the solid's failure to conduct by 'no free electrons', earns nothing; the carriers are ions and the issue is mobility.

cards.q: Identify the noncovalent interaction that holds the two strands of DNA together, and explain why gentle heating separates the strands while each strand stays intact.
cards.a: Hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (two between A and T, three between G and C), reinforced by dispersion forces between stacked bases, hold the strands together. Heating supplies enough energy to overcome these noncovalent interactions, so the strands separate, but far more energy would be needed to break the covalent bonds of the sugar-phosphate backbone within each strand, so the strands remain intact.
cards.h: → name the interaction + noncovalent vs covalent energy
cards.n: 'The strands are covalently bonded to each other' earns nothing; between the strands there are only hydrogen bonds and dispersion forces, which is why mild heat separates them.

cards.q: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
cards.a: In graphite each C bonds to three others in flat sheets, leaving one valence electron per atom delocalized over the sheet and free to move, so it carries current. In diamond each C bonds to four others in a 3-D network, so every valence electron is localized in a bond and none can move.
cards.h: → 3 bonds per C → one delocalized electron per atom → mobile; 4 bonds per C → all localized
cards.n: 'Graphite is softer so electrons move more easily' earns nothing; softness comes from sliding layers, conductivity from the delocalized electron per carbon.
o: Graphite's sp² carbons leave a p electron per atom in a delocalized system over each sheet; diamond's sp³ carbons use every valence electron in localized bonds (hybridization from Unit 2).
Conduction needs mobile charge carriers: graphite has them (delocalized electrons within layers), diamond does not.

w.a: Graphite conducts because its layers are held by weak forces that let electrons pass between them.
w.why: weak interlayer forces explain softness, not conduction; the current flows within a sheet

w.a: Diamond does not conduct because it has no valence electrons.
w.why: each carbon has four valence electrons; they are localized, not absent

w.a: Graphite conducts because it is a metal.
w.why: carbon is a nonmetal forming a covalent network

cards.q: Explain why ionic solids are brittle and shatter when struck, whereas metals bend.
cards.a: In an ionic lattice each ion is surrounded by opposite charges. A blow that shifts one layer brings like charges into line (cation over cation, anion over anion), and their Coulombic repulsion splits the crystal. In a metal the cations sit in an electron sea, so layers slide while the bonding is kept.
cards.h: → layer slips → like charges align → repulsion → fracture; metal: electron sea keeps bonding
cards.n: 'Ionic bonds are strong so the solid cracks' earns nothing; strength explains the high melting point, brittleness needs the like-charge repulsion after a layer slides.
o: Displacing a layer by one ion spacing turns attractions into repulsions between like ions, so the crystal splits along that plane.
Metallic bonding is nondirectional and the electrons move with the cores, so deformation costs little; ionic bonding is charge-alternating, so any slip creates repulsion.

w.a: Ionic solids are brittle because their bonds are weak.
w.why: ionic attractions are strong (high melting points); brittleness is about like-charge repulsion after slipping

w.a: Ionic solids are brittle because the ions are all the same size.
w.why: size is irrelevant; the alternating charges are what matter

w.a: Ionic solids shatter because the electrons leave when the crystal is struck.
w.why: there are no free electrons in an ionic solid; ions, not electrons, are displaced

cards.q: Explain why solid NaCl does not conduct electricity but a solution of NaCl in water does.
cards.a: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. In solid NaCl the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are locked in the lattice by strong Coulombic attractions, so no charge can move. On dissolving, ion-dipole attractions to water separate the ions, and the mobile hydrated ions carry current through the solution.
cards.h: → conduction needs mobile charges → ions fixed in lattice → ions freed by water → conducts
cards.n: 'Solid NaCl has no electrons free to move' earns nothing on its own; the charge carriers are ions, and the point is their mobility in the melt or solution.
o: The lattice holds every ion in place; dissolving (or melting) frees the ions, and mobile ions are what carry the current.
Conductivity tracks ion mobility: none in the rigid solid, high once water molecules surround and separate the ions.

w.a: The solution conducts because water is a good conductor of electricity.
w.why: pure water is a very poor conductor; the dissolved ions carry the current

w.a: Solid NaCl does not conduct because it has no ions until it dissolves.
w.why: the solid is already made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻; they are just immobile

w.a: The solution conducts because dissolving NaCl releases free electrons.
w.why: no electrons are released; the charge carriers are the hydrated ions

cards.q: Explain why molecular solids such as sucrose and ice do not conduct electricity, even when melted.
cards.a: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. A molecular solid is made of neutral molecules whose valence electrons are held in covalent bonds and lone pairs, with no ions present. Melting only lets the neutral molecules move past each other, so there are still no charge carriers.
cards.h: → neutral molecules → electrons localized in bonds and lone pairs → no ions or free electrons → no conduction
cards.n: 'Molecular solids have weak intermolecular forces so they cannot conduct' earns nothing; force strength sets the melting point, the absence of charge carriers sets conductivity.
o: Neither the solid nor its melt contains ions or delocalized electrons, so nothing charged can move under an applied voltage.
Unlike an ionic melt, melting a molecular solid frees molecules, not charges.

w.a: Molecular solids do not conduct because their intermolecular forces are too weak to carry current.
w.why: forces do not carry current; the issue is that no charged particles are mobile

w.a: Molecular solids do not conduct because they have no electrons.
w.why: they have plenty of electrons, all localized in bonds and lone pairs

w.a: Molten sucrose conducts because the molecules can move freely.
w.why: moving neutral molecules carry no charge

cards.q: Explain why boiling point is a more reliable indicator of intermolecular force strength than melting point.
cards.a: Boiling overcomes the intermolecular attractions completely, separating the molecules, so the boiling point tracks their strength directly. Melting only rearranges particles that stay in contact, so the melting point also depends on how well the molecules pack in the crystal, which blurs the link to force strength.
cards.h: → boiling overcomes forces completely; melting only rearranges → packing also matters for mp
cards.n: 'Melting needs less energy so it is less reliable' earns nothing; the point is that melting keeps the particles in contact and depends on crystal packing.
o: Boiling point measures the full cost of separating molecules; melting point mixes in lattice packing and symmetry effects.
Two substances with similar attractions can have very different melting points if one packs into a crystal much better, but their boiling points will be similar.

w.a: Boiling point is more reliable because it is easier to measure than melting point.
w.why: ease of measurement is not the chemical reason

w.a: Melting point is unreliable because covalent bonds break during melting.
w.why: no bonds break in melting; the particles simply become mobile

w.a: Boiling point is more reliable because gases have no intermolecular forces.
w.why: the point is that boiling overcomes them fully, not that they vanish in the gas

cards.q: Identify the six phase changes and state which are endothermic.
cards.a: Melting (fusion, solid → liquid), vaporization (liquid → gas) and sublimation (solid → gas) absorb energy: endothermic, because intermolecular attractions are loosened or overcome. Freezing, condensation and deposition are their reverses and release energy: exothermic. Each pair has enthalpy changes of equal magnitude and opposite sign.
cards.h: → six names sorted by energy sign
cards.n: 'Condensation is endothermic because the gas cools' earns nothing; forming attractions releases energy. Energy signs are Unit 6 content; phase diagrams are not assessed.

cards.q: Identify which parts of a heating curve represent increasing average kinetic energy of the particles, as opposed to increasing potential energy.
cards.a: The sloped segments, where temperature rises, represent increasing average kinetic energy of the particles (Kelvin temperature is proportional to average kinetic energy). The flat plateaus at the melting and boiling points represent increasing potential energy: the added energy loosens or overcomes intermolecular attractions while the average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, stays constant.
cards.h: → slopes = KE rising; plateaus = PE rising
cards.n: 'Temperature is constant so no energy is absorbed' earns nothing; heat is still flowing in during a plateau. Heating curves are Unit 6 content.

cards.q: Contrast a crystalline solid with an amorphous solid at the particle level, using glass as an example of the latter.
cards.a: A crystalline solid (NaCl, ice, quartz) has its particles in a regular, repeating three-dimensional lattice with long-range order, so it melts sharply at one temperature. An amorphous solid such as glass has its particles frozen in a disordered, liquid-like arrangement with no long-range order, so it softens gradually over a range of temperatures. In both, particle motion is limited to vibration and no particle translates past another.
cards.h: → long-range order vs none + melting behavior
cards.n: 'Amorphous solids are liquids that flow very slowly' earns nothing; in an amorphous solid the particles do not translate, they only vibrate about fixed, disordered positions.

cards.q: Represent, in three boxes of equal size, a particulate diagram of one pure substance as a crystalline solid, a liquid and a gas, and state what distinguishes each drawing.
cards.a: Solid: about 12 identical spheres touching in a regular array of rows, in the bottom of the box. Liquid: the same number of spheres, still touching but disordered, filling the bottom with a level surface. Gas: 3–4 spheres far apart, spread through the whole box, with motion arrows. Spacing separates the gas from the condensed phases; order separates solid from liquid; the particles are identical in all three.
cards.n: Drawing liquid particles spread apart earns nothing: liquid and solid particles both touch, only the order differs. A gas drawn as a layer at the bottom also fails.

cards.q: Describe the motion of the particles in a solid, in a liquid and in a gas.
cards.a: Solid: particles vibrate about fixed positions and do not translate past one another (crystalline or amorphous). Liquid: particles in close contact move continually, colliding and sliding past one another, so the liquid flows; their arrangement depends on the strength of the forces between them and on temperature. Gas: particles move constantly and randomly in straight lines between collisions, far apart, with minimal effect of forces between them.
cards.h: → vibrate in place; slide in contact; fly freely
cards.n: 'Particles in a solid do not move' earns nothing; they vibrate. The scored distinction is whether particles translate relative to each other.

cards.q: Estimate the ratio of the molar volume of water vapor at 100 °C and 1.00 atm to the molar volume of liquid water (density 0.96 g/mL at 100 °C), and state what the ratio shows about particle spacing.
cards.a: About 1600 to 1. Liquid: 18.0 g/mol ÷ 0.96 g/mL = 18.8 mL/mol. Vapor, ideal gas: V = nRT/P = (1 mol)(0.08206 L·atm/mol·K)(373 K)/(1.00 atm) = 30.6 L/mol = 30 600 mL/mol. Ratio 30 600/18.8 ≈ 1.6 × 10³. In the liquid the molecules are in contact, so its molar volume is close to the solid's (ice: 19.6 mL/mol); in the gas the spacing is roughly 12 times larger in each direction (∛1600 ≈ 12) and the molecules occupy a tiny fraction of the volume.
cards.n: Using 22.4 L/mol at 100 °C earns nothing for the setup; 22.4 L/mol is the value at 0 °C and 1 atm, so use PV = nRT at 373 K.

cards.q: Predict how the average spacing between the particles of a gas and their collision frequency change when the pressure on the sample is doubled at constant temperature.
cards.a: The volume halves (PV constant), so the same particles are packed into half the space: the average spacing decreases (by a factor of ∛2 ≈ 1.26 in each direction) and the number of collisions per second with the walls and with each other doubles. Average speed is unchanged, since the temperature is unchanged.
cards.h: → V halves → closer spacing → more collisions, same speed
cards.n: 'The particles move faster' earns nothing at constant temperature; only spacing and collision frequency change.

cards.q: Identify which of three particulate diagrams represents a liquid: (A) particles touching in a regular repeating array at the bottom of the box; (B) particles touching but randomly arranged, filling the bottom of the box; (C) a few widely spaced particles spread throughout the box.
cards.a: (B). Liquid particles are in close contact (so they touch and occupy the bottom of the box, like the solid) but have no long-range order and move past one another, so their arrangement is random. (A) is a crystalline solid, ordered and in contact; (C) is a gas, spread out to fill the container with large spaces between particles.
cards.n: Choosing (C) because 'liquids flow' earns nothing; flowing particles stay in contact, only a gas has large gaps.

cards.q: Identify the two factors that determine the structure a solid adopts, and give one example of each.
cards.a: The interparticle interactions and the ability of the particles to pack together. Interactions: hydrogen bonding forces water molecules into an open hexagonal lattice in ice, which is why ice is less dense than liquid water; Coulombic attraction arranges Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in an alternating array. Packing: identical metal atoms or noble-gas atoms pack as close-packed spheres, while irregularly shaped molecules or rapidly cooled melts may fail to order and form an amorphous solid.
cards.n: 'Solids form when particles stop moving' earns nothing; particles in a solid still vibrate, and the scored factors are the interactions and packing.

cards.q: Explain why temperature stays constant during the plateaus of a heating curve.
cards.a: Temperature measures the particles' average kinetic energy. During a phase change the added energy goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions, raising the particles' potential energy as they separate, so the average kinetic energy, and hence the temperature, stays the same until the change is complete.
cards.h: → T measures average KE → added energy raises PE (separating particles) → KE and T unchanged
cards.n: 'No heat is absorbed during the plateau' earns nothing; heat flows in continuously, it just goes into potential energy. Heating curves are Unit 6 content.
o: The energy supplied at the plateau is the enthalpy of fusion or vaporization, spent on loosening or separating particles rather than speeding them up.
Kinetic energy cannot rise until every attraction that must be overcome has been, so the thermometer reads the same throughout the phase change.

w.a: The temperature stays constant because the substance stops absorbing heat during the phase change.
w.why: heat is absorbed throughout; it becomes potential energy

w.a: The temperature stays constant because the covalent bonds are being broken.
w.why: phase changes overcome intermolecular attractions, not covalent bonds

w.a: The temperature stays constant because the particles stop moving while they change phase.
w.why: the particles keep the same average kinetic energy; they do not stop

cards.q: Explain why the molar volume of a liquid is close to that of its solid but hundreds of times smaller than that of its gas.
cards.a: In both solid and liquid the particles are always in close contact, so the volume per mole is set by the particles' own size and changes little on melting. In a gas the particles move freely with minimal attractions and spread through the container, so its molar volume is mostly empty space, hundreds of times larger.
cards.h: → solid and liquid: particles touching → volume ≈ particle size; gas: particles far apart → volume set by container
cards.n: 'Liquids and solids have the same volume because they have the same mass' earns nothing; mass is the same in all three phases, the point is the spacing.
o: Melting rearranges particles without separating them, so the density barely changes; vaporization separates them completely, so the density falls by a factor of about a thousand.
Condensed phases are nearly incompressible because their particles already touch; a gas is mostly empty space.

w.a: Liquids and solids have similar molar volumes because their intermolecular forces are equally strong.
w.why: force strength is not the point; close contact in both phases is

w.a: Gases have a huge molar volume because gas particles are much larger than liquid particles.
w.why: the particles are identical; the spacing between them differs

w.a: Liquids have a small molar volume because their particles are compressed by the atmosphere.
w.why: liquids are barely compressible; their particles simply touch

cards.q: Explain why a gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume, whereas a liquid has a definite volume.
cards.a: Gas particles move constantly and randomly, and the forces between them have minimal effect, so nothing holds them together: they spread to fill any container, taking its shape and volume. Liquid particles also move, but their attractions keep them in close contact, fixing the volume while letting them flow.
cards.h: → constant motion + negligible attractions → spread to fill container; liquid attractions keep contact
cards.n: 'Gases have no volume' earns nothing; a gas has the volume of its container, and the scored reason is negligible attractions plus constant motion.
o: Without attractions strong enough to hold them, moving particles keep going until a wall stops them, so the gas expands to the container's size and shape.
The liquid's attractions win over its particles' motion enough to keep them together; the gas's do not.

w.a: A gas has no definite volume because its particles are so small.
w.why: liquid particles are the same size; the spacing and lack of attraction matter

w.a: A gas takes the shape of its container because gas particles repel each other.
w.why: ideal gas particles neither attract nor repel; they simply move freely

w.a: A liquid has a definite volume because its particles cannot move.
w.why: liquid particles move constantly; attractions keep them in contact

cards.q: State the ideal gas law and the value of R.
cards.a: PV = nRT, with P in atm, V in L, n in mol and T in kelvin, where R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K); with P in torr, R = 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K); in SI energy units R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Temperature must always be in kelvin (K = °C + 273). All three values are on the AP equations sheet.
cards.n: Mixing units earns nothing: match R to the pressure unit in the problem and never put a Celsius temperature into the equation.

cards.q: State the individual gas relationships contained in the ideal gas law.
cards.a: From PV = nRT: at constant n and T, P ∝ 1/V (Boyle); at constant n and P, V ∝ T (Charles); at constant n and V, P ∝ T (Gay-Lussac); at constant P and T, V ∝ n (Avogadro). Each is a case of holding two variables fixed, so P₁V₁/(n₁T₁) = P₂V₂/(n₂T₂) covers them all.
cards.n: Every ratio demands kelvin; a Charles or Gay-Lussac ratio taken with Celsius temperatures earns nothing.

cards.q: Derive an expression for the molar mass of a gas from PV = nRT.
cards.a: M = mRT/(PV), equivalently M = dRT/P. Substitute n = m/M into PV = nRT: PV = (m/M)RT, so M = mRT/(PV); since density d = m/V, M = dRT/P. With R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K), d must be in g/L, P in atm and T in K, and M comes out in g/mol.
cards.h: → substitute n = m/M, rearrange, two forms
cards.n: Leaving density in g/mL with R in L·atm earns nothing; the units must match R, so convert to g/L and atm first.

cards.q: Compute the volume occupied by 2.00 mol of an ideal gas at 1.50 atm and 27 °C.
cards.n: Using 27 K gives 2.95 L and earns nothing; Celsius in a gas-law calculation is the single most common error.

cards.q: State Dalton's law of partial pressures.
cards.a: The total pressure of a mixture of ideal gases is the sum of the partial pressures of its components: P_total = P_A + P_B + P_C + …, where each partial pressure is the pressure that gas would exert alone in the container (P_A = n_A RT/V). It holds because ideal particles do not interact, so each gas's pressure is independent of the others.
cards.h: → sum equation + what each term means
cards.n: 'Each gas exerts the same pressure' earns nothing; each contributes in proportion to its moles, and only the SUM is the total.

cards.q: Define mole fraction and relate it to partial pressure.
cards.a: Mole fraction X_A = n_A / n_total, the moles of A divided by the total moles of gas; it is unitless and the mole fractions of a mixture sum to 1. Because each gas exerts pressure in proportion to its moles, P_A = X_A × P_total.
cards.n: Using mass fraction earns nothing; a mixture that is half oxygen by mass is not half oxygen by moles, and partial pressure follows moles.

cards.q: Apply the correction needed when a gas is collected over water.
cards.a: The collected gas is mixed with water vapor, so by Dalton's law P_gas = P_total − P_H₂O, where P_H₂O is the vapor pressure of water at the collection temperature (given in the problem). Use that corrected partial pressure in PV = nRT to find the moles of the dry gas; the water vapor's share of the pressure is not the gas you want.
cards.n: Using the total pressure earns nothing for the moles: it overstates the amount of gas collected because part of the pressure belongs to water vapor.

cards.q: Compute the total pressure of a mixture containing 0.40 mol $N_2$ and 0.20 mol $O_2$ in a 10.0 L container at 300. K.
cards.a: 1.48 atm. Ideal gases contribute pressure independently, so use the total moles: n = 0.40 + 0.20 = 0.60 mol; P = nRT/V = (0.60 mol)(0.08206 L·atm/mol·K)(300. K)/(10.0 L) = 1.48 atm.
cards.h: → total moles in one PV = nRT
cards.n: Computing each partial pressure and forgetting to add them earns nothing; either route must end at the SUM.

cards.q: Compute the partial pressure of $O_2$ in a 10.0 L container at 300. K holding 0.40 mol $N_2$ and 0.20 mol $O_2$, given a total pressure of 1.48 atm.
cards.n: Using the mass ratio 6.4 g : 11.2 g instead of the mole ratio earns nothing; partial pressures follow moles.

cards.q: $H_2$ gas is collected over water at 25°C; total pressure is 758 mmHg and water's vapor pressure at 25°C is 23.8 mmHg. Compute the partial pressure of dry $H_2$.
cards.a: 734 mmHg. By Dalton's law P_total = P(H₂) + P(H₂O), so P(H₂) = 758 − 23.8 = 734 mmHg (0.966 atm). Only this partial pressure belongs in PV = nRT for the hydrogen.
cards.n: Using 758 mmHg for the hydrogen earns nothing; part of that pressure is water vapor, so the moles of H₂ would be overstated.

cards.q: In $2Al + 6HCl \to 2AlCl_3 + 3H_2$, compute the volume of $H_2$ at STP produced from 5.40 g of Al reacting completely.
cards.h: → grams → mol Al → mol H₂ → PV = nRT
cards.n: Using 22.4 L/mol at any temperature other than 273 K earns nothing; it is a consequence of PV = nRT at STP only. The stoichiometry step is Unit 4 content.

cards.q: Compute the molar mass of a gas if 3.00 g occupies 1.68 L at 1.00 atm and 273 K.
cards.a: 40.0 g/mol. n = PV/RT = (1.00 atm)(1.68 L)/[(0.08206 L·atm/mol·K)(273 K)] = 0.0750 mol; M = m/n = 3.00 g ÷ 0.0750 mol = 40.0 g/mol, consistent with argon.
cards.h: → find n first, then M = m/n
cards.n: Dividing moles by grams (0.025) earns nothing; molar mass is grams PER mole, and a check against the periodic table catches the inversion.

cards.q: Sketch the graph of P versus V for a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant temperature, and the graph of V versus T (in kelvin) at constant pressure; describe each curve and state what it shows.
cards.a: P vs V: axes P (atm) vertical, V (L) horizontal; a downward-curving hyperbola (P = nRT/V) that never touches either axis, steep at small V and flattening at large V, showing P ∝ 1/V. V vs T: axes V (L) vertical, T (K) horizontal; a straight line through the origin with slope nR/P, showing V ∝ T; on a Celsius axis the same line would extrapolate to zero volume at −273 °C. A higher T shifts the P–V curve outward; a higher P lowers the V–T slope.
cards.h: → hyperbola never touching axes; line through origin
cards.n: Drawing P vs V as a straight line with negative slope earns nothing; a linear plot is P vs 1/V. A V–T line that misses the origin on a kelvin axis also earns nothing.

cards.q: Predict the pressure of a gas in a sealed rigid container when its temperature is raised from 27 °C to 127 °C, starting at 2.00 atm, and explain using the ideal gas law.
cards.a: 2.67 atm. With n and V fixed, PV = nRT gives P ∝ T, so P₂ = P₁ × T₂/T₁ = 2.00 atm × (400. K/300. K) = 2.67 atm. The temperatures must be converted to kelvin first (27 + 273 = 300.; 127 + 273 = 400.).
cards.n: Using the Celsius ratio 127/27 gives 9.4 atm and earns nothing; only kelvin is proportional to average kinetic energy.

cards.q: Calculate the mole fraction of each gas and the partial pressure of He in a mixture of 4.00 g He and 28.0 g N₂ that has a total pressure of 3.00 atm.
cards.a: X(He) = X(N₂) = 0.500; P(He) = 1.50 atm. n(He) = 4.00 g ÷ 4.00 g/mol = 1.00 mol; n(N₂) = 28.0 g ÷ 28.0 g/mol = 1.00 mol; each mole fraction = 1.00/2.00 = 0.500. P(He) = X(He) × P_total = 0.500 × 3.00 atm = 1.50 atm (and P(N₂) = 1.50 atm).
cards.n: Taking helium as 4/32 of the mixture by mass (X = 0.125, P = 0.375 atm) earns nothing; partial pressure follows moles, not grams.

cards.q: Calculate the partial pressure of each gas and the total pressure when 2.00 L of N₂ at 1.00 atm and 1.00 L of O₂ at 3.00 atm are both transferred into an evacuated 3.00 L container at the same temperature.
cards.a: P(N₂) = 0.667 atm, P(O₂) = 1.00 atm, P_total = 1.67 atm. Each gas expands into the 3.00 L independently at constant n and T, so P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂: N₂: 1.00 atm × 2.00/3.00 = 0.667 atm; O₂: 3.00 atm × 1.00/3.00 = 1.00 atm. Dalton: P_total = 0.667 + 1.00 = 1.67 atm.
cards.h: → Boyle for each gas, then add
cards.n: Adding 1.00 + 3.00 = 4.00 atm earns nothing; each gas's pressure must first be scaled to the new volume.

cards.q: Explain why the pressure of a fixed amount of gas doubles when its volume is halved at constant temperature.
cards.a: At constant n and T, PV = nRT fixes the product PV, so halving V doubles P. The same particles at the same average speed now occupy half the space, so each reaches a wall twice as often; twice as many collisions per second on the same wall area means twice the force per area, twice the pressure.
cards.h: → PV constant → same particles in half the space → collisions with walls twice as frequent → double P
cards.n: 'The particles move faster' earns nothing at constant temperature; the scored mechanism is more frequent collisions, not harder ones.
o: Pressure is collision force per unit area; concentrating the particles doubles the number hitting each square centimetre each second while each hit is unchanged.
Mathematically P = nRT/V with nRT fixed, so P is inversely proportional to V.

w.a: The pressure doubles because compressing the gas heats the particles and makes them hit harder.
w.why: temperature is held constant in the question; speeds do not change

w.a: The pressure doubles because the particles are squeezed together and repel each other more.
w.why: ideal gas particles do not interact; the effect is collision frequency

w.a: The pressure doubles because half the volume means half the gas escapes.
w.why: the amount of gas is fixed; nothing escapes

cards.q: Explain why the partial pressure of one gas in a mixture is unaffected by the other gases present.
cards.a: Ideal gas particles have negligible volume and neither attract nor repel one another, so each gas's particles strike the walls exactly as if the other gases were absent. Each gas's pressure depends only on its own moles, V and T (P_A = n_A RT/V), and the total is the sum of these contributions.
cards.h: → no interactions → each gas hits the walls as if alone → P_A = n_A RT/V → sum gives total
cards.n: 'Each gas takes up its own part of the container' earns nothing; every gas fills the whole volume, and the point is the absence of interactions.
o: Wall collisions by A particles are set by how many A particles there are and how fast they move; B particles neither block nor help them, so P_A is independent of B.
Dalton's law follows from PV = nRT applied to each gas separately, which is legitimate because the particles ignore each other.

w.a: The partial pressure of a gas is unaffected because each gas occupies its own region of the container.
w.why: gases mix uniformly; each fills the entire volume

w.a: The partial pressure of a gas is unaffected because all gases have the same molar mass at the same temperature.
w.why: nonsense; molar mass differs and is irrelevant to partial pressure

w.a: The partial pressure is unaffected because gases at the same temperature all exert the same pressure.
w.why: pressure depends on moles; only the mechanism (no interactions) is independent

cards.q: Explain why temperature must be expressed in kelvin, not degrees Celsius, in any gas-law calculation.
cards.a: Kelvin temperature is proportional to average kinetic energy: 0 K corresponds to zero, and doubling the kelvin temperature doubles the average kinetic energy and the pressure. Celsius has an arbitrary zero (water's freezing point), so Celsius ratios are meaningless: 400 K is twice 200 K, but 20 °C is not twice 10 °C.
cards.h: → T(K) ∝ average KE → zero of scale is physical → ratios meaningful only in kelvin
cards.n: 'Because the formula says so' or 'because Celsius can be negative' earns nothing; the point is that only kelvin is proportional to kinetic energy.
o: PV = nRT is a proportionality between P (or V) and T, and a proportionality needs a scale whose zero means zero motion, which Celsius does not have.
A Charles's-law plot of V against T is a line through the origin only on the kelvin axis; on a Celsius axis it crosses zero volume at −273 °C.

w.a: Kelvin must be used because gas-law problems always involve high temperatures.
w.why: the scale, not the size, of the temperature is the issue

w.a: Kelvin must be used because the gas constant R was measured in kelvin.
w.why: R's units follow from the physics; the physics is that T(K) is proportional to kinetic energy

w.a: Kelvin must be used because Celsius temperatures can be negative and pressure cannot.
w.why: a true observation but not the reason; the scored point is proportionality to average kinetic energy

cards.q: Explain why equal volumes of any two ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules, regardless of the identity of the gases.
cards.a: The identity of the gas does not appear in PV = nRT: at one temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy per particle, and ideal particles neither interact nor take up volume, so pressure depends only on how many particles hit the walls. Fixing P, V and T therefore fixes n = PV/RT for any gas.
cards.h: → identity absent from PV = nRT → same average KE per particle, no interactions → n = PV/RT for any gas
cards.n: 'Because all gas molecules are the same size' earns nothing; molecules differ in size, but in an ideal gas their size and mass do not affect the pressure.
o: Heavier molecules move more slowly but hit harder, and the two effects cancel exactly, so the pressure per particle is the same for every gas at a given temperature.
Avogadro's hypothesis is PV = nRT read at fixed P, V and T: n is the same for every ideal gas.

w.a: Equal volumes hold equal molecules because all gases have the same density.
w.why: densities differ (d = PM/RT); it is the molecule count, not the mass, that matches

w.a: Equal volumes hold equal molecules because gas molecules all move at the same speed.
w.why: speeds differ with mass; average kinetic energy is what matches

w.a: Equal volumes hold equal molecules because one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L.
w.why: true only at STP and it restates the claim rather than explaining it

cards.q: State the postulates of kinetic molecular theory for an ideal gas.
cards.a: 1) The volume of the particles themselves is negligible compared with the volume of the container. 2) Particles are in constant, random, straight-line motion. 3) Collisions with each other and the walls are elastic: no net kinetic energy is lost. 4) There are no attractive or repulsive forces between particles. 5) The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the kelvin temperature and is the same for every gas at that temperature.
cards.n: Omitting 'average' in postulate 5 loses the point, since individual particles have a range of energies. Postulates 1 and 4 are the ones real gases break.

cards.q: State how average kinetic energy of gas particles depends on the gas identity and temperature.
cards.a: Average kinetic energy depends ONLY on the kelvin temperature: it is proportional to T and independent of the identity or molar mass of the gas. At the same temperature He and Xe have the same average kinetic energy; because KE = ½mv², the lighter gas must have the higher average speed to make up for its smaller mass.
cards.h: → what it depends on and what it does not
cards.n: 'Same temperature means same average speed' earns nothing; only the average kinetic energy is equal, and speed scales as 1/√m.

cards.q: Explain how a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution changes when temperature increases.
cards.a: The peak shifts to higher speed (or energy) and becomes lower, and the curve broadens with a longer high-speed tail, because the average kinetic energy rises and the speeds spread over a wider range. The total area under the curve is unchanged, since it represents the fixed number of particles in the sample; the fraction of particles above any given energy increases.
cards.h: → three changes to the curve + what stays fixed
cards.n: Drawing the hotter curve taller or with the same peak position earns nothing; higher T means a lower, broader curve shifted right with the same area.

cards.q: Contrast the Maxwell-Boltzmann curves of two gases with different molar masses at the same temperature.
cards.a: The lighter gas has the broader curve, peaked at a higher speed with a lower peak height and a longer high-speed tail; the heavier gas has the narrower, taller curve peaked at a lower speed. Both distributions have the same area (same number of particles) and correspond to the same average kinetic energy, since KE = ½mv² and the larger mass pairs with the smaller speed.
cards.h: → which curve is where + the shared quantity
cards.n: Saying the heavier gas has less kinetic energy earns nothing; at one temperature the average kinetic energies are identical and only the speeds differ.

cards.q: State the equation for root-mean-square speed of a gas.
cards.a: u_rms = √(3RT/M), with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T in kelvin and M the molar mass in kg/mol, so the speed comes out in m/s. It follows from KE_avg = ½m(u_rms)² = (3/2)kT: speed rises with √T and falls with 1/√M. For N₂ at 298 K, u_rms = √(3 × 8.314 × 298/0.0280) = 515 m/s.
cards.n: Using g/mol with R in joules gives a speed too large by √1000 and earns nothing. The equation itself is not on the AP sheet; only KE = ½mv² and the proportionality are needed.

cards.q: Predict the relative average speeds of He and O₂ at the same temperature.
cards.a: He moves faster, by a factor of √(32.0/4.00) = √8.00 ≈ 2.8. At the same temperature both gases have the same average kinetic energy, ½mv², so v ∝ 1/√m: the gas with one-eighth the molar mass has √8 times the average speed.
cards.n: Answering '8 times faster' (the mass ratio without the square root) earns nothing; equal kinetic energy means the ratio of speeds is the square root of the inverse mass ratio.

cards.q: Compute the ratio of root-mean-square speeds of $H_2$ to $O_2$ at the same temperature.
cards.a: 4.00. Equal temperature means equal average kinetic energy: ½m(H₂)v(H₂)² = ½m(O₂)v(O₂)², so v(H₂)/v(O₂) = √[M(O₂)/M(H₂)] = √(32.0/2.02) = √15.8 ≈ 3.98 ≈ 4.00. H₂ molecules move about four times faster than O₂ molecules on average.
cards.h: → square root of the inverse mass ratio
cards.n: Inverting the fraction (√(2/32) = 0.25) earns nothing for the direction; the lighter gas is faster, and the ratio is √16, not 16.

cards.q: Identify what the total area under a Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution curve represents.
cards.a: The total number of particles in the sample (or the total fraction, 1, if the curve is normalized). Because the number of particles is fixed, the area stays constant when the temperature changes: a hotter sample's curve is lower and broader, not larger. The area between two speeds is the number (or fraction) of particles with speeds in that range.
cards.h: → area = particle count, unaffected by T
cards.n: Drawing the high-temperature curve with visibly more area earns nothing; the sample size does not change with temperature.

cards.q: Sketch Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions for a sample of N₂ at 300 K and at 600 K on one set of axes, labeling the axes and describing how the two curves differ.
cards.a: Horizontal axis: molecular speed (m/s) or kinetic energy; vertical axis: number (or fraction) of molecules. Each curve starts at the origin, rises to a single peak and falls with a long tail to the right (skewed). The 600 K curve has its peak at a higher speed (about √2 ≈ 1.4 times farther right), is lower at the peak, is broader, and its tail extends farther right; the two curves enclose the same area. Label each curve with its temperature.
cards.h: → skewed hump; hotter = right, lower, wider, same area
cards.n: A symmetric bell, a hotter curve that is taller, or curves of unequal area each earn nothing; the peak position scales with √T, and the area is the fixed particle count.

cards.q: Calculate the kinetic energy of one N₂ molecule (mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) moving at 515 m/s, and state how the average kinetic energy of the sample would change if the temperature were doubled.
cards.a: 6.17 × 10⁻²¹ J. KE = ½mv² = ½(4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg)(515 m/s)² = ½(4.65 × 10⁻²⁶)(2.65 × 10⁵) = 6.17 × 10⁻²¹ J (1 kg·m²/s² = 1 J). Average kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature, so doubling T doubles the average kinetic energy (and multiplies average speed by √2).
cards.h: → ½mv² with SI units, then KE ∝ T
cards.n: Using the molar mass 28.0 g in ½mv² earns nothing; the mass must be that of one molecule in kg to give joules per molecule.

cards.q: Identify which curve on a Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution at 300 K belongs to Ne and which to Xe: curve 1 peaks at a lower speed and is taller and narrower; curve 2 peaks at a higher speed and is broader with a longer tail. Justify the assignment.
cards.a: Curve 1 is Xe; curve 2 is Ne. At the same temperature both gases have the same average kinetic energy, ½mv², so the heavier Xe (131 g/mol) must have the lower average speed and the lighter Ne (20.2 g/mol) the higher one; the Ne speeds are also spread over a wider range, giving the broader, lower curve. The two curves enclose the same area if the samples have the same number of atoms.
cards.h: → equal KE → heavier peaks at lower speed
cards.n: Assigning the taller curve to Ne 'because lighter atoms are faster so more reach the peak' earns nothing; taller and narrower belongs to the slower, heavier gas.

cards.q: Predict, using kinetic molecular theory, how the pressure of a gas in a rigid container changes when the temperature is raised, and identify two changes in the wall collisions that cause it.
cards.a: The pressure rises. Raising the temperature raises the average kinetic energy and so the average speed of the particles, so (1) each particle reaches the walls more often, and (2) each collision transfers more momentum, a harder push. More frequent and more forceful collisions on the same wall area give a greater force per area, and with V and n fixed, P ∝ T.
cards.h: → faster particles → more frequent and harder collisions
cards.n: Naming only 'more collisions' earns half at most; at higher temperature the collisions are both more frequent and more forceful, and the container's volume does not change.

cards.q: Compare the average speed of N₂ molecules at 1200 K with that at 300 K, and state the ratio of their average kinetic energies.
cards.a: The average speed at 1200 K is twice that at 300 K, and the average kinetic energy is 4 times as large. Average kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature, so KE(1200)/KE(300) = 1200/300 = 4; since KE = ½mv² for the same molecules, v ∝ √KE ∝ √T, and √4 = 2.
cards.n: Answering 'four times faster' earns nothing; the energy quadruples but the speed only doubles.

cards.q: Describe what a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows: the quantity on each axis, the meaning of the peak, and why the curve is not symmetric.
cards.a: Horizontal axis: particle speed (or kinetic energy); vertical axis: number or fraction of particles at that speed. The peak is the most probable speed; the average speed lies slightly to its right. The curve is skewed because speeds cannot fall below zero but have no upper limit, so a few particles form a long high-speed tail: a sample at one temperature holds particles with many different energies.
cards.h: → axes, peak = most probable, long right tail
cards.n: 'All particles at a given temperature have the same kinetic energy' earns nothing; the temperature fixes the average, and the distribution shows the spread.

cards.q: Explain the origin of gas pressure in terms of kinetic molecular theory.
cards.a: Gas pressure is the force per unit area from the particles' constant collisions with the container walls. Each collision transfers momentum to the wall; countless collisions per second add up to a steady force. More particles, a smaller volume or a higher temperature raise the collision rate or force, and so raise P.
cards.h: → particles in constant motion → collide with walls → momentum transfer → force per area
cards.n: 'Pressure comes from the weight of the gas' or 'from particles pushing on each other' earns nothing; the scored mechanism is wall collisions.
o: Every wall collision delivers an impulse; summed over the enormous number of collisions each second, the impulses become a continuous force on the wall, and force per area is pressure.
KMT postulates constant random motion and elastic collisions; the walls feel those collisions as pressure.

w.a: Gas pressure comes from the gas particles repelling each other and pushing outward.
w.why: ideal gas particles do not interact; pressure comes from wall collisions

w.a: Gas pressure is the weight of the gas pressing down on the bottom of the container.
w.why: pressure acts equally on all walls, including the top; it is collisional

w.a: Gas pressure is caused by the heat energy stored in the gas.
w.why: vague; the mechanism is momentum transfer in collisions

cards.q: Explain why He and O₂ at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy but different average speeds.
cards.a: Kelvin temperature is proportional to average kinetic energy for any gas, so at one temperature He and O₂ have equal average ½mv². An O₂ molecule has 8 times the mass of a He atom, so its average v² must be 8 times smaller: O₂ moves at about 1/√8, roughly a third, of helium's average speed.
cards.h: → T fixes average KE → KE = ½mv² → same KE with larger m needs smaller v
cards.n: 'Heavier gases have less kinetic energy at the same temperature' earns nothing; the energies are equal by definition of temperature.
o: Temperature is a statement about average kinetic energy, not speed; the speed follows from the mass through KE = ½mv².
Equal ½mv² with m(O₂) = 8 m(He) forces v(He)/v(O₂) = √8 ≈ 2.8.

w.a: They have different speeds because oxygen molecules are polar and slow down.
w.why: O₂ is nonpolar, and polarity does not enter KMT for an ideal gas

w.a: They have the same speed because they are at the same temperature.
w.why: temperature fixes the average kinetic energy, not the speed

w.a: Helium has more kinetic energy because it moves faster.
w.why: its higher speed exactly compensates its smaller mass; the energies are equal

cards.q: Explain why the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at a higher temperature is lower and broader rather than simply shifted to the right.
cards.a: The area under the curve is the number of particles, which heating does not change. At the higher temperature the speeds spread over a wider range, with a longer fast tail, so the same area is distributed over more speeds; to keep that area fixed, the curve must be lower at its peak as it widens.
cards.h: → area = fixed particle count → wider spread of speeds at higher T → same area over more speeds → lower peak
cards.n: 'The curve gets lower because fewer particles are present at high temperature' earns nothing; the count is fixed, the spread is what widens.
o: Heating raises the average energy and the variety of energies; spreading a fixed number of particles over more speeds necessarily flattens the peak.
Constant area under a wider curve means a lower maximum; the peak also moves right because the most probable speed rises with √T.

w.a: The curve is lower at high temperature because some particles escape the container.
w.why: the sample is closed; the particle count is constant

w.a: The curve is lower because fast particles have less kinetic energy.
w.why: faster particles have more kinetic energy, not less

w.a: The curve simply shifts to the right because every particle speeds up by the same amount.
w.why: speeds spread out, they do not shift uniformly, and the area constraint forces a lower peak

cards.q: Explain why, at the same n, V and T, a container of Xe exerts the same pressure as a container of He even though Xe atoms are 33 times heavier.
cards.a: Pressure is momentum delivered to the walls per unit time. At the same temperature both gases have the same average kinetic energy, so the heavy Xe atoms move more slowly: they reach the walls less often, but each hit carries more momentum. The effects cancel, so the pressures are equal; mass is absent from PV = nRT.
cards.h: → same average KE → Xe slower but heavier → fewer collisions × more momentum each → same pressure
cards.n: 'Xe exerts more pressure because it is heavier' or 'He exerts more because it is faster' each earn nothing; the compensation between speed and mass is the point.
o: Momentum per collision scales with m·v while collision frequency scales with v, so the product m·v² per particle is what sets pressure, and that is fixed by temperature.
The ideal gas law contains n, not m: only the number of particles and their average kinetic energy matter for pressure.

w.a: Xe exerts more pressure because its heavier atoms hit the walls harder.
w.why: they hit harder but less often; the effects cancel

w.a: He exerts more pressure because its atoms move faster and hit the walls more often.
w.why: more often but more gently; the effects cancel

w.a: The pressures are equal because both gases have the same average speed at the same temperature.
w.why: the average kinetic energies are equal, the speeds are not

cards.q: Explain the two conditions under which a real gas deviates most from ideal behavior.
cards.a: High pressure and low temperature. At high pressure the particles are crowded, so their own volume is no longer negligible: the free space is less than V and PV/nRT rises above 1. At low temperature, near condensation, the slow particles feel intermolecular attractions that pull them back from the walls, so the pressure is lower than ideal and PV/nRT falls below 1. Gases are most ideal at low P and high T.
cards.h: → two conditions, each with its cause and its direction
cards.n: Naming 'high pressure and low temperature' without saying particle volume for one and attractions for the other earns nothing; the conditions alone are not the reasoning.

cards.q: Explain the effect of intermolecular attractions on the measured pressure of a real gas.
cards.a: Attractions make the measured pressure LOWER than PV = nRT predicts. A molecule moving toward the wall is pulled back by its neighbors, so it strikes the wall less often and with less force than an ideal particle would. The effect is largest when the molecules are slow (low temperature) and close together (moderate to high pressure), near the conditions at which the gas condenses; the ratio PV/nRT then falls below 1.
cards.h: → direction of the error + collision mechanism
cards.n: 'Attractions make the molecules stick together so the volume is smaller' earns nothing for a pressure question; the scored mechanism is softer, less frequent wall collisions.

cards.q: Explain the effect of finite particle volume on a real gas at very high pressure.
cards.a: The molecules themselves occupy a significant fraction of the container, so the empty space available for them to move in is less than the measured volume V. The gas is therefore harder to compress than an ideal gas and its pressure is higher than PV = nRT predicts for that V: the ratio PV/nRT rises above 1. This effect dominates only at very high pressure, when the free volume becomes comparable to the particle volume.
cards.h: → direction of the error + free-volume mechanism
cards.n: 'The particles are bigger at high pressure' earns nothing; the particle volume is constant, what shrinks is the free space around them.

cards.q: Identify which gases deviate most from ideal behavior and why.
cards.a: Gases with strong intermolecular attractions deviate most: polar and especially hydrogen-bonding molecules (H₂O, NH₃), and large, highly polarizable molecules (Cl₂, CO₂, SF₆), whose strong dispersion forces and larger particle volumes both matter. Small, barely polarizable gases (He, H₂, Ne) behave most ideally. A high boiling point is a quick proxy: the easier a gas is to liquefy, the more it deviates.
cards.h: → two categories of deviant gases + the ideal ones
cards.n: 'Heavy gases deviate more' earns nothing; the causes are stronger attractions (polarity, hydrogen bonding, polarizability) and larger particle volume.

cards.q: Explain what a measured compressibility factor Z less than 1 indicates about a real gas.
cards.a: Z = PV/nRT < 1 means the gas's PV product is smaller than ideal: at the measured V the pressure is lower than PV = nRT predicts (or at the measured P the gas occupies less volume). Intermolecular attractions are pulling molecules back from the walls, softening wall collisions, and this effect outweighs the finite-volume effect. Z = 1 is ideal behavior, and Z > 1 means the particle volume effect dominates.
cards.n: 'Z < 1 means the gas is smaller than ideal' earns nothing without naming the attractions that lower the pressure.

cards.q: Interpret a graph of PV/nRT (vertical axis) against pressure (horizontal axis, 0 to 800 atm) for one mole of a real gas at 300 K: the curve starts at 1.00 near 0 atm, falls to a minimum of 0.80 at about 150 atm, rises back through 1.00 at about 350 atm and reaches 1.50 at 800 atm. Identify the cause of the dip and of the rise, and describe how the curve for He would differ.
cards.a: Near 0 atm the molecules are far apart, so the gas is ideal (1.00). The dip below 1 is caused by intermolecular attractions: at moderate pressure the molecules are close enough that neighbors pull them back from the walls, lowering the pressure. The rise above 1 is caused by the molecules' own volume, which dominates once the gas is highly compressed. He, with almost no attractions, shows little or no dip and rises above 1 from low pressure.
cards.n: Attributing the dip to particle volume, or describing the shape without a cause for each feature, earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the postulate of kinetic molecular theory that fails when a gas is compressed to very high pressure, and the one that fails as the gas is cooled toward its condensation point.
cards.a: At very high pressure the postulate that the particles' own volume is negligible compared with the container fails: the molecules occupy a large fraction of the space, so the free volume is less than V. As the gas is cooled toward condensation the postulate that there are no attractive forces between particles fails: the slow-moving molecules are pulled toward one another, which lowers the wall pressure and, at the condensation point, holds them together as a liquid.
cards.h: → negligible volume fails; no attractions fails
cards.n: Citing 'elastic collisions' or 'random motion' as the failing postulate earns nothing; the two that break are negligible particle volume and no attractions.

cards.q: Predict whether the pressure calculated from PV = nRT for 1.00 mol of CO₂ in a 1.00 L container at 300. K (24.6 atm) will be higher or lower than the measured pressure, and justify the prediction.
cards.a: The calculated 24.6 atm is HIGHER than the measured pressure (about 22 atm). At 1 mol/L and 300 K, CO₂ molecules are close together and CO₂ is easily liquefied, so their dispersion attractions are significant: a molecule heading for the wall is pulled back by its neighbors and hits less often and less hard. The finite volume of CO₂ raises the pressure, but at this density that effect is smaller than the attractions.
cards.h: → ideal P too high; attractions soften collisions
cards.n: 'Real gases always exceed the ideal pressure because molecules have volume' earns nothing; here attractions dominate. The 22 atm is a van der Waals estimate.

cards.q: Predict whether $NH_3$ or $CH_4$ deviates more from ideal gas behavior at the same temperature and pressure, and explain.
cards.a: NH₃ deviates more.
