Its molecules hydrogen bond (H on N attracted to a neighbor's N lone pair), far stronger than the weak dispersion forces between nonpolar CH₄ molecules, so NH₃ molecules are pulled back from the walls more and its pressure falls further below ideal. Their masses (17, 16 g/mol) are nearly equal.
cards.h: → NH₃ hydrogen bonds → stronger attractions → pressure further below ideal
cards.n: 'NH₃ is heavier' earns nothing (they are nearly equal); the point needs hydrogen bonding named as the stronger attraction.
o: NH₃ condenses at −33 °C and CH₄ at −161 °C; the gas nearer its condensation point has the stronger attractions and deviates more.
Deviation from ideality below Z = 1 scales with intermolecular attraction, and hydrogen bonding in NH₃ far exceeds CH₄'s dispersion forces.

w.a: CH₄ deviates more because it has more hydrogen atoms and therefore more hydrogen bonding.
w.why: C–H hydrogens cannot hydrogen bond; CH₄ is nonpolar

w.a: They deviate equally because their molar masses are almost the same.
w.why: mass is not the cause; the type of intermolecular force is

w.a: NH₃ deviates more because its molecules are larger and take up more space.
w.why: the sizes are similar; the scored cause is hydrogen bonding, not particle volume

cards.q: Predict which gas deviates more from ideal behavior at high pressure: He or $Cl_2$, and explain.
cards.a: Cl₂ deviates more. Its 34 electrons make it far more polarizable than He (2 electrons), so its dispersion attractions are much stronger and pull molecules back from the walls; and each Cl₂ molecule is much larger, so at high pressure its own volume takes a bigger share of the container. Tiny He stays nearly ideal.
cards.h: → Cl₂: more electrons → stronger dispersion, plus larger volume → both deviations bigger
cards.n: 'Cl₂ is heavier' earns nothing; name more electrons and polarizability (attractions) and the larger particle volume.
o: Both sources of non-ideality, attractions and particle volume, are larger for Cl₂, so whichever dominates at the given pressure, Cl₂ is further from Z = 1.
Cl₂ liquefies at −34 °C under 1 atm while He needs 4 K; the gas that is easier to condense has the stronger attractions.

w.a: He deviates more because its atoms move faster and collide with the walls more violently.
w.why: speed is set by temperature and is not a source of non-ideality

w.a: Cl₂ deviates more because it is a polar molecule with dipole-dipole forces.
w.why: Cl₂ is nonpolar; its attractions are dispersion forces

w.a: They deviate equally because both are nonpolar with only dispersion forces.
w.why: dispersion strength differs enormously with electron count

cards.q: Explain why a real gas behaves more ideally as its temperature is raised at constant pressure.
cards.a: Heating raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Once it is large compared with the energy of attraction, a molecule approaching the wall is barely slowed by its neighbors, so attractions hardly affect the pressure. Heating at constant P also expands the gas, making particle volume a smaller share of V.
cards.h: → higher T → KE ≫ attraction energy → attractions negligible → PV/nRT → 1
cards.n: 'Hot gases have no intermolecular forces' earns nothing; the forces are still there, they are simply overwhelmed by the kinetic energy.
o: Attractions matter only when molecules linger near each other; fast molecules fly past too quickly for a weak attraction to change their momentum much.
The KMT postulate 'no attractions' becomes a good approximation once kinetic energy dwarfs the attraction energy, which is what heating achieves.

w.a: Hot gases are ideal because heating breaks the intermolecular forces permanently.
w.why: attractions are not broken; they just become negligible next to kinetic energy

w.a: Hot gases are ideal because the molecules expand and become lighter.
w.why: molecules do not change size or mass with temperature

w.a: Hot gases are ideal because higher temperature raises the pressure to the ideal value.
w.why: the pressure rises for any gas; the point is the ratio of kinetic to attraction energy

cards.q: Explain why every real gas approaches ideal behavior as its pressure approaches zero.
cards.a: At very low pressure the molecules are, on average, very far apart. Their own volume becomes a negligible fraction of the container, and they are rarely close enough for attractions to act, so both KMT assumptions, negligible particle volume and no attractions, hold, and PV/nRT → 1 for every gas.
cards.h: → low P → large spacing → particle volume negligible and attractions rarely act → both KMT assumptions hold
cards.n: 'At low pressure there are fewer molecules so fewer errors' earns nothing; the point is the large spacing making both volume and attractions negligible.
o: Attractions fall off steeply with distance and the excluded volume is fixed, so a dilute gas satisfies both ideal assumptions.
The PV/nRT curves of all gases converge on 1 at the low-pressure end of the graph because their molecules are effectively isolated there.

w.a: Gases are ideal at low pressure because the molecules stop moving.
w.why: they move just as fast; they are simply far apart

w.a: Gases are ideal at low pressure because low pressure means low temperature.
w.why: pressure and temperature are independent variables here

w.a: Gases are ideal at low pressure because there are too few molecules to exert intermolecular forces.
w.why: fewer molecules is not the reason; the greater distance between them is

cards.q: Define molarity and give its equation.
cards.a: Molarity (M) is the number of moles of solute per liter of SOLUTION: M = n(solute) / V(solution in L), in mol/L, written M. The volume is the final volume of the whole solution, so 1.00 M means 1.00 mol of solute dissolved and diluted to a total of 1.00 L, not 1.00 mol added to 1.00 L of solvent. It is the most common way to express concentration in the laboratory.
cards.n: Using the volume of solvent added instead of the final solution volume earns nothing. Molality and percent by mass or volume are not assessed on the AP exam.

cards.q: Apply the dilution equation and state what it assumes.
cards.a: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, where 1 is the concentrated stock and 2 the diluted solution. It assumes the moles of solute do not change: adding solvent increases the volume but adds or removes no solute, so n = M₁V₁ before equals n = M₂V₂ after. Any volume unit works if both volumes use it, and V₂ is the final total volume, not the volume of water added.
cards.n: Taking V₂ as the water added earns nothing: 10.0 mL of stock diluted with 90.0 mL of water has V₂ = 100.0 mL, not 90.0 mL.

cards.q: Compute the concentration of each ion in 0.20 M CaCl₂.
cards.a: [Ca²⁺] = 0.20 M and [Cl⁻] = 0.40 M. CaCl₂ is a soluble ionic compound that dissociates completely, CaCl₂(s) → Ca²⁺(aq) + 2 Cl⁻(aq), so each liter holds 0.20 mol Ca²⁺ and 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 mol Cl⁻, a total ion concentration of 0.60 M.
cards.n: Giving [Cl⁻] = 0.20 M by ignoring the subscript earns nothing, and so does writing the chloride as Cl₂; it is released as two separate Cl⁻ ions.

cards.q: State how to prepare 500.0 mL of 0.250 M NaCl from solid.
cards.a: Weigh out 7.31 g of NaCl: n = 0.250 mol/L × 0.5000 L = 0.125 mol, and 0.125 mol × 58.44 g/mol = 7.31 g. Transfer it to a 500.0 mL volumetric flask, dissolve it in about half that volume of distilled water, then add water until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the calibration mark; stopper and invert to mix.
cards.n: Adding the solid to 500.0 mL of water earns nothing, since the final volume would then exceed 500.0 mL; a beaker cannot deliver the four significant figures asked for.

cards.q: Compute the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.500 mol of NaOH in enough water to make 2.00 L of solution.
cards.a: 0.250 M. M = n/V = 0.500 mol ÷ 2.00 L = 0.250 mol/L. The 2.00 L is the volume of the finished solution, which is exactly the volume molarity requires.
cards.n: Inverting the ratio (4.00 L/mol) or dropping the unit M earns nothing; molarity is moles on top, liters of solution underneath.

cards.q: Compute the final volume needed to dilute 50.0 mL of 6.00 M HCl down to 0.500 M.
cards.a: 600. mL. V₂ = M₁V₁/M₂ = (6.00 M)(50.0 mL)/(0.500 M) = 600. mL of final solution, so 550. mL of water is added to the 50.0 mL of stock. The 0.300 mol of HCl is unchanged; a twelvefold increase in volume gives a twelvefold drop in concentration.
cards.n: Answering 550 mL confuses the water added with the final volume the question asks for.

cards.q: Compute the molarity after mixing 100. mL of 0.300 M HCl with 200. mL of 0.150 M HCl.
cards.a: 0.200 M. Moles add, concentrations do not: n = (0.100 L)(0.300 M) + (0.200 L)(0.150 M) = 0.0300 + 0.0300 = 0.0600 mol HCl in V = 0.100 + 0.200 = 0.300 L (volumes of dilute aqueous solutions are taken as additive), so M = 0.0600 mol ÷ 0.300 L = 0.200 M.
cards.n: Averaging 0.300 and 0.150 to get 0.225 M earns nothing; it ignores the unequal volumes. Only moles add.

cards.q: Calculate the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 11.7 g of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) in water and diluting to a final volume of 250.0 mL.
cards.a: 0.801 M. n = 11.7 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol = 0.2002 mol NaCl; V = 250.0 mL = 0.2500 L; M = 0.2002 mol ÷ 0.2500 L = 0.801 M, three significant figures as set by 11.7 g.
cards.h: → grams → moles, mL → L, then divide
cards.n: Dividing grams by liters (46.8 g/L) or by 250.0 instead of 0.2500 L earns nothing; convert mass to moles and mL to L first.

cards.q: Calculate the number of chloride ions in 25.0 mL of 0.150 M AlCl₃ solution.
cards.a: 6.77 × 10²¹ Cl⁻ ions. n(AlCl₃) = 0.0250 L × 0.150 mol/L = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol; each AlCl₃ releases 3 Cl⁻, so n(Cl⁻) = 1.125 × 10⁻² mol; × 6.022 × 10²³ ions/mol = 6.77 × 10²¹ ions.
cards.n: Stopping at formula units (2.26 × 10²¹) earns nothing; the question asks for chloride ions, three per AlCl₃.

cards.q: Determine the concentration of each ion (or of the dissolved molecules) in: 0.10 M Na₂SO₄ · 0.30 M Al(NO₃)₃ · 0.050 M (NH₄)₂SO₄ · 0.15 M MgCl₂ · 0.20 M KMnO₄ · 0.40 M C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) · 0.12 M Al₂(SO₄)₃ · 0.25 M Ca(NO₃)₂
cards.a:
0.10 M Na₂SO₄ → [Na⁺] = 0.20 M, [SO₄²⁻] = 0.10 M
0.30 M Al(NO₃)₃ → [Al³⁺] = 0.30 M, [NO₃⁻] = 0.90 M
0.050 M (NH₄)₂SO₄ → [NH₄⁺] = 0.10 M, [SO₄²⁻] = 0.050 M
0.15 M MgCl₂ → [Mg²⁺] = 0.15 M, [Cl⁻] = 0.30 M
0.20 M KMnO₄ → [K⁺] = 0.20 M, [MnO₄⁻] = 0.20 M
0.40 M glucose → 0.40 M intact C₆H₁₂O₆ molecules, no ions (nonelectrolyte)
0.12 M Al₂(SO₄)₃ → [Al³⁺] = 0.24 M, [SO₄²⁻] = 0.36 M
0.25 M Ca(NO₃)₂ → [Ca²⁺] = 0.25 M, [NO₃⁻] = 0.50 M
cards.h: → molarity × each subscript; polyatomic ions stay whole
cards.n: Splitting a polyatomic ion (SO₄²⁻ into S and O) or ignoring subscripts earns nothing; a molecular solute such as glucose gives no ions at all.

cards.q: Describe how a solution differs from a heterogeneous mixture, and identify the phase of each of these solutions: air, brass, carbonated water.
cards.a: A solution (homogeneous mixture) is mixed at the particle level, so its composition and macroscopic properties (color, density, concentration) are the same in every sample; a heterogeneous mixture's properties depend on where it is sampled (sand in water, oil floating on vinegar). Solutions exist in every phase: air is a gaseous solution (O₂ and Ar in N₂), brass a solid solution (Zn in Cu), carbonated water a liquid solution (CO₂ in water).
cards.n: 'A solution is always a liquid' earns nothing; air and alloys such as brass are solutions too.

cards.q: Predict whether the actual concentration of a NaCl solution is higher or lower than the intended 0.250 M if the student adds water above the calibration mark of the volumetric flask, and explain.
cards.a: Lower than 0.250 M. The mass, and so the moles, of NaCl is correct, but the volume of solution is larger than the flask's stated volume; since M = n/V, the same moles divided by a larger volume give a smaller molarity. Pouring off the excess does not fix it, because the liquid removed carries solute with it; the solution must be remade.
cards.h: → same n, larger V → smaller M
cards.n: Suggesting the extra liquid be pipetted out earns nothing; it is solution, not water, and removes solute along with it.

cards.q: Explain why diluting a solution lowers its molarity even though no solute is removed.
cards.a: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution. Dilution adds only solvent, so the moles of solute stay the same while the volume of solution grows; the same moles spread through more liters give fewer moles per liter. That constant number of moles is why M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
cards.h: → solvent added → n unchanged, V larger → n/V smaller → M₁V₁ = M₂V₂
cards.n: 'The solute gets weaker' earns nothing; the solute particles are unchanged, only their number per liter falls.
o: The number of solute particles is fixed, but they now occupy a larger volume, so each liter holds fewer of them.
Because n = MV is constant during a dilution, M must fall in proportion as V rises.

w.a: Diluting lowers the molarity because some of the solute is destroyed by the added water.
w.why: no solute is lost; the moles are unchanged

w.a: Diluting lowers the molarity because water reacts with the solute particles.
w.why: dilution is a physical change; nothing reacts

w.a: Diluting lowers the molarity because the solute particles become smaller.
w.why: particle size is irrelevant; particles per liter falls

cards.q: Explain why a 0.10 M CaCl₂ solution contains more dissolved particles per liter than a 0.10 M NaCl solution.
cards.a: Both are soluble ionic compounds that dissociate completely. Each CaCl₂ releases three ions (Ca²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻), so 0.10 M CaCl₂ holds 0.30 mol of ions per liter; each NaCl releases two (Na⁺ + Cl⁻), so 0.10 M NaCl holds 0.20 mol per liter. Equal molarity counts formula units, not particles.
cards.h: → complete dissociation → 3 ions vs 2 per formula unit → 0.30 M vs 0.20 M particles
cards.n: Stop at the particle count: freezing-point and boiling-point effects of particle number are colligative properties, which are not assessed on the AP exam.
o: Particle concentration = molarity × ions per formula unit: 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 M for CaCl₂ versus 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 M for NaCl.
The subscripts of the formula set how many ions each dissolved formula unit releases.

w.a: They contain the same number of particles because both solutions are 0.10 M.
w.why: molarity counts formula units, not the ions released

w.a: CaCl₂ contains more particles because calcium is heavier than sodium.
w.why: mass does not change the count; the ion ratio does

w.a: CaCl₂ gives more particles because a Cl₂ molecule is released intact.
w.why: chloride is released as two separate Cl⁻ ions

cards.q: Explain what a correct particulate diagram of aqueous NaCl must show.
cards.a: Separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a 1:1 ratio with no NaCl units, each surrounded by water molecules oriented by ion-dipole attraction: the δ− O end of water toward Na⁺, the δ+ H ends toward Cl⁻. Water molecules far outnumber the ions, the number of ions reflects the concentration, and Na⁺ is drawn smaller than Cl⁻.
cards.n: Drawing NaCl pairs or lattice fragments earns nothing, and so does water with its H atoms toward Na⁺; each ion must face the correct end of the water dipole.

cards.q: Contrast the particulate representations of a strong electrolyte and a nonelectrolyte in water.
cards.a: A strong electrolyte (KBr) is drawn as fully separated, hydrated ions in the formula ratio, with no intact formula units; those mobile ions are why the solution conducts. A nonelectrolyte (glucose, ethanol) is drawn as intact, neutral molecules dispersed among water molecules, often with dashed hydrogen bonds between their –OH groups and water, and no ions at all.
cards.h: → ions in ratio vs intact neutral molecules
cards.n: Drawing glucose split into C, H and O atoms or into ions earns nothing; dissolving a molecular solute separates molecules from each other, never atoms within a molecule.

cards.q: Contrast the particulate diagram of a strong acid HA in water with that of a weak acid HA at the same concentration.
cards.a: Strong acid: essentially no intact HA; every HA has given its proton to water, so the diagram shows equal numbers of H₃O⁺ and A⁻ among the water molecules. Weak acid: mostly intact HA molecules with only one or two H₃O⁺/A⁻ pairs per ten or more HA, because it ionizes only slightly. Both diagrams contain the same total number of A units (HA + A⁻), reflecting equal concentrations.
cards.h: → all ions vs mostly intact + equal totals
cards.n: Drawing the weak acid fully ionized, or with unequal numbers of H₃O⁺ and A⁻, earns nothing. Acid strength is borrowed from Unit 8.

cards.q: Explain what a correct particulate diagram of aqueous ammonia, a weak base, must show.
cards.a: Mostly intact NH₃ molecules among many water molecules, with only a few NH₄⁺ and OH⁻ ions and exactly one OH⁻ for each NH₄⁺, because NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ proceeds only slightly. Hydrogen bonds (dashed lines) may be shown from water's H to the N lone pair and from NH₃'s H to a water O.
cards.h: → mostly molecules, a few matched ion pairs
cards.n: Drawing NH₃ fully converted to ions, or NH₄⁺ without a matching OH⁻, earns nothing. Weak-base behavior is borrowed from Unit 8.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, a particulate diagram of aqueous K₂SO₄ that contains six potassium ions, including how the water molecules around each kind of ion are oriented.
cards.a: Six K⁺ and three SO₄²⁻ ions, all separated from one another, with each sulfate drawn as one intact unit (an S bonded to four O), not as separate S and O atoms. Around each K⁺, water molecules point their δ− O atoms inward; around each SO₄²⁻, they point δ+ H atoms inward. Many more water molecules than ions fill the space.
cards.h: → 2:1 ion ratio, intact sulfate, oriented water
cards.n: Splitting SO₄²⁻ into S and O ions, or drawing K₂ pairs, earns nothing; the 2:1 ratio of K⁺ to intact SO₄²⁻ is what is scored.

cards.q: Represent the interactions between methanol (CH₃OH) and water in a particulate diagram of their solution, identifying the atoms joined by each interaction.
cards.a: Intact CH₃OH and H₂O molecules, no ions. Dashed lines (hydrogen bonds) run from the H of methanol's O–H to a lone pair on a water O, and from an H of water to a lone pair on methanol's O; every dashed line joins an H bonded to O with an O on a different molecule. The CH₃ group touches its neighbors only through dispersion forces.
cards.h: → dashed H···O lines between different molecules
cards.n: Drawing a hydrogen bond from a C–H hydrogen, or along the covalent O–H bond itself, earns nothing; the dashed line links an O–H hydrogen to an O on another molecule.

cards.q: Determine the molarity of MgCl₂ and of Cl⁻ represented by a particulate diagram of 1.0 L of solution that shows 3 Mg²⁺ ions and 6 Cl⁻ ions, if each drawn particle stands for 0.10 mol.
cards.a: [MgCl₂] = 0.30 M and [Cl⁻] = 0.60 M. 3 Mg²⁺ × 0.10 mol = 0.30 mol Mg²⁺, and each Mg²⁺ came from one MgCl₂, so 0.30 mol MgCl₂ in 1.0 L is 0.30 M. 6 Cl⁻ × 0.10 mol = 0.60 mol in 1.0 L is 0.60 M, twice [MgCl₂], as the formula requires.
cards.n: Counting all nine ions as MgCl₂ (0.90 M) earns nothing; formula units are counted by the Mg²⁺ ions, one per MgCl₂.

cards.q: Identify the two errors in a student's particulate diagram of CaCl₂(aq) that shows four Ca²⁺ ions and four Cl⁻ ions, with the hydrogen atoms of every nearby water molecule pointing toward each Ca²⁺ ion.
cards.a: (1) The ion ratio is wrong: CaCl₂ releases two Cl⁻ for each Ca²⁺, so four Ca²⁺ require eight Cl⁻, and only then is the drawing electrically neutral. (2) The orientation of water around Ca²⁺ is wrong: the δ+ H ends would be repelled by the cation; the δ− O ends must face Ca²⁺, while H ends face the Cl⁻ ions.
cards.n: Fixing the ratio by adding Cl₂ molecules earns nothing; chlorine is present only as separate Cl⁻ ions.

cards.q: Represent how a particulate diagram of 0.40 M KCl changes when the solution is diluted to 0.20 M, if both diagrams show the same small volume of solution.
cards.a: Same-size boxes: the 0.40 M box shows, say, 4 K⁺ and 4 Cl⁻ among the water molecules; the 0.20 M box shows 2 K⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ with correspondingly more water molecules in their place. Halving the concentration halves the number of solute particles in any fixed volume, while the ions stay separate, hydrated and in a 1:1 ratio.
cards.h: → same box, half the ions, more water
cards.n: Drawing the same number of ions spread farther apart, or smaller ions, earns nothing when the boxes are the same volume; the scored feature is half as many solute particles.

cards.q: Describe what a correct particulate diagram shows for each solute dissolved in water: KBr · C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (sucrose) · HNO₃ · HF · Na₂CO₃ · CH₃OH · NH₃ · Mg(NO₃)₂ · C₂H₅OH · NH₄Cl
cards.a:
KBr → separate K⁺ and Br⁻ in a 1:1 ratio; water O toward K⁺, water H toward Br⁻
sucrose → intact C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ molecules hydrogen bonded to water; no ions
HNO₃ → strong acid: H₃O⁺ and NO₃⁻ in a 1:1 ratio; no intact HNO₃
HF → weak acid: mostly intact HF with a few H₃O⁺ and F⁻ pairs
Na₂CO₃ → Na⁺ and intact CO₃²⁻ in a 2:1 ratio
CH₃OH → intact molecules hydrogen bonded to water; no ions
NH₃ → weak base: mostly intact NH₃ with a few NH₄⁺ and OH⁻ pairs
Mg(NO₃)₂ → Mg²⁺ and intact NO₃⁻ in a 1:2 ratio
C₂H₅OH → intact molecules hydrogen bonded to water; no ions
NH₄Cl → intact NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ in a 1:1 ratio
cards.h: → per case: ions in formula ratio, or intact molecules
cards.n: Drawing ionic formula units intact, or breaking polyatomic ions apart, earns nothing. Strong versus weak acids and bases (HNO₃, HF, NH₃) are borrowed from Unit 8.

cards.q: Explain why the water molecules around a dissolved Na⁺ ion point their oxygen atoms toward it, while those around a Cl⁻ ion point their hydrogen atoms toward it.
cards.a: Water is polar: its O carries a partial negative charge and its H atoms partial positive charges. Opposite charges attract (Coulomb's law), so the δ− O end is drawn toward the positive Na⁺ and the δ+ H ends toward the negative Cl⁻; the reverse orientation would put like charges together and be repulsive.
cards.h: → water has δ− O and δ+ H → opposite charges attract → O faces cation, H faces anion
cards.n: 'Oxygen is attracted to sodium because they bond' earns nothing; the attraction is an ion-dipole force, not a chemical bond.
o: Each ion-dipole attraction is strongest when the oppositely charged end of the water dipole faces the ion: O for a cation, H for an anion.
The partial charges within water, not its zero net charge, decide which end each ion attracts.

w.a: Water's oxygen points toward Na⁺ because oxygen and sodium form an ionic bond.
w.why: no bond forms; it is an ion-dipole attraction

w.a: Water's hydrogens point toward Cl⁻ because they are the heavier end of the molecule.
w.why: mass is irrelevant; the sign of the partial charge sets orientation

w.a: The water molecules around both ions point the same way because water is neutral overall.
w.why: the partial charges inside water decide its orientation

cards.q: Explain why a particulate diagram of dissolved sucrose shows intact molecules, while one of dissolved NaCl shows separate ions.
cards.a: Sucrose is a molecular solid: dissolving overcomes only the attractions between sucrose molecules, replaced by hydrogen bonds to water, and the covalent bonds within each molecule stay intact. NaCl is ionic: ion-dipole attractions to water pull the lattice's Na⁺ and Cl⁻ apart, so separate hydrated ions appear.
cards.h: → molecular solid: only IMFs overcome → molecules; ionic solid: ion-dipole separates the ions → ions
cards.n: 'Sucrose is too big to break apart' earns nothing; dissolving never breaks covalent bonds, and NaCl's particles were ions to begin with.
o: Dissolving separates the particles a solid is made of: molecules for sucrose, ions for NaCl.
A sucrose solution does not conduct and a NaCl solution does, consistent with neutral molecules in one diagram and ions in the other.

w.a: Sucrose stays intact because covalent bonds are stronger than ionic bonds.
w.why: no bonds break in either case; bond strength is not the point

w.a: NaCl splits into ions because water breaks its covalent bond.
w.why: NaCl has no covalent bond; its ions are separated

w.a: Sucrose breaks into C, H and O atoms that are surrounded by water.
w.why: molecules stay intact on dissolving

cards.q: Define the retention factor $(R_f)$ in paper or thin-layer chromatography.
cards.a: $R_f = \frac{d_{spot}}{d_{front}}$: the distance from the origin line to the center of a component's spot divided by the distance from the origin line to the solvent front. It is unitless and lies between 0 and 1. With the same stationary phase, solvent and temperature, a given compound always has the same $R_f$, so matching values help identify components.
cards.h: → ratio of two distances + its range
cards.n: Measuring from the bottom edge of the plate, or dividing the solvent distance by the spot distance (a value above 1), earns nothing.
x: Rf = spot distance / solvent front distance

cards.q: Predict which component travels farthest on a polar stationary phase with a nonpolar mobile phase.
cards.a: The least polar component travels farthest (highest $R_f$). It is only weakly attracted to the polar stationary phase and has dispersion attractions similar to those of the nonpolar solvent, so it spends most of its time dissolved in the moving phase. Polar components are held by dipole-dipole or hydrogen-bond attractions to the stationary phase and stay near the origin.
cards.h: → least polar + attractions to both phases
cards.n: 'The lightest component travels farthest' earns nothing; the order follows the relative strength of attractions to the two phases, not mass.

cards.q: Decide which separation technique to use for: sand in water, salt in water, and two miscible liquids.
cards.a: Sand in water: filtration, because the sand is undissolved solid too coarse to pass through the paper. Salt in water: evaporation or distillation, because a solution passes straight through a filter but water vaporizes while the ionic salt does not. Two miscible liquids: (fractional) distillation, because different intermolecular forces give them different vapor pressures and boiling points.
cards.n: Choosing filtration for salt water earns nothing; the dissolved ions pass through the filter with the water.

cards.q: Compute the $R_f$ value for a chromatography spot that travels 4.5 cm while the solvent front travels 9.0 cm.
cards.a: $R_f$ = 0.50. $R_f$ = spot distance ÷ solvent-front distance = 4.5 cm ÷ 9.0 cm = 0.50, with no units: the component moved half as far as the solvent.
cards.n: An answer above 1 (2.0) is impossible; it means the two distances were inverted or measured from different lines.

cards.q: Predict which of two dyes has the higher $R_f$ value on a polar (silica) TLC plate with a nonpolar mobile solvent: a polar dye or a nonpolar dye.
cards.a: The nonpolar dye. The Si–OH groups on silica attract a polar dye through hydrogen bonding and dipole-dipole forces and hold it back; a nonpolar dye has only weak dispersion attractions to the silica and dissolves well in the nonpolar solvent, so it spends more time in the moving phase and travels farther.
cards.h: → claim + attractions to plate and to solvent
cards.n: Stating the result without comparing the dye's attractions to BOTH phases earns nothing for the justification.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, the developed TLC plate (polar silica, nonpolar solvent) for a mixture of a nonpolar hydrocarbon dye and a polar alcohol dye whose $R_f$ values are 0.75 and 0.20, with the solvent front 8.0 cm above the origin.
cards.a: An upright plate with a pencil origin line near the bottom and the solvent-front line 8.0 cm above it. Both spots lie in the lane above the original sample spot: the nonpolar hydrocarbon dye ($R_f$ 0.75) centered 0.75 × 8.0 = 6.0 cm above the origin, the polar alcohol dye ($R_f$ 0.20) 0.20 × 8.0 = 1.6 cm above it; nothing remains on the origin line.
cards.h: → origin, front, two spots at computed heights
cards.n: Placing the polar dye higher earns nothing on a polar plate with a nonpolar solvent, and a spot above the solvent front is impossible.

cards.q: Interpret a TLC plate (polar silica, nonpolar solvent) on which an unknown mixture gives spots at $R_f$ 0.15, 0.48 and 0.81, while standards X, Y and Z run on the same plate give 0.15, 0.60 and 0.81. Identify the components and rank them by polarity.
cards.a: The mixture contains X (0.15) and Z (0.81) plus one component (0.48) that matches no standard; Y is absent. Polarity, most to least: X > the unidentified component > Z. On a polar plate with a nonpolar solvent, the more polar a component, the more strongly the stationary phase holds it and the lower its $R_f$.
cards.h: → match to standards, then low R_f = more polar
cards.n: Matching $R_f$ values from a different plate or solvent earns nothing; values are comparable only under identical conditions, and a match is evidence, not proof.

cards.q: Describe the order in which a hydrocarbon, a ketone and an alcohol of similar size leave a column packed with polar silica when a nonpolar solvent is used, and explain the order.
cards.a: Hydrocarbon first, ketone second, alcohol last. A component moves down the column only while dissolved in the flowing solvent. The hydrocarbon has only dispersion attractions and is barely held by the silica; the ketone's C=O dipole is held by dipole-dipole attractions; the alcohol's O–H hydrogen bonds to the surface Si–OH groups most strongly, so it lags behind.
cards.n: 'The largest molecule comes out last' earns nothing; elution order follows attraction to the stationary phase relative to the solvent, not size.

cards.q: Identify the two errors in a paper chromatography procedure in which the student draws the origin line in ink and stands the paper in a solvent whose surface is above the origin line, and give the effect of each.
cards.a: (1) Ink contains dyes that dissolve in the solvent and travel up the paper, adding spots that are not from the sample; the origin line must be drawn in pencil, since graphite does not dissolve. (2) With the solvent above the origin, the sample spots dissolve into the solvent pool instead of being carried up the paper, so they are lost or smeared; the origin must sit above the solvent surface.
cards.h: → two errors, each with its effect
cards.n: 'The ink will smudge' earns nothing; the problem is that the ink's own components are separated along with the sample.

cards.q: Explain why a component that is strongly attracted to the stationary phase has a small $R_f$ value.
cards.a: A component moves only while it is dissolved in the mobile phase. Its molecules keep switching between being held on the stationary phase and dissolving in the solvent; strong stationary-phase attractions mean most of the time is spent held, so while the solvent front rises the component travels only a short distance.
cards.h: → strong attraction to stationary phase → more time held → less time moving with solvent → small R_f
cards.n: 'It is too heavy to move' earns nothing; the distance traveled depends on the balance of attractions to the two phases.
o: $R_f$ reflects the fraction of time a component spends in the mobile phase; strong stationary-phase attractions shrink that fraction.
Components compete between the two phases, and the one whose attractions favor the stationary phase lags behind the solvent front.

w.a: It has a small R_f because it is the heaviest molecule in the mixture.
w.why: mass does not set R_f; the relative attractions do

w.a: It has a small R_f because it does not dissolve in anything.
w.why: it must dissolve to move at all; it is simply held more

w.a: It has a small R_f because it evaporates before it can travel.
w.why: evaporation is not the mechanism; adsorption to the stationary phase is

cards.q: Explain why replacing hexane with a more polar solvent increases the $R_f$ values of polar compounds on a silica TLC plate.
cards.a: A polar solvent forms dipole-dipole or hydrogen-bond attractions with polar compounds and competes with them for the polar sites on the silica. The compounds are then held less by the stationary phase and spend more time dissolved in the moving solvent, so they travel farther and their $R_f$ values rise.
cards.h: → polar solvent attracts polar solutes and competes for silica sites → less time held → higher R_f
cards.n: 'The solvent moves faster' earns nothing; $R_f$ is a ratio to the solvent front, so only a shift in relative attractions changes it.
o: When the solvent's intermolecular forces resemble the compounds' own, the balance of attractions shifts toward the mobile phase and the compounds move with it.
A polar eluent both dissolves polar compounds well and displaces them from the polar silica surface.

w.a: R_f rises because a polar solvent evaporates more slowly and has more time to carry the spots.
w.why: R_f is a ratio to the solvent front, so timing cancels

w.a: R_f rises because the polar solvent makes the silica nonpolar.
w.why: the plate stays polar; the solvent competes for its sites

w.a: R_f rises because polar solvents are heavier and push the spots farther.
w.why: mass is irrelevant; attractions decide

cards.q: Explain why the first vapor collected when a hexane-octane mixture is distilled is rich in hexane.
cards.a: Both are nonpolar with only London dispersion forces, but octane has more electrons and a longer chain, so its dispersion attractions are stronger. Hexane molecules escape the liquid more easily, so hexane has the higher vapor pressure (bp 69 °C vs 126 °C) and the vapor, and the first distillate, is rich in hexane.
cards.h: → fewer electrons in hexane → weaker dispersion → higher vapor pressure → vapor enriched in hexane
cards.n: 'Hexane is lighter so it rises first' earns nothing; the scored cause is weaker intermolecular attractions giving a higher vapor pressure.
o: Distillation exploits differences in intermolecular attraction: the component with the weaker attractions vaporizes preferentially.
At every temperature the lower-boiling liquid has the higher vapor pressure, so it makes up a larger share of the vapor.

w.a: Hexane distills first because its covalent bonds break at a lower temperature.
w.why: no bonds break on boiling; attractions between molecules are overcome

w.a: Hexane distills first because it is polar and octane is not.
w.why: both are nonpolar; their dispersion strengths differ

w.a: The first vapor is pure hexane because octane cannot evaporate below 126 °C.
w.why: octane has a vapor pressure below its boiling point, so the vapor is enriched, not pure

cards.q: State the 'like dissolves like' rule and explain it energetically.
cards.a: Substances with similar intermolecular interactions tend to be miscible or soluble in one another. Dissolving replaces solute-solute and solvent-solvent attractions with solute-solvent attractions; when the new attractions are comparable in type and strength to those broken, mixing costs little energy and the greater dispersal of the particles drives it. Ionic and polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents, nonpolar solutes in nonpolar solvents.
cards.n: Writing 'like dissolves like' alone earns nothing; the answer must name the interactions broken and formed (for example, ion-dipole attractions replacing the lattice).

cards.q: Predict the solubility of NaCl, I₂, and CH₃OH in water versus in hexane.
cards.a: NaCl dissolves in water, where ion-dipole attractions replace the lattice attractions, but not in hexane, which offers only weak ion-induced dipole attractions. I₂ dissolves in hexane (dispersion with dispersion) but only slightly in water, whose hydrogen bonds it cannot replace. CH₃OH is miscible with water through hydrogen bonding and only partly miscible with hexane (two layers form at room temperature).
cards.h: → three solutes × two solvents, interaction named
cards.n: Labeling the solvents polar or nonpolar without naming the solute-solvent interaction in each case earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain the three energy steps involved in forming a solution.
cards.a: (1) Separate the solute particles, overcoming solute-solute attractions: endothermic. (2) Separate the solvent particles to make room, overcoming solvent-solvent attractions: endothermic. (3) Form solute-solvent attractions: exothermic. The enthalpy of solution is the sum: exothermic when the new attractions are stronger than those broken, endothermic when weaker.
cards.h: → two endothermic steps + one exothermic step
cards.n: Calling step 1 'breaking bonds' for a molecular solute earns nothing; only intermolecular attractions are overcome. The energy bookkeeping is borrowed from Unit 6 (6.1.A.4).

cards.q: Define saturated, unsaturated, and supersaturated solutions.
cards.a: Unsaturated: less solute dissolved than the maximum at that temperature, so more will dissolve. Saturated: the maximum is dissolved, and any undissolved solid is in dynamic equilibrium with the solution, dissolving and crystallizing at equal rates. Supersaturated: more dissolved than the saturated amount, an unstable state made by cooling a hot saturated solution; a seed crystal makes the excess crystallize.
cards.h: → three definitions, each tied to the maximum
cards.n: 'In a saturated solution dissolving stops' earns nothing; both processes continue at equal rates. Dynamic equilibrium is borrowed from Unit 7.

cards.q: Recall the solubility rules for compounds that are generally SOLUBLE in water.
cards.a: All sodium, potassium, ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻) salts are soluble in water. That is the one rule the AP exam expects (4.7.A.5): if a question depends on the solubility of any other salt, it supplies the information, for example as a Ksp value or an observed precipitate.
cards.n: Rote solubility rules beyond the Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ salts are excluded from the exam (Unit 4 exclusion statement); this card is borrowed from Unit 4.

cards.q: Predict whether dissolving a salt in water is exothermic overall if the hydration energy released exceeds the lattice energy that must be broken.
cards.a: Exothermic overall. More energy is released as ion-dipole attractions form between the ions and water (hydration) than is absorbed to separate the ions of the lattice, so the net enthalpy change is negative and the solution warms.
cards.h: → compare energy released with energy absorbed
cards.n: Concluding 'so it dissolves because it is exothermic' earns nothing; entropy matters too, and salts such as NH₄NO₃ dissolve endothermically. Energy signs are borrowed from Unit 6.

cards.q: Explain why ethanol is completely miscible with water while octanol is only slightly soluble in water.
cards.a: Ethanol's –OH group hydrogen bonds with water, and its short two-carbon chain disrupts little of water's hydrogen-bond network, so the new attractions match those broken. Octanol has the same single –OH on an eight-carbon nonpolar chain that attracts water only through weak dispersion forces; dissolving it would break many water-water hydrogen bonds without replacing them, so only about 0.5 g dissolves per liter.
cards.n: 'Octanol is too big' earns nothing; name hydrogen bonding for the –OH group and dispersion-only attractions for the long chain.

cards.q: Predict whether $CaCO_3$ or $NaNO_3$ is more soluble in water, using standard solubility rules.
cards.a: NaNO₃ is more soluble. Every sodium salt and every nitrate salt is soluble in water, the solubility rule the AP exam expects you to know. CaCO₃ contains none of Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ or NO₃⁻, so no rule guarantees it dissolves, and in fact it is only sparingly soluble: chalk and limestone are CaCO₃.
cards.n: 'All calcium salts are insoluble' earns nothing (Ca(NO₃)₂ is soluble). Rules beyond the Na⁺/K⁺/NH₄⁺/NO₃⁻ one are not assessed; borrowed from Unit 4.

cards.q: Predict whether each pair mixes (miscible, or the solid dissolves), naming the main solute-solvent attraction: ethanol + water · hexane + water · I₂ + CCl₄ · I₂ + water · KBr + water · KBr + hexane · hexane + octane · acetone + water · NH₃ + water · naphthalene (C₁₀H₈) + benzene · glucose + water · CCl₄ + water
cards.a:
ethanol + water → miscible; hydrogen bonding in both directions
hexane + water → immiscible; only weak dispersion and dipole-induced dipole, too weak to replace water's hydrogen bonds
I₂ + CCl₄ → soluble; dispersion with dispersion
I₂ + water → only slightly soluble; dipole-induced dipole is weak
KBr + water → soluble; ion-dipole
KBr + hexane → insoluble; only weak ion-induced dipole
hexane + octane → miscible; dispersion only in both
acetone + water → miscible; water's O–H hydrogen bonds to acetone's C=O oxygen, plus dipole-dipole
NH₃ + water → very soluble; hydrogen bonding
naphthalene + benzene → soluble; dispersion with dispersion
glucose + water → soluble; hydrogen bonds with its five –OH groups
CCl₄ + water → immiscible; only dispersion and dipole-induced dipole
cards.h: → match the dominant attractions of solute and solvent
cards.n: Answering 'soluble' without the solute-solvent attraction earns nothing on an FRQ; acetone accepts hydrogen bonds from water but has no O–H of its own to donate.

cards.q: Predict where the iodine ends up when a brown aqueous solution of I₂ is shaken with hexane in a separatory funnel and the layers are allowed to separate, and justify the prediction.
cards.a: Most of the I₂ moves into the hexane layer, which turns violet, while the water layer fades. Nonpolar I₂ forms strong dispersion attractions with nonpolar hexane, similar to the I₂-I₂ and hexane-hexane attractions, but only weak dipole-induced dipole attractions with water. Hexane (about 0.66 g/mL) floats as the top layer above the water.
cards.h: → claim + the attractions in each layer
cards.n: 'The iodine sinks because it is heavy' earns nothing; the iodine goes to the layer whose intermolecular attractions most resemble its own.

cards.q: Explain why the water solubility of straight-chain alcohols falls as the carbon chain lengthens.
cards.a: Only the –OH group hydrogen bonds with water; the hydrocarbon chain attracts water only by weak dispersion forces and disrupts water's hydrogen bonding. Each added CH₂ enlarges the nonpolar part, so solute-water attractions fall further short of the water-water hydrogen bonds broken, and solubility drops.
cards.h: → one –OH H-bonds, the chain cannot → longer chain disrupts more water H-bonds → weaker net attraction → less soluble
cards.n: 'Longer alcohols are heavier' earns nothing; the point is the growing nonpolar part that cannot hydrogen bond with water.
o: As the chain grows, the alcohol's intermolecular forces become more like hexane's (dispersion) and less like water's (hydrogen bonding), so it mixes less with water.
Methanol, ethanol and propanol are miscible with water, 1-butanol dissolves to about 7 g per 100 mL and 1-hexanol to about 0.6 g per 100 mL, tracking the nonpolar share of the molecule.

w.a: Longer alcohols are less soluble because they have fewer –OH groups.
w.why: each has one –OH; the nonpolar part grows

w.a: Longer alcohols are less soluble because their molecules are too large to fit between water molecules.
w.why: size alone is not the point; the chain's inability to hydrogen bond is

w.a: Longer alcohols are less soluble because their C–C bonds break in water.
w.why: no bonds break on dissolving

cards.q: Explain why NaCl dissolves readily in water but not in hexane.
cards.a: In water, strong ion-dipole attractions (water's O toward Na⁺, H toward Cl⁻) compensate for the strong ion-ion attractions of the lattice, so the ions separate. Nonpolar hexane offers only weak ion-induced dipole attractions, far too weak to pay for pulling the ions apart, so NaCl stays solid.
cards.h: → water: ion-dipole ≈ lattice attractions → ions separate; hexane: weak ion-induced dipole → lattice stays
cards.n: 'Like dissolves like' without naming ion-dipole attractions in water, and their absence in hexane, earns nothing.
o: Dissolving is favorable only when solute-solvent attractions are comparable to solute-solute ones; only water's dipoles can approach the Coulombic attractions within NaCl.
Hexane molecules have no permanent dipole to orient around an ion, so the ions gain almost nothing by leaving the lattice.

w.a: NaCl does not dissolve in hexane because hexane is too dense to let the ions through.
w.why: density is irrelevant; the attractions decide

w.a: NaCl dissolves in water because water breaks the covalent bonds in NaCl.
w.why: NaCl is ionic; ion-dipole attractions separate its ions

w.a: NaCl does not dissolve in hexane because hexane is a liquid and NaCl is a solid.
w.why: water is a liquid too; the type of attraction is the difference

cards.q: Explain why hexane and water form two layers instead of mixing.
cards.a: Mixing would break many strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules, but hexane can offer water only weak dispersion and dipole-induced dipole attractions in return. The attractions gained are far weaker than those lost, so water molecules stay hydrogen bonded to one another and hexane forms a separate layer.
cards.h: → mixing breaks water-water H-bonds → replaced only by weak dispersion → unfavorable → two layers
cards.n: 'Hexane and water repel each other' earns nothing; they attract weakly, just far less than water attracts water.
o: Water's hydrogen bonding and hexane's dispersion-only attractions are too dissimilar; substances with similar intermolecular interactions mix, and these do not.
Hexane attracts water about as weakly as it attracts itself, but water attracts water far more strongly, so the liquids separate.

w.a: Hexane and water separate because hexane molecules repel water molecules.
w.why: the attraction is weak, not a repulsion

w.a: Hexane and water separate because hexane is less dense than water.
w.why: density decides which layer is on top, not whether they mix

w.a: Hexane and water separate because polar molecules cannot touch nonpolar ones.
w.why: they touch and attract weakly; water-water hydrogen bonds are simply not replaced

cards.q: Identify the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing photon energy.
cards.a: Radio < microwave < infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-ray < gamma ray. Photon energy rises as frequency rises and wavelength falls (E = hν = hc/λ); within the visible range (about 700 nm to 400 nm) red photons have the least energy and violet the most.
cards.h: → seven regions in order + the λ link
cards.n: Listing the regions by increasing wavelength reverses the answer; energy and wavelength run in opposite directions.

cards.q: Identify the molecular transition probed by microwave, infrared, and UV-visible radiation.
cards.a: Microwave radiation causes transitions between rotational energy levels (the molecule rotates faster). Infrared causes transitions between vibrational levels (bonds stretch and bend more). Ultraviolet and visible radiation cause transitions between electronic energy levels (an electron is promoted to a higher-energy orbital). The energy gaps increase in the same order: rotational < vibrational < electronic.
cards.h: → three regions → three kinds of transition
cards.n: Swapping infrared and microwave (IR → rotation) is the classic error and earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify the spectral region and the type of transition caused when a molecule absorbs radiation of each wavelength or frequency: 254 nm · 2.45 × 10⁹ Hz (microwave oven) · 5.8 µm · 520 nm · 1.0 cm · 15 µm · 190 nm · 650 nm
cards.a:
254 nm → ultraviolet → electronic transition
2.45 × 10⁹ Hz (λ = c/ν = 0.122 m) → microwave → rotational transition
5.8 µm → infrared → vibrational transition (C=O stretching absorbs near here)
520 nm → visible (green) → electronic transition
1.0 cm → microwave → rotational transition
15 µm → infrared → vibrational transition (CO₂ bending absorbs here)
190 nm → ultraviolet → electronic transition
650 nm → visible (red) → electronic transition
cards.h: → λ → region → rotation, vibration or electronic
cards.n: Calling 5.8 µm microwave because it is 'long' earns nothing; µm wavelengths are infrared, mm to cm are microwave, and visible spans 400–700 nm.

cards.q: Rank the spacing between rotational, vibrational and electronic energy levels of a molecule, and match each to the region of photons it absorbs.
cards.a: Rotational < vibrational < electronic. Closely spaced rotational levels match low-energy microwave photons (about 2 × 10⁻²³ J at λ = 1 cm); vibrational spacings match infrared photons (about 2 × 10⁻²⁰ J at 10 µm); the widely spaced electronic levels match ultraviolet-visible photons (about 4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J at 500 nm, 1 × 10⁻¹⁸ J at 200 nm), from E = hc/λ.
cards.h: → order + region + a rough photon energy for each
cards.n: Ranking electronic levels as the most closely spaced reverses the order; an absorbed photon must match the gap, so the largest gaps need UV-visible photons.

cards.q: Explain why an infrared spectrum can be used to identify the functional groups present in a molecule.
cards.a: An infrared photon is absorbed when its energy matches the spacing between vibrational levels of a bond. Each kind of bond (O–H, C=O, C–H) vibrates at its own characteristic frequency, so a molecule absorbs infrared radiation at the frequencies of the bonds it contains, and absorption peaks at those positions reveal which groups are present.
cards.h: → each bond type vibrates at its own frequency
cards.n: 'Infrared breaks the bonds so they can be identified' earns nothing; infrared photons only excite vibrations and are far too weak to break bonds.

cards.q: Identify the region of the electromagnetic spectrum a chemist should use to (a) detect whether a sample contains a C=O bond, (b) measure the concentration of a colored dye in solution, (c) study the rotation of gas-phase HCl molecules, and (d) promote an electron in a colorless compound such as benzene.
cards.a: (a) Infrared: C=O stretching is a vibrational transition. (b) Visible: a colored dye absorbs visible light through an electronic transition. (c) Microwave: rotational transitions. (d) Ultraviolet: a colorless compound absorbs no visible light, so its electronic gaps are larger and need UV photons.
cards.n: Choosing ultraviolet for (b) because 'UV has more energy' earns nothing; the dye's color shows its electronic transition lies in the visible range.

cards.q: Explain why infrared radiation can make a molecule vibrate but cannot promote its electrons to higher energy levels.
cards.a: A molecule absorbs a photon only if its energy equals the gap between two of the molecule's energy levels. Infrared photon energies match vibrational spacings but are far smaller than the gaps between electronic levels, so infrared excites vibrations but cannot promote an electron; that takes UV-visible photons.
cards.h: → absorbed energy must match a gap → IR energy fits vibrational gaps → far below electronic gaps
cards.n: 'Infrared is too weak' earns nothing unless it compares the energy per photon with the electronic energy gap.
o: Electronic gaps correspond to photons of roughly 100–700 nm; infrared wavelengths are longer, so each photon's energy (hc/λ) is too small.
Energy is ordinarily absorbed one photon at a time, so a brighter infrared source adds photons without making any one of them energetic enough.

w.a: Infrared cannot cause electronic transitions because it is invisible.
w.why: ultraviolet is invisible too and does; photon energy decides

w.a: Infrared causes vibrations because infrared radiation is heat.
w.why: heating is a consequence; the point is matching the vibrational gap

w.a: A brighter infrared lamp would promote electrons.
w.why: intensity adds photons, not energy per photon

cards.q: Explain, in terms of the transitions microwave photons cause, why a microwave oven heats food that contains water.
cards.a: Microwave photon energies match the spacing of rotational levels, so polar water molecules absorb them and rotate faster (in the liquid, they twist back and forth faster). Colliding with neighbors, they pass the energy on, raising the particles' average kinetic energy: the temperature rises.
cards.h: → microwave energy matches rotational gaps → water rotates faster → collisions share energy → higher T
cards.n: 'Microwaves break the water molecules' earns nothing; microwave photons are far too low in energy to break bonds or promote electrons.
o: Microwaves are the lowest-energy photons molecules commonly absorb, and they excite rotation; collisions turn that rotational energy into thermal energy.
The absorbed energy per photon is tiny, but enormous numbers of absorptions by polar water molecules add up to heating.

w.a: Microwaves heat food by exciting electrons to higher energy levels.
w.why: electronic transitions need UV-visible photons

w.a: Microwaves heat food by making the O–H bonds vibrate until they break.
w.why: vibrations need infrared photons, and no bonds break

w.a: Microwaves heat food because microwaves are hot radiation.
w.why: radiation is not hot; energy is absorbed through rotational transitions

cards.q: State the two equations relating photon energy, frequency, and wavelength.
cards.a: E = hν and c = λν, which combine to E = hc/λ. Here h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s (both on the AP equations sheet), ν is in s⁻¹ (Hz), λ in meters and E in joules per photon. Energy is proportional to frequency and inversely proportional to wavelength.
cards.n: Writing E = hλ confuses frequency with wavelength, and putting nm straight into c = λν earns nothing; convert to meters (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m).

cards.q: Explain the relationship between a photon's wavelength and its energy.
cards.a: They are inversely proportional: E = hc/λ, so halving the wavelength doubles the energy of each photon. Short-wavelength, high-frequency photons such as ultraviolet carry more energy each than long-wavelength photons such as red light or microwaves.
cards.n: 'Per photon' is load-bearing: a bright red lamp can deliver more total energy than a dim UV lamp, yet each red photon carries less.

cards.q: Compute the energy of a photon with wavelength 663 nm (h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s).
cards.n: Leaving λ in nm gives 3.00 × 10⁻²⁸ J, a billionfold error; convert to meters first.

cards.q: Explain the photoelectric effect and the role of the threshold frequency.
cards.a: Light striking a metal ejects electrons only if each photon's energy, hν, is at least the energy that binds an electron to the metal (the work function, φ). The threshold frequency ν₀ = φ/h is the lowest frequency that ejects electrons: below it none leave at any intensity, and above it each photon's excess energy, hν − φ, becomes the electron's kinetic energy.
cards.h: → one photon per electron + minimum energy
cards.n: 'Brighter light ejects faster electrons' earns nothing; intensity sets the number of electrons. The effect is not named in the CED but applies E = hν (3.12.A.1–2), as PES does.

cards.q: Compute the kinetic energy of an electron ejected in the photoelectric effect.
cards.a: KE = hν − φ, the photon's energy minus the work function φ needed to free the electron. Example: 200. nm light gives E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.00 × 10⁸) ÷ (2.00 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 9.94 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; on a metal with φ = 6.90 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, KE = 9.94 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 6.90 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.04 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
cards.n: A negative result means the photon is below threshold and no electron leaves; comparing J per photon with kJ/mol without Avogadro's number earns nothing.

cards.q: Predict whether decreasing the wavelength of light above the threshold frequency increases the kinetic energy of ejected photoelectrons, their number, or both.
cards.a: Only the kinetic energy (for the same number of photons per second). A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and more energy per photon, E = hc/λ, and since KE = hν − φ each ejected electron leaves with more energy. The number ejected per second is set by the number of photons arriving, the intensity, not by their wavelength.
cards.h: → energy per photon vs number of photons
cards.n: 'Both increase' earns nothing; one photon ejects at most one electron, so with the same photon rate the electron count is unchanged.

cards.q: Calculate the frequency of light with a wavelength of 486 nm.
cards.n: Multiplying c by λ (146 m²/s) earns nothing; frequency is c divided by λ, with units s⁻¹.

cards.q: Calculate the wavelength, in nm, of a photon with an energy of 4.00 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and identify its region of the spectrum.
cards.a: 497 nm, visible (blue-green). λ = hc/E = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m/s) ÷ (4.00 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) = 4.97 × 10⁻⁷ m = 497 nm, inside the 400–700 nm visible range.
cards.n: Using λ = E/h or leaving the answer as 4.97 × 10⁻⁷ with no unit conversion earns nothing for the nm value.

cards.q: Calculate the change in energy of a hydrogen atom that emits a photon of wavelength 656 nm, and state its sign.
cards.a: ΔE = −3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The photon carries E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m/s) ÷ (6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and emission lowers the atom's energy by exactly that amount, so the sign is negative: an electron has dropped to a lower energy level.
cards.h: → photon energy, then sign from emission
cards.n: Giving the atom +3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J earns nothing for the sign; the photon carries away what the atom loses.

cards.q: Calculate the energy of one mole of photons of 250. nm ultraviolet light, in kJ/mol.
cards.a: 479 kJ/mol. One photon: E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m/s) ÷ (2.50 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 7.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. One mole: 7.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 4.79 × 10⁵ J/mol = 479 kJ/mol, comparable to typical bond energies (C–C about 348 kJ/mol).
cards.h: → E per photon × Avogadro's number, J → kJ
cards.n: Stopping at 7.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and calling it kJ/mol earns nothing; E = hν gives energy per photon, and bond energies are per mole.

cards.q: Explain why increasing light intensity below the threshold frequency ejects no electrons.
cards.a: Each electron is ejected by absorbing one photon, and one photon's energy is E = hν. Below the threshold frequency that energy is less than the energy binding the electron, so no single absorption frees it. Higher intensity means more photons, not more energy per photon, so still no electrons leave.
cards.h: → one photon per electron → hν below binding energy → more photons, same energy each → none ejected
cards.n: 'The light is not strong enough' earns nothing unless 'strong' means energy per photon; intensity sets the number of photons.
o: Energy arrives in packets of hν; an electron cannot pool several too-small packets, so only frequency, not brightness, can reach the threshold.
A wave model predicts that bright enough light of any color would eventually eject electrons; the sharp threshold shows light is absorbed as photons.

w.a: Brighter light would eventually eject electrons if it shone long enough.
w.why: below threshold no electrons leave at any intensity or time

w.a: No electrons are ejected because the metal reflects low-frequency light.
w.why: the issue is energy per photon versus binding energy

w.a: Intense light below threshold ejects slow electrons with little kinetic energy.
w.why: below threshold no electrons are ejected at all

cards.q: Explain why an atom absorbs or emits light only at specific wavelengths.
cards.a: An atom's electrons can occupy only certain energy levels, so the atom's energy can change only by the differences between them. Absorbing or emitting a photon changes the atom's energy by exactly the photon's energy, E = hν = hc/λ, so only photons matching an allowed difference appear: specific wavelengths.
cards.h: → quantized levels → ΔE(atom) = E(photon) → only matching hν → specific λ
cards.n: 'The electrons only like certain colors' earns nothing; the answer needs energy conservation between atom and photon. Quantized levels are borrowed from Unit 1.
o: Each spectral line corresponds to one allowed transition, with wavelength λ = hc/ΔE for that energy gap.
A continuous range of wavelengths would require a continuous range of atomic energies, which quantized levels do not allow.

w.a: Atoms emit only certain wavelengths because the air absorbs all the others.
w.why: the lines come from the atom's energy gaps, not from filtering

w.a: Atoms emit specific wavelengths because each electron has its own color.
w.why: the photon's energy equals an energy difference, not an electron property

w.a: Atoms emit specific wavelengths because photons can only have certain wavelengths.
w.why: photons can have any wavelength; the atom's allowed energy changes restrict them

cards.q: Explain why ultraviolet light can damage molecules in skin while visible light of much greater intensity does not.
cards.a: Damage requires one molecule to absorb enough energy to break a bond or start a reaction, and energy is absorbed one photon at a time. A UV photon, with its higher frequency, carries a large enough E = hν; each visible photon carries too little, and higher intensity adds photons without raising the energy of each.
cards.h: → damage needs energy per molecule → one photon at a time → UV hν large enough, visible hν too small
cards.n: 'UV is stronger light' earns nothing unless 'stronger' means more energy per photon; visible light can deliver more total energy.
o: E = hc/λ: a 300 nm photon carries about 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (about 400 kJ/mol), a 600 nm photon only half that, below what many bonds need.
Intensity sets how many photons arrive; frequency sets the energy of each, and only the energy of each decides whether a bond can break.

w.a: UV light is more dangerous because it has a longer wavelength than visible light.
w.why: UV has the shorter wavelength

w.a: Bright visible light is harmless because it carries less total energy than UV.
w.why: it can carry more total energy; energy per photon is the point

w.a: UV damages skin because it is hotter than visible light.
w.why: temperature is not the mechanism; photon energy is

cards.q: State the Beer-Lambert law and define each term.
cards.a: A = εbc. A is absorbance (no units); ε is the molar absorptivity (M⁻¹ cm⁻¹), a constant for one species at one wavelength that measures how strongly it absorbs; b is the path length of light through the sample (cm, usually 1.00 cm); c is the molar concentration of the absorbing species (M). With b and wavelength held fixed, A is directly proportional to c.
cards.n: Treating ε as something that changes with concentration earns nothing; it depends only on the absorbing species and the wavelength.

cards.q: Apply a Beer-Lambert calibration curve to find an unknown concentration.
cards.a: Measure the absorbance of several standards of known concentration at one wavelength (λmax) in the same cuvette, plot A (vertical) against c (horizontal), and draw the best-fit straight line, which passes through the origin with slope εb. Measure the unknown's A under the same conditions and read its c from the line, or compute c = A ÷ slope.
cards.h: → standards → A-vs-c line → read the unknown
cards.n: Plugging a textbook ε into A = εbc when calibration data are given earns nothing; an unknown above the top standard must be diluted, not extrapolated.

cards.q: Predict what happens to absorbance when a colored solution is diluted by half.
cards.a: The absorbance is halved, for example from 0.640 to 0.320. With the wavelength and path length unchanged, A = εbc makes A directly proportional to c; halving the concentration halves the number of absorbing particles in the light path.
cards.h: → A ∝ c at fixed b and λ
cards.n: Answering that absorbance doubles, or that transmittance halves, earns nothing; A tracks concentration directly.

cards.q: Compute the absorbance of a solution that transmits 1.0% of the incident light (T = 0.010).
cards.a: A = 2.00. A = −log T = −log(0.010) = 2.00: only 1 photon in 100 reaches the detector, which is why very high absorbances are hard to measure precisely.
cards.h: → A = −log T with T as a decimal
cards.n: Entering 1.0 (the percent) instead of 0.010 gives A = 0 and earns nothing. A = −log T is not on the AP equations sheet; the exam uses A = εbc.

cards.q: Compute the concentration of a solution with absorbance 0.500, given ε = 5.00×10³ M⁻¹cm⁻¹ and a 1.00 cm cell.
cards.a: 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ M. c = A ÷ (εb) = 0.500 ÷ [(5.00 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹)(1.00 cm)] = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ M; the cm cancel, and a unitless A divided by M⁻¹ leaves M.
cards.n: Multiplying A by εb (2.50 × 10³) earns nothing; rearrange before substituting and check that the answer is a small, sensible molarity.

cards.q: Compute the molar absorptivity ε of a solution with A = 0.450, c = 3.00×10⁻⁴ M, in a 1.00 cm cell.
cards.a: 1.50 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹. ε = A ÷ (bc) = 0.450 ÷ [(1.00 cm)(3.00 × 10⁻⁴ M)] = 1.50 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹. Because ε is fixed for this species at this wavelength, every standard in a set should give the same value.
cards.h: → rearrange to ε = A/(bc), units included
cards.n: Dropping the units M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ loses the point on an FRQ; a unitless ε cannot make A come out unitless.

cards.q:
Calculate the concentration of an unknown solution whose absorbance is 0.380, using these standards measured at 510 nm in a 1.00 cm cuvette:
concentration (M) · absorbance
1.00 × 10⁻⁴ · 0.152
2.00 × 10⁻⁴ · 0.305
3.00 × 10⁻⁴ · 0.455
4.00 × 10⁻⁴ · 0.610
cards.a: 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ M. The standards lie on a straight line through the origin with slope ≈ 0.152 per 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ M = 1.52 × 10³ M⁻¹ (= εb), so c = A ÷ slope = 0.380 ÷ 1.52 × 10³ M⁻¹ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ M, between the second and third standards. With b = 1.00 cm, ε = 1.52 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹.
cards.h: → slope of A vs c, then c = A ÷ slope
cards.n: Averaging the four concentrations, or reading a value outside the range of the standards, earns nothing; the slope (εb) is what converts A into c.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, a calibration curve for four standards of a dye (1.0, 2.0, 3.0 and 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, with absorbances 0.12, 0.24, 0.36 and 0.48), and show how an unknown with A = 0.30 is read from it.
cards.a: Horizontal axis: concentration (M), 0 to 5.0 × 10⁻⁵; vertical axis: absorbance (no units), 0 to 0.60. Plot the four points and draw one straight best-fit line through the origin, slope εb = 1.2 × 10⁴ M⁻¹. From A = 0.30 on the vertical axis go across to the line, then down to the horizontal axis: c = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ M.
cards.h: → labelled axes, one line through the origin, read-off
cards.n: Joining the points dot to dot, swapping the axes, or leaving out the origin earns nothing; the calibration line is a single best fit through (0, 0).

cards.q:
Determine the wavelength at which to set the spectrophotometer to measure a red dye, from its absorbance spectrum:
wavelength (nm) · absorbance
400 · 0.08
450 · 0.21
500 · 0.55
520 · 0.68
540 · 0.61
600 · 0.19
650 · 0.05
cards.a: 520 nm, the wavelength of maximum absorbance (A = 0.68). There ε is largest, so the calibration line is steepest and each change in concentration gives the largest change in absorbance: the greatest sensitivity. The dye absorbs green light near 520 nm, which is why it looks red.
cards.n: Choosing 650 nm because the dye looks red earns nothing; a red solution transmits red light and absorbs it only weakly.

cards.q: Predict whether each error makes the calculated concentration of an unknown too high, too low, or unaffected (standards measured correctly unless stated): fingerprints on the unknown's cuvette · unknown added to a cuvette still wet with distilled water · unknown measured in a 2.00 cm cuvette, standards in 1.00 cm · unknown read at a wavelength away from λmax, standards at λmax · standards and unknown all read at the same off-peak wavelength · unknown left uncovered so some solvent evaporated · air bubble in the light path of the unknown
cards.a:
fingerprints → too high: smudges block light, so the measured A is too large
wet cuvette → too low: the water dilutes the unknown, so A is too small
2.00 cm cuvette → too high: A doubles with b, so c comes out twice the true value
unknown off λmax → too low: ε is smaller there, so A is too small for the line built at λmax
all at one off-peak wavelength → unaffected: the line was built at that wavelength; only sensitivity drops
solvent evaporated → too high: the sample itself became more concentrated, so A rises
air bubble → too high: scattered light never reaches the detector and is read as absorbed
cards.h: → does the error raise or lower the measured A?
cards.n: Answering 'inaccurate' without a direction earns nothing; trace each error to the measured A, then use A ∝ c to state the direction.

cards.q: Explain why absorbance is measured at the wavelength of maximum absorbance.
cards.a: At λmax the molar absorptivity ε is largest, so A changes most per unit change in concentration (the steepest calibration line): sensitivity is greatest and small concentration differences are easiest to detect. The peak of the absorbance curve is also flat, so a slight error in the wavelength setting barely changes A.
cards.h: → ε largest at λmax → steepest A-vs-c line → greatest sensitivity; flat peak → least wavelength error
cards.n: 'Because that is the color of the solution' earns nothing; a solution absorbs the complementary color, and the reason is the maximum ε.
o: The slope of the calibration line is εb, so the wavelength with the largest ε gives the largest slope and the most precise readings.
Near the peak the absorbance barely changes with wavelength, so drift in the instrument's wavelength setting has little effect.

w.a: λmax is used because at that wavelength the solution absorbs all of the light.
w.why: it absorbs the most, not all; A stays measurable

w.a: λmax is used because Beer's law only works at one wavelength.
w.why: it holds at any fixed wavelength; λmax gives the best sensitivity

w.a: λmax is used because it is the wavelength of the solution's color.
w.why: a solution appears the complementary color of what it absorbs

cards.q: Explain why doubling the path length of the cuvette doubles the measured absorbance of the same solution.
cards.a: Absorbance is proportional to the number of absorbing particles the light meets. A cuvette twice as long, filled with the same solution, puts twice as many absorbing molecules or ions in the light's path, so twice as much light is absorbed: in A = εbc, ε and c are unchanged, so A doubles when b doubles.
cards.h: → longer path → twice as many absorbing particles in the beam → A ∝ b
cards.n: 'The light gets tired traveling farther' earns nothing; the point is the number of absorbing particles in the light path.
o: Path length and concentration play the same role: each is proportional to the number of absorbing particles in the beam.
With the same species at the same wavelength, ε is constant, so A scales directly with b.

w.a: Absorbance doubles because the longer cuvette holds a more concentrated solution.
w.why: the concentration is the same; only the path length changes

w.a: Absorbance stays the same because the solution has not changed.
w.why: A depends on path length as well as concentration

w.a: Absorbance doubles because light slows down in a longer cuvette.
w.why: light speed is not the mechanism; the particle count in the path is

cards.q: Explain why a spectrophotometer is zeroed with a blank cuvette containing only the solvent before samples are measured.
cards.a: The cuvette walls and the solvent absorb or scatter a little light too. Zeroing on a solvent blank sets that background to A = 0, so each later reading measures only the light absorbed by the dissolved species, the quantity A = εbc relates to its concentration, and a solution with c = 0 reads A = 0.
cards.h: → solvent and cuvette absorb a little → blank sets that to zero → A reflects only the solute → A ∝ c
cards.n: 'The blank calibrates the machine' earns nothing unless it says what is removed: the absorbance of the solvent and the cuvette.
o: Beer's law applies to the absorbing species alone, so every other contribution to the reading must be subtracted by the blank.
Blanking makes the calibration line pass through the origin, so A is proportional to c.

w.a: The blank is measured so that the spectrophotometer can warm up before the real samples.
w.why: the blank removes background absorbance; warming up is separate

w.a: The blank is measured so that the solvent absorbs all of the light first.
w.why: the blank sets the solvent's small absorbance to zero

w.a: The blank is used because the solvent has the highest absorbance of anything in the cuvette.
w.why: the solvent absorbs very little; it is subtracted, not maximized

cards.q: Explain why the calibration standards and the unknown must be measured at the same wavelength.
cards.a: Molar absorptivity ε depends on wavelength: a species absorbs different wavelengths to different extents. The calibration line's slope is εb at the wavelength used; read at another wavelength, the unknown has a different ε, so its concentration gives a different A and the line converts it to a wrong concentration.
cards.h: → ε depends on λ → slope εb valid only at the calibration λ → another λ gives the wrong c
cards.n: 'So the colors match' earns nothing; the scored idea is that ε, and so the slope of A versus c, changes with wavelength.
o: A = εbc is a straight line in c only while ε and b are constant, and changing the wavelength changes ε.
Each wavelength has its own calibration line; reading an unknown against the wrong one mixes two different ε values.

w.a: The wavelength must match because different wavelengths travel different distances through the cuvette.
w.why: the path length is set by the cuvette, not the wavelength

w.a: The wavelength must match because the concentration of the solution changes with wavelength.
w.why: the concentration is fixed; ε changes

w.a: The wavelength does not matter because Beer's law holds at every wavelength.
w.why: it holds at each wavelength, but with a different ε

cards.q: Contrast a physical change with a chemical change at the particulate level.
cards.a: Physical change: only the attractions between particles are disrupted; the particles themselves are unchanged (melting, boiling, dissolving). Chemical change: bonds within particles break and new bonds form, so different substances exist afterward.
cards.n: Dissolving NaCl in water is classified as a physical change on the AP exam even though the ions separate.

cards.q: Identify the macroscopic evidence that a chemical change has occurred.
cards.a: Gas evolved that is not simply boiling, a precipitate forming, a permanent color change, a temperature change with no external heating, light emitted, or a new odor. Confirmation requires showing a new substance is present.
cards.n: Bubbles alone can mean boiling; AP wants evidence tied to the formation of a new substance.

cards.q: Explain why dissolving an ionic solid in water is treated as a physical change.
cards.a: Water molecules pull the ions apart by ion-dipole attraction. The ions are chemically unchanged and can be recovered unchanged by evaporating the water, so only interparticle attractions were disrupted.
cards.n: The equation is still written with an arrow and state symbols, so an arrow alone is not evidence that a chemical change occurred.

cards.q: Define a net ionic equation.
cards.a: An equation showing only the species that actually change: soluble strong electrolytes are written as separated aqueous ions and all spectator ions are cancelled. Both mass and total charge must balance.
cards.h: → what is kept, what is cancelled
cards.n: Charge balance is scored separately; a net ionic equation with unbalanced charge earns no credit.

cards.q: Define a spectator ion.
cards.a: An ion that is present in the same aqueous, unchanged form both before and after the reaction, so it cancels out of the complete ionic equation and does not appear in the net ionic equation.
cards.n: Spectator status belongs to the reaction, not the ion. Nitrate sits out here but is itself reduced when copper reacts with nitric acid.

cards.q: State which species are written as separated ions and which are kept as complete formulas in an ionic equation.
cards.a: Separate: strong acids, strong bases, and soluble ionic salts labeled (aq). Keep intact: all solids (s), liquids (l), gases (g), weak acids, weak bases, and molecular compounds such as water.
cards.n: Writing a weak acid such as CH3COOH as separated ions is one of the most common AP scoring errors.

cards.q: Write the net ionic equation for aqueous silver nitrate mixed with aqueous sodium chloride.
cards.a: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Sodium ion and nitrate ion are spectators and are omitted.
cards.n: Charge balances as well as mass here: 1+ and 1- sum to zero on the left, matching the neutral solid on the right.

cards.q: State the solubility guidelines most often required on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Always soluble: Group 1 cations, NH4⁺, NO3⁻, ClO4⁻, and most acetates. Generally insoluble: most carbonates, phosphates, sulfides, and hydroxides, plus the halides of Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, and Hg2²⁺.
cards.n: No solubility table is provided on the exam, so the always-soluble rules must be memorized.

cards.q: Explain what makes a solute a strong electrolyte and why that matters for ionic equations.
cards.a: A strong electrolyte dissociates essentially completely into free ions in water (strong acids, strong bases, soluble salts). Because it truly exists as separate ions in solution, it is written in separated ionic form.
cards.n: Weak acids and weak bases stay whole, so acetic acid is written as a molecule in a net ionic equation while HCl is split into ions.

cards.q: Explain what a particulate diagram drawn after a precipitation reaction must show.
cards.a: The precipitate drawn as a neutral cluster of alternating cations and anions, the spectator ions still drawn as separate hydrated ions in correct relative numbers, and any leftover excess reactant ions still in solution.
cards.n: Students routinely forget to draw the excess reactant ions that survive after the limiting reactant is used up.

cards.q: State the relationship used to convert between mass and moles of a substance.
cards.a: n = m / M, where n is moles, m is mass in grams, and M is molar mass in g/mol. Mole ratios taken from the balanced equation then connect moles of one species to moles of another.
cards.n: Moles are the hub of every stoichiometry road map. A ratio taken straight from coefficients to masses skips that hub and fails.

cards.q: Explain why the coefficients of a balanced equation give mole ratios rather than mass ratios.
cards.a: Coefficients count particles, and a mole is a fixed number of particles. Masses of equal particle counts differ because molar masses differ, so masses must be converted to moles before the ratio is applied.
cards.n: Gas VOLUME ratios at the same temperature and pressure do follow the coefficients directly, since equal volumes hold equal moles.

cards.q: Define the limiting reactant and state how to identify it.
cards.a: The reactant consumed completely first, which sets the maximum amount of product. Identify it by dividing the moles of each reactant by its coefficient in the balanced equation; the smallest quotient is the limiting reactant.
cards.n: Compare moles divided by coefficients, never raw masses and never raw moles.

cards.q: State how to find the amount of excess reactant remaining after a reaction goes to completion.
cards.a: Remaining moles = initial moles of the excess reactant minus the moles consumed, where moles consumed = moles of limiting reactant times the coefficient ratio. Multiply by molar mass if grams are requested.
