A unimolecular step has rate = k[A], first order, so k = (M/s)/M = s⁻¹. The molecularity of an elementary step fixes its order, and the order fixes the units of k.
cards.n: Giving s⁻¹ for both earns nothing; the second concentration factor in a bimolecular step removes one power of M from k.

cards.q: Explain why elementary reactions involving the simultaneous collision of three or more particles are rare.
cards.a: An elementary step requires all its reactant particles to meet in one event with enough energy and the right orientation. Three particles arriving at the same point at the same instant, correctly aligned, is far less probable than two, so reactions almost always proceed through uni- and bimolecular steps.
cards.h: → all reactants must meet at once → three-body coincidence improbable → sequences of 1- and 2-body steps instead
cards.n: 'Three molecules cannot fit together' earns nothing; the argument is about the low probability of a simultaneous, correctly oriented three-body collision.
o: Bimolecular collisions are already only a small fraction effective; requiring a third particle at the same instant multiplies in another small probability.
A mechanism of two bimolecular steps can accomplish what a termolecular step would, so nature rarely uses the improbable three-body route.

w.a: Termolecular steps are rare because three reactants would violate the law of conservation of mass.
w.why: mass conservation is unrelated; the issue is collision probability

w.a: Termolecular steps are rare because gas molecules never collide with more than one partner.
w.why: they can, just very rarely at the same instant with the right orientation

w.a: Termolecular steps are rare because they would have a rate law of third order, which is impossible.
w.why: third-order rate laws exist (e.g. 2 NO + O₂); the rarity is about the single collision event

cards.q: Explain why the rate law of an elementary step can be written directly from its coefficients, when the rate law of an overall reaction cannot.
cards.a: An elementary step is one collision, so its rate is proportional to how often the required particles meet: each participant's concentration raised to the number of those particles, its coefficient. An overall equation is the net sum of several steps, so its rate is set by the slowest step, not the net stoichiometry.
cards.h: → elementary = one collision → rate ∝ collision frequency ∝ [each]^(count) → overall = sum of steps
cards.n: 'Because elementary steps are simpler' earns nothing; the point is that the step's stoichiometry IS the collision, so exponents count colliding particles.
o: For a step A + B → products, the number of A–B encounters per second doubles when either concentration doubles, which is exactly rate = k[A][B].
The overall reaction's rate law reflects only the species in the rate-determining step, which may involve intermediates or omit some reactants entirely.

w.a: Any balanced equation's coefficients give the rate law exponents as long as the reaction is fast.
w.why: speed is irrelevant; only a single elementary step licenses the rule

w.a: Elementary steps use coefficients because their rate constants are always equal to one.
w.why: k has nothing to do with it and is rarely 1

w.a: Overall reactions cannot use coefficients because they do not have a rate law.
w.why: every reaction has a rate law; it just must be measured

cards.q: Explain why an observed rate law of rate = k[A] for the reaction 2 A → B shows that the reaction does not occur as a single elementary step.
cards.a: If 2 A → B were one elementary event, two A particles would collide and the rate law would be rate = k[A]². The observed first-order law means the rate-determining event involves only one A particle, so the reaction must proceed by several steps with a slow step unimolecular in A.
cards.h: → elementary 2A → rate ∝ [A]² → observed [A]¹ ≠ → not one step
cards.n: 'It is not elementary because B is a product' earns nothing; the argument compares the predicted elementary order (2) with the observed order (1).
o: A first-order rate law says that doubling [A] doubles the rate; a bimolecular collision of two A would quadruple it.
The rate law is evidence about the mechanism: a mismatch with the coefficients rules out the one-step picture.

w.a: The reaction is not elementary because its rate law does not include B.
w.why: products are absent from forward rate laws whether or not the step is elementary

w.a: The reaction could still be elementary; the rate law just happens to be first order.
w.why: an elementary 2A step must be second order

w.a: The reaction is not elementary because 2 A → B has a coefficient of 2.
w.why: elementary steps can have coefficient 2 (2 NO → N₂O₂); the issue is the mismatch with the observed order

cards.q: Define the collision model of reaction rates.
cards.a: The collision model states that reactant particles must collide for bonds to break and form, and that only a fraction of collisions succeed. The rate of an elementary reaction equals the collision frequency multiplied by the fraction of collisions that have energy at least equal to the activation energy and by the fraction with an orientation that lets the bonds rearrange. Concentration sets the frequency; temperature sets the energy fraction.
cards.n: 'Particles must collide' alone earns nothing; the point is that only collisions with sufficient energy AND correct orientation produce products.

cards.q: State the two requirements for a collision to result in reaction.
cards.a: (1) Sufficient energy: the colliding particles' kinetic energy along the line of collision must be at least the activation energy, so the transition state can be reached. (2) Correct orientation: the particles must meet with the atoms that will bond facing each other, so the bonds can rearrange. A collision lacking either simply bounces apart.
cards.n: 'They must hit hard enough' covers only the energy criterion; omitting orientation loses the second point.

cards.q: Define the steric (orientation) factor in the collision model and explain why it is usually less than 1.
cards.a: The steric factor is the fraction of sufficiently energetic collisions that also have the orientation needed for the bonds to rearrange. It is less than 1 because most collisions, even energetic ones, bring the wrong atoms together: for NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ an O atom of NO₂ must strike the C atom of CO, and a collision by the N end or at the O end of CO cannot transfer the oxygen.
cards.h: → fraction correctly oriented, with a concrete example
cards.n: 'Energy is all that matters' earns nothing; both energy and orientation are required, and the steric factor tracks the second.

cards.q: Describe the features of a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve for the kinetic energies of particles in a sample, and what each feature represents.
cards.a: Axes: kinetic energy on the horizontal axis, number (or fraction) of particles with that energy on the vertical axis. The curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak at the most probable energy, then falls in a long tail toward high energy without reaching zero. The total area under the curve is the total number of particles; the area under the curve to the right of a vertical line at Ea is the fraction of particles (collisions) with energy sufficient to react.
cards.h: → axes, origin, peak, tail, two areas
cards.n: Labeling the peak 'the activation energy' earns nothing; the peak is the most probable energy, and Ea is a separate vertical line usually far out in the tail.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, the Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions for the same gas at 300 K and at 400 K on one set of axes, with the activation energy of a reaction marked, and state what the drawing shows about the reaction rate.
cards.a: Axes: kinetic energy (horizontal), number of particles (vertical). Both curves start at the origin. 300 K: a tall, narrow peak at lower energy, dropping off quickly. 400 K: a lower, broader peak shifted right, with a fatter tail reaching higher energy; the areas under both are equal. A vertical Ea line lies right of both peaks; the area beyond it is clearly larger for 400 K, so a larger fraction of collisions can react and the rate is higher.
cards.h: → two equal-area curves; hotter one lower, right; Ea line
cards.n: Drawing the hotter curve taller or shifting the Ea line earns nothing; the same number of particles is redistributed, and Ea is fixed by the reaction.

cards.q: Identify which curve is at the higher temperature and which sample reacts faster, with reasons: two Maxwell–Boltzmann curves for the same gas are drawn on one graph; curve X has a tall peak at low energy and a short tail, curve Y a lower peak further right with a longer tail; a vertical line marks Ea to the right of both peaks.
cards.a: Curve Y is the higher temperature: raising T raises the average kinetic energy, spreading the particles over a wider range, so the peak shifts right and lowers (the area, the number of particles, is fixed). Sample Y reacts faster because the area under Y to the right of the Ea line is larger, so a greater fraction of its collisions has energy at least Ea.
cards.h: → broader/right = hotter; larger area past Ea = faster
cards.n: Choosing X 'because its peak is higher' earns nothing; peak height is not energy, the position and the tail area beyond Ea are what matter.
x: Y is hotter and reacts faster

cards.q: Compare the fraction of effective collisions for two reactions run at the same temperature, one with an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol and one with 100 kJ/mol, and predict which is faster if their collision frequencies and orientation requirements are similar.
cards.a: The 50 kJ/mol reaction has the larger fraction of effective collisions and is faster. At a given temperature the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution is fixed; the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea is the tail area beyond Ea, and a vertical line at 50 kJ/mol leaves far more area to its right than a line at 100 kJ/mol. With similar frequency and orientation factors, the larger energetic fraction gives the larger rate constant.
cards.h: → same curve, lower Ea line → larger tail area → larger k
cards.n: 'The 100 kJ/mol reaction releases more energy so it is faster' earns nothing; Ea is a barrier, not an energy released, and ΔH does not set the rate.

cards.q: Predict how cooling a reaction mixture from 350 K to 300 K changes the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution and the fraction of collisions that have energy at least equal to the activation energy.
cards.a: The distribution narrows: the peak becomes taller and moves to lower energy, and the high-energy tail shrinks, while the total area stays the same. The vertical line at Ea does not move, so the area beyond it, the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea, falls sharply; fewer effective collisions per second means a lower rate and a smaller rate constant.
cards.h: → peak taller and left → smaller area past fixed Ea
cards.n: Moving the Ea line to the right 'because it is harder to react when cold' earns nothing; Ea belongs to the reaction and is unchanged by temperature.

cards.q: Describe the orientation requirement for the reaction NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) to occur in a single collision, and identify a collision geometry that fails even with sufficient energy.
cards.a: An oxygen atom of NO₂ must strike the carbon atom of CO so that the C–O bond can form as the N–O bond breaks, transferring the O atom. A collision in which the nitrogen end of NO₂ hits CO, or in which the oxygen end of CO faces NO₂, cannot form the new C–O bond in that geometry and the molecules bounce apart, no matter how energetic the collision.
cards.h: → which atoms must meet; one failing geometry
cards.n: 'The molecules must hit each other' earns nothing; name the atoms that must make contact for the new bond to form.

cards.q: Describe, in terms of the collision model, the three factors whose product determines the rate of an elementary reaction, and name the experimental variable that mainly controls each.
cards.a: Rate = (collision frequency) × (fraction with energy ≥ Ea) × (fraction correctly oriented). Frequency is controlled mainly by concentration (and a solid's surface area) and rises slightly with T. The energetic fraction is controlled by temperature, through the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, and by Ea, which a catalyst lowers. The orientation fraction is set by molecular structure; a catalyst that holds reactants in place can raise it.
cards.n: Attributing the temperature effect to 'more collisions' alone earns nothing; the dominant effect of temperature is on the fraction with energy above Ea.

cards.q: Explain why a modest increase in temperature produces a large increase in reaction rate.
cards.a: Raising T shifts the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution toward higher energy. Because Ea lies in the sparse high-energy tail, the area beyond Ea grows by a far larger factor than the average energy does, so the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea, and with it k and the rate, rises sharply.
cards.h: → distribution shifts right → tail area past Ea grows disproportionately → many more effective collisions
cards.n: 'Higher temperature means more collisions' alone earns nothing; the scored idea is the larger FRACTION of collisions with energy above Ea.
o: The rate constant depends exponentially on Ea/T, so a few percent more thermal energy multiplies the fraction of particles that can clear the barrier.
Only the fastest particles react; warming the sample moves many particles from just below Ea to just above it, a large relative change in that small group.

w.a: A small temperature rise speeds the reaction a lot because the molecules collide much more often.
w.why: collision frequency rises only slightly; the energetic fraction is what grows sharply

w.a: A small temperature rise speeds the reaction because it lowers the activation energy.
w.why: Ea is fixed by the reaction pathway; temperature changes how many collisions exceed it

w.a: A small temperature rise speeds the reaction because the reactant concentrations increase.
w.why: concentrations are unchanged by temperature in a closed system

cards.q: Explain how a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows the effect of temperature on rate.
cards.a: The curve plots number of particles against kinetic energy; the area beyond the fixed Ea line is the fraction able to react. Raising T lowers and broadens the peak and shifts it right, so that area grows: more collisions have sufficient energy, more are effective, and the rate rises.
cards.h: → area beyond Ea = reactive fraction → hotter curve shifts right → area grows → faster
cards.n: Saying the hotter curve 'moves Ea to the left' earns nothing; Ea is fixed by the reaction, only the fraction of particles beyond it changes.
o: Since the total area is fixed, moving particles into the high-energy tail necessarily increases the fraction past Ea, which is the fraction of effective collisions.
At two temperatures the same Ea line cuts off a small tail at low T and a much larger one at high T, which is why k is strongly temperature dependent.

w.a: The distribution shows the effect of temperature because the hotter curve has a higher peak, meaning more energetic particles.
w.why: the hotter curve has a LOWER peak; the tail beyond Ea is what carries the effect

w.a: The distribution shows that at higher temperature all particles have enough energy to react.
w.why: even at high T only a fraction exceed Ea; the fraction grows, it does not become 1

w.a: The distribution shows that the activation energy decreases at higher temperature.
w.why: Ea is a property of the reaction, not the temperature

cards.q: Explain why the reaction between two large, complex molecules typically has a smaller steric (orientation) factor than a reaction between two small atoms.
cards.a: In a large molecule the bonds that must break and form lie in a small reactive region, so only collisions that bring those atoms together in the right alignment react; most strike elsewhere and bounce off. Two small atoms have no directional structure, so almost any energetic collision succeeds.
cards.h: → small reactive site on a big molecule → few orientations work → small fraction
cards.n: 'Big molecules move slower so they collide less' earns nothing; the steric factor is about the fraction of collisions with the right orientation, not their frequency.
o: Reaction needs a particular geometry of approach; the more atoms a molecule has, the smaller the fraction of its surface that is the reactive site.
Enzymes exist precisely to fix this: they hold a large substrate in the one orientation that reacts, raising the effective orientation factor.

w.a: Large molecules have a smaller steric factor because they need more activation energy.
w.why: Ea is the energy criterion; the steric factor is the orientation criterion

w.a: Large molecules have a smaller steric factor because they collide less often.
w.why: frequency is a separate factor; orientation is about which collisions count

w.a: Small atoms have a steric factor of zero because they have no bonds to orient.
w.why: backwards: with no orientation requirement the factor approaches 1

cards.q: Explain why, in most reactions, only a small fraction of the collisions between reactant particles leads to a reaction.
cards.a: A collision reacts only if it has energy ≥ Ea and brings the reacting atoms together in the right orientation. At ordinary temperatures Ea lies far out in the thin tail of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, so few collisions are energetic enough, and only some of those are aligned.
cards.h: → need E ≥ Ea AND right orientation → Ea in the sparse tail → small fraction × small fraction
cards.n: 'Collisions are rare' earns nothing; gas molecules collide billions of times per second. The point is that few collisions meet BOTH criteria.
o: The rate constant is the product of a collision frequency factor and a small exponential fraction that clears Ea, and the orientation factor shrinks it further.
If every collision reacted, most gas-phase reactions would be over in nanoseconds; observed rates are far slower because the energy and orientation filters remove almost all collisions.

w.a: Only a few collisions react because most molecules are moving too slowly to collide at all.
w.why: they do collide, constantly; they lack the energy or alignment to react

w.a: Only a few collisions react because the products immediately turn back into reactants.
w.why: reversibility is a separate matter; the small fraction is about the forward event

w.a: Only a few collisions react because the activation energy is used up by the first collisions.
w.why: Ea is a barrier height, not a consumable quantity

cards.q: Explain why raising the temperature of a reaction from 298 K to 308 K can roughly double its rate even though the average kinetic energy of the particles rises by only about 3%.
cards.a: The rate follows the fraction of collisions with energy above Ea, which lies in the thin high-energy tail, not the average energy. A 3% rise in average energy shifts the curve slightly right, but the small tail area beyond Ea can double, so effective collisions roughly double.
cards.h: → rate tracks tail area past Ea, not average → small shift → large relative growth of a small tail
cards.n: 'The rate doubles because the collisions are 3% more frequent' earns nothing; the 3% is the average energy change, and the rate follows the tail fraction.
o: Because the fraction above Ea falls off exponentially with Ea/T, a modest change in T produces a large proportional change in that fraction.
Most particles never react at either temperature; the rate is decided by the few in the tail, and their number is very sensitive to temperature.

w.a: The rate doubles because the particles collide twice as often at 308 K.
w.why: collision frequency rises by only a few percent

w.a: The rate doubles because at 308 K the activation energy is half as large.
w.why: Ea does not change with temperature

w.a: The rate doubles because heating adds a catalyst-like energy to the reaction.
w.why: heat changes the energy distribution, it does not change the pathway

cards.q: Define activation energy.
cards.a: Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum energy colliding particles must have to reach the transition state and go on to products. On a reaction energy profile it is the vertical distance from the reactant energy level up to the peak (the transition state); the reverse reaction has its own Ea measured from the product level up to the same peak.
cards.h: → minimum energy to reach the peak; measured from reactants
cards.n: Measuring Ea from the zero of the energy axis, or from the products for the forward reaction, earns nothing; it is the climb from the reactants to the peak.
x: minimum energy to reach the transition state

cards.q: Define the activated complex and distinguish it from an intermediate.
cards.a: The activated complex (transition state) is the highest-energy arrangement of atoms along the reaction coordinate, at the peak of the energy profile, with old bonds partly broken and new bonds partly formed; it cannot be isolated because it exists only for the instant of a collision. An intermediate is a real species that sits in an energy minimum (a valley) between two peaks, formed in one elementary step and consumed in a later one, and can sometimes be detected.
cards.h: → peak vs valley; partial bonds vs real species
cards.n: Calling the valley a transition state, or saying an intermediate has partial bonds, earns nothing; peaks are transition states, valleys are intermediates.

cards.q: State the Arrhenius equation and identify each symbol.
cards.a: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT). k is the rate constant; A is the frequency factor, which combines the collision frequency and the fraction of collisions with the correct orientation; Ea is the activation energy; R is the gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K); T is the absolute temperature in kelvin. The exponential factor is the fraction of collisions with energy at least Ea, so k grows with T and shrinks with Ea.
cards.h: → equation, then five symbols with meanings
cards.n: The CED excludes calculations with this equation; know what each factor means (A = frequency × orientation; the exponential = energetic fraction), not how to solve for Ea.

cards.q: Identify the forward activation energy, reverse activation energy, and ΔH on a reaction energy profile.
cards.a: Ea(forward) is the vertical rise from the reactant energy level to the peak; Ea(reverse) is the rise from the product level to the same peak; ΔH (the overall energy change) is the product level minus the reactant level, negative if products lie lower (exothermic). The three are linked: ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse).
cards.h: → three vertical distances and their relation
cards.n: Reading ΔH as the peak height, or Ea(reverse) as the drop from peak to reactants, earns nothing; each quantity is a specific vertical distance.

cards.q: Predict how doubling the activation energy affects the rate constant at a fixed temperature, using the Arrhenius equation.
cards.a: k decreases sharply, by far more than half. In k = A·e^(−Ea/RT) the activation energy sits in a negative exponent, so doubling Ea squares the already small exponential factor: a much smaller fraction of collisions has enough energy to reach the transition state. On the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve the Ea line moves right into the thin tail, leaving very little area beyond it.
cards.h: → Ea in the exponent → k falls far more than half
cards.n: 'k halves because Ea doubled' earns nothing; the dependence is exponential, not inverse. Quantifying the drop would be an Arrhenius calculation, which the CED excludes.

cards.q: Compute the ratio k2/k1 if raising temperature increases the rate constant from 0.010 to 0.040 s⁻¹.
cards.a: k₂/k₁ = 0.040 s⁻¹ ÷ 0.010 s⁻¹ = 4.0. The rate constant, and therefore the rate at any given concentration, has quadrupled, because at the higher temperature a larger fraction of collisions has energy at least equal to the activation energy. The units cancel, so the ratio is dimensionless.
cards.n: Reporting the difference (0.030 s⁻¹) earns nothing; a ratio is asked. Solving this ratio for Ea would be an Arrhenius calculation, which the CED excludes.

cards.q: Explain how to tell from a reaction energy profile whether the overall reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
cards.a: Compare the energy level of the products (right end) with that of the reactants (left end). If the products lie lower, energy was released and the reaction is exothermic, ΔH < 0; if the products lie higher, energy was absorbed and the reaction is endothermic, ΔH > 0. The height of the peak is irrelevant to this; it sets the rate, not the sign of ΔH.
cards.h: → compare end levels; ignore the peak
cards.n: Judging exothermic 'because the peak is high' earns nothing; the barrier height is Ea, not ΔH.

cards.q: Draw, in words precise enough to sketch, the reaction energy profile for an exothermic elementary reaction whose reactants sit at 0 kJ/mol, transition state at +80 kJ/mol and products at −40 kJ/mol, labeling Ea(forward), Ea(reverse) and ΔE.
cards.a: Axes: reaction coordinate (horizontal), potential energy in kJ/mol (vertical). Start with a flat segment at 0 labeled reactants; a single smooth hump rises to a peak at +80 labeled transition state; the curve descends to a flat segment at −40 labeled products, lower than the start. Label the vertical arrow from 0 up to 80 as Ea(forward) = 80 kJ/mol, the arrow from −40 up to 80 as Ea(reverse) = 120 kJ/mol, and the arrow from 0 down to −40 as ΔE = −40 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → one hump; three labeled arrows with values
cards.n: An unlabeled hump earns little; the points are for the correct relative levels and the three arrows measured from the right baselines.

cards.q: Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction for (a) a reaction with Ea(forward) = 75 kJ/mol and ΔH = −50 kJ/mol, and (b) a reaction with Ea(forward) = 120 kJ/mol and ΔH = +30 kJ/mol.
cards.a: (a) 125 kJ/mol; (b) 90 kJ/mol. The peak is shared, so Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH. (a) 75 − (−50) = 125 kJ/mol: the products lie 50 kJ/mol below the reactants, so climbing back to the peak is 50 kJ/mol harder. (b) 120 − 30 = 90 kJ/mol: the products lie 30 kJ/mol above the reactants, so the reverse climb is shorter.
cards.h: → Ea(rev) = Ea(fwd) − ΔH, watch the sign
cards.n: Adding ΔH with the wrong sign (75 − 50 = 25 kJ/mol) earns nothing; for an exothermic reaction the reverse barrier is LARGER than the forward one.

cards.q: Describe what the reaction coordinate represents and what is happening to the bonds at the transition state of the elementary step NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂.
cards.a: The reaction coordinate is the horizontal axis of the energy profile: a single variable that tracks the progress of the set of atomic motions converting reactants to products, from separated reactants on the left to separated products on the right. At the transition state, the highest-energy point, one N–O bond of NO₂ is partly broken and a new C–O bond to the carbon of CO is partly formed; the O atom is shared between N and C in a fleeting, unstable arrangement.
cards.h: → progress variable; partial bonds at the peak
cards.n: Calling the reaction coordinate 'time' earns nothing; it measures structural progress along the pathway, not elapsed time.

cards.q: Compare two elementary reactions at the same temperature: reaction A has Ea = 40 kJ/mol and ΔH = +10 kJ/mol; reaction B has Ea = 80 kJ/mol and ΔH = −90 kJ/mol. Determine which is faster and explain whether ΔH matters.
cards.a: Reaction A is faster. The rate of an elementary reaction depends on the fraction of collisions with energy above Ea, and a 40 kJ/mol barrier leaves far more of the Maxwell–Boltzmann tail beyond it than an 80 kJ/mol barrier does. ΔH does not matter for the rate: B releases much more energy overall, but its particles must first climb the higher barrier. ΔH sets the heights of the end levels, not the peak.
cards.h: → lower Ea → larger fraction past Ea; ΔH irrelevant
cards.n: 'B is faster because it is more exothermic' earns nothing; thermodynamics (ΔH) and kinetics (Ea) are independent.

cards.q: Determine Ea(forward), Ea(reverse) and ΔE for a single-step reaction whose energy profile has the reactant level at 20 kJ/mol, the peak at 95 kJ/mol and the product level at 60 kJ/mol, and classify the reaction as exothermic or endothermic.
cards.a: Ea(forward) = 95 − 20 = 75 kJ/mol; Ea(reverse) = 95 − 60 = 35 kJ/mol; ΔE = 60 − 20 = +40 kJ/mol, endothermic because the products lie above the reactants. Check: Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse) = 75 − 35 = +40 kJ/mol = ΔE.
cards.h: → three subtractions, then sign of ΔE
cards.n: Reporting Ea(forward) as 95 kJ/mol (the peak's absolute height) earns nothing; Ea is measured from the reactant level.

cards.q: Explain why the activation energy of the reverse reaction is larger than the activation energy of the forward reaction for an exothermic reaction.
cards.a: Forward and reverse reactions pass through the same transition state, the single peak on the profile. In an exothermic reaction the products lie below the reactants, so climbing from the lower product level to that shared peak is a longer climb than from the reactant level: Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + |ΔH|.
cards.h: → same peak for both directions → products lower → longer climb back → Ea(rev) = Ea(fwd) + |ΔH|
cards.n: 'The reverse reaction is endothermic so it needs more energy' is the conclusion restated; the point is the shared peak and the lower starting level.
o: ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse); with ΔH negative, Ea(reverse) must exceed Ea(forward).
On the profile the drop from peak to products is the reverse barrier, and it is the forward barrier plus the extra height the products fell below the reactants.

w.a: The reverse activation energy is larger because the reverse reaction has a different, higher transition state.
w.why: both directions share the same transition state

w.a: The reverse activation energy is larger because the products are more stable, so they react faster.
w.why: more stable products react SLOWER; and stability is not the mechanism of the larger barrier

w.a: The reverse activation energy is always larger, for every reaction.
w.why: for an endothermic reaction the reverse barrier is smaller

cards.q: Explain why the transition state of an elementary reaction cannot be isolated and studied as a stable compound.
cards.a: The transition state is the maximum on the energy profile, an arrangement with bonds partly broken and partly formed. Any motion along the reaction coordinate lowers its energy, so it collapses at once to reactants or products; nothing holds it. Isolable species, including intermediates, sit in energy minima.
cards.h: → energy maximum → no barrier to leaving → falls apart instantly → only minima are isolable
cards.n: 'It is too reactive' earns nothing; the reason is that it sits at an energy maximum with partial bonds, not in a well.
o: A species can be isolated only if it must overcome an activation energy to change; the transition state has none in either direction.
Its lifetime is a single bond vibration, roughly 10⁻¹³ s, far too short to accumulate or characterize.

w.a: The transition state cannot be isolated because it is an intermediate that reacts too fast.
w.why: an intermediate sits in a valley and can sometimes be isolated; the transition state is a peak

w.a: The transition state cannot be isolated because it has no atoms, only energy.
w.why: it is a real arrangement of atoms with partial bonds

w.a: The transition state cannot be isolated because it only forms at very high temperature.
w.why: it forms in every successful collision at any temperature

cards.q: Explain why the rate of an elementary reaction depends on temperature.
cards.a: To react, colliding particles need enough energy to reach the transition state. As T rises, more particles move into the high-energy tail of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, so the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea grows sharply; that fraction is the exponential factor in k = A·e^(−Ea/RT).
cards.h: → need E ≥ Ea → fraction past Ea grows with T → k = A·e^(−Ea/RT) rises
cards.n: 'Hotter particles collide more' alone earns nothing; the scored reasoning is the larger proportion of collisions energetic enough to reach the transition state.
o: The proportion of particles that can climb the barrier, not the barrier itself, changes with temperature, and that proportion sets k.
On the profile the peak height is fixed; raising T gives more collisions the energy to reach it per second.

w.a: The rate depends on temperature because heating lowers the activation energy.
w.why: Ea is a property of the pathway; temperature changes the fraction that exceeds it

w.a: The rate depends on temperature only because hotter molecules collide more frequently.
w.why: the frequency change is small; the energetic fraction dominates

w.a: The rate depends on temperature because ΔH becomes more negative when heated.
w.why: ΔH is nearly temperature independent and does not set the rate

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with a large negative ΔH, such as the combustion of methane, can be extremely slow at room temperature.
cards.a: The rate is set by the activation energy, not ΔH. Combustion has a high barrier because strong C–H and O=O bonds must be partly broken to reach the transition state, and at room temperature almost no collisions have that much energy. ΔH is the energy drop after the barrier is crossed.
cards.h: → rate set by Ea, not ΔH → high barrier → negligible fraction past Ea at 298 K → slow
cards.n: 'It is slow because it needs a spark' restates the observation; the point is that a large barrier leaves almost no energetic collisions at room temperature.
o: Thermodynamics says how far downhill the products lie; kinetics says how high the hill in between is, and the two are independent.
A spark supplies the energy for the first collisions to reach the transition state; the heat released then keeps the temperature, and the energetic fraction, high.

w.a: Methane burns slowly at room temperature because its ΔH is not negative enough.
w.why: ΔH is very negative; the barrier, not the energy release, controls the rate

w.a: Methane burns slowly at room temperature because oxygen is a catalyst that is missing.
w.why: oxygen is a reactant, not a catalyst, and it is present

w.a: Methane does not react at all at room temperature because the reaction is endothermic.
w.why: combustion is strongly exothermic; slow is not the same as endothermic

cards.q: Define a reaction mechanism.
cards.a: A reaction mechanism is the sequence of elementary steps (single collisions or decompositions) by which reactants are converted to products. Its components may include reactants, products, intermediates (formed in one step, consumed in a later one) and catalysts (consumed then regenerated). A valid mechanism's steps must add up to the overall balanced equation, and its rate-determining step must predict the observed rate law.
cards.h: → sequence of elementary steps + two requirements
cards.n: 'The way a reaction happens' earns nothing; name the elementary steps and the requirement that they sum to the overall equation.

cards.q: Define a reaction intermediate.
cards.a: An intermediate is a species produced in one elementary step and consumed in a later step, so it is present only while the reaction is occurring and cancels out when the steps are added; it does not appear in the overall balanced equation. Unlike a transition state, it sits in an energy minimum (a valley between peaks on the profile) and can sometimes be detected. Its concentration never appears in a final rate law.
cards.h: → made in one step, used in a later one; absent from overall
cards.n: Calling the transition state an intermediate earns nothing: the intermediate is a real species in a valley, the transition state is the peak.

cards.q: Contrast a reaction intermediate with a catalyst in terms of where each appears in a mechanism.
cards.a: An intermediate first appears as a PRODUCT of an early step and is consumed as a reactant in a later step. A catalyst first appears as a REACTANT of an early step, is consumed there, and is regenerated as a product of a later step. Both cancel when the steps are added and so are absent from the overall equation; the order of appearance tells them apart.
cards.n: 'Both cancel out' alone earns nothing; the point is the ORDER: intermediate made first, catalyst used first.

cards.q: Identify the intermediate in this mechanism: Step 1: $NO_2 + F_2 \to NO_2F + F$; Step 2: $F + NO_2 \to NO_2F$.
cards.a: F (the fluorine atom). It is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, so it cancels when the steps are added and is absent from the overall equation 2 NO₂ + F₂ → 2 NO₂F. NO₂ and F₂ are reactants (consumed, not regenerated) and NO₂F is the product.
cards.h: → species made in one step, used in the next
cards.n: Naming NO₂F 'because it appears in both steps' earns nothing; NO₂F is formed in both and never consumed, so it is the product.

cards.q: Identify the overall reaction obtained by summing two elementary steps: Step 1 (slow) $A+B \to C$; Step 2 (fast) $C+B \to D$.
cards.a: A + 2B → D. Adding the steps gives A + B + C + B → C + D; C appears on both sides (produced in step 1, consumed in step 2) and cancels as the intermediate, leaving A + 2B → D. The two B's come from one B consumed in each step.
cards.h: → add, cancel the intermediate, collect like terms
cards.n: Leaving C in the overall equation or writing A + B → D (forgetting the second B) earns nothing; only the intermediate cancels.

cards.q: Describe the four kinds of species that can appear in a reaction mechanism and how to recognize each from the list of elementary steps.
cards.a: Reactants: consumed in some step, never regenerated; on the left of the overall equation. Products: formed, never consumed; on the right. Intermediates: formed in an earlier step and consumed in a later one; they cancel and are absent from the overall equation. Catalysts: consumed in an earlier step and regenerated in a later one; they also cancel, but are present before the reaction starts and unchanged at the end.
cards.n: Classifying every species that cancels as an intermediate earns nothing; a catalyst also cancels but is used FIRST and regenerated LATER.

cards.q: Determine the overall equation and identify every intermediate for the mechanism: Step 1: 2 NO → N₂O₂; Step 2: N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂O + H₂O; Step 3: N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O.
cards.a: Overall: 2 NO + 2 H₂ → N₂ + 2 H₂O. Intermediates: N₂O₂ (formed in step 1, consumed in step 2) and N₂O (formed in step 2, consumed in step 3). Adding the steps: 2 NO + N₂O₂ + H₂ + N₂O + H₂ → N₂O₂ + N₂O + H₂O + N₂ + H₂O; cancelling N₂O₂ and N₂O from both sides leaves the overall equation. There is no catalyst: nothing is consumed first and regenerated later.
cards.h: → add three steps, cancel two intermediates
cards.n: Listing H₂O as an intermediate because it is formed twice earns nothing; it is never consumed, so it is a product with coefficient 2.
x: 2 NO + 2 H2 -> N2 + 2 H2O; N2O2 and N2O

cards.q: Determine whether the proposed mechanism Step 1: NO₂ + F₂ → NO₂F + F; Step 2: F + F → F₂ is consistent with the overall reaction 2 NO₂ + F₂ → 2 NO₂F, and explain.
cards.a: It is not consistent. Adding the steps gives NO₂ + F₂ + 2 F → NO₂F + F + F₂; cancelling F₂ and one F leaves NO₂ + F → NO₂F, which is not the overall equation: F is left over rather than cancelling, only one NO₂F forms, and F₂ is regenerated as if it were a catalyst. A mechanism must sum exactly to the overall equation with every intermediate cancelling.
cards.h: → add the steps; compare to the overall equation
cards.n: Accepting the mechanism 'because it uses the right substances' earns nothing; the steps must sum to the overall equation.

cards.q: Identify which proposed mechanism for NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) is supported by the observation that NO₃ can be detected in the reacting mixture: Mechanism 1, a single step NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂; or Mechanism 2, Step 1: 2 NO₂ → NO₃ + NO, Step 2: NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂.
cards.a: Mechanism 2. Detecting NO₃ shows that this species forms during the reaction; Mechanism 2 produces NO₃ as an intermediate (formed in step 1, consumed in step 2), while Mechanism 1 involves no NO₃ at any point. Evidence of an intermediate supports the mechanism that includes it; it does not by itself prove every detail of that mechanism.
cards.h: → which mechanism contains the detected species
cards.n: The CED excludes how the detection data are collected; the scored idea is that an observed intermediate supports the mechanism that predicts it.

cards.q:
Identify the intermediate(s), the catalyst if any, and the overall equation for each mechanism:
(a) 2 NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂
(b) Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂; ClO + O → Cl + O₂
(c) H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻; H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + I⁻
(d) O₃ → O₂ + O; O + O₃ → 2 O₂
cards.a:
(a) → intermediate NO₃; no catalyst; overall NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ (one NO₂ cancels)
(b) → intermediate ClO; catalyst Cl (consumed in step 1, regenerated in step 2); overall O₃ + O → 2 O₂
(c) → intermediate IO⁻; catalyst I⁻; overall 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂
(d) → intermediate O (oxygen atom); no catalyst; overall 2 O₃ → 3 O₂
cards.n: In (a), the NO₂ regenerated in step 2 is not a catalyst: two NO₂ are consumed and only one returns, so NO₂ is a net reactant.

cards.q: Explain why a reaction intermediate does not appear in the overall balanced equation.
cards.a: An intermediate is produced by one elementary step and consumed by a later one, so it is a product in one step and a reactant in another. When the steps are added it occurs on both sides and cancels; it exists only while the reaction runs and is neither a starting material nor a final product.
cards.h: → made in one step, used in another → both sides on addition → cancels
cards.n: 'Because it is unstable' earns nothing; instability is not why it cancels. It cancels because it is both formed and consumed.
o: The overall equation shows only net change, and an intermediate undergoes no net change: everything made is used up.
On the energy profile an intermediate is a valley between two peaks, a stop along the way, not an endpoint.

w.a: An intermediate does not appear in the overall equation because it is a catalyst.
w.why: a catalyst also cancels, but it is consumed first and regenerated; an intermediate is the reverse

w.a: An intermediate does not appear in the overall equation because it exists in too small an amount to count.
w.why: its amount is irrelevant; it cancels because it is formed and then consumed

w.a: An intermediate does not appear because it is the same thing as the transition state.
w.why: it is a real species in an energy minimum, not the peak

cards.q: Explain why detecting a proposed intermediate during a reaction supports one mechanism over another, yet does not prove that mechanism.
cards.a: A mechanism predicts which transient species exist, so detecting one supports a mechanism that produces it and counts against one that does not. But other mechanisms might form the same species, and detection says nothing about step order or rates, so it shows consistency, not proof.
cards.h: → prediction of a transient species confirmed → supports; other mechanisms possible → not proof
cards.n: 'It proves the mechanism because the intermediate is there' earns nothing; a mechanism can only be supported or ruled out.
o: Failing to detect an intermediate can rule a mechanism out; detecting it can only add support, because the same species may arise in several pathways.
Consistency with the rate law and with the observed intermediates together build a case; each is necessary evidence, neither is sufficient.

w.a: Detecting the intermediate proves the mechanism because intermediates can only form one way.
w.why: different mechanisms can share an intermediate

w.a: Detecting the intermediate is irrelevant because intermediates cancel out of the overall equation.
w.why: cancelling from the net equation is exactly why seeing it is informative about the steps

w.a: Detecting the intermediate proves the mechanism as long as the rate law also fits.
w.why: even both together only support; another mechanism could match both

cards.q: Explain why a proposed mechanism whose elementary steps do not add up to the overall balanced equation must be rejected.
cards.a: The overall equation is the observed net change: what is consumed and formed, in what mole ratios. A mechanism claims to be the molecular events producing that change, so its steps must sum exactly to it with intermediates cancelling; otherwise it describes a different reaction, whatever its rate law.
cards.h: → overall equation = observed net change → steps must sum to it → otherwise a different reaction
cards.n: 'It must be rejected because mechanisms have to be balanced' is circular; the point is that the steps must reproduce the observed stoichiometry.
o: Atoms and charge are conserved in every step, so a set of steps that fails to give the overall equation is either incomplete or describes other products.
Summing to the overall equation is the first of two tests; only a mechanism that passes it is then checked against the rate law.

w.a: A mechanism can still be accepted if it predicts the correct rate law, even if the steps do not sum to the overall equation.
w.why: both tests are required; a wrong sum means the wrong reaction

w.a: The steps do not need to sum to the overall equation because intermediates are not real.
w.why: intermediates are real and cancel precisely because they are formed and consumed

w.a: A mechanism is rejected if its steps sum to the overall equation, because then there is no intermediate.
w.why: backwards; summing correctly is required, and intermediates cancel in the sum

cards.q: Define the rate-determining step.
cards.a: The rate-determining (rate-limiting) step is the slowest elementary step in a mechanism. Because the later steps can go no faster than the supply of species from the slow step, it acts as a bottleneck and sets the overall rate; the observed rate law is the rate law of that step, written from its molecularity, after any intermediate has been replaced using an earlier fast equilibrium.
cards.h: → slowest step → bottleneck → its rate law is observed
cards.n: 'The first step' earns nothing; the rate-determining step is the SLOWEST step, wherever it falls.

cards.q: State the predicted rate law when the first elementary step of a mechanism is the slow step.
cards.a: The overall rate law is the rate law of that first step, written from its molecularity, because every later step is fast and only consumes what the slow step supplies. For a slow first step A + B → C the prediction is rate = k[A][B]; for 2A → C, rate = k[A]². No intermediate appears because the first step involves only original reactants.
cards.h: → slow step's coefficients become the exponents
cards.n: Writing the rate law from the OVERALL equation's coefficients earns nothing; use only the slow step's reactants.

cards.q: Apply rate-determining-step logic: if the slow step 1 is $NO_2 + F_2 \to NO_2F + F$, write the predicted rate law.
cards.a: rate = k[NO₂][F₂]. The slow first step is a bimolecular collision of one NO₂ with one F₂, so its rate, and the overall rate, is first order in each. The fast second step (F + NO₂ → NO₂F) does not affect the rate law. This matches the experimental rate law for 2 NO₂ + F₂ → 2 NO₂F, which is NOT k[NO₂]²[F₂].
cards.h: → exponents from the slow step's reactants
cards.n: Writing rate = k[NO₂]²[F₂] from the overall coefficients earns nothing; the second NO₂ reacts after the bottleneck.

cards.q: State the two criteria a proposed mechanism must satisfy to be acceptable.
cards.a: (1) The elementary steps must add up to the overall balanced equation, with every intermediate cancelling. (2) The mechanism must predict the experimentally observed rate law: the rate law of its rate-determining step, with intermediates eliminated, must match the measured orders. Meeting both makes the mechanism consistent with the evidence, not proven.
cards.h: → sums correctly + predicts the rate law
cards.n: Offering only 'it must be balanced' earns half at most; the rate-law test is the one that rejects most wrong mechanisms.

cards.q: Determine whether the mechanism Step 1 (slow): 2 NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; Step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ is consistent with the overall reaction NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ and with its observed rate law, rate = k[NO₂]².
cards.a: It is consistent on both counts. Sum: 2 NO₂ + NO₃ + CO → NO₃ + NO + NO₂ + CO₂; cancelling NO₃ (intermediate) and one NO₂ gives NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂, the overall equation. The slow step is a bimolecular collision of two NO₂, so its rate law is rate = k₁[NO₂]², matching the observation; CO is absent because it reacts only in the fast step after the bottleneck.
cards.h: → check the sum, then the slow step's rate law
cards.n: Saying 'consistent because both contain NO₂ and CO' earns nothing; show the cancellation and derive k[NO₂]² from the slow step.

cards.q: Predict the effect on the initial rate of NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) of doubling [CO] at constant [NO₂], given the mechanism Step 1 (slow): 2 NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; Step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂.
cards.a: No change. The rate law is that of the slow step, rate = k[NO₂]², which contains no CO; CO reacts only in the fast second step with the NO₃ supplied by the slow step, so doubling [CO] cannot speed up the bottleneck. (Doubling [NO₂] instead would quadruple the rate.)
cards.h: → CO not in the slow step → order 0 in CO
cards.n: 'The rate doubles because CO is a reactant' earns nothing; being a reactant does not put a species in the rate law.

cards.q: Determine which of two proposed mechanisms for 2 NO₂ + F₂ → 2 NO₂F is consistent with the observed rate law rate = k[NO₂][F₂]. Mechanism A: slow NO₂ + F₂ → NO₂F + F, fast F + NO₂ → NO₂F. Mechanism B: slow 2 NO₂ → N₂O₄, fast N₂O₄ + F₂ → 2 NO₂F.
cards.a: Mechanism A is consistent; B is rejected. Both sum to the overall equation (A cancels F, B cancels N₂O₄). A's slow step is NO₂ + F₂, predicting rate = k[NO₂][F₂], which matches. B's slow step is 2 NO₂ → N₂O₄, predicting rate = k[NO₂]², zero order in F₂, which contradicts the observed first order in F₂. A is supported (not proven); B cannot be right.
cards.h: → sum check for both, then slow-step rate law vs observed
cards.n: Choosing B 'because its intermediate N₂O₄ is a known compound' earns nothing; the rate law contradicts it.

cards.q: Determine the rate law and the units of k for the iodide-catalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, given the mechanism Step 1 (slow): H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻; Step 2 (fast): H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + I⁻.
cards.a: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻], second order overall, k in M⁻¹·s⁻¹. The slow first step is a bimolecular collision of H₂O₂ with I⁻, so both appear to the first power. I⁻ is the catalyst (consumed in step 1, regenerated in step 2) and is absent from the overall equation 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂, yet it belongs in the rate law because it takes part in the rate-determining step.
cards.h: → slow step reactants, including the catalyst
cards.n: Writing rate = k[H₂O₂]² from the overall coefficients earns nothing; only the slow step's reactants set the orders.

cards.q: Determine the rate law for the destruction of ozone by chlorine atoms, given the mechanism Step 1 (slow): Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂; Step 2 (fast): ClO + O → Cl + O₂, and identify the role of Cl and of ClO.
cards.a: rate = k[Cl][O₃]. The slow first step is bimolecular in Cl and O₃, so each is first order. Cl is a catalyst: consumed in step 1, regenerated in step 2, absent from the overall equation O₃ + O → 2 O₂, but present in the rate law because it is in the slow step. ClO is the intermediate, formed in step 1 and consumed in step 2; it appears in neither the overall equation nor the rate law.
cards.h: → slow-step rate law; catalyst vs intermediate
cards.n: Putting ClO in the rate law, or leaving Cl out because 'it is not in the overall equation', earns nothing.

cards.q: Write the predicted rate law for each mechanism, in which the first step is slow: (a) slow A + A → B, fast B + C → D · (b) slow X → Y + Z, fast Y + W → V · (c) slow NO + Cl₂ → NOCl₂, fast NOCl₂ + NO → 2 NOCl · (d) slow 2 O₃ → 3 O₂ in one step · (e) slow Br⁻ + H₂O₂ → BrO⁻ + H₂O, fast BrO⁻ + H₂O₂ → Br⁻ + H₂O + O₂ · (f) slow (CH₃)₃CBr → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻, fast (CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH
cards.a:
(a) → rate = k[A]²
(b) → rate = k[X]
(c) → rate = k[NO][Cl₂] (overall 2 NO + Cl₂ → 2 NOCl, not k[NO]²[Cl₂])
(d) → rate = k[O₃]² (if it truly were one bimolecular step)
(e) → rate = k[Br⁻][H₂O₂] (Br⁻ is a catalyst in the slow step)
(f) → rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]; OH⁻ absent, order 0, because it reacts after the slow step
cards.h: → exponents = slow-step coefficients; later species absent
cards.n: In (f), including [OH⁻] because 'it is a reactant' earns nothing; OH⁻ enters only after the bottleneck.

cards.q: Explain why the rate law of a multistep reaction is set by its slowest elementary step.
cards.a: The steps occur in sequence, so the slow step's product is the raw material for every later step, and fast steps can consume it only as fast as it is supplied. The overall rate is the rate of this bottleneck, so the rate law is the slow step's, written from the species that collide in it.
cards.h: → sequential steps → later steps wait for the slow step's output → bottleneck sets rate
cards.n: 'Because the slow step takes the most time' restates the claim; the point is that later steps cannot proceed faster than the slow step supplies them.
o: Like an assembly line, the throughput of the whole line equals the throughput of its slowest station.
Species that enter only in fast steps after the bottleneck do not change the rate, which is why they are absent from the rate law.

w.a: The rate law is set by the slowest step because that step has the largest rate constant.
w.why: the slow step has the SMALLEST rate constant

w.a: The rate law is set by the first step, whichever step is slow.
w.why: if a later step is slow, its rate law (with intermediates substituted) applies

w.a: The rate law is set by the slowest step because the fast steps do not occur.
w.why: the fast steps occur; they simply wait on the slow step's output

cards.q: Explain why CO does not appear in the rate law for NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g), rate = k[NO₂]², even though CO is a reactant.
cards.a: The rate-determining step is the slow collision of two NO₂ molecules, 2 NO₂ → NO₃ + NO, with no CO in it. CO reacts only in the fast second step with NO₃ from the slow step, so extra CO cannot make products form faster than NO₃ is supplied: the rate depends on [NO₂]² alone.
cards.h: → CO reacts after the slow step → cannot speed the bottleneck → order 0
cards.n: 'CO is not in the rate law because it is a gas' or 'because its coefficient is 1' earns nothing; the reason is where it enters the mechanism.
o: Experimentally, doubling [CO] at fixed [NO₂] leaves the initial rate unchanged, which is what a zero-order dependence means.
A reactant appears in the rate law only if it takes part in the rate-determining step or an equilibrium before it; CO does neither.

w.a: CO does not appear because it is in excess and its concentration is constant.
w.why: the rate law is zero order in CO at any concentration; excess is a different situation

w.a: CO does not appear because it is an intermediate.
w.why: CO is a reactant in the overall equation, not a species formed and consumed

w.a: CO does not appear because the reaction is elementary.
w.why: if it were elementary the rate law would be k[NO₂][CO]

cards.q: Explain why a mechanism that correctly predicts the observed rate law and sums to the overall equation is said to be consistent with the data rather than proven.
cards.a: A correct mechanism must sum to the overall equation and predict the rate law, so failing either rules a mechanism out. But more than one set of steps can give the same sum and rate law, so passing both shows only that it has not been disproved; more evidence can strengthen the case, never close it.
cards.h: → tests can disprove but several mechanisms can pass → consistent, not proven
cards.n: 'It is proven because it matches the experiment' earns nothing; matching is consistency, and a rival mechanism might match too.
o: For 2 NO + O₂ → 2 NO₂, a termolecular single step and a two-step pre-equilibrium mechanism both predict rate = k[NO]²[O₂]; the rate law cannot decide between them.
Science supports models by failing to falsify them; a mechanism is a model of unseen molecular events.

w.a: A mechanism is proven once its rate law matches, because the rate law is unique to each mechanism.
w.why: different mechanisms can share a rate law

w.a: A mechanism can never be tested because elementary steps cannot be observed.
w.why: rate laws and intermediates test mechanisms; they can be disproved

w.a: A mechanism is consistent only if it has exactly two steps.
w.why: the number of steps is irrelevant to consistency

cards.q: Explain why increasing the concentration of a species that reacts only in a fast step after the rate-determining step has no effect on the overall reaction rate.
cards.a: That species reacts with the intermediate made in the slow step, and the fast step already consumes the intermediate almost as soon as it forms. Adding more cannot make the intermediate appear faster, because its supply is fixed by the slow step, so the rate is unchanged: the order is zero.
cards.h: → fast step already keeps up → supply of intermediate is the limit → extra reactant idle
cards.n: 'It has no effect because it is not in the balanced equation' earns nothing; it IS in the equation. It is absent from the rate law because of where it enters the mechanism.
o: The fast step's rate constant is large, so even a small concentration of that species clears the intermediate quickly; more of it just waits.
Only the concentrations of species that collide in the slow step, or that set the concentration of its reactants through a prior equilibrium, appear in the rate law.

w.a: It has no effect because the fast step is already at equilibrium.
w.why: an irreversible fast step is not at equilibrium; it simply keeps pace with the slow step

w.a: It has no effect because the species is a catalyst.
w.why: it is consumed, so it is a reactant, not a catalyst

w.a: It has a small effect that is usually ignored.
w.why: the effect is zero: the rate law has no term for it

cards.q: Explain how to derive the rate law when a fast reversible step precedes the rate-determining step.
cards.a: Write the rate law of the slow step from its molecularity; it contains an intermediate. Because step 1 is fast and reversible, treat it as at equilibrium: set its forward rate equal to its reverse rate (k₁[reactants] = k₋₁[intermediate]), or use K₁, and solve for the intermediate's concentration in terms of the reactants. Substitute into the slow-step rate law and combine the constants (k = k₂k₁/k₋₁ = k₂K₁) so the final law contains only reactants (and any catalyst).
cards.h: → slow-step law; step 1 forward = reverse; substitute
cards.n: Leaving the intermediate in the final rate law earns nothing; the equilibrium step exists to eliminate it. This uses the equilibrium ideas of Unit 7.

cards.q: Determine the rate law for 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g) from the mechanism Step 1 (fast, reversible): 2 NO ⇌ N₂O₂; Step 2 (slow): N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2 NO₂.
cards.a: rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. Slow step: rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂], but N₂O₂ is an intermediate. Step 1 is a fast equilibrium, so k₁[NO]² = k₋₁[N₂O₂], giving [N₂O₂] = (k₁/k₋₁)[NO]² = K₁[NO]². Substituting: rate = k₂K₁[NO]²[O₂] = k[NO]²[O₂], with k = k₂k₁/k₋₁. The prediction is second order in NO and first order in O₂, matching experiment, without a termolecular step.
cards.h: → slow-step law, replace [N₂O₂] via step-1 equilibrium
cards.n: Writing rate = k[N₂O₂][O₂] as the final answer earns nothing; the intermediate must be replaced by reactant concentrations.

cards.q: Determine the rate law for 2 NO(g) + Br₂(g) → 2 NOBr(g) from the mechanism Step 1 (fast, reversible): NO + Br₂ ⇌ NOBr₂; Step 2 (slow): NOBr₂ + NO → 2 NOBr.
cards.a: rate = k[NO]²[Br₂]. Slow step: rate = k₂[NOBr₂][NO]. Fast equilibrium in step 1: k₁[NO][Br₂] = k₋₁[NOBr₂], so [NOBr₂] = (k₁/k₋₁)[NO][Br₂]. Substituting: rate = k₂(k₁/k₋₁)[NO][Br₂][NO] = k[NO]²[Br₂], with k = k₂k₁/k₋₁. Second order in NO because one NO enters through the equilibrium and one in the slow step.
cards.n: Reporting rate = k[NO][Br₂] (forgetting the NO in the slow step) or leaving [NOBr₂] earns nothing; track every NO.

cards.q: Determine the rate law for H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2 HI(g) from the mechanism Step 1 (fast, reversible): I₂ ⇌ 2 I; Step 2 (slow): H₂ + 2 I → 2 HI, and describe the molecularity of the slow step.
cards.a: rate = k[H₂][I₂]. Slow step: rate = k₂[H₂][I]². Fast equilibrium: k₁[I₂] = k₋₁[I]², so [I]² = (k₁/k₋₁)[I₂] = K₁[I₂]. Substituting: rate = k₂K₁[H₂][I₂] = k[H₂][I₂], first order in each and identical to what a single bimolecular step would predict. The slow step as written is termolecular (H₂ + I + I), which is rare; the actual mechanism is usually taken to involve further bimolecular steps.
cards.n: Writing rate = k[H₂][I]² as final, or k[H₂][I₂]² from squaring the wrong thing, earns nothing; [I]², not [I₂], is what the equilibrium replaces.

cards.q: Determine the rate law, in terms of A, B and D, for the mechanism Step 1 (fast, reversible): A + B ⇌ C; Step 2 (slow): C + D → E, using the pre-equilibrium approximation.
cards.a: rate = k[A][B][D], with k = k₂K₁ = k₂k₁/k₋₁. The slow step gives rate = k₂[C][D], but C is an intermediate. Treating step 1 as at equilibrium, k₁[A][B] = k₋₁[C], so [C] = K₁[A][B]. Substituting eliminates C: rate = k₂K₁[A][B][D]. The reaction is first order in each of A, B and D and third order overall; the overall equation is A + B + D → E.
cards.h: → [C] = K₁[A][B], substitute into the slow-step law
cards.n: A final rate law containing [C] earns nothing; the point of the approximation is to express the intermediate in terms of reactants.

cards.q: Identify the approximation that allows the concentration of the intermediate N₂O₂ to be replaced in the mechanism 2 NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast), N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2 NO₂ (slow), and state the equation it justifies.
cards.a: The pre-equilibrium (fast-equilibrium) approximation: because step 1 is fast in both directions and step 2 removes N₂O₂ only slowly, step 1 stays essentially at equilibrium, so its forward and reverse rates are equal: k₁[NO]² = k₋₁[N₂O₂]. This gives [N₂O₂] = (k₁/k₋₁)[NO]² = K₁[NO]², an expression in reactant concentrations only, to substitute into the slow-step rate law.
cards.h: → name it; forward rate = reverse rate of step 1
cards.n: Saying 'the intermediate is used up immediately' describes the opposite situation (a fast second step) and earns nothing here.

cards.q: Determine whether the observed rate law rate = k[NO]²[O₂] for 2 NO + O₂ → 2 NO₂ can distinguish between Mechanism 1, a single termolecular step 2 NO + O₂ → 2 NO₂, and Mechanism 2, fast 2 NO ⇌ N₂O₂ followed by slow N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2 NO₂, and identify which is more plausible.
cards.a: It cannot distinguish them: both predict rate = k[NO]²[O₂] (Mechanism 1 directly from its molecularity; Mechanism 2 from k₂K₁[NO]²[O₂] after substituting the pre-equilibrium). Mechanism 2 is more plausible because a simultaneous three-body collision with correct orientation is very improbable, whereas two bimolecular steps are common; detecting N₂O₂ would support Mechanism 2 further.
cards.h: → same rate law from both; prefer bimolecular steps
cards.n: Claiming the rate law proves Mechanism 1 'because the exponents match the coefficients' earns nothing; matching coefficients is a coincidence Mechanism 2 also produces.

cards.q: Predict the factor by which the rate of 2 NO + O₂ → 2 NO₂ changes when [NO] is doubled at constant [O₂], given the mechanism fast 2 NO ⇌ N₂O₂, slow N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2 NO₂, and explain using the mechanism.
cards.a: The rate quadruples (×4). The slow step's rate is k₂[N₂O₂][O₂], and the pre-equilibrium fixes [N₂O₂] = K₁[NO]², so doubling [NO] quadruples the equilibrium concentration of the intermediate that feeds the slow step. The overall rate law rate = k[NO]²[O₂] says the same: 2² = 4.
cards.n: Answering ×2 'because NO is in one step at a time' earns nothing; the equilibrium makes the intermediate concentration depend on [NO] squared.

cards.q: Explain why an intermediate cannot appear in an experimentally determined rate law.
cards.a: Rate laws are found by varying the concentrations the experimenter prepares, but an intermediate is absent at the start and is formed and consumed during the run, so it cannot be set and is rarely measurable. Its concentration is re-expressed in terms of reactants, for example through a fast prior equilibrium.
cards.h: → rate law from controllable concentrations → intermediate not present at t = 0 → substitute it out
cards.n: 'Intermediates are too unstable' earns nothing; the reason is that only reactant (and catalyst) concentrations are set and measured in a rate experiment.
o: The intermediate's concentration is itself determined by the reactant concentrations through the earlier steps, so those reactants are the true variables.
A useful rate law predicts the rate from what you put in the flask; an intermediate is not something you put in.

w.a: An intermediate cannot appear because it cancels out of the overall balanced equation.
w.why: cancelling from the equation is about stoichiometry; catalysts also cancel yet can appear in rate laws

w.a: An intermediate cannot appear because its concentration is always zero.
w.why: it is present, in small amounts, while the reaction runs

w.a: An intermediate cannot appear because rate laws contain only products.
w.why: rate laws contain reactants (and sometimes catalysts)

cards.q: Explain why the pre-equilibrium approximation is valid when the first step of a mechanism is fast and reversible and the second step is slow.
cards.a: Step 1 runs fast in both directions, so the intermediate is formed and turned back into reactants many times before the slow step consumes it. The slow step drains so little that step 1 stays essentially at equilibrium, so its forward and reverse rates can be set equal to solve for the intermediate.
cards.h: → fast forward and reverse → slow step drains little → step 1 stays at equilibrium
cards.n: Applying the approximation when the FIRST step is slow earns nothing; then the intermediate is consumed as fast as it forms and no equilibrium is established.
o: The rates of step 1 forward and reverse are both large compared with the rate of step 2, so the small leak through step 2 is a negligible perturbation of the equilibrium.
Equilibrium is a balance of forward and reverse rates, and a fast reversible step reaches that balance long before the slow step has done much.

w.a: The approximation works because the slow step is at equilibrium.
w.why: the FIRST (fast) step is at equilibrium; the slow step is treated as irreversible

w.a: The approximation works because the intermediate is consumed as soon as it forms.
w.why: that describes a fast second step; here the second step is slow

w.a: The approximation works for any mechanism with two steps.
w.why: it requires a fast reversible step before the slow one

cards.q: Explain why the rate law for 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g) is third order overall even though elementary reactions of three particles are rare.
cards.a: No three-body collision is needed. In 2 NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast), N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2 NO₂ (slow), the slow step is bimolecular, but the equilibrium makes [N₂O₂] proportional to [NO]², so rate = k₂K₁[NO]²[O₂]. Two bimolecular steps together produce third-order kinetics.
cards.h: → bimolecular slow step + [N₂O₂] ∝ [NO]² → third order without a termolecular collision
cards.n: 'The reaction is termolecular' earns nothing; a rate law's overall order is not the molecularity of any single step.
o: The overall order counts every reactant concentration that influences the slow step, directly or through a prior equilibrium, so it can exceed the molecularity of that step.
Orders are experimental; molecularity is a property of one elementary step, and only for a single elementary step must the two coincide.

w.a: The rate law is third order because the reaction is a single termolecular step.
w.why: a three-body collision is improbable; the two-step mechanism explains the order without it

w.a: The rate law is third order because there are three molecules in the balanced equation.
w.why: coefficients do not give orders; the mechanism does

w.a: The rate law cannot really be third order, because third order is impossible.
w.why: third-order rate laws are observed; this reaction is the standard example

cards.q: Explain why the experimentally measured rate constant for a reaction with a pre-equilibrium mechanism is a combination of constants rather than the rate constant of a single step.
cards.a: The observed law is the slow step's law with the intermediate replaced through step 1's equilibrium: rate = k₂[C][D] becomes k₂(k₁/k₋₁)[A][B][D]. Experiment measures the whole product k₂k₁/k₋₁ as k, because the rate reflects both how much intermediate forms and how fast it reacts.
cards.h: → substitute [C] = (k₁/k₋₁)[A][B] → constants multiply → observed k = k₂k₁/k₋₁
cards.n: Reporting the observed k as 'k₂' earns nothing; the equilibrium constant of step 1 is folded into it.
o: Experiment sees only the overall proportionality between rate and reactant concentrations, and that proportionality is the product of the step constants.
Changing temperature changes k₁, k₋₁ and k₂ all at once, so the observed k carries the temperature dependence of the whole sequence.

w.a: The observed rate constant is the sum of the rate constants of the steps.
w.why: substitution multiplies the constants; nothing is added

w.a: The observed rate constant equals the rate constant of the slow step alone.
w.why: the pre-equilibrium constant K₁ multiplies it

w.a: The observed rate constant equals the equilibrium constant K₁.
w.why: K₁ scales the intermediate concentration; k₂ still sets how fast it reacts

cards.q: Identify the rate-determining step from a multi-step reaction energy profile.
cards.a: The rate-determining step is the elementary step with the largest activation energy: the hump whose climb from the level immediately before it (the reactants or the preceding valley) up to its own peak is greatest. That step has the smallest fraction of collisions energetic enough to cross its barrier, so it has the smallest rate constant and is the slowest step in the sequence.
cards.h: → one hump per step; biggest climb from its own valley
cards.n: Measuring each peak from the zero of the energy axis, or picking the step with the most negative ΔE, earns nothing; each step's Ea starts at the level before its hump.
x: the step with the largest activation energy

cards.q: Explain what the valleys between peaks on a multi-step energy profile represent.
cards.a: Each valley between two peaks is a reaction intermediate: a real species with complete bonds sitting at a local energy minimum, formed by the elementary step on its left and consumed by the step on its right. Because it must climb a barrier to go either forward or back, it persists briefly and can sometimes be detected. The peaks on either side are transition states, which cannot be.
cards.n: Calling a valley a transition state or 'activated complex' earns nothing; transition states are the peaks, and the species in a valley is an intermediate.

cards.q: Identify whether the taller of two activation-energy humps on a mechanism's energy profile tells you if that step is exothermic or endothermic.
cards.a: It does not. A hump's height is that step's activation energy, which sets how fast the step goes. Whether the step is exothermic or endothermic depends only on whether the level after the hump (the next valley or the products) lies below or above the level before it; a tall hump can belong to an exothermic step and a short hump to an endothermic one.
cards.h: → no; compare the levels before and after the hump
cards.n: 'The taller hump is the endothermic step because it absorbs more energy' earns nothing; Ea (the barrier) and ΔE (end minus start) are independent.

cards.q: A two-step mechanism has step 1 with ΔH = +40. kJ/mol and step 2 with ΔH = -65 kJ/mol. Compute the overall ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic.
cards.a: −25 kJ/mol, exothermic. The steps add to the overall equation, so their enthalpy changes add: ΔH = (+40.) + (−65) = −25 kJ/mol. On the profile the intermediate's valley sits 40 kJ/mol above the reactants and the products end 25 kJ/mol below the reactants; the heights of the humps (the activation energies) never enter the sum.
cards.h: → add the step values, then read the sign
cards.n: Adding the activation energies, or averaging the two ΔH values, earns nothing. Borrows the additivity of enthalpy changes (Hess's law, Unit 6).

cards.q: Determine the number of elementary steps, intermediates and transition states in a mechanism whose energy profile, read left to right, shows reactants, then three peaks separated by two valleys, then products.
cards.a: Three elementary steps, two intermediates, three transition states. Each peak is the transition state of one elementary step, so three peaks mean three steps. Each valley between two peaks is an intermediate formed by one step and consumed by the next, so two valleys mean two intermediates. The reactant and product levels at the ends are not intermediates.
cards.h: → peaks = steps = transition states; inner valleys
cards.n: Counting the reactant and product plateaus as intermediates (four), or the valleys as steps, earns nothing; only a valley between two peaks is an intermediate.

cards.q: Draw, in words precise enough to sketch, the energy profile for a two-step reaction with reactants at 0 kJ/mol in which step 1 has Ea = 90 kJ/mol and ΔE = +30 kJ/mol and step 2 has Ea = 20 kJ/mol and ΔE = −80 kJ/mol. Label the rate-determining step and the overall ΔE.
cards.a: Axes: reaction coordinate (horizontal), potential energy in kJ/mol (vertical). Reactants flat at 0; hump 1 peaks at +90 (transition state 1) and falls to a valley at +30 (the intermediate); hump 2 rises from +30 to a peak at +50 (transition state 2) and falls to products flat at −50. Label step 1 rate-determining (climb 90 vs 20 kJ/mol) and a downward arrow from 0 to −50 as ΔE = −50 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → five levels in order, two humps, two labels
cards.n: Drawing hump 2 from the zero line (peak at +20) earns nothing; step 2's Ea is measured from where step 2 starts, the valley at +30.

cards.q: Determine the activation energy of each step, the overall ΔE, the rate-determining step, and whether the intermediate is more or less stable than the reactants, for a two-step energy profile with reactants at 50 kJ/mol, first peak at 120 kJ/mol, a valley at 70 kJ/mol, second peak at 100 kJ/mol and products at 10 kJ/mol.
cards.a: Ea(step 1) = 120 − 50 = 70 kJ/mol; Ea(step 2) = 100 − 70 = 30 kJ/mol; overall ΔE = 10 − 50 = −40 kJ/mol, exothermic. Step 1 is rate-determining because its barrier is larger. The intermediate at 70 kJ/mol lies 20 kJ/mol above the reactants, so it is less stable than the reactants (step 1 is endothermic, +20 kJ/mol) and far less stable than the products.
cards.h: → subtract levels step by step; compare barriers
cards.n: Taking step 2's Ea as 100 − 50 = 50 kJ/mol (from the reactants) earns nothing; step 2 starts in the valley at 70 kJ/mol.
x: 70 and 30 kJ/mol; −40 kJ/mol; step 1; less stable

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, an energy profile consistent with this mechanism for an overall exothermic reaction: Step 1 (fast, reversible): A + B ⇌ C; Step 2 (slow): C + D → E.
cards.a: Axes: reaction coordinate, potential energy. Reactants (A + B + D) on a plateau; a small first hump leads to a valley labeled C (the intermediate), drawn a little above the reactants so the climbs over hump 1 in both directions are small (fast, reversible). From the C valley a much larger second hump rises to the highest peak on the diagram (slow, rate-determining), then the curve falls to products E, below the reactant plateau (ΔE < 0).
cards.h: → small hump, valley C, big hump, products below start
cards.n: A tall first hump with a small second one contradicts 'step 1 fast'; the rate-determining step must show the largest climb from its own starting level.

cards.q: Determine the rate law for the mechanism Step 1: NO + Br₂ → NOBr₂; Step 2: NOBr₂ + NO → 2 NOBr, given that its energy profile shows a first hump whose climb from the reactants is 20 kJ/mol, a valley for NOBr₂ lying 5 kJ/mol above the reactants, and a second hump whose climb from that valley is 60 kJ/mol.
cards.a: rate = k[NO]²[Br₂]. Step 2 has the largest climb (60 kJ/mol), so it is rate-determining; step 1's barriers are small both ways (20 kJ/mol forward, 20 − 5 = 15 kJ/mol back from the valley), so it is a fast equilibrium. Slow step: rate = k₂[NOBr₂][NO]; the equilibrium gives [NOBr₂] = K₁[NO][Br₂]; substituting gives rate = k₂K₁[NO]²[Br₂].
cards.h: → largest climb = slow step; pre-equilibrium first
cards.n: Writing rate = k[NO][Br₂] from step 1 earns nothing; the profile shows step 1 is fast. The substitution uses the equilibrium expression of Unit 7 (see 5.9).

cards.q: Predict how the energy profile of a two-step reaction, and the identity of its rate-determining step, change when the reaction is run at a higher temperature.
cards.a: Neither changes, to a good approximation. The energies of the reactants, intermediate, transition states and products, and so each step's activation energy and ΔE, belong to the pathway, not to the temperature. Raising T increases the fraction of collisions able to cross every barrier, so both steps and the overall reaction go faster, but the step with the largest barrier is still the slowest.
cards.h: → profile fixed; more collisions cross each barrier
cards.n: 'The humps shrink at higher temperature' earns nothing; only a catalyst (a new pathway) changes the profile. Temperature changes how many collisions can cross.

cards.q: Explain why the elementary step with the largest activation energy is the rate-determining step of a multistep reaction.
cards.a: The larger a step's barrier, the smaller the fraction of collisions with energy at least equal to its Ea, so that step has the smallest rate constant and runs slowest. Because the steps occur in sequence, the others can go no faster than this step supplies or removes species: it sets the overall rate.
cards.h: → biggest Ea → fewest collisions over the barrier → smallest k → bottleneck for the sequence
cards.n: 'It is the slowest because its peak is highest on the graph' earns nothing without linking barrier size to the fraction of effective collisions.
o: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve, the Ea line of the largest barrier sits farthest into the tail, leaving the smallest area beyond it.
A chain of steps runs only as fast as its slowest link, and the link with the highest barrier has the fewest successful crossings per second.

w.a: The step with the largest activation energy is rate-determining because it releases the most energy.
w.why: barrier height is not energy released

w.a: The rate-determining step is always the first hump, because every later step has to wait for it.
w.why: the slow step is the largest barrier, wherever it falls
