cards.n: Trap: mixing two solutions always dilutes each concentration before you can compute Q.

cards.q: Identify the correct Kc expression for the heterogeneous equilibrium $CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$.
cards.a: Kc = $[CO_2]$. Both solids are omitted because their concentrations are constant, leaving only the gas-phase species in the expression.
cards.n: Because only one gas appears, the equilibrium pressure of $CO_2$ above the two solids is fixed at any given temperature.

cards.q: Explain why a very large K value lets you assume a reaction goes essentially to completion before setting up an ICE table in reverse.
cards.a: When K is very large, equilibrium lies so far toward products that treating the reaction as if it finishes and then reverses slightly by a small amount x simplifies the algebra with little error.
cards.n: Run the limiting-reactant stoichiometry to completion first, then use those product amounts as the new initial row of the table.

cards.q: Predict the shift in $N_2(g)+3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$ (exothermic) when both temperature and pressure are raised together.
cards.a: Raising pressure shifts toward $NH_3$ (fewer moles), while raising temperature shifts away from it since the forward reaction is exothermic; the two disturbances push in opposite directions.
cards.n: When two disturbances oppose each other, Le Chatelier alone gives no net direction; say that explicitly rather than guessing one.

cards.q: Compute the molar solubility of $CaF_2$ ($K_{sp}=3.9\times10^{-11}$) in 0.10 M NaF solution.
cards.a: With $[F^{-}] \approx 0.10$ M fixed by the common ion, $K_{sp}=s(0.10)^2$, so $s = 3.9\times10^{-11}/0.010 = 3.9\times10^{-9}$ M, far less soluble than in pure water.
cards.h: → common ion fixes [F-], solve for s
cards.n: The common ion enters squared here, so it suppresses solubility far more sharply than it would for a 1:1 salt such as AgCl.

cards.q: Reaction 1: $2X \rightleftharpoons Y$, K = 25. Reaction 2: $Y \rightleftharpoons 2Z$, K = 0.20. Compute the equilibrium constant for $2Z \rightleftharpoons 2X$.
cards.a: 0.20. Reversing both given reactions and adding them gives $2Z \to Y \to 2X$; K = (1/K2)(1/K1) = (5.0)(0.040) = 0.20.
cards.n: Reversing a reaction inverts its K, so do that before multiplying; adding the two constants instead is the usual error.

cards.q: Given $A \rightleftharpoons B$ with K = 0.25, compute K for $3B \rightleftharpoons 3A$.
cards.a: 64. Reversing gives $B \rightleftharpoons A$ with K' = 1/0.25 = 4.0; multiplying all coefficients by 3 raises K to the third power: $4.0^3 = 64$.
cards.n: Reversing inverts K and scaling raises it to that power, and the two operations are applied in sequence, never added together.

cards.q: Predict whether the molar solubility of $CaF_2$ increases, decreases, or stays the same when solid $Ca(NO_3)_2$ is added to a saturated $CaF_2$ solution.
cards.a: It decreases. Adding $Ca(NO_3)_2$ raises $[Ca^{2+}]$, a common ion with $CaF_2$; by Le Chatelier's principle the dissolution equilibrium shifts back toward solid $CaF_2$, lowering its solubility.
cards.h: → the common ion here is Ca2+, not F-
cards.n: Common-ion problems can add either ion of the salt; check which ion the added compound actually shares.

cards.q: Identify what a graph of forward and reverse reaction rates versus time shows at the moment equilibrium is reached.
cards.a: The forward and reverse rate curves intersect and become equal; after that point both rates stay constant and equal, even though the reaction keeps proceeding in both directions.
cards.n: Equal forward and reverse rates do not mean equal concentrations; equilibrium concentrations are set by K, not by the rates being equal.

cards.q: Compute Kc for $2NO(g)+O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)$ given [NO]=0.020 M, $[O_2]=0.010$ M, $[NO_2]=0.40$ M at equilibrium.
cards.n: The coefficient 2 becomes a squared term on both NO and $NO_2$, and dropping either exponent shifts the answer by orders of magnitude.

cards.q: Predict whether a reaction with K = 3.0×10⁸ goes nearly to completion or barely proceeds, and justify.
cards.a: It goes nearly to completion. Such a large K means the equilibrium mixture is overwhelmingly products, so essentially all limiting reactant is converted.
cards.n: A very large K describes the equilibrium position, not reaction speed; the reaction could still be slow to reach that state.

cards.q: $Ag_2CrO_4$ has $K_{sp}=1.1\times10^{-12}$. Compute its molar solubility in pure water.
cards.n: Molar solubility is not Ksp, and comparing two salts by Ksp alone is valid only when they share the same ion ratio.

cards.q: Predict whether the solubility of $Mg(OH)_2$ increases or decreases as the solution pH is lowered, and explain.
cards.a: Solubility increases. Added $H^+$ reacts with and removes $OH^-$ from solution; by Le Chatelier's principle the dissolution equilibrium shifts to replace the consumed hydroxide, dissolving more $Mg(OH)_2$.
cards.n: Name the acid-base reaction that removes the anion rather than just citing Le Chatelier; readers want the removed species identified.

cards.q: Explain why a salt can dissolve spontaneously in water even when its dissolution is endothermic $(ΔH°_soln$ > 0).
cards.a: Dissolution greatly increases entropy as an ordered solid becomes dispersed ions in solution; if TΔS° exceeds $ΔH°_soln,$ ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is still negative, making the process spontaneous despite absorbing heat.
cards.h: → ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; entropy can win
cards.n: A positive ΔH does not rule out spontaneity; the entropy term can still make ΔG negative.

cards.q: Define the equilibrium constant K and state what distinguishes it from the reaction quotient Q.
cards.a: K is the value of the mass-action expression using equilibrium concentrations, a fixed number at a given temperature; Q uses the same expression at any moment, so Q equals K only when the system is at equilibrium.
cards.n: On the AP exam, writing Q when equilibrium concentrations are meant (or the reverse) is a frequent point-losing mix-up.

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with very fast forward and reverse rates can still have a small equilibrium constant.
cards.a: K depends on the ratio of the rate constants ($k_{forward}/k_{reverse}$), not their absolute size; if both rates are fast but the reverse rate constant is much larger, K is small even though equilibrium is reached quickly.
cards.h: → K depends on the ratio $k_forward/k_reverse,$ not their size
cards.n: Fast kinetics tells you how quickly equilibrium is reached, not where the equilibrium position lies.

cards.q: Predict the shift when the temperature of an equilibrium mixture is lowered for a reaction with ΔH° = 0.
cards.a: No shift occurs. Since K depends on temperature only through ΔH°, a thermoneutral reaction's K does not change with temperature, so the equilibrium position stays the same.
cards.n: Temperature is the only disturbance that actually changes K; every other stress moves Q back toward a K that never moved.

cards.q: State why the equilibrium constant expression uses equilibrium concentrations raised to the stoichiometric coefficients, not initial concentrations.
cards.a: The expression is defined to give a constant value only once the system has reached equilibrium; the coefficients set the exponents to match the reaction's stoichiometry, but only equilibrium concentrations make the ratio equal K.
cards.n: Using initial concentrations instead of equilibrium concentrations in this expression is one of the most common ICE-table errors.

cards.q: Explain why macroscopic properties like concentration and color remain constant at equilibrium even though the forward and reverse reactions continue.
cards.a: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reaction rates have become equal, so reactants are converted to products at exactly the same rate products convert back to reactants. The two changes cancel at the molecular level, so no net change in any concentration is observed macroscopically.
cards.h: → equal rates, not a stopped reaction
cards.n: Write no net change, never that the reaction stops; a stopped reaction is the most heavily penalized phrase on equilibrium free-response.

cards.q: For an elementary reversible reaction with forward rate constant $k_f = 4.0\times10^{-2}$ and reverse rate constant $k_r = 2.0\times10^{-3}$, compute K.
cards.n: This relationship only holds for a genuinely elementary (single-step) reaction, not an overall reaction.

cards.q: Compute Kc for $2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)$ given equilibrium concentrations $[SO_2]=0.20$ M, $[O_2]=0.10$ M, $[SO_3]=0.60$ M.
cards.n: The coefficient 2 becomes an exponent on both $SO_2$ and $SO_3$, while $O_2$ carries the power 1 and is easy to over-square.

cards.q: Predict whether a reaction with $K = 4.0\times10^{-9}$ goes nearly to completion or barely proceeds, and justify.
cards.a: It barely proceeds. Such a tiny K means the equilibrium concentrations of products are far smaller than those of reactants, so the reaction mixture at equilibrium is overwhelmingly reactants.
cards.n: A tiny K still means some product forms; saying no reaction occurs is wrong, since every species is present at equilibrium.

cards.q: Identify what a particulate diagram of a reaction mixture at equilibrium should show when K is very large ($K \ge 10^{8}$).
cards.a: Mostly product particles with only a few reactant particles remaining, since a very large K means the equilibrium position lies far toward products.
cards.n: Contrast with a system where K ≈ 1: that diagram would show comparable numbers of reactant and product particles.

cards.q: Explain why adding more reactant to a system at equilibrium makes Q momentarily less than K, and connect this to the resulting shift.
cards.a: Adding reactant increases a denominator term in the Q expression without immediately changing the products, so Q drops below its equilibrium value K. Since Q < K, the forward reaction is favored and the system shifts toward products until Q rises back to equal K.
cards.h: → how Q moves, then the shift
cards.n: Q < K always means the system shifts forward (toward products); Q > K always means it shifts backward.

cards.q: Explain how decreasing the volume of a gaseous equilibrium with unequal moles of gas on each side changes Q relative to K, and use that to justify the resulting shift.
cards.a: Shrinking the volume raises every concentration, but the side with the larger stoichiometric total is affected more strongly. This pushes Q away from K toward the side with fewer moles of gas, so the system shifts toward whichever side has fewer gas particles until Q returns to K.
cards.h: → Q versus K, then a direction
cards.n: The Q argument is the rigorous version of the Le Chatelier shortcut, and readers award the reasoning point for showing it.

cards.q: Predict whether the molar solubility of $CaCO_3$ increases or decreases as the solution pH is lowered, and explain.
cards.a: Solubility increases. The carbonate ion is a basic anion that reacts with added $H_3O^{+}$ to form $HCO_3^{-}$ and eventually $H_2CO_3$, removing $CO_3^{2-}$ from solution and shifting the dissolution equilibrium forward by Le Chatelier's principle.
cards.n: Any salt with a conjugate-base anion of a weak acid becomes more soluble in acidic solution.

cards.q: Explain why the solubility of AgCl is essentially unaffected by the solution's pH.
cards.a: $Cl^{-}$ is the conjugate base of the strong acid HCl, so it is far too weak a base to react with $H_3O^{+}$ in solution. Since neither the added acid nor the anion shifts the dissolution equilibrium, changing pH has no meaningful effect on AgCl's solubility.
cards.n: Contrast this with $CaCO_3$ or $Mg(OH)_2$, whose basic anions are consumed by acid, so their solubility does climb as pH falls.

cards.q: Given ΔH°soln = +15.0 kJ/mol and ΔS°soln = +65.0 J/(mol·K) at 298 K, compute ΔG°soln and determine whether dissolution is spontaneous.
cards.a: -4.37 kJ/mol, spontaneous. ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS° = 15.0 - (298)(0.0650) = 15.0 - 19.4 = -4.37 kJ/mol, a negative value, so dissolution is spontaneous at 298 K.
cards.n: Convert the entropy term from J to kJ before subtracting; skipping that makes the TΔS° term a thousand times too large.

cards.q: Contrast the Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, and Lewis definitions of an acid.
cards.a: Arrhenius: produces H⁺ in water. Bronsted-Lowry: donates a proton (H⁺) to another species. Lewis: accepts a pair of electrons. Each definition is broader than the one before it.
cards.n: Species like BF3 and metal cations are Lewis acids without being acids by the other two definitions.

cards.q: Define a conjugate acid-base pair.
cards.a: Two species whose formulas differ by exactly one H⁺. The acid becomes its conjugate base when it donates the proton; the base becomes its conjugate acid when it accepts one.
cards.n: The charge also differs by one unit; the conjugate base always carries one more negative charge.

cards.q: Identify the conjugate acid and the conjugate base of HCO3⁻.
cards.a: Conjugate acid: H2CO3 (add H⁺). Conjugate base: CO3²⁻ (remove H⁺). HCO3⁻ can act as either an acid or a base, so it is amphiprotic.
cards.h: → one gains H, one loses H
cards.n: HCO3⁻, HSO4⁻, H2PO4⁻, and H2O are the amphiprotic species AP questions use most.

cards.q: Define an amphiprotic species and give an example.
cards.a: A species that can either donate or accept a proton, depending on its reaction partner. Water is the classic example: it acts as a base toward HCl and as an acid toward NH3.
cards.n: Amphoteric is the broader term (acts as acid or base by any definition); amphiprotic specifically involves H⁺.

cards.q: State the seven strong acids that ionize essentially completely in water.
cards.a: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4 (first proton only), HClO4, and HClO3.
cards.n: HF is NOT strong. For H2SO4 only the first ionization is complete; the second has Ka2 about 1.2×10⁻².

cards.q: State which bases are treated as strong bases in AP Chemistry.
cards.a: The hydroxides of Group 1 metals (LiOH, NaOH, KOH, RbOH, CsOH) and the soluble Group 2 hydroxides Ca(OH)2, Sr(OH)2, and Ba(OH)2. Group 2 hydroxides release 2 mol OH⁻ per formula unit.
cards.n: Forgetting to double [OH⁻] for Ba(OH)2 or Ca(OH)2 is a standard pH error.

cards.q: Explain the autoionization of water and write its equilibrium constant.
cards.a: 2H2O(l) ⇌ H3O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), with Kw = [H3O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. Water is omitted because it is the pure liquid solvent.
cards.n: Kw holds in every aqueous solution, so knowing one of [H⁺] or [OH⁻] always gives the other.

cards.q: Explain how Kw and the pH of pure water change when the temperature is raised above 25 °C.
cards.a: Autoionization is endothermic, so raising the temperature shifts it right: Kw increases and the pH of pure water falls below 7.00. The water is still neutral because [H3O⁺] still equals [OH⁻].
cards.h: → Kw up, pH down, still neutral
cards.n: Neutral means [H3O⁺] = [OH⁻], not pH = 7; pH 7 is neutral only at 25 °C.

cards.q: State the definitions of pH and pOH and the relationship between them at 25 °C.
cards.a: pH = -log[H3O⁺] and pOH = -log[OH⁻], with [H3O⁺] = $10^(-pH).$ At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.00 and pKw = 14.00.
cards.n: pH + pOH = 14.00 only at 25 °C, since it comes from Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.025 M HNO3.
cards.a: HNO3 is a strong acid, so [H3O⁺] = 0.025 M and pH = -log(0.025) = 1.60.
cards.n: For a strong monoprotic acid, [H3O⁺] equals the acid molarity - no ICE table is needed.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.010 M Ba(OH)2 at 25 °C.
cards.a: Ba(OH)2 is a strong base giving 2 OH⁻ per formula unit, so [OH⁻] = 0.020 M. pOH = -log(0.020) = 1.70, and pH = 14.00 - 1.70 = 12.30.
cards.n: The factor of 2 is the whole point of this question type; skipping it gives 12.00 instead of 12.30.

cards.q: Explain the significant-figure rule for a pH value.
cards.a: Only the digits to the right of the decimal point in a pH count as significant. A concentration known to 2 significant figures gives a pH written with 2 decimal places, such as 0.025 M → pH 1.60.
cards.n: Writing pH 1.6 for a 2-sig-fig concentration loses a point on free response.

cards.q: Compute [H3O⁺] in a solution whose pH is 4.30.
cards.n: A pH change of 1 unit is a factor of 10 in [H3O⁺]; a change of 0.30 is a factor of 2.

cards.q: State the acid dissociation constant expression for a weak acid HA in water.
cards.a: HA + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + A⁻, with $K_{a} = \frac{[H_{3}O^{+}][A^{-}]}{[HA]}$. Water is omitted as the solvent.
cards.n: A larger Ka means a stronger weak acid and therefore a lower pH at the same concentration.

cards.q: State the base ionization constant expression for a weak base B in water.
cards.a: B + H2O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻, with $K_{b} = \frac{[BH^{+}][OH^{-}]}{[B]}$. Water is omitted as the solvent.
cards.n: Kb calculations give [OH⁻] and pOH first; convert to pH at the very end.

cards.q: State the relationship between Ka and Kb for a conjugate acid-base pair.
cards.a: Ka × Kb = Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, and equivalently pKa + pKb = 14.00.
cards.n: This is how you get Kb for an anion like F⁻ from the Ka of HF; the pair must be conjugates.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid, Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵.
cards.n: x is 1.3% of 0.10 M, so the approximation passes the 5% check.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.10 M NH3, Kb = 1.8×10⁻⁵.
cards.n: For a weak base the ICE solution gives [OH⁻]; converting straight to pH without pOH is a common slip.

cards.q: Define percent ionization of a weak acid and state how to calculate it.
cards.a: Percent ionization = ([H3O⁺] at equilibrium / [HA] initial) × 100%. It measures the fraction of acid molecules that have actually donated a proton.
cards.n: Strong acids are 100% ionized by definition; weak acids at typical concentrations are usually a few percent.

cards.q: Explain how the percent ionization of a weak acid changes as the solution is diluted.
cards.a: Percent ionization increases on dilution, even though [H3O⁺] falls and the pH rises. Ka is fixed, so as [HA] drops the fraction ionized must rise to keep the quotient constant.
cards.h: → goes up while pH also goes up
cards.n: Dilution raises percent ionization but never makes a weak acid strong; Ka is unchanged.

cards.q: Compute Ka for a 0.20 M weak acid whose measured pH is 3.00.
cards.n: Working backward from pH to Ka is a standard lab-based free-response task.

cards.q: Explain the relationship between the strength of an acid and the strength of its conjugate base.
cards.a: The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base, because Ka × Kb = Kw is fixed. The conjugate bases of strong acids (Cl⁻, NO3⁻) are so weak they have no measurable basicity in water.
cards.n: This is why NaCl solutions are neutral but NaF solutions are basic.

cards.q: Explain the trend in binary acid strength (HX) down a group and across a period.
cards.a: Down a group, acid strength increases because the H-X bond gets longer and weaker (HF < HCl < HBr < HI). Across a period, strength increases with electronegativity, which stabilizes the conjugate base (CH4 < NH3 < H2O < HF).
cards.n: Bond strength dominates within a group; conjugate-base stability (electronegativity) dominates within a period.

cards.q: Explain how the number of terminal oxygen atoms affects the strength of an oxyacid.
cards.a: More terminal oxygens pull electron density away from the O-H bond and delocalize the negative charge of the conjugate base, stabilizing it. Acid strength therefore rises with the number of oxygens.
cards.n: HClO < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4 spans about ten orders of magnitude in Ka.

cards.q: Explain the inductive effect on acid strength using CH3COOH and CCl3COOH.
cards.a: The three highly electronegative chlorines withdraw electron density through the sigma bonds, spreading out the negative charge on the carboxylate conjugate base and stabilizing it. CCl3COOH is therefore the much stronger acid.
cards.n: Any argument about acid strength should end with the stability of the conjugate base.

cards.q: Rank HClO, HClO2, HClO3, and HClO4 from weakest to strongest acid and justify the order.
cards.a: HClO < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4. Each added terminal oxygen increases the oxidation number of chlorine and delocalizes charge in the conjugate base, making the O-H bond more polar and the anion more stable.
cards.n: Same central atom means the only variable is the number of oxygens.

cards.q: Predict whether a salt formed from a strong acid and a strong base gives an acidic, basic, or neutral solution.
cards.a: Neutral. Both ions are conjugates of strong species (for example Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from NaOH and HCl), so neither hydrolyzes water. The pH is 7 at 25 °C.
cards.n: Group 1 cations and the anions of strong acids are always spectators.

cards.q: Predict the acid-base character of a solution of sodium acetate, NaC2H3O2.
cards.a: Basic. Na⁺ is a spectator, but acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so C2H3O2⁻ + H2O ⇌ HC2H3O2 + OH⁻ produces hydroxide.
cards.h: → one word plus the hydrolysis equation
cards.n: Salt of weak acid + strong base is always basic; use Kb = Kw/Ka to find its pH.

cards.q: Predict the acid-base character of a solution of ammonium chloride, NH4Cl.
cards.a: Acidic. Cl⁻ is a spectator, but NH4⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH3, so NH4⁺ + H2O ⇌ NH3 + H3O⁺ lowers the pH.
cards.h: → one word plus the hydrolysis equation
cards.n: Small highly charged metal cations such as Al³⁺ and Fe³⁺ also make solutions acidic.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.10 M NaF given Ka(HF) = 7.2×10⁻⁴.
cards.n: You must convert Ka to Kb first; using Ka directly on the anion is the classic mistake.

cards.q: Define a buffer solution.
cards.a: A solution containing appreciable amounts of both a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) that resists large changes in pH when small amounts of strong acid or strong base are added.
cards.n: A weak acid alone is not a buffer; the conjugate base must also be present.

cards.q: Explain at the particle level how a buffer resists a change in pH.
cards.a: Added H3O⁺ is consumed by the conjugate base (A⁻ + H3O⁺ → HA + H2O); added OH⁻ is consumed by the weak acid (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H2O). Because the strong species is converted into a weak one, the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] shifts only slightly and the pH barely moves.
cards.n: Full credit requires writing both reactions, not just saying the buffer 'absorbs' the addition.

cards.q: Define the equivalence point of a titration and contrast it with the endpoint.
cards.a: The equivalence point is where moles of added titrant exactly equal the stoichiometric amount needed to react with the analyte. The endpoint is where the indicator changes color - an experimental estimate of the equivalence point.
cards.n: A well-chosen indicator makes the endpoint fall within the steep region so the two nearly coincide.

cards.q: Describe the shape of a strong acid-strong base titration curve.
cards.a: It starts at very low pH, rises slowly, then jumps almost vertically through a very steep region, and levels off at high pH. The equivalence point is at pH = 7.00 at 25 °C, at the midpoint of the vertical section.
cards.h: → pH at the equivalence point plus curve shape
cards.n: Only the strong-strong case has an equivalence point at exactly pH 7.

cards.q: Describe the shape of a weak acid-strong base titration curve.
cards.a: It starts at a moderate pH, rises quickly, then flattens into a buffer region, passes through a smaller vertical jump, and reaches an equivalence point at pH > 7 because the solution contains the weak acid's conjugate base.
cards.h: → buffer plateau plus basic equivalence point
cards.n: The weaker the acid, the higher the equivalence-point pH and the shorter the vertical jump.

cards.q: State what is true about the pH at the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration.
cards.a: At half-equivalence, exactly half the weak acid has been converted to its conjugate base, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa.
cards.n: This is the standard way to determine Ka experimentally from a titration curve.

cards.q: Explain why the equivalence point of a weak base-strong acid titration falls below pH 7.
cards.a: At equivalence all the weak base has been converted to its conjugate acid (for example NH3 to NH4⁺). That conjugate acid hydrolyzes water to produce H3O⁺, so the solution is acidic.
cards.n: Whatever species remains at the equivalence point determines the pH there.

cards.q: Compute the molarity of an HCl solution if 25.0 mL requires 32.5 mL of 0.100 M NaOH to reach the equivalence point.
cards.a: mol NaOH = 0.0325 L × 0.100 M = 3.25×10⁻³ mol. The reaction is 1:1, so mol HCl = 3.25×10⁻³ mol and M = 3.25×10⁻³/0.0250 L = 0.130 M.
cards.n: Always convert to moles first; the mole ratio is 1:1 only for monoprotic-monobasic pairs.

cards.q: Describe the titration curve of a diprotic weak acid with a strong base.
cards.a: It shows two buffer regions and two equivalence points, one for each proton, separated by a vertical jump. The second equivalence point requires twice the titrant volume of the first, and its pH is higher.
cards.n: Distinct steps appear only when Ka1 is roughly 10³ times Ka2 or more; otherwise the steps blur together.

cards.q: Define an acid-base indicator and state its useful pH range.
cards.a: An indicator is a weak acid (HIn) whose acid and base forms have different colors. It changes color over roughly pH = pKa ± 1, where the ratio [In⁻]/[HIn] moves from about 1:10 to 10:1.
cards.h: → weak acid plus a range formula
cards.n: Because the indicator is itself a weak acid, add only a couple of drops so it does not consume titrant.

cards.q: Decide how to choose an appropriate indicator for a titration.
cards.a: Choose an indicator whose pKa is close to the pH at the equivalence point, so its color change (pKa ± 1) occurs inside the steep vertical portion of the curve.
cards.n: Phenolphthalein (pKa about 9) suits weak acid-strong base; methyl red (pKa about 5) suits weak base-strong acid.

cards.q: Identify a suitable indicator for the titration of acetic acid with NaOH and justify the choice.
cards.a: Phenolphthalein. Its color change spans about pH 8.2-10.0, which brackets the equivalence-point pH (above 7) for a weak acid titrated with a strong base.
cards.h: → one indicator name plus its range
cards.n: Methyl orange would change color far too early, in the buffer region, and underestimate the volume.

cards.q: State the definition of pKa and how it relates to acid strength.
cards.a: pKa = -log(Ka), so Ka = $10^(-pKa).$ A smaller pKa means a larger Ka and a stronger acid; each unit of pKa is a factor of 10 in acid strength.
cards.n: Ranking acids by pKa reverses the ranking by Ka; the strongest acid has the lowest pKa.

cards.q: Predict which form of a conjugate pair predominates when the solution pH is below, equal to, or above the pKa.
cards.a: pH < pKa: the protonated acid form HA predominates. pH = pKa: the two forms are present in equal amounts. pH > pKa: the deprotonated base form A⁻ predominates.
cards.n: A difference of 2 pH units from pKa means roughly a 100:1 ratio of the favored form.

cards.q: State the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation and the conditions under which it applies.
cards.a: $pH = pK_{a} + \log\frac{[A^{-}]}{[HA]}$. It applies to a buffer, where both the weak acid and its conjugate base are present in appreciable, comparable amounts.
cards.n: Because the volume is shared, you may substitute moles of A⁻ and HA directly for concentrations.

cards.q: Compute the pH of a buffer that is 0.20 M in HC2H3O2 and 0.40 M in NaC2H3O2, given Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵.
cards.n: A 2:1 base-to-acid ratio always raises the pH exactly 0.30 unit above the pKa.

cards.q: Compute the pH after 0.010 mol NaOH is added to 1.00 L of a buffer containing 0.100 mol HA and 0.100 mol A⁻ (pKa = 4.75).
cards.a: OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻: HA becomes 0.090 mol and A⁻ becomes 0.110 mol. pH = 4.75 + log(0.110/0.090) = 4.75 + 0.09 = 4.84.
cards.n: Do the limiting-reactant neutralization in moles before applying Henderson-Hasselbalch.

cards.q: Predict the pH of a buffer in which the weak acid and its conjugate base are present in equal concentrations.
cards.a: pH = pKa, because the log of the ratio 1 is zero. This is also the composition of maximum buffering ability.
cards.n: Equal concentrations, not equal volumes; check the moles of each component.

cards.q: Define buffer capacity.
cards.a: The amount of strong acid or strong base a buffer can neutralize before its pH changes significantly. It depends on the absolute concentrations of the buffer components, not just their ratio.
cards.n: Two buffers can share a pH yet have very different capacities if one is far more concentrated.

cards.q: Explain what conditions maximize buffer capacity.
cards.a: High concentrations of both components and a [A⁻]/[HA] ratio close to 1, which means a pH close to the pKa. Capacity falls off sharply once the ratio passes about 10:1 either way.
cards.n: Buffer capacity is largest at pH = pKa and is effectively exhausted outside pKa ± 1.

cards.q: Decide how to choose a weak acid to prepare a buffer of a target pH.
cards.a: Pick a weak acid whose pKa is within about 1 unit of the target pH, then set the [A⁻]/[HA] ratio with Henderson-Hasselbalch to fine-tune the value.
cards.n: Choosing an acid whose pKa is far from the target forces an extreme ratio and a very weak buffer.

cards.q: Explain why diluting a buffer with water barely changes its pH.
cards.a: Dilution lowers [HA] and [A⁻] by the same factor, so their ratio - and therefore the log term in Henderson-Hasselbalch - is unchanged. The pH stays essentially constant while the buffer capacity drops.
cards.n: Dilution is the cleanest illustration that pH depends on the ratio while capacity depends on the amounts.

cards.q: Identify the Lewis acid and the Lewis base in the reaction BF3 + NH3 → F3B-NH3.
cards.a: NH3 is the Lewis base because it donates its lone pair; BF3 is the Lewis acid because its electron-deficient boron accepts that pair to form a coordinate covalent bond.
cards.n: No proton is transferred here, so only the Lewis definition classifies this as an acid-base reaction.

cards.q: Identify two laboratory ways to prepare a buffer of a given pH.
cards.a: (1) Mix a weak acid with a soluble salt of its conjugate base in the desired mole ratio. (2) Partially neutralize a weak acid with a limited amount of strong base (or a weak base with limited strong acid), leaving both forms present.
cards.n: In method 2 the strong reagent must be the limiting reactant, otherwise no weak-acid form remains.

cards.q: Explain why the successive Ka values of a polyprotic acid decrease sharply.
cards.a: Each proton is removed from a species that is one unit more negative than the last, so the remaining protons are held more tightly by electrostatic attraction. Ka1 >> Ka2 >> Ka3, typically by factors of about 10⁵.
cards.n: Because Ka1 dominates, the pH of a polyprotic acid solution can usually be computed from the first ionization alone.

cards.q: Identify the pH region on a weak acid-strong base titration curve where the solution acts as an effective buffer.
cards.a: The buffer region spans from just after the start of titration to just before the equivalence point, where significant, comparable amounts of both the weak acid and its conjugate base coexist.
cards.n: Buffering is strongest at half-equivalence, where the ratio is 1, and it disappears the moment the equivalence point is passed.

cards.q: Compute the pH at the half-equivalence point of a titration of a weak acid with $K_a = 4.5\times10^{-4}$.
cards.a: At half-equivalence, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa = -log(4.5x10⁻⁴) = 3.35.
cards.n: Neither the acid's concentration nor the titrant volume enters this; Ka alone fixes the pH at the half-equivalence point.

cards.q: Identify the titration-curve feature used to read off pKa directly, without any calculation.
cards.a: The pH at the half-equivalence point, half the volume needed to reach the equivalence point, equals pKa directly, since [HA] = [A⁻] there.
cards.n: Find the equivalence volume first and then halve it; reading pKa at the equivalence point instead is the usual misstep.

cards.q: Rank three weak acids by the pH of their 0.10 M solutions, given $K_a$ values $1.8\times10^{-5}$, $6.3\times10^{-3}$, and $4.0\times10^{-8}$.
cards.a: The acid with $K_a=6.3\times10^{-3}$ gives the lowest pH (strongest, most ionized), and $K_a=4.0\times10^{-8}$ gives the highest pH (weakest), with $1.8\times10^{-5}$ in between.
cards.n: The equal 0.10 M concentrations make this a fair comparison; at different concentrations a larger Ka need not give the lower pH.

cards.q: Compute the pH of a buffer made from 0.30 mol $NH_3$ and 0.20 mol $NH_4Cl$ in 1.00 L, given $K_b(NH_3)=1.8\times10^{-5}$.
cards.n: Trap: Henderson-Hasselbalch always uses the conjugate ACID's pKa, so a base buffer needs Kb converted first.

cards.q: Compute the pH change when 0.020 mol HCl is added to 1.00 L of a buffer with 0.200 mol $CH_3COOH$ and 0.200 mol $CH_3COO^{-}$ ($K_a=1.8\times10^{-5}$).
cards.a: Before: pH = pKa = 4.74. After HCl consumes acetate: [HA]=0.220, [A⁻]=0.180, pH = 4.74 + log(0.180/0.220) = 4.65. The pH drops only 0.09 units.
cards.h: → add strong acid moles to HA, subtract from A-
cards.n: The size of the change is the point: 0.020 mol of HCl in 1.00 L of plain water would instead sit near pH 1.7.

cards.q: Compute the pH at the equivalence point of titrating 0.10 M $CH_3COOH$ with NaOH if the resulting acetate concentration is 0.050 M ($K_b=5.6\times10^{-10}$).
cards.a: Treat acetate as a weak base: $[OH^{-}] = \sqrt{K_b \times C} = \sqrt{(5.6\times10^{-10})(0.050)} = 5.3\times10^{-6}$ M. pOH = 5.28, so pH = 8.72.
cards.h: → equivalence point of a weak acid titration is basic
cards.n: This is the same reasoning used for the equivalence point of any weak acid-strong base titration.

cards.q: Rank $HClO_4$, $HClO_3$, and $HClO_2$ by acid strength, and justify using terminal oxygen atoms.
cards.a: $HClO_4 > HClO_3 > HClO_2$. More terminal oxygen atoms pull electron density away from the O-H bond and stabilize the resulting conjugate base by delocalizing its negative charge.
cards.n: The same reasoning explains why $HClO_4$ beats $H_2SO_4$ beats $H_3PO_4$ across different central atoms too.

cards.q: Predict the acid-base character of a solution of $NaH_2PO_4$.
cards.a: Slightly acidic. $H_2PO_4^{-}$ is amphiprotic, but its Ka acting as an acid is larger than its Kb acting as a base, so the acidic character dominates.
cards.n: Compare Ka2 of phosphoric acid against the ion's Kb; running the same comparison for $Na_2HPO_4$ instead gives a basic solution.

cards.q: Compute the pH of 0.50 M HF, given $K_a=7.2\times10^{-4}$.
cards.n: The shortcut assumes x is negligible next to 0.50 M; check afterward that percent ionization stays under about 5 percent.

cards.q: Compute the pOH of a solution with pH = 9.40 at 25 °C.
cards.n: The sum of 14.00 holds only at 25 °C, because Kw itself grows as temperature rises and pure water's neutral pH drops below 7.

cards.q: Identify the two Bronsted-Lowry conjugate acid-base pairs in $HCO_3^{-}+H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3+OH^{-}$.
cards.a: $HCO_3^{-}$/$H_2CO_3$ is one pair, with $HCO_3^{-}$ as the base and $H_2CO_3$ its conjugate acid; $H_2O$/$OH^{-}$ is the other, with water as the acid and $OH^{-}$ its conjugate base.
cards.n: Conjugate partners differ by exactly one $H^{+}$ and one unit of charge; a pair differing by two protons is not a conjugate pair.

cards.q: Predict which buffer has the greater capacity: one with 0.10 mol each of HA and A⁻, or one with 1.0 mol each of HA and A⁻ in the same volume.
cards.a: The 1.0 mol buffer has greater capacity. More moles of both the weak acid and conjugate base are available to absorb added acid or base before the ratio, and pH, shift significantly.
cards.n: Capacity depends on the moles of buffer components present, not on the pH they set.

cards.q: Explain why the pH jump near the equivalence point is smaller for a weak acid-strong base titration than for a strong acid-strong base titration.
cards.a: The weak acid's conjugate base buffers the solution right up until just before equivalence, resisting the pH change, so the vertical jump is smaller and the equivalence point itself is above pH 7.
cards.n: The equivalence point is still where moles match; a pH above 7 there is the signature of a weak acid being titrated.

cards.q: Predict whether a solution of $NH_4F$ is acidic, basic, or neutral, given $K_a(NH_4^+)=5.6\times10^{-10}$ and $K_b(F^-)=1.4\times10^{-11}$.
cards.a: Acidic. Both ions hydrolyze, but $K_a(NH_4^+) > K_b(F^-)$, so the solution ends up slightly acidic overall.
cards.h: → compare Ka of the cation to Kb of the anion
cards.n: Both ions react here, so naming only one is incomplete; the explicit comparison of Ka against Kb is the justification readers want.

cards.q: Predict whether an aqueous solution of $Na_2CO_3$ tests as acidic, basic, or neutral, and identify the ion responsible.
cards.a: Basic. Carbonate, $CO_3^{2-}$, is the conjugate base of the weak acid $HCO_3^-$ and hydrolyzes water to produce $OH^-$; $Na^+$ does not react with water.
cards.n: Both ions of $Na_2CO_3$ could in principle react with water, but $Na^+$ does not hydrolyze; only the anion determines the solution's character here.

cards.q: Identify why $Al(OH)_3$ is classified as an amphoteric substance.
cards.a: It reacts as a base with strong acids (forming $Al^{3+}$ and water) and as an acid with strong bases (forming the soluble $Al(OH)_4^-$ ion), so it can neutralize either an acid or a base.
cards.n: Amphoteric metal hydroxides like $Al(OH)_3$ react with both strong acid and strong base, unlike a simple amphiprotic ion.

cards.q: Identify the products when $HSO_3^-$ reacts as an acid with $OH^-$, and as a base with $H_3O^+$.
cards.a: As an acid: $HSO_3^- + OH^- \to SO_3^{2-} + H_2O$. As a base: $HSO_3^- + H_3O^+ \to H_2SO_3 + H_2O$. $HSO_3^-$ can donate or accept a proton.
cards.n: Whether $HSO_3^-$ acts as an acid or a base depends entirely on what it reacts with, not on any single fixed property of the ion.

cards.q: Compute the ratio $[A^-]/[HA]$ needed to buffer a solution at pH = 5.20 using an acid with pKa = 4.70.
cards.a: 3.16. From Henderson-Hasselbalch, $[A^-]/[HA] = 10^{(pH-pKa)} = 10^{0.50} = 3.16$.
cards.n: A ratio above 1 means more conjugate base than acid, matching a pH that sits above the pKa; use that as a quick sanity check.

cards.q: 500. mL of 0.200 M $CH_3COOH$ needs $NaC_2H_3O_2$ added to reach pH = 5.05 (pKa = 4.745). Compute the mass of $NaC_2H_3O_2$ (M = 82.0 g/mol) needed.
cards.h: → Henderson-Hasselbalch for the ratio, then moles to mass
cards.n: The 500. mL volume cancels because both species share it, so the ratio can be applied to moles directly with no dilution step.

cards.q: Explain what happens to a buffer's ability to resist pH change once enough strong acid has been added to consume nearly all its conjugate base.
cards.a: The buffer loses its capacity; with little or no conjugate base left to neutralize further acid, additional acid causes a large, uncontrolled pH drop instead of a small, buffered change.
cards.h: → what happens once capacity is gone
cards.n: A buffer works only while both the weak acid and conjugate base remain present in significant amounts.

cards.q: Predict which buffer has greater overall capacity: a large excess of conjugate base over acid, or equal amounts of each, at equal total concentration.
cards.a: The one with equal amounts has greater overall capacity against both acid and base. A skewed ratio resists one direction (added acid) well but is weak against added base.
cards.n: A skewed conjugate-base-to-acid ratio still buffers well against acid alone; true balanced protection against both acid and base needs a ratio near 1.

cards.q: Compute the pKa of a weak acid with $K_a=6.3\times10^{-5}$.
cards.n: A Ka between $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-4}$ has to give a pKa between 4 and 5, which catches most calculator slips instantly.

cards.q: Compute the Ka of a weak acid whose pKa is 3.75.
cards.n: The negative exponent is easy to lose: it is $10^{-3.75}$, not $10^{3.75}$, since Ka for a weak acid must be far below 1.

cards.q: Explain why a solution made only from $NH_4Cl$ is not a buffer, even though $NH_4^+$ is a weak acid.
cards.a: A buffer needs comparable amounts of both a weak acid and its conjugate base; $NH_4Cl$ supplies only $NH_4^+$ with no significant $NH_3$ present, so it cannot resist added base the way a true buffer can.
cards.n: Add some $NH_3$, or half-neutralize the ammonium with strong base, and the very same solution does become a buffer.

cards.q: Compute the percent ionization of a 0.050 M weak acid with $K_a=2.0\times10^{-4}$.
cards.a: 6.3%. $x=\sqrt{K_aC}=\sqrt{(2.0\times10^{-4})(0.050)}=3.2\times10^{-3}$ M; percent ionization = $3.2\times10^{-3}/0.050 \times 100$.
cards.n: Percent ionization falls as concentration rises, so a more concentrated weak acid ionizes in a smaller fraction despite its lower pH.

cards.q: Predict which is the stronger acid, $H_2SO_3$ or $H_2SO_4$, using the number of terminal oxygens on sulfur.
cards.a: $H_2SO_4$. It has more terminal (non-hydroxyl) oxygen atoms than $H_2SO_3$, which pull electron density from the O-H bonds more strongly, making the proton easier to remove.
cards.n: Adding one more terminal oxygen per sulfur atom, not one more hydrogen, is what drives the extra acid strength here.

cards.q: Explain why a Lewis acid must have an empty orbital available to accept an electron pair, using $BF_3$ as an example.
cards.a: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair to form a new bond, which requires an unoccupied orbital to hold it; boron in $BF_3$ has only 6 valence electrons and an empty p orbital, letting it accept a lone pair from a Lewis base like $NH_3$.
cards.n: A Lewis base needs a lone pair to donate; a Lewis acid needs an empty orbital to accept one, and the two roles are not interchangeable.

cards.q: Compute $[OH^{-}]$ in a solution whose pOH is 5.60.
cards.n: A pOH of 5.60 means the solution is basic, since pH works out to 8.40; check the exponent's sign against that before finishing.

cards.q: Compute the $pK_b$ of the conjugate base of a weak acid with $pK_a = 4.60$.
cards.a: 9.40. At 25°C, $pK_a + pK_b = 14.00$ for a conjugate acid-base pair, so $pK_b = 14.00 - 4.60 = 9.40$.
cards.n: The relationship holds only for a genuine conjugate pair at 25 °C, not for any two unrelated acids and bases you happen to be given.

cards.q: Predict which is the stronger acid: one with $pK_a = 3.2$ or one with $pK_a = 8.1$.
cards.a: The acid with $pK_a = 3.2$ is stronger. A lower pKa corresponds to a larger Ka, meaning greater ionization and a stronger acid.
cards.n: Each pKa unit is a factor of ten in Ka, so these two acids differ in strength by nearly five orders of magnitude.

cards.q: Define a buffer solution and state the two components required to make one.
cards.a: A buffer is a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It requires a significant concentration of both a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) present together.
cards.n: A strong acid and its conjugate base cannot buffer, because the conjugate base of a strong acid is far too weak to accept protons.

cards.q: Compute the pH of a buffer containing 0.20 M acetic acid ($K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}$) and 0.30 M sodium acetate.
cards.n: Trap: the ratio inside the log is [conjugate base]/[acid], not the reverse.

cards.q: Define entropy in terms of the dispersal of matter and energy.
cards.a: Entropy (S) measures the number of ways the energy and particles of a system can be arranged - its degree of dispersal or disorder. A larger number of accessible microstates means higher entropy.
cards.n: Unlike enthalpy, absolute entropies can be measured, and every pure substance above 0 K has S° > 0.

cards.q: Identify the changes that increase the entropy of a chemical system.
cards.a: Melting or vaporizing, dissolving a solid or liquid, increasing temperature, increasing the volume available to a gas, increasing the number of moles of gas, and forming larger or more complex molecules.
cards.n: Increasing moles of gas is the single most reliable indicator of a positive ΔS in an AP reaction.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° for 2NO2(g) → N2O4(g) and justify it.
cards.a: Negative. Two moles of gas become one mole of gas, so the particles have fewer accessible arrangements and the system becomes more ordered.
cards.n: Always count gas moles first; if they change, that dominates the sign of ΔS.

cards.q: Rank solid, liquid, and gas phases of the same substance by molar entropy.
cards.a: S(gas) >> S(liquid) > S(solid). The jump from liquid to gas is far larger than from solid to liquid because vaporization dramatically increases the volume and freedom of the particles.
cards.n: Dissolving a gas in a liquid decreases entropy, which is why gas solubility falls as temperature rises.

cards.q: State how to calculate the standard entropy change of a reaction from absolute entropies.
cards.a: ΔS°rxn = ΣnS°(products) - ΣnS°(reactants), where each standard molar entropy is multiplied by its balanced coefficient. Units are usually J/(mol·K).
cards.n: S° values are absolute, not formation values, so elements in their standard states have nonzero S°.

cards.q: Explain why S° of an element in its standard state is not zero, unlike ΔH°f.
cards.a: Standard entropy is an absolute quantity measured from the third-law reference point of a perfect crystal at 0 K, so any substance above 0 K has positive S°. ΔH°f is defined as a relative change, and forming an element from itself involves no change.
cards.n: Setting S° of O2 to zero is a common error that ruins a ΔS° calculation.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l) given S° values of 131, 205, and 70. J/(mol·K).
cards.n: The sign makes sense: three moles of gas become two moles of liquid.

cards.q: State the Gibbs free energy equation and what each term contributes.
cards.a: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, where ΔH is the enthalpy change, T is the absolute temperature in kelvin, and ΔS is the entropy change. ΔG combines the enthalpy and entropy drives into a single criterion.
cards.n: ΔH is usually in kJ/mol while ΔS is in J/(mol·K); convert before subtracting.

cards.q: Define a thermodynamically favorable process in terms of ΔG.
cards.a: A process is thermodynamically favorable when ΔG < 0. If ΔG > 0 the reverse process is favorable, and if ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium.
cards.n: AP says 'thermodynamically favorable', not 'spontaneous', and favorable never implies fast.

cards.q: State how to calculate ΔG°rxn from standard free energies of formation.
cards.a: ΔG°rxn = ΣnΔG°f(products) - ΣnΔG°f(reactants). ΔG°f of any element in its standard state is zero.
cards.n: You can also get ΔG° by combining ΔH° and ΔS° with ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°; both routes should agree.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0.
cards.a: ΔG is negative at all temperatures, so the reaction is thermodynamically favorable at every temperature. Both the enthalpy and entropy terms favor the products.
cards.n: Combustion reactions that produce more gas moles are the standard example.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0.
cards.a: ΔG is positive at all temperatures, so the reaction is never thermodynamically favorable; only the reverse reaction is favorable.
cards.n: If a question shows this sign pattern, no temperature change can make the reaction go.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0.
cards.a: ΔG is negative only at low temperatures, where the favorable -ΔH term outweighs the unfavorable -TΔS term. Raising T eventually makes ΔG positive.
cards.n: Freezing and condensation belong here: exothermic but entropy-decreasing.

cards.q: State the temperature dependence when ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0.
cards.a: ΔG is negative only at high temperatures, where the -TΔS term becomes large enough to overcome the unfavorable positive ΔH.
cards.n: Melting, boiling, and many dissolutions are endothermic but entropy-driven.

cards.q: Compute the temperature at which a reaction with ΔH° = +58.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +176 J/(mol·K) becomes thermodynamically favorable.
cards.a: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 58,000 J/mol ÷ 176 J/(mol·K) = 330. K. Above about 330 K, ΔG < 0.
cards.h: → temperature in kelvin near room temperature
cards.n: The crossover temperature is where ΔG = 0, which is also where K = 1.

cards.q: Explain the unit precaution required when using ΔG = ΔH - TΔS.
cards.a: Tabulated ΔH is in kJ/mol but ΔS is in J/(mol·K), so ΔS must be divided by 1000 (or ΔH multiplied by 1000) before subtracting. Temperature must be in kelvin, never Celsius.
cards.n: A factor-of-1000 error here produces an answer off by three orders of magnitude and the wrong sign conclusion.

cards.q: Contrast thermodynamic control and kinetic control of a reaction.
cards.a: Thermodynamic control means the outcome is determined by which products have the lowest free energy (most negative ΔG). Kinetic control means the outcome is determined by which pathway has the lowest activation energy, regardless of ΔG.
cards.n: A reaction can be highly favorable yet not occur because its activation energy is too large.

cards.q: Explain why diamond does not visibly convert to graphite even though ΔG° for the conversion is negative.
cards.a: The conversion is thermodynamically favorable but under kinetic control: breaking and rearranging the covalent network requires an enormous activation energy, so the rate is effectively zero at room temperature.
cards.n: Any 'favorable but does not happen' question is answered by a large activation energy.

cards.q: State the relationship between standard free energy change and the equilibrium constant.
cards.a: ΔG° = -RT ln K, with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T in kelvin. Equivalently, K = $e^(-ΔG°/RT).$
cards.n: Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) here, not 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K), and convert ΔG° to joules.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔG° from the magnitude of K.
cards.a: K > 1 gives ln K > 0 and therefore ΔG° < 0 (products favored). K < 1 gives ΔG° > 0 (reactants favored). K = 1 gives ΔG° = 0.
cards.n: The dividing line is K = 1, not K = 0; a small but nonzero K still means positive ΔG°.

cards.q: State the equation relating ΔG under nonstandard conditions to ΔG° and Q.
cards.a: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient at the moment of interest.
cards.h: → standard value plus a correction term
cards.n: This is the thermodynamic parent of the Nernst equation.

cards.q: Explain what ΔG equals at equilibrium and what that implies about Q.
cards.a: At equilibrium ΔG = 0, so 0 = ΔG° + RT ln Q, which requires Q = K. ΔG° is generally not zero at equilibrium; only the instantaneous ΔG is.
cards.n: Confusing ΔG with ΔG° is the most common error in this topic; ΔG° is fixed at a given temperature.

cards.q: Compute K at 298 K for a reaction with ΔG° = -22.8 kJ/mol.
cards.n: Roughly, every 5.7 kJ/mol of negative ΔG° at 298 K multiplies K by about 10.

cards.q: Explain how coupled reactions can drive a thermodynamically unfavorable process.
cards.a: An unfavorable reaction (ΔG > 0) is paired with a favorable one (ΔG << 0) that shares a common intermediate. The free energies add, and if the sum is negative the overall coupled process is favorable.
cards.n: The two reactions must share a species so they truly combine; otherwise their ΔG values do not add.

cards.q: Identify a common example of a coupled reaction and the source of the driving free energy.
cards.a: Extracting iron from Fe2O3 is unfavorable alone, but coupling it to the highly favorable oxidation of carbon to CO/CO2 makes the overall smelting reaction favorable. In biology, ATP hydrolysis is coupled to unfavorable biosynthesis.
cards.h: → one industrial and one biological case
cards.n: Electrolysis is a related idea: external electrical work supplies the free energy an unfavorable redox reaction lacks.

cards.q: Contrast a galvanic (voltaic) cell with an electrolytic cell.
cards.a: A galvanic cell runs a thermodynamically favorable redox reaction (E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0) and produces electrical energy. An electrolytic cell uses an external power supply to force an unfavorable reaction (E°cell < 0, ΔG° > 0).
cards.n: In both cell types oxidation still occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

cards.q: Identify which electrode is the anode and which is the cathode in any electrochemical cell.
cards.a: Oxidation always occurs at the anode; reduction always occurs at the cathode. This is true for both galvanic and electrolytic cells.
cards.n: Mnemonic: AN OX and RED CAT. Only the electrode signs differ between cell types, not the chemistry.

cards.q: State the direction of electron flow and of current in the external circuit of a galvanic cell.
cards.a: Electrons flow through the external wire from the anode to the cathode. Conventional current is defined in the opposite direction, from cathode to anode.
cards.n: Electrons never travel through the salt bridge; only ions move there.

cards.q: Explain the function of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell.
cards.a: It completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality by allowing ions to migrate between half-cells. Without it, charge builds up in each compartment and current stops almost immediately.
cards.n: A common free-response answer point is that the cell stops working if the salt bridge is removed.

cards.q: Identify the direction that cations and anions migrate through a salt bridge.
cards.a: Cations migrate toward the cathode compartment, where positive charge is being consumed by reduction. Anions migrate toward the anode compartment, where positive metal ions are being produced.
cards.n: Cations move toward the cathode - both words start with the same sound.

cards.q: Identify the electrode charge signs in galvanic versus electrolytic cells.
cards.a: Galvanic: the anode is negative and the cathode is positive. Electrolytic: the anode is positive and the cathode is negative, because the external supply drives the charges.
cards.n: The signs flip between cell types even though anode = oxidation never changes.

cards.q: State the cell notation convention for a galvanic cell.
cards.a: Anode | anode electrolyte || cathode electrolyte | cathode, with oxidation on the left and reduction on the right. A single bar is a phase boundary and the double bar is the salt bridge. Example: Zn | Zn²⁺(1 M) || Cu²⁺(1 M) | Cu.
cards.n: An inert electrode such as Pt is written at the far left or far right when no solid conductor is produced.

cards.q: State how to calculate the standard cell potential from tabulated half-cell potentials.
cards.a: E°cell = E°(cathode) - E°(anode), using standard reduction potentials for both half-reactions as written in the table.
cards.n: Do NOT multiply a half-cell potential by the coefficient used to balance electrons; E° is intensive.

cards.q: Compute E°cell for a Zn/Cu galvanic cell given E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = -0.76 V.
cards.a: Copper has the higher reduction potential, so it is the cathode: E°cell = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V. Zinc is oxidized at the anode.
cards.n: In a galvanic cell the species with the more positive reduction potential is always the cathode.

cards.q: Explain why a standard reduction potential is not multiplied when a half-reaction is scaled.
cards.a: E° is an intensive property - energy per unit charge - so it does not depend on how much substance reacts. Only ΔG°, which is extensive, scales with the coefficients through ΔG° = -nFE°.
cards.n: Doubling a half-reaction doubles n and doubles ΔG°, but leaves E° unchanged.

cards.q: State the equation linking standard free energy change and standard cell potential.
cards.a: ΔG° = -nFE°, where n is the moles of electrons transferred in the balanced reaction and F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻. A positive E° corresponds to a negative ΔG°.
cards.n: With E° in volts and F in C/mol, ΔG° comes out in joules; divide by 1000 for kJ.

cards.q: State what the sign of E°cell tells you about a redox reaction.
cards.a: E°cell > 0 means the reaction is thermodynamically favorable as written and the cell is galvanic. E°cell < 0 means it is unfavorable and would require an electrolytic cell.
cards.n: E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0, and K > 1 always travel together.

cards.q: Rank species as oxidizing or reducing agents using a table of standard reduction potentials.
cards.a: The more positive the standard reduction potential, the stronger the oxidizing agent (it is most easily reduced). The more negative the potential, the stronger the reducing agent in its reduced form.
cards.n: F2 sits at the top as the strongest oxidizing agent; Li is the strongest common reducing agent.

cards.q: State qualitatively how cell potential responds to nonstandard concentrations (the Nernst relationship).
cards.a: E = E° - (RT/nF) ln Q. As Q increases (more product, less reactant) E decreases; as Q decreases E increases. When Q = K, E = 0 and the cell is dead.
cards.n: A battery going flat is exactly the cell reaching equilibrium, where E = 0 and ΔG = 0.

cards.q: Predict the effect on cell potential of increasing the concentration of a product ion in a galvanic cell.
cards.a: Q increases, so E decreases below E°. By Le Chatelier reasoning, adding product pushes the cell closer to equilibrium and reduces its driving force.
cards.n: Increasing a reactant concentration has the opposite effect and raises E above E°.

cards.q: Define a concentration cell.
cards.a: An electrochemical cell whose two half-cells contain the same species at different concentrations. The chemical reaction is the same on both sides, so E° = 0, and the potential comes entirely from the concentration difference.
cards.n: A concentration cell runs until the two concentrations become equal, at which point E = 0.

cards.q: Predict which half-cell of a concentration cell acts as the anode.
cards.a: The dilute half-cell is the anode. Oxidation there raises its ion concentration, while reduction at the concentrated cathode lowers that side, driving the two toward equality.
cards.n: Trace the direction the system must move to equalize the concentrations; that identifies the anode.

cards.q: Explain why E° for a concentration cell is exactly zero while the measured E is not.
cards.a: Both half-reactions are the same, so E°(cathode) - E°(anode) = 0. The measured potential comes from the -(RT/nF) ln Q term, which is nonzero whenever the two concentrations differ.
cards.n: Concentration-cell voltages are small, typically a few hundredths of a volt.

cards.q: State the equations used for electrolysis stoichiometry.
cards.a: q = I × t (charge in coulombs from current in amperes and time in seconds), and moles of electrons = q/F with F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻. Then use the half-reaction to convert moles of electrons to moles of substance.
cards.h: → two equations plus a mole ratio
cards.n: Time must be in seconds; a problem stated in minutes or hours needs conversion first.

cards.q: Compute the mass of copper deposited when 2.00 A flows for 30.0 minutes through a Cu²⁺ solution.
cards.n: The 2 in the half-reaction halves the moles of metal; forgetting it doubles the answer.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° for $CaCO_3(s) \to CaO(s)+CO_2(g)$ and justify.
cards.a: ΔS° is positive. A solid decomposes into a solid plus a gas, and forming a gas from a solid dramatically increases the number of accessible microstates.
cards.n: Counting moles of gas is the fastest entropy check on the exam, and going from no gas to one mole settles this sign immediately.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° when a gas dissolves into a liquid solvent, such as $CO_2(g) \to CO_2(aq)$.
cards.a: ΔS° is negative. The gas loses its large translational freedom once confined among solvent molecules, decreasing the number of accessible microstates.
cards.n: This is why warm soda goes flat faster: rising temperature favors the higher-entropy gas escaping.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $N_2(g)+3H_2(g) \to 2NH_3(g)$ given S° = 192, 131, and 193 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.n: S° values are absolute and positive for every substance, so elements do not drop out of this sum the way they do for ΔH°f.

cards.q: Compute the crossover temperature at which ΔG° = 0 for a reaction with ΔH° = -92.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -199 J/(mol·K).
cards.a: $T=\Delta H^{\circ}/\Delta S^{\circ} = -92000/-199 = 462$ K. Below 462 K the reaction is favorable; above it, ΔG° turns positive.
cards.n: Trap: ΔH must be converted to joules to match ΔS's J/K units before dividing.

cards.q: Compute ΔG° at 298 K for a reaction with ΔH° = -92.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -199 J/(mol·K).
cards.a: ΔG° = -92000 - (298)(-199) = -92000 + 59302 = -32.7 kJ/mol. The reaction is thermodynamically favorable at 298 K.
cards.h: → ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, convert units first
cards.n: Both terms are negative here, so the reaction is favorable only while T stays low; raising the temperature eventually flips the sign.

cards.q: Contrast a reaction that is thermodynamically favorable but kinetically slow with one that is favorable in both senses, using an everyday example.
cards.a: Paper burning is thermodynamically favorable (ΔG°<0) but kinetically slow without a spark, since it has a high activation barrier. Acid-base neutralization is favorable both ways and is instant.
cards.n: Favorability and speed are set by different quantities, free energy versus activation energy, which is why favorable can still mean slow.

cards.q: Compute K at 298 K for a reaction with ΔG° = +11.4 kJ/mol.
cards.h: → solve for ln K, then exponentiate
cards.n: A ΔG° this close to zero corresponds to a K well below 1, so the reaction favors reactants only modestly.

cards.q: Decide whether a cell with $E_{cell} < 0$ under the given conditions is operating as a galvanic or an electrolytic cell.
cards.a: It must be operating as an electrolytic cell. A negative cell potential means the reaction is not thermodynamically favorable on its own, so an external power source must be forcing it to run.
cards.n: The sign links straight to ΔG° = -nFE°: a negative potential means a positive ΔG°, so the process cannot run unassisted.

cards.q: Compute E°cell for a cell built from $Ag^{+}/Ag$ (E° = +0.80 V) and $Fe^{2+}/Fe$ (E° = -0.44 V), and identify the cathode.
cards.a: $Ag^{+}$ has the higher reduction potential, so it is reduced at the cathode. E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0.80 - (-0.44) = 1.24 V.
cards.h: → higher E° is reduced, at the cathode
cards.n: Never multiply E° by the coefficients used to balance electrons; cell potential is intensive, unlike ΔG°, which does scale.

cards.q: Compute ΔG° for the Ag/Fe cell above (E°cell = 1.24 V) if the balanced equation transfers 2 mol electrons.
cards.n: A positive E° always pairs with a negative ΔG°, since the two are connected by a negative sign in ΔG°=-nFE°.

cards.q: Predict the effect on $E_cell$ of increasing $[Zn^{2+}]$ at the anode of a Zn/Cu galvanic cell while $[Cu^{2+}]$ stays fixed.
cards.a: $E_{cell}$ decreases. Raising an anode product concentration increases Q, and by the Nernst relationship a larger Q makes $E=E^{\circ}-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$ smaller.
cards.n: This is the Nernst equation's qualitative content: rising Q at any point always pulls E away from E°.

cards.q: Compute the moles of electrons passed when a current of 3.00 A flows for 965 seconds.
cards.n: Time must already be in seconds for this to work, since an ampere is one coulomb per second and nothing per minute.

cards.q: Compute the mass of silver deposited when 0.0300 mol of electrons passes through a cell containing $Ag^{+}$.
cards.a: $Ag^{+}$ requires 1 electron per ion, so mol Ag = 0.0300 mol. Mass = 0.0300 x 107.9 = 3.24 g.
cards.n: Copper(II) would need twice as many electrons per mole deposited, since $Cu^{2+}$ requires 2 e- per ion.

cards.q: Predict how $E_{cell}$ changes as a galvanic cell operates and its reaction approaches equilibrium.
cards.a: $E_{cell}$ decreases toward zero. As the reaction proceeds, Q approaches K, and the driving force for electron flow shrinks until $E_{cell}=0$ at equilibrium, when the battery is dead.
cards.n: A cell at equilibrium can no longer do electrical work, even though the chemical species are still present.

cards.q: For a cathode half-reaction $MnO_4^-+8H^++5e^- \to Mn^{2+}+4H_2O$, predict the effect on $E_{cell}$ of decreasing $[H^+]$.
cards.a: $E_{cell}$ decreases. Lower $[H^+]$ makes the reduction of $MnO_4^-$ less favorable, lowering the effective potential of that half-reaction and thus the overall cell potential.
cards.h: → H+ is a reactant in this half-reaction
cards.n: Eight protons appear in this half-reaction, so permanganate's potential is unusually sensitive to pH compared with most reductions.

cards.q: Explain why iron corrodes (rusts) readily in the presence of both water and dissolved oxygen.
cards.a: Water and oxygen enable a galvanic process: iron is oxidized to $Fe^{2+}$ at anodic regions, while dissolved $O_2$ is reduced at cathodic regions on the same surface; the products further react to form iron oxide (rust).
cards.n: Rusting requires both water and oxygen together; iron in perfectly dry air, or fully submerged in oxygen-free water, corrodes far more slowly.

cards.q: Apply electrolytic cell setup to electroplate a spoon with silver: identify which electrode the spoon must be connected to.
cards.a: The cathode. Reduction of $Ag^+$ to solid Ag occurs at the cathode, so the spoon must be the cathode for silver metal to deposit onto its surface.
cards.n: Connecting the object to the anode instead of the cathode would oxidize (dissolve) it rather than plate it.

cards.q: Explain how connecting zinc metal to iron protects the iron from corrosion (cathodic protection).
cards.a: Zinc is more easily oxidized than iron, so it becomes the anode and is oxidized preferentially while iron becomes the protected cathode; the zinc corrodes away first, sacrificing itself to prevent the iron from oxidizing.
cards.h: → zinc acts as a sacrificial anode
cards.n: Any metal more easily oxidized than iron will do, which is why galvanized steel and magnesium anodes on ship hulls work the same way.

cards.q: Predict whether coupling a favorable reaction (ΔG°₁ = −80. kJ/mol) with an unfavorable one (ΔG°₂ = +20. kJ/mol) gives an overall favorable process.
cards.a: Yes. The overall ΔG° = ΔG°₁ + ΔG°₂ = −80. + 20. = −60. kJ/mol, which is negative, so the coupled process is thermodynamically favorable overall.
cards.h: → yes or no, plus the sum
cards.n: Simple addition of ΔG° values works because Gibbs free energy is a state function; that shortcut does not apply directly to K values, which multiply instead.

cards.q: Compute the moles of electrons transferred in a redox reaction with ΔG° = −212 kJ/mol and $E°_{cell}=+1.10$ V.
cards.n: Faraday's constant (96500 C/mol) converts between charge and moles of electrons in both electrolysis and cell-potential problems.

cards.q: Compute the mass of chromium plated when 4.50 A flows for 2.00 hours through a $Cr^{3+}$ solution.
cards.n: Convert the hours to seconds first; leaving t in hours makes the deposited mass come out 3600 times too small.

cards.q: Identify which half-reaction, iron oxidation or oxygen reduction, occurs at the anodic region of a corroding iron surface.
cards.a: Iron oxidation, $Fe \to Fe^{2+}+2e^-$, occurs at the anodic region; oxygen reduction occurs at separate cathodic regions on the same metal surface.
cards.n: Oxidation always happens at the anode, whether in a battery, an electrolytic cell, or a corroding metal surface.

cards.q: Predict how increasing the electrode surface area affects $E_{cell}$, with concentrations unchanged.
cards.a: $E_{cell}$ is unaffected. Cell potential is a thermodynamic quantity depending only on concentrations and temperature; electrode surface area changes the rate of electron transfer, not the potential.
cards.h: → the effect, plus what changes instead
cards.n: A common trap is assuming larger electrodes give a higher voltage; surface area affects current and rate, not $E_{cell}$.

cards.q: Compute ΔG° at 298 K for a reaction with K = 5.0×10⁻³.
cards.n: A K below 1 must give a positive ΔG°, so check that sign before trusting the arithmetic, and report the answer in kJ rather than J.

cards.q: Identify how to choose two half-reactions from a standard reduction potential table to produce the largest possible $E°_{cell}$.
cards.a: Pair the half-reaction with the most positive reduction potential (as the cathode) with the one having the most negative reduction potential, run in reverse as the anode; their difference gives the maximum $E°_{cell}$.
cards.h: → two table entries, then a difference
cards.n: A reduction potential table already accounts for reversing a half-reaction as the anode; you never flip the sign of the table entries themselves before comparing.

cards.q: Explain why the mass of metal deposited during electrolysis depends on the total charge passed but not on the cell voltage.
cards.a: Faraday's laws relate deposited mass to moles of electrons, which depend only on current × time (charge); voltage affects the energy required to drive the reaction, not the stoichiometric amount of product formed per electron.
cards.n: A higher-voltage power supply does not by itself deposit more metal; only increasing the current or the time increases the total charge passed.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔS° for $2H_2(g) + O_2(g) \to 2H_2O(l)$ and justify.
cards.a: Negative. Three moles of gas become zero moles of gas as a much more ordered liquid forms, so the system becomes far more ordered and entropy decreases.
cards.n: Liquid water is specified rather than vapor, which makes the decrease even larger than the change in moles of gas alone suggests.

cards.q: Identify two examples of processes that decrease the entropy of a chemical system.
cards.a: A gas condensing into a liquid, and a reaction in which the total moles of gas decrease (such as $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \to 2NH_3(g)$) both decrease entropy, since particles become more ordered or more constrained.
cards.n: A system's entropy is allowed to fall; the second law constrains the system plus its surroundings together, not the system by itself.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \to 2SO_3(g)$ given S° = 248, 205, and 257 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.n: The negative sign makes sense: 3 mol of gas becomes 2 mol of gas, a more ordered arrangement.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $CaCO_3(s) \to CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$ given S° = 92.9, 39.8, and 213.7 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.n: S° for a solid is small but never zero, unlike ΔH°f for an element; only a perfect crystal at 0 K has an entropy of zero.

cards.q: Compute ΔS° for $N_2O_4(g) \to 2NO_2(g)$ given S° = 304 and 240 J/(mol·K) respectively.
cards.n: One mole of gas becoming two should give a positive value, which is a fast check that the subtraction ran in the right order.

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with a large negative ΔG° can still proceed too slowly to observe at room temperature.
cards.a: ΔG° describes only the thermodynamic favorability, the relative stability of reactants versus products; it says nothing about the activation energy barrier between them. A high activation energy can make even a very favorable reaction extremely slow, regardless of how negative ΔG° is.
cards.n: ΔG° tells you where the equilibrium lies, not how fast the system gets there.

cards.q: Contrast the kinetic product of a reaction with the thermodynamic product when a reaction can form two different products.
cards.a: The kinetic product forms fastest, through the pathway with the lowest activation energy, but is not necessarily the most stable. The thermodynamic product is the most stable, lowest-energy product, but may form through a slower pathway with a higher activation energy.
cards.n: Short times and low temperatures favor the kinetic product, while long times and higher temperatures let the thermodynamic one win.

cards.q: Predict how raising the temperature of a reaction that can form either a kinetic or a thermodynamic product shifts the product distribution.
cards.a: Raising the temperature shifts the distribution toward the thermodynamic product. Extra thermal energy lets the system overcome the higher activation-energy barrier and reach true equilibrium, favoring the more stable product rather than the kinetically fastest one.
cards.h: → direction of the shift, plus reason
cards.n: Reversibility is the real mechanism: extra heat lets the kinetic product revert, so the system can settle into the more stable one.

cards.q: Explain why increasing temperature reliably speeds up a reaction's rate, while its effect on thermodynamic favorability depends on the sign of ΔS°.
cards.a: Higher temperature always gives more particles enough kinetic energy to clear the activation-energy barrier, so rate always increases with temperature. But in ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°, raising T only pushes ΔG° more negative if ΔS° is positive; if ΔS° is negative, raising T makes ΔG° less favorable.
cards.n: Faster is not more: for an exothermic reaction, raising T speeds the approach to an equilibrium that holds less product, since K falls.

cards.q: Explain what value K must equal whenever ΔG° = 0, and what that special case means physically.
cards.a: K must equal 1, since ΔG° = -RT ln K forces ln K = 0 when ΔG° = 0. Physically, it means the standard-state mixture of reactants and products (all at 1 M or 1 atm) is already at equilibrium.
cards.n: This does not mean any mixture is at equilibrium, only the standard-state one; a real mixture at other concentrations still shifts.

cards.q: Define a coupled reaction system and state the requirement for the two reactions to be linked.
cards.a: A coupled reaction system pairs a thermodynamically unfavorable reaction with a strongly favorable one so the overall two-step process is spontaneous. The two reactions must share a common intermediate species that is produced by one and consumed by the other.
cards.n: Biology runs on this: ATP hydrolysis is the favorable partner that drives unfavorable synthesis reactions inside cells.

cards.q: A cell couples reaction 1 $(ΔG°_1$ = -62 kJ/mol) with reaction 2 $(ΔG°_2$ = +38 kJ/mol). Compute the overall ΔG° and determine whether the coupled process is spontaneous.
cards.a: -24 kJ/mol, spontaneous. ΔG°overall = $ΔG°_1$ + $ΔG°_2$ = -62 + 38 = -24 kJ/mol, a negative value.
cards.n: Free energies add only because ΔG is a state function; the corresponding equilibrium constants would multiply instead of adding.

cards.q: Explain why the two reactions in a coupled system must share a common intermediate species.
cards.a: The shared intermediate is what physically links the two reactions into a single overall process; without it, they would just be two independent reactions running side by side, and the favorable one could not drive the unfavorable one forward.
cards.n: The intermediate has to cancel when the two equations are added, exactly as in Hess's law, or the ΔG° values do not legitimately combine.

cards.q: State the minimum condition on the sum of the individual ΔG° values for a coupled pair of reactions to be spontaneous overall.
cards.a: The sum of the two ΔG° values must be negative: $ΔG°_1$ + $ΔG°_2$ < 0. The favorable reaction's ΔG° must be negative enough to outweigh the unfavorable reaction's positive ΔG°.
cards.n: This condition is the algebraic requirement behind every coupled-reaction spontaneity question.

cards.q: Compute the time required to deposit 2.50 g of nickel from a $Ni^{2+}$ solution using a current of 3.00 A (M(Ni) = 58.69 g/mol, 2 mol $e^{-}$ per mol Ni).
cards.n: Trap: multiply by the number of moles of electrons per mole of metal before converting to charge, since $Ni^{2+}$ requires 2 electrons, not 1.

cards.q: State the overall format of the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Section I: 60 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes, worth 50% of the score. Section II: 7 free-response questions in 1 hour 45 minutes, worth 50%. Total testing time is 3 hours 15 minutes.
cards.n: Both sections weight equally at 50%, unlike some AP exams where FRQs outweigh MC.

cards.q: State what Section I of the AP Chemistry exam contains.
cards.a: 60 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes: some stand alone, others come in sets of 2 to 5 questions that share one stimulus, such as a graph, data table, or particulate diagram.
cards.n: That's 1.5 minutes per question on average - don't let one question in a set stall the rest.

cards.q: State the calculator rule for Section I of the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: No calculator of any kind is permitted on Section I. Every multiple-choice question is designed to be solved with arithmetic you can do by hand or by estimation.
cards.h: → allowed or not, plus why it's feasible
cards.n: If a multiple-choice question seems to need a calculator, you are missing a shortcut or an estimate, not a device.

cards.q: State the calculator rule for Section II of the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: A four-function, scientific, or graphing calculator is permitted for all of Section II, both long and short free-response questions. A graphing calculator is not required.
cards.n: Calculators are Section II only - the opposite of the MC section.

cards.q: State what reference materials are provided during the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: A periodic table and an equations and constants sheet are provided in the exam booklet for both Section I and Section II. You do not need to bring or memorize either.
cards.n: The equations sheet is not comprehensive - it has gas laws, thermo, equilibrium, and electrochemistry formulas but still expects reaction stoichiometry and dimensional analysis cold.

cards.q: Identify what is on the AP Chemistry equations and constants sheet.
cards.a: Physical constants (R, F, Avogadro's number, Kw), and formulas for gas laws, thermochemistry (q, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG), equilibrium constant expressions, acid-base relationships (pH, pKa), and electrochemistry (E°cell, Nernst equation).
cards.h: → constants list plus five formula categories
cards.n: Know when to reach for it - many students waste time deriving a formula that's already printed on the sheet.

cards.q: State what is not allowed or not provided on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: No calculator on Section I, no personal notes, textbooks, or phones at any point, and no extra data tables beyond what a question supplies - only the periodic table and equations sheet are given.
cards.n: Everything beyond the two provided sheets has to already be in your head.

cards.q: Contrast the two multiple-choice question styles on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Standalone questions test one idea in isolation. Question sets give one shared stimulus - a graph, table, structure, or experimental description - and ask 2 to 5 questions off of it, so a misread of the stimulus costs several questions at once.
cards.h: → standalone vs. set, and the risk of a set
cards.n: Read a set's stimulus once, carefully, before touching any of its questions.

cards.q: Explain what a 'reasoning' multiple-choice question on the AP Chemistry exam tests, as opposed to a calculation question.
cards.a: It asks you to predict a direction or compare outcomes - which way equilibrium shifts, which sample has the higher boiling point, which trend is correct - using a concept, with no arithmetic needed to pick the answer.
cards.h: → what it asks, plus why no math is needed
cards.n: Since Section I bans calculators, a large share of questions are built to be reasoned through, not computed.
