cards.q: State the structure of Section II of the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: 7 free-response questions in 1 hour 45 minutes: 3 long questions worth 10 points each, then 4 short questions worth 4 points each. Long questions get about 23 minutes; short questions get about 9 minutes.
cards.h: → 3 long plus 4 short, points, time each
cards.n: Long questions are worth two and a half short questions - budget time to match, not evenly across all 7.

cards.q: State how the two long free-response questions early in Section II typically differ.
cards.a: Question 1 usually gives experimental or numeric data and asks you to interpret and manipulate it through calculation. Question 2 usually asks you to use or create particulate-level models - drawings, Lewis structures, or representations - to explain a phenomenon.
cards.h: → Q1 is data and math, Q2 is models and particles
cards.n: The exact order can shift slightly by year, but data-heavy first and model-heavy second has been the pattern.

cards.q: State what the third long free-response question on the AP Chemistry exam usually asks.
cards.a: It typically asks you to make a scientific claim and justify it with evidence and reasoning, often tied to an experimental design or a proposed procedure - sometimes including an error-analysis part.
cards.n: This is the question most likely to have a part asking you to propose or evaluate a lab procedure.

cards.q: State what the four short free-response questions on the AP Chemistry exam cover.
cards.a: Each is worth 4 points and covers one topic in depth - typically drawn from equilibrium or acids and bases, thermodynamics or electrochemistry, kinetics, and a laboratory-based task such as experimental design or error analysis.
cards.h: → 4 points each, rotating topics, one lab-based
cards.n: Don't assume every short question is quick - a 4-point question can still have three sub-parts.

cards.q: Explain how Section I and Section II combine into your final AP Chemistry score.
cards.a: Your raw score on each section is converted to a scale and weighted equally: 50% from the 60 multiple-choice questions and 50% from the 46 possible points across the 7 free-response questions. The two weighted scores combine into a composite that maps to the 1-5 AP score.
cards.h: → two 50% weighted scores combine into a composite
cards.n: Because the sections are equal-weighted, an FRQ point and an MC point end up worth about the same to your final score, even though FRQs feel harder.

cards.q: State the guessing penalty on the AP Chemistry multiple-choice section.
cards.a: There is no penalty for a wrong answer - only correct answers add points. An unanswered question and a wrong answer are scored the same, at zero.
cards.h: → no penalty, blank equals wrong either way
cards.n: Always fill in every bubble, even a pure guess, before time runs out.

cards.q: Explain what readers reward on the data-interpretation long free-response question (typically Q1) and the most common way students lose points on it.
cards.a: Readers reward correct setup shown for every calculation, not just final numbers, plus correct units and sig figs at each step. Skipping intermediate steps is the most common loss - a bare final answer with no shown work often earns no credit even when it's numerically correct.
cards.h: → reward is shown setup at each step; trap is no work shown
cards.n: Even a wrong final number with clearly shown correct setup can still earn most of that part's points.

cards.q: Explain what readers reward on the particulate or model long free-response question (typically Q2) and the most common way students lose points on it.
cards.a: Readers reward a drawing or model that is quantitatively consistent with the given scenario - correct particle counts and ratios - and clearly labelled. The most common loss is drawing chemically reasonable particles that don't match the numbers implied by the problem.
cards.h: → reward is a consistent, labelled model; trap is a plausible but wrong count
cards.n: A drawing can look like good chemistry and still score zero if the particle count contradicts the given stoichiometry.

cards.q: Explain what readers reward on the claim-justify long free-response question (typically Q3) and the most common way students lose points on it.
cards.a: Readers reward a clear claim tied to specific evidence from the scenario, plus reasoning that names a chemistry principle. The most common loss is confident, well-organized prose that never actually states the reasoning connecting evidence to claim.
cards.h: → reward is claim, evidence, and a named principle; trap is no explicit reasoning link
cards.n: Long, well-written paragraphs without an explicit reasoning sentence often score lower than short answers that hit all three parts.

cards.q: Explain what a standalone multiple-choice question on the AP Chemistry exam rewards, compared to a question in a set.
cards.a: It tests one fact or skill in isolation, worth exactly one point regardless of difficulty, with no partial credit and no dependency on any other question - a wrong answer costs nothing beyond that single point.
cards.h: → one isolated point, no partial credit, no spillover
cards.n: Don't over-invest time on one hard standalone question - it's worth the same as an easy one.

cards.q: Explain what the Models and Representations science practice asks you to do on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Connect a particulate-level model (atoms, molecules, ions drawn as particles) to a macroscopic property, or explain why a given representation - Lewis structure, orbital diagram, particulate diagram - is or isn't accurate.
cards.h: → particle picture linked to an observable property
cards.n: This shows up most in Long FRQ 2 and in particulate-drawing multiple-choice sets.

cards.q: Explain what the Question and Method science practice asks you to do.
cards.a: Propose or evaluate an experimental procedure: identify the variable being tested, what should be held constant, what should be measured, and whether a proposed method actually answers the question asked.
cards.n: This is the practice behind experimental-design free-response prompts.

cards.q: Explain what the Representing Data and Phenomena science practice asks you to do.
cards.a: Build or read a graph or table accurately: choose a sensible scale, plot points correctly, label both axes with units, and describe the trend the data shows.
cards.h: → build or read a graph or table correctly
cards.n: An unlabeled axis or a missing unit forfeits this practice's point even when the data itself is right.

cards.q: Explain what the Model Analysis science practice asks you to do.
cards.a: Use a model or representation to make a prediction or justify a claim - for example, using a particulate diagram of a solution to predict whether a precipitate forms, and explaining why.
cards.h: → use a model to predict or justify
cards.n: This pairs a model (Models and Representations) with reasoning (Argumentation) - many rubrics require both together.

cards.q: Explain what the Mathematical Routines science practice asks you to do.
cards.a: Carry out the correct calculation for the chemistry involved - stoichiometry, equilibrium, thermodynamics, kinetics, or electrochemistry - with correct setup, correct units, and the right number of significant figures.
cards.h: → correct setup, correct units, correct sig figs
cards.n: A numeric answer with no units or the wrong sig figs commonly loses this practice's point even when the number itself is right.

cards.q: Explain what the Argumentation science practice asks you to do.
cards.a: State a claim, support it with specific evidence from data or a given scenario, and explain the reasoning that connects that evidence to the claim using a chemistry principle.
cards.h: → claim, evidence, reasoning - three connected parts
cards.n: This is the most commonly lost point on the exam - students give a claim and evidence but skip the reasoning that ties them together.

cards.q: Explain how to earn a justification point on an AP Chemistry free-response question.
cards.a: State the specific chemistry principle that explains the result - intermolecular forces, Le Chatelier's principle, oxidation states, relative bond strength - and connect it explicitly to the data or scenario given. Restating the data alone does not earn it.
cards.h: → name the principle and connect it to the data
cards.n: The single most common way to lose this point: describing what the data shows without saying why it happens.

cards.q: Explain the three parts a claim-evidence-reasoning response needs to earn full credit on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: A claim that directly answers the question, evidence that is a specific number or observation from the problem, and reasoning that uses a chemistry principle to explain why that evidence supports that claim. All three must be present and connected.
cards.h: → claim, evidence, reasoning - all three, connected
cards.n: A claim with no evidence, or evidence with no reasoning, earns partial or no credit even if the final claim is correct.

cards.q: Explain what a labelled particulate drawing needs to earn full credit.
cards.a: The correct number and ratio of each particle type, particles drawn in the correct phase (spacing appropriate to solid, liquid, or gas), and a key or label identifying which symbol is which species.
cards.h: → correct count and ratio, correct phase, a key
cards.n: A drawing with the right particles but no key, or the wrong count from a mole ratio, typically loses the point.

cards.q: Explain what a graph needs to earn full credit on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Both axes labelled with a quantity and a unit, a scale that uses most of the grid and fits all the data, points plotted accurately, and a line or curve that matches the requested trend.
cards.h: → labelled axes with units, a fitted scale, an accurate plot
cards.n: Correctly plotted data with an unlabeled axis or missing unit still loses the point - label first.

cards.q: Explain how units and significant figures are scored on AP Chemistry free-response calculations.
cards.a: Most numeric answers need the correct unit and a significant-figure count matching the least precise given value to earn full credit; some rubrics award this as its own point, separate from the setup and the number.
cards.h: → correct unit and sig figs matching the data
cards.n: A correct number with no unit, or four sig figs from data given to two, commonly costs a point that has nothing to do with your math.

cards.q: Explain how an early wrong answer affects later parts of the same AP Chemistry free-response question.
cards.a: Later parts are usually scored for consistency, not just correctness: if you use your wrong earlier answer correctly in a later calculation, you can still earn that later part's points.
cards.h: → consistent use of a wrong value can still score
cards.n: Never leave a later part blank just because an earlier part went wrong - carry your number forward and keep working.

cards.q: Explain what an experimental-design free-response prompt on the AP Chemistry exam asks for.
cards.a: A specific, testable procedure: what to measure, what to change, what to hold constant, and how the collected data would answer the stated question - not a general description of 'doing an experiment.'
cards.h: → specific procedure: vary, hold constant, measure
cards.n: Vague procedures like 'test different amounts and compare' rarely earn the point - name the actual measurement and quantities.

cards.q: Explain what an error-analysis free-response prompt on the AP Chemistry exam asks for.
cards.a: Identify one specific, plausible source of experimental error - not human error like 'made a mistake' - and explain the direction it pushes the calculated result: too high or too low, with reasoning.
cards.h: → one specific source, plus the direction of its effect
cards.n: Generic answers like 'measurement error' or 'human error' earn nothing; the error must be specific and its direction justified.

cards.q: Explain how to pace Section I of the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: You have about 1.5 minutes per question. Answer the questions you know immediately, mark and skip any that need more thought, and return to marked questions only after finishing a first full pass.
cards.h: → 1.5 min per question, first pass then return
cards.n: There's no penalty for guessing, so never leave a bubble blank at the end.

cards.q: Explain the first move to make when you reach a multiple-choice question set on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Read the entire shared stimulus once before looking at any of its questions - a graph's axes, a table's units, or an experiment's setup - since every question in the set depends on reading it correctly.
cards.h: → read the whole stimulus before any question
cards.n: Jumping straight to question one and reading the stimulus in pieces is the main way sets go wrong.

cards.q: Explain how to pace Section II of the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Budget about 23 minutes per long question and 9 minutes per short question. Since long questions are worth more, protect their time - don't let a stuck short question eat into a long question's time.
cards.h: → 23 min for long, 9 min for short, protect the long ones
cards.n: Points are awarded per part, so a slow first part isn't worth stalling the rest of that same question.

cards.q: Explain what to do in the first two minutes of any AP Chemistry free-response question.
cards.a: Read every sub-part, (a) through the end, before writing anything, note what data or values are given once and reused, and mark which parts are calculation versus explanation so you know where to spend time.
cards.h: → read all parts first, spot shared given data
cards.n: Many multi-part questions reuse the same given data across parts - missing that means re-deriving numbers you already have.

cards.q: Decide when to abandon a free-response part and move on during the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: If a calculation setup won't resolve after about a minute of trying, write down your setup and a reasonable estimate, state any assumption you're making, and move to the next part - a stated setup can still earn credit.
cards.h: → write the setup and an assumption, then move on
cards.n: A blank answer earns nothing; a shown setup with a wrong final number often still earns partial credit.

cards.q: Decide when to guess and move on during Section I of the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: If a question isn't clicking after roughly two passes, eliminate any answer choice you can rule out, guess among what's left, mark it, and move on - don't let one question consume time meant for four others.
cards.n: Time spent stuck on one MC question is time taken directly from other questions worth the same one point.

cards.q: A 2.35 g sample of impure CaCO3 is heated until it fully decomposes to CaO and CO2. The mass of CO2 released is 0.891 g. Calculate the percent by mass of CaCO3 in the original sample.
cards.a: mol CO2 = 0.891/44.01 = 0.02025 mol (1 pt: correct mol CO2). mol CaCO3 = mol CO2, mass CaCO3 = 0.02025 x 100.09 = 2.03 g (1 pt: correct 1:1 ratio and mass). %CaCO3 = 2.03/2.35 x 100 = 86.2% (1 pt: correct percent, 3 sig figs).
cards.h: → three points: mol CO2, mass CaCO3 from the ratio, percent with sig figs
cards.n: Losing the ratio point is common when students forget the 1:1 mole ratio between CaCO3 and CO2 in the decomposition.

cards.q: In the reaction 2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3, 5.40 g Al is mixed with 8.00 g Cl2. Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the theoretical yield of AlCl3 in grams.
cards.a: mol Al = 5.40/26.98 = 0.200 mol; mol Cl2 = 8.00/70.90 = 0.113 mol (1 pt: both mol values). Required Cl2 for 0.200 mol Al is 0.300 mol > 0.113 mol available, so Cl2 is limiting (1 pt: correct reactant with comparison shown). mol AlCl3 = 0.113 x (2/3) = 0.0753 mol, mass = 10.0 g (1 pt: correct theoretical yield).
cards.h: → three points: both mol values, limiting reactant with comparison, theoretical yield
cards.n: The limiting-reactant point requires showing the comparison, not just naming the answer.

cards.q: A student dilutes 25.0 mL of 6.00 M HCl to a final volume of 250.0 mL. Calculate the molarity of the diluted solution and explain whether this is a physical or chemical change.
cards.a: M1V1 = M2V2: (6.00)(25.0) = M2(250.0), M2 = 0.600 M (1 pt: correct dilution calculation). Physical change, because dilution only adds solvent - no bonds are broken or formed and HCl's identity is unchanged (1 pt: correct classification with reasoning).
cards.h: → two points: dilution math, physical-change reasoning
cards.n: The classification point needs a reason, not just the word 'physical.'

cards.q: A 0.500 g sample of a metal M reacts completely with excess HCl to produce 0.0206 mol of H2 gas. If M forms M2+ ions, calculate the molar mass of M and identify a plausible element.
cards.a: mol M = mol H2 = 0.0206 mol, since M + 2HCl -> MCl2 + H2 is 1:1 with H2 (1 pt: correct mole-ratio reasoning). Molar mass = 0.500/0.0206 = 24.3 g/mol (1 pt: correct calculation). Consistent with magnesium (1 pt: plausible element matching the value).
cards.h: → three points: mole ratio, molar mass, identified element
cards.n: Students often assume a 1:1 ratio with HCl instead of with H2 - check the gas, not the acid.

cards.q: A synthesis has a theoretical yield of 4.20 g of product but only 3.65 g is recovered. Calculate the percent yield and identify one plausible reason the actual yield is lower than theoretical.
cards.a: %yield = 3.65/4.20 x 100 = 86.9% (1 pt: correct percent yield, proper sig figs). Plausible reason: some product was lost during transfer or filtration, or a competing side reaction consumed some reactant (1 pt: one specific, plausible cause, not 'human error').
cards.h: → two points: percent yield, one specific plausible cause
cards.n: A vague reason like 'experimental error' does not earn the second point - name a real mechanism for loss.

cards.q: Using rate data at varied [A] and [B], determine the order of reaction with respect to A, given that doubling [A] while holding [B] constant quadruples the initial rate.
cards.a: Rate ratio = 4 when [A] doubles: 4 = 2^n, so n = 2 (1 pt: correct exponent from the ratio). The reaction is second order in A (1 pt: correct order stated), meaning rate depends on [A]^2, not a fixed increment.
cards.h: → two points: exponent from the ratio, stated order
cards.n: Show the ratio-to-exponent step - stating 'second order' with no work rarely earns full credit.

cards.q: The rate law for a reaction is rate = k[A]^2, with k = 0.0450 L/(mol·s). Calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.200 M, including correct units.
cards.a: rate = (0.0450)(0.200)^2 = 1.80x10^-3 (1 pt: correct substitution and calculation). Units: L/(mol·s) x mol^2/L^2 = mol/(L·s) (1 pt: correctly derived units), so rate = 1.80x10^-3 mol/(L·s).
cards.h: → two points: correct number, correctly derived units
cards.n: Units for k depend on overall order - copying 'M/s' by habit instead of deriving it is the usual error.

cards.q: A reaction is run at two temperatures and the rate constant increases sharply with temperature. Explain this result in terms of the Arrhenius equation and collision theory.
cards.a: Claim: k increases because more molecules have kinetic energy exceeding Ea at the higher temperature (1 pt). Evidence: k = Ae^(-Ea/RT) shows k rises as T rises for fixed Ea (1 pt: equation as evidence). Reasoning: a larger fraction of collisions are then properly oriented and energetic enough to react, raising the frequency of successful collisions (1 pt: reasoning).
cards.h: → three points: claim, the equation as evidence, reasoning about collisions
cards.n: Saying only 'higher temperature means faster molecules' without linking to Ea and successful collisions loses the reasoning point.

cards.q: A proposed two-step mechanism has a slow first step and a fast second step. Identify which step is rate-determining and explain what that means for the overall rate law.
cards.a: The slow step is rate-determining (1 pt: correct step identified). The overall rate law is written using only the reactants of that slow step, since the fast step doesn't limit how quickly product forms overall (1 pt: correct reasoning about what governs the rate law).
cards.h: → two points: which step, why it sets the rate law
cards.n: If the slow step's rate law includes an intermediate, that intermediate must be replaced using the fast pre-equilibrium step - a common follow-up trap.

cards.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20.0 minutes. Calculate what fraction of the original reactant remains after 60.0 minutes.
cards.a: 60.0/20.0 = 3 half-lives (1 pt: correct number of half-lives). Fraction remaining = (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 0.125 (1 pt: correct fraction, meaning 12.5% remains).
cards.h: → two points: number of half-lives, resulting fraction
cards.n: An integrated rate law also works here, but the half-life shortcut is faster and just as valid for full credit.

cards.q: A reaction's rate constant is 0.0250 s^-1 at 300 K and rises to 0.0975 s^-1 at 320 K. Explain what this trend suggests about the reaction's activation energy without calculating it.
cards.a: Claim: the reaction has a meaningfully large, positive activation energy (1 pt). Reasoning: k nearly quadruples over a 20 K rise, so the rate is highly sensitive to temperature, which by the Arrhenius equation indicates a large Ea - a low-Ea reaction would rise far less over the same change (1 pt: reasoning linking sensitivity to Ea's size).
cards.h: → two points: claim of large Ea, reasoning from sensitivity to T
cards.n: This tests interpreting the Arrhenius relationship conceptually - no calculator or ln needed to answer it.

cards.q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), Kc = 0.500 at a given temperature. At equilibrium [N2] = 0.20 M and [H2] = 0.30 M. Calculate [NH3] at equilibrium.
cards.a: Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3): 0.500 = [NH3]^2/(0.20 x 0.30^3) (1 pt: correct expression and substitution). 0.500 = [NH3]^2/0.0054, [NH3] = 0.052 M (1 pt: correct final concentration, correct sig figs).
cards.h: → two points: correct Kc expression and substitution, correct answer
cards.n: Forgetting to cube [H2] because it looks like a lot of exponent work is the most common slip here.

cards.q: For an exothermic equilibrium, predict and justify the effect on the equilibrium position of increasing the temperature.
cards.a: Claim: the equilibrium shifts toward reactants (1 pt: correct direction). Reasoning: treating heat as a product of an exothermic reaction, raising temperature adds heat, so the system shifts to consume it, per Le Chatelier's principle, favoring the reverse reaction (1 pt: heat-as-product reasoning tied to Le Chatelier).
cards.h: → two points: correct direction, heat-as-product reasoning
cards.n: Just naming 'Le Chatelier's principle' without the heat-as-product logic usually earns the claim but not the reasoning point.

cards.q: A saturated solution of PbCl2 has [Pb2+] = 1.6x10^-2 M at equilibrium. Calculate Ksp for PbCl2, given PbCl2(s) ⇌ Pb2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq).
cards.a: [Cl-] = 2 x [Pb2+] = 3.2x10^-2 M (1 pt: correct stoichiometric relationship for Cl-). Ksp = [Pb2+][Cl-]^2 = (1.6x10^-2)(3.2x10^-2)^2 = 1.6x10^-5 (1 pt: correct expression and calculated value).
cards.h: → two points: [Cl-] from stoichiometry, Ksp expression and value
cards.n: Forgetting to double [Pb2+] for [Cl-], or forgetting to square [Cl-] in Ksp, are the two places this is usually lost.

cards.q: At a certain moment, Q = 12.0 and Kc = 4.50 for a reaction. Decide which direction the reaction will proceed to reach equilibrium and justify your answer.
cards.a: Claim: the reaction proceeds in reverse, toward reactants (1 pt: correct direction). Reasoning: since Q > K, there is proportionally too much product compared to equilibrium, so the system shifts to consume product and form reactant until Q falls to equal K (1 pt: reasoning comparing Q to K correctly).
cards.h: → two points: correct direction, Q-vs-K reasoning
cards.n: Mixing up which direction Q > K favors is common - Q too big means too much product, so it must go backward.

cards.q: A buffer contains equal moles of a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A-. Explain why adding a small amount of strong base changes the buffer's pH only slightly.
cards.a: Claim: pH changes only slightly (1 pt). Reasoning: added OH- reacts with HA to form more A- and water, consuming the added base while only slightly changing the HA-to-A- ratio, and since pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), a small ratio change gives a small pH change (1 pt: mechanism linked to the pH relationship).
cards.h: → two points: claim, mechanism tied to the ratio-pH relationship
cards.n: The reasoning point needs the ratio-to-pH link, not just 'the buffer resists the change.'

cards.q: 0.0300 mol of PCl5 is placed in a 2.00 L container and allowed to reach equilibrium: PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g). At equilibrium, 0.0120 mol of PCl5 remains. Calculate Kc.
cards.a: Change: 0.0300 - 0.0120 = 0.0180 mol PCl5 reacted, forming 0.0180 mol each of PCl3 and Cl2 (1 pt: correct ICE amounts). Concentrations: [PCl5]=0.0060 M, [PCl3]=[Cl2]=0.0090 M; Kc = (0.0090)^2/0.0060 = 0.0135 (1 pt: correct concentrations and Kc).
cards.h: → two points: ICE table amounts, concentrations converted and Kc calculated
cards.n: Forgetting to divide moles by the 2.00 L volume before plugging into Kc is the most common slip here.

cards.q: Calculate the pH of a 0.150 M solution of a weak acid HA with Ka = 1.80x10^-5.
cards.a: x^2/0.150 ≈ 1.80x10^-5, approximation valid since Ka is small (1 pt: correct ICE setup with valid approximation). x = [H+] = sqrt(1.80x10^-5 x 0.150) = 1.64x10^-3 M (1 pt: correct [H+]). pH = -log(1.64x10^-3) = 2.784 (1 pt: correct pH, three decimal places to match three sig figs in [H+]).
cards.n: pH carries as many DECIMAL places as [H+] has SIGNIFICANT figures: 1.64x10^-3 M is three sig figs, so pH = 2.784, not 2.79.

cards.q: 25.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. Calculate the pH at the equivalence point and explain why it has that value.
cards.a: At equivalence, moles HCl equal moles NaOH exactly, leaving only NaCl in solution (1 pt: correct species identified). Na+ and Cl- are both spectator ions from a strong acid and strong base, so the solution is neutral: pH = 7.00 (1 pt: correct pH and reasoning that it IS 7 here, unlike a weak-acid titration).
cards.h: → two points: species present at equivalence, pH with reasoning
cards.n: Strong-acid/strong-base equivalence points are neutral - only a weak-acid or weak-base titration gives a non-7 equivalence pH.

cards.q: A buffer is made from 0.250 mol CH3COOH and 0.150 mol CH3COONa in 1.00 L of solution. Ka for acetic acid is 1.80x10^-5. Calculate the buffer's pH.
cards.a: pKa = -log(1.80x10^-5) = 4.74 (1 pt: correct pKa). pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 4.74 + log(0.150/0.250) = 4.74 - 0.22 = 4.52 (1 pt: correct Henderson-Hasselbalch setup and answer).
cards.n: The ratio goes conjugate base over acid - flipping it is the most common sign error here.

cards.q: On a titration curve for a weak acid titrated with a strong base, identify the point at half of the equivalence volume and explain what quantity can be read there.
cards.a: At half-equivalence, moles of acid remaining equal moles of conjugate base formed, so [HA] = [A-] and pH = pKa (1 pt: correct identification of equal concentrations). This lets you read pKa directly off the graph at that volume (1 pt: correct value read from the curve).
cards.h: → two points: why [HA] equals [A-] there, what you read off
cards.n: Students often look for pKa at the equivalence point instead of halfway to it - halfway is where the ratio is exactly 1.

cards.q: A 0.0800 M solution of a weak base B has a pH of 11.20. Calculate Kb for the base.
cards.h: → two points: [OH-] from pH, Kb calculation
cards.n: Going from pH straight to [OH-] without writing pOH explicitly is where sign errors creep in.

cards.q: Using Hess's law, calculate ΔH for 2A + B -> C, given: A + B -> D, ΔH = -120 kJ; A + D -> C, ΔH = +40 kJ.
cards.a: Add the two given equations directly: (A+B->D) + (A+D->C) gives 2A+B->C after D cancels (1 pt: correct manipulation and cancellation shown). ΔH_overall = -120 + 40 = -80 kJ (1 pt: correct summed value with correct sign).
cards.h: → two points: shown cancellation of intermediates, summed ΔH
cards.n: Full credit needs the equation manipulation shown, not just the two numbers added - a bare sum with no setup often loses the first point.

cards.q: A reaction has ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. Decide under what temperature conditions this reaction is spontaneous, and justify using ΔG = ΔH - TΔS.
cards.a: Claim: spontaneous at high temperature (1 pt). Reasoning: ΔH is positive (unfavorable) and ΔS is positive (favorable), so ΔG = ΔH - TΔS turns negative only once TΔS exceeds ΔH, which happens at sufficiently high T (1 pt: reasoning shown from the equation's sign behavior).
cards.h: → two points: high-T claim, sign reasoning from ΔG=ΔH-TΔS
cards.n: Reciting the four sign-combination cases from memory, without showing why this case flips at high T, misses the reasoning point.

cards.q: A 50.0 g sample of water at 25.0°C absorbs 2510 J of heat. Calculate the final temperature, using c = 4.18 J/(g·°C).
cards.a: q = mcΔT: 2510 = (50.0)(4.18)(ΔT) (1 pt: correct setup). ΔT = 2510/209 = 12.0°C (1 pt: correct ΔT). Final T = 25.0 + 12.0 = 37.0°C (1 pt: correct final temperature, not just ΔT).
cards.h: → three points: setup, ΔT, final temperature
cards.n: Reporting ΔT as the final answer instead of adding it to the initial temperature is a common way to lose the last point.

cards.q: Explain, in terms of particles, why ΔS is positive when solid CO2 sublimes directly to CO2 gas.
cards.a: Claim: entropy increases (1 pt). Reasoning: gas particles are far apart and free to move through far more possible positions and arrangements than particles fixed in the ordered solid lattice, so the number of accessible microstates rises sharply (1 pt: reasoning about particle freedom and microstates, not just 'gases have more entropy').
cards.n: Saying only 'gases are more disordered than solids' without connecting to particle motion or microstates usually earns partial credit at best.

cards.q: Calculate ΔG° for a reaction at 298 K given ΔH° = -92.0 kJ and ΔS° = -199 J/K, and decide whether the reaction is spontaneous at this temperature.
cards.a: Convert ΔS° to kJ/K: -0.199 kJ/K (1 pt: correct unit conversion). ΔG° = -92.0 - (298)(-0.199) = -32.7 kJ (1 pt: correct calculation). Since ΔG° < 0, the reaction is spontaneous at 298 K (1 pt: conclusion tied to the sign of ΔG°).
cards.h: → three points: unit conversion, ΔG° value, spontaneity conclusion
cards.n: Forgetting to convert ΔS° from J/K to kJ/K before combining with ΔH° in kJ is the single most common error here.

cards.q: Given E° = +0.80 V for Ag+ + e- -> Ag and E° = -0.76 V for Zn2+ + 2e- -> Zn, calculate E°cell for a voltaic cell built from these two half-reactions.
cards.a: Ag+/Ag has the higher, more positive E°, so it is the cathode (reduction); Zn2+/Zn is the anode (oxidation) (1 pt: correct cathode and anode identification). E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56 V (1 pt: correct value and sign).
cards.h: → two points: cathode/anode identification, E°cell value
cards.n: E°cell uses the reduction potentials as given - don't flip the sign on the anode's value before subtracting.

cards.q: Balance the following half-reaction in acidic solution: MnO4- -> Mn2+, and state the number of electrons transferred.
cards.a: Balance O with H2O, H with H+, then charge with electrons: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O (1 pt: correctly balanced atoms and charge). 5 electrons are transferred (1 pt: correct count matching the balanced equation).
cards.h: → two points: fully balanced equation, electron count
cards.n: Balancing charge last, after atoms, avoids the common error of guessing the electron count first.

cards.q: A cell has E°cell = 1.10 V. Calculate Ecell at 298 K when [Zn2+] = 0.0100 M and [Cu2+] = 1.50 M for Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, n = 2.
cards.a: Ecell = E°cell - (0.0592/n) log([Zn2+]/[Cu2+]) (1 pt: correct Nernst setup with correct Q). Ecell = 1.10 - (0.0296) log(0.0100/1.50) = 1.10 + 0.0644 = 1.16 V (1 pt: correct final voltage).
cards.h: → two points: correct Nernst setup, correct final voltage
cards.n: Q uses products over reactants, just like equilibrium Q - putting Cu2+ on top instead of Zn2+ is the usual sign flip.

cards.q: A constant current of 2.50 A is passed through molten AlCl3 for 3.00 hours. Calculate the mass of aluminum deposited, given Al3+ + 3e- -> Al.
cards.a: Charge = It = (2.50)(3.00x3600) = 2.70x10^4 C (1 pt: correct total charge). mol e- = 2.70x10^4/96485 = 0.280 mol (1 pt: correct moles of electrons). mol Al = 0.280/3 = 0.0933 mol, mass = 2.52 g (1 pt: correct mass using the 3-electron ratio).
cards.h: → three points: total charge, mol electrons, mass via the 3e- ratio
cards.n: Forgetting to divide by 3 for the electrons-per-Al ratio is the single most common error in electrolysis mass problems.

cards.q: For a reaction with E°cell = -0.30 V, decide whether the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions and justify your answer.
cards.a: Claim: the reaction is not spontaneous under standard conditions (1 pt). Reasoning: a negative E°cell corresponds to a positive ΔG°, since ΔG° = -nFE°cell, and a positive ΔG° means nonspontaneous as written (1 pt: reasoning linking the sign of E°cell to the sign of ΔG°).
cards.h: → two points: nonspontaneous claim, E°cell-to-ΔG° link
cards.n: The reasoning point needs the ΔG° = -nFE°cell relationship stated, not just 'negative E means nonspontaneous.'

cards.q: A rigid container holds N2 and H2 in a 1:3 ratio that react completely via N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. Draw the labelled particulate picture after the reaction and state how many of each particle remain.
cards.a: Starting with 2 N2 and 6 H2 (1:3 ratio), full reaction consumes all of both (1 pt: correct complete-reaction reasoning), producing 4 NH3 particles with 0 N2 and 0 H2 remaining, drawn as 4 distinct particles with a key labeling the symbol (1 pt: correct count, phase, and labelled key).
cards.h: → two points: correct reacted amounts, correctly drawn and labelled particles
cards.n: Even with the count right, a drawing with no key identifying which shape is N2, H2, or NH3 loses the second point.

cards.q: Given concentration-versus-time data for a reactant that shows a straight line when ln[A] is plotted against time, state what this reveals about the reaction order and sketch its key features.
cards.a: A linear ln[A] vs. time plot means the reaction is first order in A (1 pt: correct order from the linear form). The graph should have time on the x-axis, ln[A] on the y-axis with units, a straight line with negative slope, and that slope equal to -k (1 pt: correctly labelled axes and slope identified as -k).
cards.h: → two points: order from linearity, labelled axes with slope equal to -k
cards.n: Forgetting that the slope equals negative k, not k itself, is a common omission on this graph type.

cards.q: Propose a controlled experiment a student could run to determine the effect of catalyst surface area on the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
cards.a: Use the same volume and concentration of H2O2 and the same mass of catalyst in each trial, varying only particle size (powder vs. chunks) (1 pt: identifies manipulated and controlled variables). Measure the volume of O2 produced over a fixed time interval, or the time to collect a fixed gas volume, for each particle size (1 pt: specific, measurable response variable and method).
cards.h: → two points: manipulated and controlled variables, specific measurement
cards.n: Stating 'measure how fast the reaction goes' without naming what you actually measure will not earn the second point.

cards.q: In a calorimetry experiment to measure ΔH of a reaction, some heat escapes to the surroundings before the calorimeter is sealed. Decide how this affects the calculated ΔH and justify your answer.
cards.a: Claim: the calculated magnitude of ΔH is too small (1 pt). Reasoning: heat lost before sealing is never measured by the calorimeter, so the recorded temperature change is smaller than the true one, making the calculated q, and therefore ΔH, smaller than actual (1 pt: reasoning tracing lost heat to a smaller measured ΔT and ΔH).
cards.h: → two points: direction of the effect, reasoning through ΔT
cards.n: The reasoning must trace the specific error to the measured ΔT, not just assert that the final answer is 'off.'

cards.q: A student measures the mass of a sample as 12.60 g and its volume as 4.3 mL. Calculate the density and report it with the correct number of significant figures.
cards.a: density = 12.60/4.3 = 2.930... g/mL (1 pt: correct division). Volume has only 2 sig figs, so the answer must round to 2 sig figs: 2.9 g/mL (1 pt: correctly rounded to match the least precise measurement).
cards.h: → two points: correct division, rounded to the least precise measurement's sig figs
cards.n: Reporting all the calculator's digits, or rounding to the mass's sig figs instead of the volume's, both lose the second point.

cards.q: A reaction absorbs 45.0 kJ of heat and the surroundings do 12.0 kJ of work on the system. Calculate ΔE for the system using the first law of thermodynamics.
cards.a: ΔE = q + w = 45.0 + 12.0 (1 pt: correct sign convention, both positive since heat is absorbed and work is done on the system). ΔE = 57.0 kJ (1 pt: correct final value with unit).
cards.h: → two points: correct signs for q and w, correct total
cards.n: The sign convention flips depending on whether work is done on or by the system - read the scenario carefully before assigning + or -.

cards.q: A galvanic cell is written as Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s). Identify the anode, the cathode, and the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
cards.a: By cell-notation convention, the anode (oxidation) is on the left, Zn, and the cathode (reduction) is on the right, Cu (1 pt: correct anode/cathode from notation). Electrons flow through the external wire from anode to cathode, from Zn to Cu (1 pt: correct direction of electron flow).
cards.h: → two points: anode and cathode from notation, electron-flow direction
cards.n: Electrons flow toward the cathode in the wire, even though conventional current is defined the opposite way - don't mix the two up.
